Preface

Safety assurance of software systems has never been as selected a problem as it is today. Practitioners and researchers who work on the problem face a challenge unique to modern software systems: uncertainties. For one, the cyber- physical nature of modern software systems—as exemplified by automated driving systems—mandates environmental uncertainties to be addressed and the resulting hazards to be mitigated. Furthermore, the abundance of statistical machine-learning components—massive numerical computing units for statistical reasoning such as deep neural networks—makes systems hard to explain, understand, analyse, or verify.

Facing the challenge of these physical and statistical uncertainties, no single established method for software safety and reliability would suffice. Rigorous formal verification requires formal modelling of every detail of the target system, which is impossible under uncertainties. Testing suffers from uncertainties, too: notably, it is unclear to what degree of safety assurance a given test result should translate. Therefore, modern efforts towards safe software systems must unite techniques from different disciplines—formal methods, software science, software engineering, control theory, machine learning, etc.—in a way driven by real-world examples and supported by a common theoretical ground.

This book is the first to provide a comprehensive overview of such united and interdisciplinary efforts. Driven by automated driving systems as a leading example, the book describes diverse techniques to specify, model, test, analyse, and verify modern software systems. Coming out of a collaboration between industry and basic academic research, the book covers both practical analysis techniques (readily applicable to existing systems) and more long-range design techniques (that call for new designs but bring a greater degree of assurance). It consists of eleven chapters covering a variety of topics and techniques. Their diversity reflects the diversity of facets of safety assurance of modern software systems. Each chapter is written by experts of the corresponding field. Although there are loose connections between chapters, our intention is that each chapter is self-contained and can be read independent of others.

The book’s exposition aims at giving high-level intuitions and use-cases of each technique, rather than technical details, with plenty of pointers for interested readers.

Chapter Overview

Here is a very high-level overview of the content of each chapter. Readers are encouraged to read it first and choose which chapter to read. As we have previously mentioned, there are no technical dependencies between chapters, therefore each chapter can be read without reading others.

Chapter 1: Optimisation-Based Falsification—Showcasing Black-Box Techniques for System Safety

We start out with an exposition of a concrete technique, namely optimisation- based falsification. It is a prototypical formal technique to tackle uncertainties in modern software systems. Notably, it is a safety assurance method that does not require formal modelling (i.e., a white-box system model).

Falsification is a search-based testing task where, given a black-box system model M and a specification φ on its output, one searches for an input signal σ such that the corresponding output signal M(σ) violates φ. This task is clearly omnipresent in safety assurance efforts.

The emphasis of the chapter is on the crucial role played by formal logic as a specification formalism. Falsification relies on formal specification—an important branch of formal methods—and specifications play various roles, from serving as interpretable presentations of objective functions to enhancing search heuristics exploiting logical structures.

Summarising, this chapter: (1) introduces a technique that is widely applicable to various safety assurance problems, and (2) demonstrates how formal methods can broaden its realm to those uncertain settings where white-box system models are unavailable.

Chapter 2: Monitoring Temporal Specifications

We continue with another concrete technique that stems out from formal methods but does not require white-box system models. The technique is called monitoring: given an execution log σ of a target system and a formal specification φ, monitoring returns if (or in which part) σ satisfies φ. This task too is omnipresent in real-world safety assurance efforts—one generates many execution logs σ and check if nothing is wrong there.

This task of monitoring may not sound too challenging: indeed, in the current industry practice, it is solved mostly by ad-hoc coding specific to individual φ. This is problematic at least for two reasons. For one, such an ad-hoc and repetitive coding effort is often inefficient. For another, such ad-hoc coding usually does not explicate the specification φ, which is undesired in terms of explainability and accountability.

The chapter discusses techniques that are generic; in particular, the implemented monitor works for any specification φ expressed in a certain formalism. The techniques are derived from automata theory—one of the key theoretical backgrounds of formal methods—and the algorithms discussed here exploit latest theoretical developments for the purpose of (1) accommodating more expressive specification formalisms and (2) making the output more informative (e.g., from Boolean verdicts to quantitative ones).

Chapter 3: Formal Specification of Temporal Properties

In Chapter 3, we take a step back, and give a comprehensive introduction of a foundational element that underlies both of Chapters 1 and 2, namely a formalism for expressing various specifications. We are particularity interested in temporal logics. Temporal logics extend usual propositional logics (with operators such as ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘not’, etc.) with so-called temporal operators (‘some time within 3 seconds’, ‘always henceforth’, etc.); they are important since many modern software systems—especially cyber-physical systems—operate on time-series data.

The exposition here is pedagogical, starting with basic logics and gradually moving on to the logic used in Chapter 1 called signal temporal logic (STL). In its way, we also emphasise some basic principles of formal logic, such as separation of syntax and semantics, structural induction, etc.

Chapter 4: Testing for Machine Learning-Based Systems

Testing is a principal safety assurance method, for both conventional and modern software systems. Its major advantage is that testing can be conducted if an executable model or code is available: one can press a button and then let

the target system run. This is in stark contrast with some formal verification techniques that would require experts spend months or even years for manual efforts on rigorous white-box modeling.

Machine learning-based systems, as one archetype of modern software systems, pose special challenges to the methodology of testing. One example is the absence of test oracles that tell whether a test result is pass or fail, for example, we may not know the ‘‘right answer’’ for recommendation function. The chapter starts with an overview of (conventional) testing, exhibits some major challenges that they encounter in machine learning-based systems, and then discusses several techniques.

Chapter 5: Safety Standards and Safety Assurance Framework for ADS

This chapter discusses an approach to system safety from a very different direction, namely that of industry standards and social norms. It in particular focuses on international safety standards and safety assurance frameworks for automated driving vehicles.

For one, safety standards in the automotive domain are a well-established field, where a massive amount of technical and organisational effort has resulted in a variety of international standards that are used by a massive industry as guidances. For another, the whole field of automotive safety standards is currently trying to find its new shape, in the rise of automated driving. Therefore, we believe that the trends in the field are instructive when we think more generally about how new kinds of software systems—i.e., new information technologies— should gain social acceptance.

Chapter 6: Uncertainty-wise Testing

This chapter is another testing chapter—after Chapter 4—and its focus is how to deal with uncertainties. Uncertainties are a characteristic of modern software systems, especially cyber-physical systems where uncertainties can arise from imperfect sensing, an unexpected variety of physical environments, human interaction, etc.

Such uncertainties pose unique challenges to safety assurance methods. In this chapter, focusing on model-based testing, a framework is introduced in which various uncertainties are explicitly modeled and then tested and monitored so that they are resolved in field tests and operation.

Chapter 7: Decision Making for Automated Driving

In this chapter, we focus on a specific yet representative application domain, namely automated driving. Automated driving is an emerging technology with big social and economic impacts, and thus its safety is of wide public interest. Given that automated driving cars operate on public roads where there are a lot of uncertainties, automated driving is a prototypical application domain of the techniques discussed in this book.

The chapter introduces basics on decision making for automated driving. Starting with the usual hierarchy of decision making, it discusses some common techniques—most of them coming from control theory—on motion planning and its safety verification. The chapter ends with an extensive section on the technique called responsibility-sensitive safety (RSS), which is a rigorous framework for safety verification that (1) is based on mathematical proofs and (2) successfully embraces uncertainties (which are often a critical blocker of proof-based approaches).

Chapter 8: Formal Modelling

The chapter discusses formal modelling—a crucial ‘‘preparation step’’ for many techniques discussed in the book—where we build a mathematical (formal) model of a target system. Such models are typically implemented in a software tool and thus is amenable to automated analysis, such as testing and formal verification.

In the automotive and cyber-physical domains, modelling tools such as Simulink and Modelica are widely used. The ‘‘models’’ built in these tools— together with most digital twins—are principally for the purpose of numeric simulation. In contrast, in formal modelling, one seeks logical models which expose structural information.

Formal modelling is a costly and laborious task in general; thus a disciplined methodology is needed. The chapter discusses two major approaches. One is domain-specific modelling, and the chapter discusses a modelling language called CREST that is tailored for small cyber-physical applications. The other is with stepwise refinement, where one starts with a coarse-grained high-level model and gradually adds details that are needed. The chapter uses a specific modelling language called Event-B for illustration.

Chapter 9: Theorem Proving at Work

The chapter discusses another fundamental methodology, namely theorem proving. It refers to a body of machine-assisted techniques to write mathematical proofs; in the context of the current book, these proofs are for theorems that state safety of target systems.

The chapter first makes a general introduction to theorem proving. After reviewing the basics of formal logic (i.e., formal languages in which mechanised proofs are written), two major approaches are discussed: interactive theorem proving and automated theorem proving. The introduction given here is general and goes beyond the scope of this book (namely Safety Assurance under Uncertainties); so it can be read by wider audience who are interested in theorem proving in general.

The chapter proceeds to introduce two specific approaches that are tailored to the book’s scope. One is theorem proving for continuous and hybrid systems, where conventional discrete techniques get combined with ideas from control theory to accommodate continuous dynamics. The other is theorem proving with model refinement: continuing the introduction of Event-B in Chapter 8, it is discussed how safety proofs can be established iteratively along gradually refined system models.

Chapter 10: Search-Based Analysis and Engineering

The book takes a turn to the software engineering direction where safety assurance is often conducted by testing (although the use of theorem proving is definitely present there). The chapter in particular focuses on search-based techniques, where (1) problems in software engineering and safety assurance get translated to optimisation problems and (2) the latter are solved by advanced optimisation solvers. Objectives in such a scenario include discovering a rare fault, test coverage, etc.

The discussion of the chapter is pinned down by the specific application domain, namely automated driving systems, since it exposes many real-world needs and challenges for search-based testing techniques. The chapter introduces a number of concrete techniques that have been applied to the automated driving domain. It must be clear, however, that those techniques have wider applicability beyond this specific domain.

Chapter 11: Fault Localisation and Understanding

The topic of the final chapter is fault localisation. After a problem is found in a target system using the techniques discussed in other chapters (testing, monitoring, formal verification etc.), one needs to localize the cause of the problem so that it can be properly addressed. In particular, in complex systems in modern days that consist of numerous components, it is a big challenge to identify which component (line of code, class, etc.) is the source of a problem. Fault localisation is a body of techniques for this purpose, developed in the field of software engineering.

The chapter first introduces the basic ideas of spectrum-based fault localisation (SBFL), an empirical method to suggest which components are likely to be faulty. SBFL is a well-established technique for software systems expressed as programs; however, in modern systems—such as automated driving and machine learning-based systems, i.e., systems of the book’s focus— the methodology encounters several issues. The chapter discusses those issues, and exhibits two examples of adaptation of SBFL to those particular domains.

1.1 Introduction

1.1.1 Cyber-Physical Systems

Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) refer to physical systems with digital control of computers. With the rapid development of computer technologies, especially artificial intelligence in the last decade, the collaboration between physical and digital components of systems is getting much closer than ever, giving birth to many applications of CPS. These applications are facilitating people’s daily lives: for example, domestic robots save people’s time from household duties; automated driving cars give people easier and safer driving experiences; unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are used for photography, package delivery, or even fire fighting; some advanced medical devices, such as artificial pancreas, assist people to fight with diseases. Indeed, it has already been such an era: machines are equipped with “brains”, and thus they behave not only mechanically, but also intelligently.

From a mathematical perspective, CPS are also called hybrid systems: they combine discrete and continuous dynamics together in a single system. Discrete dynamics exhibits stepwise behaviours, and it is empowered by computer software. Continuous dynamics exhibits continuous behaviours, and it is given by traditional physical systems. In general, computer software is used to monitor and control the behaviours of the physical systems, based on a set of logical rules. The physical systems execute the commands, and then provide feedback information back to the computer system. Therefore, they do not work independently, but closely interact with each other.

1.1.2 Quality Assurance of CPS

Quality assurance of CPS products is a topic of great significance. Firstly, many CPS applications are safety-critical, and their failures can cause unacceptable consequences. For example, many CPS serve as transportation facilities, such as airplanes, trains, cars, etc. System faults of these applications can cause huge financial damages or even loss of human lives. Moreover, software systems themselves are prone to errors; so far, it is still a challenging task to guarantee the quality of software products. In history, there have been many tragedies due to the system failures caused by software errors, such as the well-known Apollo 13 Accident.

Verifying software systems is hard, and it is still one of the major research topics in computer science. CPS, as a family of complicated systems, pose many new challenges in their quality assurance. We list some of the major challenges below:

  • Infinite state space. Due to the existence of physical components, the system state space of CPS is usually infinite. This feature poses challenges in modelling and reasoning about the system. New formalisms have been invented for modelling hybrid systems, such as hybrid automata [35], Simulink,
  • Complex dynamics. White-box methods based on the knowledge of system dynamics and rigorous mathematical proofs are considered as a highly reliable approach to system quality assurance. However, the dynamics equations of CPS are typically so complicated that even if they are known, there is still a huge barrier to obtain a tractable method for their verification.
  • Scalability. Scalability refers to the ability to extend reasoning techniques from small models to systems of much larger magnitude. As real-world CPS products are usually large and complex, how to develop scalable techniques remains a big challenge.
  • Black-box components. Nowadays, many CPS products are produced by commercialised collaborations, so they contain black-box components. A black-box component indicates that the internal dynamics of the component are not accessible. One reason is that those components include confidential techniques; also, modern CPS are produced by interdisciplinary collaborations, where one individual is not supposed to hold all the domain expertise. As a consequence, the black-box nature gives rise to more uncertainties and makes the system less understandable compared to the white-box models.
  • Environmental uncertainties. In practice, environmental noises can be introduced into the system execution in many ways, and the uncertainties brought by them are an important issue that needs to be considered. Even worse, they are typically difficult to model or handle. First, few formal models can precisely describe them; second, considering during reasoning is also complicated.

1.1.3 Verification vs. Testing

Classic approaches to quality assurance of software systems include verification and testing, which exemplify different philosophies. In this section, we introduce these two techniques.

1.1.3.1 Verification

Formal verification is a quality assurance approach that has been widely used in applications such as cryptographic protocols, digital circuits, etc. It applies mathematical tools to derive rigorous proofs for the properties of interest, and by that, it provides reliable conclusions.

For instance, model checking [15] is a basic verification approach to quality assurance of traditional software systems. In general, it models the system under consideration with some formalism (e.g., finite state automata), and transforms the verification problem into a reachability analysis problem (that can be solved by graph search).

As CPS usually have infinite system states, abstraction is inevitable in their modelling. Such abstraction retains the major features of the systems, but ignores some concrete events in the system executions. For instance, hybrid automata are a formalism for modelling hybrid systems. See Fig. 1.1 for an example of using a hybrid automaton to describe the dynamics of a bouncing ball [40]. The continuous state transformations are encoded within the node, while the discrete state transformations are represented by the edges.

Although verification gives elegant formalization and rigorous guarantees, it also has some fatal weaknesses: first, scalability is a major problem, and due to that, the class of models and specifications that can be handled is limited; second, verification usually relies on the knowledge of system dynamics, and so it is not suited for modern CPS that contain many black-box components. Therefore, the use of formal verification to quality assurance of CPS is highly constrained; more practical methodologies are necessarily needed.

1.1.3.2 Testing

Testing is the dual process of verification. Instead of verifying that a system satisfies a requirement, testing aims to find a counterexample showing that the system violates the requirement. In that way, testing exposes the fact that the system has the potential to behave unexpectedly, and so it requires repairing or redesigning. In some cases when verification is hard to apply testing is potentially a viable solution to understanding the behaviours of systems; indeed, searching for one specific case is usually easier than exploring the whole system thoroughly.

Testing has also been applied to quality assurance of traditional software systems for a long time, and there have been many techniques that proved to be effective, such as search-based testing [34, 44], model-based testing [59], etc. Notably, testing includes methodologies suited for not only the white-box but also the black-box systems. In this regard, testing is a feasible candidate approach to solving the quality assurance problem of CPS.

1.1.4 Optimisation-Based Falsification as a Practical Quality Assurance Method

Falsification was born in such a context: when computer scientists found it infeasible to verify CPS via system state exploration, they started to pursue a countermeasure that directly searches for the unexpected system state. Breach [22], a representative falsification tool, was named as the abbreviation of “barbaric reachability” [17]. Indeed, this approach is straightforward, but effective.

A typical falsification tool, e.g., Breach, takes as input a model, a specification, a time budget, and some other configurations, such as the shape and range of input signals. To get the tool run, the user only needs to push a button. After execution, the tool will output a counterexample input signal if it manages to find one that violates the specification, or it reports that no counterexample is found within the time budget. A usage scenario of falsification is shown in Section 1.2.

Falsification has been widely adopted in industry and actively studied in academia. Its application domain covers automotive systems, avionics, etc. In the future, due to its low constraint to the system (black-box suffices), it has the potential to be more widely applied.

1.2 A Usage Scenario: An Automotive System

In this section, we present a usage scenario which engineers may encounter in practice. Suppose an engineer is designing a car in a Simulink development environment (an introduction to Simulink is given in Section 1.3). As Fig. 1.2 shows, the car model

Now a task is given to the engineer. They would like this car to satisfy the following safety property: whenever the gear is 4 (a relatively high gear value), the speed should never be too low, say lower than 35 km/h. This is a reasonable requirement for the car, because, once the car runs at a high gear with a low speed, it will harm some components, and even threaten the safety of the entire system.

This is not a trivial problem for the engineer, as the car consists of so many blocks that operate according to complicated dynamics. Tentatively, the engineer comes up with the following alternative strategies:

  • Figure out the reachable set via reasoning about the dynamics of the system components, to determine whether there exist some states that violate the property;
  • Feed the system with some example traces of throttle and brake, and check whether the output violates the property.

The former refers to verification, which is infeasible to apply to such a complex system; the latter is a more feasible testing approach, however, performing it manually is expensive, and the correctness of those examples is not sufficient. The engineer needs an automatic testing technique, that either says that the system is safe providing different tests as a support of the claim, or reports an unexpected behaviour to show that the system is unsafe.

1.2.1 Counterexamples via Optimisation-Based Falsification

In this section, we show how falsification can help the engineer with that problem.

Let us say the engineer decides to use the falsification tool Breach [22], a representative falsification tool. As shown in Fig. 1.3, Breach takes a model (usually expressed in Simulink), a specification (in Signal Temporal Logic (STL), which we will illustrate later in Section 1.3.1.3), and some other parameters, such as the time budget, the shape of the input signals, the choice of the optimisation algorithm, etc., as inputs; it then performs the falsification workflow shown in Fig. 1.8, and outputs a result—either a success in falsifying the specification with an input signal u or a failure to do so.

In an experiment, the engineer gives the automatic transmission model in Fig. 1.2 to Breach as the system model under test, and then expresses the desired property in STL, namely □ [0,30] (gear = 4 → speed > 35); the engineer sets the time budget as 100 seconds, and uses CMA-ES as the optimiser. The engineer can then start the falsification process, and wait for a while to obtain the results.

Breach displays a running instance as reported in Fig. 1.4. On the top of the figure, there are four columns, respectively recording the number of simulations, the total time consumed so far, the robustness value resulting from the current input signal, and the best (i.e., smallest) robustness over the input signal history. It is clear that the best robustness is decreasing, which means that Breach is gradually approaching a falsifying input. After 204 simulations (53.2 seconds), Breach succeeded in finding a falsifying input, shown on the bottom of the figure, with the robustness –0.198605. This result demonstrates that the car designed in Fig. 1.2 is not safe as expected, and the engineer needs to redesign related components to fix some existing problems.

1.3 Optimisation-Based Falsification—An Overview

As we mentioned earlier, falsification is a testing-based approach for quality assurance of CPS. Compared to verification, it does not need the exploration of the whole state space; instead, it pursues one counterexample that refutes the system specification. In this section, we overview the classical workflow of falsification.

1.3.1 Problem Setting

We firstly introduce the basic problem setting of falsification that has been considered in the literature [1, 7, 9, 19, 22, 24, 30, 41, 45, 54, 65, 66, 70, 71]. The inputs to the problem consist of a system model M and a specification φ. The problem consists in answering the question whether there exists an input signal u such that the corresponding output signal M(u) violates the specification φ.

1.3.1.1 System Models

The falsification problem concerns a model, i.e., the system under test. We usually treat the model as a black box, which means that we do not access its internal dynamics, but the only way we evaluate it is by providing input signals and observing the corresponding output signals. This setting makes falsification very practical, in that its usage is not limited to any specific type of model—knowing the inputs and outputs of a model suffices.

In industry, Simulink, a toolbox by MathWorks, is a commonly used development environment for modelling CPS. It provides a visualised interface for fast prototyping. An example of Simulink model is shown in Fig. 1.2. The ports 1 and 2 are input signals for the system, namely throttle and brake; the ports 3, 4 and 5 are output signals, namely speed, RPM (rounds per minute), and gear. It is composed of several blocks, and each of them can have several sub-blocks embedded. When an input signal is provided, the model can be executed and then output signals will be generated.

Since a black-box model suffices, system models for falsification are not limited to Simulink. Recently, have been many studies on applying falsification in the domain of testing of automated driving system [25, 33, 57, 58]. In these works, system models are based on more complicated types of simulators. PSY-TaLiRo [56] is also developed as a falsification tool in Python to accommodate the use of falsification in those emerging types of simulators.

1.3.1.2 Input Signals

With the black-box setting, falsification boils down to searching for a specific input signal such that the corresponding output signal violates the system specification. Here, a signal is a time-variant function. As the time domain is continuous, it is impossible to synthesise an input signal by providing its value at each moment. Therefore, we adopt a parametrised representation of input signals as an approximation of them. Commonly-used representations include piecewise constant (see Fig. 1.5a), piecewise linear (see Fig. 1.5b), pulse signals (Fig. 1.5c), etc.

We elaborate on piecewise constant signals as an example. In Fig. 1.5a, the signal is composed of three constants. In practice, piecewise constant signals can be obtained by sampling the real signals at intervals; as a result, the number of samples, usually called control points, decides how closely the piecewise constant signal approximates the real one.

In falsification, after fixing the type of representation and hyperparameters such as the number of control points, the task is reduced to searching for a finite set of parameter values that identify an input signal.

1.3.1.3 Specifications

Specifications are used to describe the requirements to a system, regarding safety, comfort, performance, etc. In some cases, they can be described in a natural language, e.g., when discussing requirements with non-expert stakeholders. However, natural languages usually suffer from the ambiguity issue: the same sentence can be interpreted in a completely different way by different people. Moreover, natural language processing is a non-trivial burden for computer systems, and it is unreasonable to involve this process into the loop of quality assurance. Therefore, formal languages that are easily understandable by computer systems are necessary.

Since the behaviours of CPS are usually constrained by temporal requirements, temporal logics are the best choice of formal language to express those requirements. Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) [47] is a well-known formalism for reasoning about systems with discrete state transitions. Signal Temporal Logic (STL) [23], as an extension of LTL, is a widely-adopted specification language in most falsification literature. Compared to LTL, STL uses an equality/inequality expression to replace the atomic proposition, and extends the discrete time step to a continuous time domain. The bridges between LTL and STL include metric temporal logics (MTL) [39], metric interval temporal logics (MITL) [8]. Other formalisms are mostly developed on top of these languages. For instance, AvSTL [5], IA-STL [32], etc.

The feature that enables temporal logics to express temporal properties is the use of temporal operators, namely, always (or □), eventually (or ♢) and until (or U). For example, the property in Section 1.2 is expressed in STL as follows:


▫( gear =4→ speed >35)

Here, □ is the always temporal operator, requiring the proposition gear = 4 → speed > 35 to be true at every moment. Moreover, STL introduces quantitative semantics, which plays an important role in the optimisation-based falsification. In the next section, we will elaborate on the quantitative STL robust semantics.

1.3.2 Quantitative STL Robustness

The Boolean satisfaction of temporal logics is easy to understand. In the context of hybrid systems, it is a relation between a signal w and an STL formula φ—we write w |= φ if w satisfies φ, and w ⊭ φ otherwise. The quantitative semantics of STL introduces quantities into the relation, which is called robustness. We write [w,φ] as the robustness of a signal w to φ; its formal definition is given in Section 3.4.4.

Compared to the Boolean satisfaction, the quantitative semantics does not only say whether u satisfies φ or not, but also indicates how robustly u satisfies or violates φ. See the examples inTable 1.1.

Table 1.1 Boolean satisfaction w |= φ and quantitative robustness values of three signals of speed for the STL formula φ ≡ □ [0,30] (speed < 120)
signal w

 

 

 
w |= φ True True False
[w,φ] 30 10 −10

There are three signals of speed, and we reason about their satisfaction to the temporal property


▫[0, 30]( speed  < 120)

that is, “during the time bound [0, 30], the speed is always below 120”. It is clear that the first two signals satisfy the property, while the third one violates it, which corresponds to the Boolean satisfaction shown in the second row. Furthermore, although both the first two signals satisfy the property, intuitively the second one is more vulnerable to perturbations than the first one, in the sense that once a small change happens to the signal, it may violate the property. This intuition is embodied by the robustness in the third row. These values are computed from the margin between the peak point of each signal and the threshold 120. The robustness 30 of the first signal shows that this signal is more robust than the second one whose robustness is 10. Moreover, we can see that when the robustness is negative (as the case of the third signal), the property is violated.

This is a simple case where the sub-formula (speed < 120) is an atomic proposition. However, in practice, we need to handle specifications that are much more complicated, such as the one in Section 1.3.1.3:


▫( gear =4→ speed >35)

where the sub-formula is an implication. Whatever specification it is, STL the robust semantics, given a signal, always returns a real number indicating the quantitative satisfaction or violation of the signal to the specification. This quantity will be utilised as a guidance in the optimisation-based falsification, which will be introduced in the next section.

1.3.3 Stochastic Optimisation-Based Falsification

As we introduced before, the quantitative STL robust semantics returns a quantity that guides the optimisation-based falsification. In this section, we shed a light on this procedure.

Optimisation, in general, is a technique that is used to search for the minimum (or maximum) value of an objective function in an input space. Falsification is formalised as an optimisation problem as follows:


$$\begin{array}{l} {\,\underset{\mathbf{u}}{minimise}\,\,\,\,\,\lbrack\,\,\,\,\lbrack\,\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{u}),\varphi\,\rbrack\,\,\,\,\rbrack\,\,} \\ {\,~subject\ to~\,\,\,\,\mathbf{u} \in \text{Ω}\,} \\ \end{array}$$

where u stands for an input signal, M(u) stands for the corresponding output signal, ϕ is the specification, and Ω stands for a valid range of input signal u. We can see that here the robustness of the output signal M(u) towards the specification ϕ is treated as the objective function, and optimisation aims to minimise the robustness as much as possible. Once a negative robustness value is found, which indicates that the system specification is violated, then we are done.

A large number of optimisation algorithms have been proposed in the literature. Many of these algorithms are based on the knowledge of the objective function. For instance, gradient descent exploits the gradient information of the objective function to find a direction by which the objective function value can quickly descend. However, in our case, since the system model is black-box, no internal information is available. Therefore, we need to consider another family of optimisation algorithms, which is called stochastic optimisation.

1.3.3.1 Stochastic Optimisation

Stochastic optimisation is a family of optimisation techniques that implement diverse metaheuristic strategies. These algorithms introduce randomness into the search process, so that the optimisation is stochastic—different executions of the same algorithm with different random seeds lead to different outcomes. This feature enhances an algorithm’s ability of reaching the optimisation goal—even if it fails to reach the goal, one can start a new trial and hope that the different execution can bring a successful result.

Metaheuristics refers to a family of heuristic strategies that can be applied to solve a class of problems, and in our context, these strategies are used to achieve the optimisation goals effectively and efficiently. Compared to random sampling, these algorithms are goal-driven and thus more efficient, i.e., they usually achieve the optimisation goal with less number of samples than random sampling.

Various metaheuristic strategies can be adopted in stochastic optimisation. Specifically, these strategies are usually inspired by biological or natural processes, e.g., genetic algorithms, simulated annealing [46], etc. Although metaheuristic strategies are often problem-independently applicable, the performances of these strategies can be problem-dependent and, moreover, there is no global best performer. This has been stated by the famous “no free lunch” [60] theorem for optimisation, which indicates that performance gains usually come with costs.

Let us firstly take a look at how hill climbing works, as depicted in Fig. 1.7. It starts with initial some random samplings and obtains their objective function values; then, it analyses these values and conjectures the direction where the objective function potentially descends; based on that, it comes up with the next sample following that direction. This loop is repeated until a time budget is exhausted; hopefully, by that time, the optimisation goal (i.e., a negative robustness value in our case) can be achieved. Just as the name indicates, this process is like a hill climbing (upwards or downwards).

There are several reasons why these stochastic optimisation algorithms are selected for falsification. Firstly, as we mentioned before, they are applicable to black-box models. Besides that, efficiency and scalability issues are also important. Usually the system simulation that, given an input signal, generates the corresponding output signal is computationally expensive, so in practice it is preferred if an algorithm works out efficiently with a small number of simulations. Also, we expect the algorithms to be scalable enough, so that the same workflow can be smoothly applied to systems of larger scale (e.g., with more input signals, system components, etc.). Although stochastic optimisation algorithms also suffer from this scalability issue, the effect is much less severe compared to state exploration-based techniques such as verification.

The details of some commonly used optimisation algorithms are listed below:

  • Global Nelder-Mead [42] The Nelder-Mead method makes use of the simplex algorithm to perform a local search. It is specialised in searching for a local optimum, but it is unable to jump out to search for the global optimum (see Fig 1.6). Global Nelder-Mead introduces a probabilistic restart mechanism, so that it is possible for the search to be reinitialised elsewhere and thus not trapped in local optima.

  • Simulated Annealing [46] Simulated annealing is inspired by the physical process of heating a material and then cooling it down to bring it to a stable status. The algorithm starts with random sampling, and accepts all new samples that have lower robustness; meanwhile, it also accepts the samples that have higher robustness, according to a specific mechanism called temperature. The temperature is initially high, and decreases as the optimisation goes on. By the temperature mechanism, the algorithm is able to jump out of the local optimum.
  • CMA-ES [11] CMA-ES is the abbreviation for Covariance Matrix Adaption Evolutionary Strategy, belonging to the family of evolutionary strategies that are inspired by Darwin’s theory of evolution; these techniques evolve a set of possible solutions by mutating and recombining those that have higher fitness values. CMA-ES employs a multivariate normal distribution to approximate the objective function, and updates its covariance matrix according to the information learned by performing mutations and crossovers.

1.3.3.2 Evaluation Metrics for Stochastic Optimisation-Based Falsification Algorithms

In the previous section, we have introduced a number of optimisation algorithms. In general, according to the “no free lunch” [60] theorem of optimisation, none of the optimisation algorithms can outperform the others in all cases.

As these optimisation algorithms are stochastic, different falsification trials with different random seeds can produce different results. Taking this feature into account, in order to evaluate an algorithm, we usually run it multiple times and analyse the results statistically.

We consider two metrics, namely effectiveness (if an algorithm can find an answer) and efficiency (how fast an algorithm manages to find an answer). In general, we prioritise the effectiveness rather than the efficiency of an algorithm, because the ultimate goal of falsification is to find falsifying inputs, as long as the time budget is not run out. These two aspects are embodied by the following two measurements.

  • Falsification success rate: It refers to the percentage of the trials that succeed in finding falsifying inputs within the budget, over the total number of trials. A high success rate certificates the effectiveness of an algorithm, in the sense that it manages to find falsifying inputs with a high probability. Instead, a low success rate indicates that the algorithm is not effective, or vulnerable to random seeds, thus not stable.
  • Time consumption: For successful trials, the time consumption is computed as the time when the algorithm returns a falsifying input. Unsuccessful trials usually terminate because the time budget expires; however, there are also cases in which the optimisation algorithm meets other internal termination criteria, e.g., local optimum, and thus quits before the timeout.

Therefore, there are two ways of computing time consumption: one is by computing the average time consumption of only successful trials; the other one is by taking also unsuccessful trials into consideration, and thus computing the average time consumption of both successful and unsuccessful trials, in the latter case taking time budget as their values.

The advantage of the first method is that it reflects the efficiency of algorithms better, e.g., in the case that a “greedy” algorithm is fast but not effective; the second method integrates effectiveness into efficiency, exemplifying the principle that only if one is effective it can be efficient. Both methods are adopted in literature, especially the former one.

Note that these two metrics are not independent—as the success rate metric is subject to the parameter of budget, in many cases, high effectiveness (i.e., a high falsification success rate) can only be achieved when high efficiency is achieved.

1.3.4 Workflow Summary

So far, we have gone through the workflow of the optimisation-based falsification technique, as illustrated in Fig. 1.8. The model accepts an input signal given by the optimiser, and runs simulation to generate an output signal; the robustness that reflects the relation between the output signal and the system specification is computed according to the STL robust semantics; the optimiser then tries to minimise the robustness by proposing new input signals. This loop keeps on iterating until a falsifying input is found, or the pre-specified budget is run up.

1.4 Tools and Applications of Optimisation-Based Falsification

We first describe what tools are currently available, and what applications have been targeted. Scientific observations that underlie these tools, together with topics of future research, are in the next section.

1.4.1 Tools

Over the years, the methodology of falsification has proved to be effective in practice. There have been several tools developed following the workflow depicted in Fig. 1.8, such as Breach [22] and S-TaLiRo [9]. In this section, we give an introduction to these two representative tools.

We present a comparison between Breach and S-TaLiRo inTable 1.2. Since both tools are mainly developed in Matlab, they provide Matlab API and take Simulink models as the basic supported systems under test. However, the type of models they support is not limited to Simulink; with proper interfacing efforts, they theoretically support any type of black-box models. Both tools provide a nice documentation and some example scripts for facilitating the usage.

They differ in many implementation details. For example, Breach implements Signal Temporal Logic (STL) as the specification language, while S-TaLiRo adopts Metric Interval Temporal Logic (MITL) [31]. Breach allows users to write specification directly using the STL syntax, while S-TaLiRo provides a template for specifications and users need to transform their specifications in that format. In addition to the syntactic differences, the two tools also adopt different algorithms for (offline) monitoring of specifications, and this can lead to some performance differences in some cases. Moreover, these tools are used for research purposes—their authors include new research outcomes in them, so they also differ in falsification algorithms and they keep evolving over time.

There is an annual friendly competition, held with the workshop of Applied Verification for Continuous and Hybrid Systems (ARCH).

1.4.3 Adoption in Industry

The falsification methodology has been adopted by many industrial manufacturers, such as Toyota [37], Bosch [33], Airbus [16], etc. Toyota was one of the earliest manufacturers that applied this methodology. In [37], they present a fuel control system, and list several requirements that the system is supposed to satisfy; they test those requirements with S-TaLiRo, and experiments show that in most cases S-TaLiRo does not find any violation, so they conclude that “the quality of the manual abstractions that we performed vis-à-vis high-level requirements is reasonable”. Bosch has also been working on this for several years. They have been trying to apply the technique in testing automated driving systems. In [33], they present their practical experience, in particular they give several interesting tips, such as “simulation is costly”, “many properties can be formalised by formulas of simple form”, etc., which are helpful for practitioners. Airbus [16] recently collaborated with academia on a project for testing their products. In their work, they apply Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), a technique introduced into falsification by us [65].

1.5 Scientific Challenges and Highlights in Optimisation-Based Falsification

Falsification has proved to be effective in revealing unexpected behaviours of CPS, and it has been adopted by manufacturers such as Toyota [37], Bosch [33], etc. However, the methodology is not perfect yet. In this section, we list and elaborate on the shortcomings, and we also review the existing literature to show the recent progress on those topics.

1.5.1 Exploration and Exploitation

The trade-off between exploration and exploitation is the core of the search techniques. Exploration prefers to cover the search space as broadly as possible, rather than focusing on a specific local area. Exploitation, instead, is the opposite; it eagerly searches for local minima, without considering big jumps in the search space. Given a limited time budget, it is a challenge how to balance between exploration and exploitation.

As introduced in Section 1.3.3.1, falsification employs hill-climbing optimisation as the optimiser, which is known as an algorithm that favours exploitation. This bias affects the falsification performance severely, and so it attracts plenty of research attention. We classify these works according to the methodologies they use, and introduce them in the following sections.

1.5.1.1 Metaheuristics for Exploration

This line of works makes use of metaheuristics to avoid pure exploitation. Many metaheuristic-based approaches implement a mechanism that triggers a jump when the search falls into a local optimum. For example, the strategies in Section 1.3.3.1, namely global Nelder-Mead, Simulated Annealing [46], and CMA-ES, adopt different metaheuristics, respectively. In [10], the authors apply the famous ant colony optimisation to falsification, in which the search takes a small probability to start a new exploration. In [19], the authors propose to use tabu search for falsification. The algorithm maintains a tabu list during the search, which is a memory structure that records the sampling history to guarantee that the same local optimum is not visited twice. Cross entropy [49] is an importance sampling method that initially explores the search space and then performs biased sampling in the promising area. Its application to falsification is studied in [50]. S-TaLiRo implements the stochastic optimisation with the adaptive restart mechanism [43] to avoid trapping into local optima.

1.5.1.2 Coverage-Guided Metrics

Coverage is an important concept in traditional software testing. Originally, it is used to measure how much of a program is executed by a test suite. In the case that no error is found in the program, the larger coverage a test suite achieves, the more reliable the testing result can be considered. Some falsification techniques are developed based on the coverage notion, with the aim of avoiding local optima. These techniques employ coverage as a guidance for the search—the search aims not only at minimizing the robustness, but also at enlarging the coverage of the search space. In this way, the search can avoid pure exploitation that can only lead to a small coverage.

As hybrid systems deal with infinite search spaces, it remains the problem of how to define the coverage metric in this context. Different coverage definitions have been proposed. In [21], coverage is defined based on the internal states of Simulink models, and it is included as a part of the objective function so that the search is guided by both robustness and coverage. In [24], the coverage is defined by star discrepancy, a measure for evaluating how well-distributed a set of samples are. In [3], a coverage notion is defined based on classification of the input space according to robustness values. This work balances well between exploration and exploitation because it considers not only the coverage of input space but also robustness. Moreover, a recent work [69] of ours targets a specific type of hybrid systems that adopts deep neural networks (DNNs) as controllers. In [69], we define coverage metrics based on the intermediate outputs of the DNN controllers, and explore the system behavior space guided by the coverage.

1.5.1.3 Machine Learning for Falsification

Machine learning techniques have been applied everywhere, and some researchers have also introduced it into falsification. In general, this line of work learns a model from data; based on that, it proposes new samples with the aim of exploring the search space effectively. Specifically, two machine learning techniques have been studied heavily in falsification, namely, Bayesian optimisation and reinforcement learning. Bayesian optimisation makes use of Gaussian Process Regression [48] to

Bayesian optimisation makes use of Gaussian Process Regression [48] to learn the objective function (i.e., robustness in our context); this results in a Gaussian process over the search space. Gaussian process is a model in which every point in the search space has a Gaussian distribution; in this context, it predicts the probability distribution of the robustness at each point. Bayesian optimisation then samples at some potentially interesting places, where low robustness is likely to locate. The sampling strategy, known as acquisition function, guarantees the balance between exploration and exploitation. This technique has been studied in [2, 4, 6, 18, 54].

Reinforcement learning is a hot spot in the machine learning community in recent years. It tries to learn the best policy—a sequence of actions—that an agent can take, from the interactions between the agent and the environment. There is also a trade-off between exploration and exploitation in reinforcement learning: when the agent decides which action to take for the next step, the choice is either to explore an action that has not been taken before, or to exploit an already taken action further to get more reliable feedback. The default mechanism of handling the trade-off in reinforcement learning is ε-greedy. In recent years, this technique has been applied to falsification [7, 38].

1.5.2 Robust Semantics Definition

The definition of robust semantics in our context plays the role of objective functions for the optimisation, and thus it affects the performance of the entire framework significantly. The current widely-used STL robust semantics refers to the spatial robustness (see Section 3.4.4 for the definition and see the example inTable 1.1). There also exists another formalism [23] that captures the temporal robustness; intuitively, it characterises the level of satisfaction of a signal to a property from the perspective of time. These two formalisms are suited for different use cases. In [5], the authors propose a way that takes both perspectives into account, resulting in the Averaged STL (AvSTL). While the computation of spatial or temporal robustness is just a matter of obtaining a vertical or horizontal distance, AvSTL requires to compute the integration of the signal over a certain interval; the authors then design a specific algorithm for that purpose. Their experiments show the strength of that semantics in solving falsification problems.

Another line of work aims to tackle a different problem, that is, the robust semantics for Boolean connectives. In the STL robustness definition, when it comes to the robustness for Boolean connectives, it makes a comparison between the robustness values of different sub-formulas—for conjunctive it takes the minimum, and for disjunctive it takes the maximum (see Section 3.4.4 for details). However, this yields a problem: if the sub-formulas concern with different signals ranging over different scales (e.g., the formula in Section 1.3.2 that involves gear and speed), then the comparison becomes unfair, because one can always mask the other one. This is the so-called scale problem. In [68], we show that a naive signal rescaling (normalization) approach does not always work in solving this problem. We have done a line of work [66, 67] solving this problem. Our main idea is to treat the two operands of the connectives as incomparable, and design a reward to decide which one to adopt on the fly. The details will be elaborated in Section 1.6.2.

1.5.3 Input Constraints

In Section 1.3.3.1, we explained that hill-climbing optimisation relies on random sampling at its initial stage. Typically, random sampling works in a search space that is unconstrained (usually a hyperrectangle), and so does hill-climbing optimisation. In this way, falsification can return any input signal that violates the system specification in the search space, once it manages to find one. However, in reality, there usually exist some logical constraints among input signals. One example is that, in an automotive system (e.g., the one in Fig. 1.2), the throttle and brake cannot be pushed simultaneously. Such constraints also exist in other literature about CPS products; for example in [14], the authors test an assisted driving system under different environment and system parameters; there is a constraint—“when there is no fog, the visibility range is set to maximum”—that restricts the system inputs. Sometimes, the engineers also desire to impose some conditions on the input when testing systems; for example in [37], the authors aim to test a system under the condition that throttle increases monotonically. In the presence of such constraints, input signals produced by falsification should be guaranteed to satisfy them; otherwise, those signals would be meaningless.

There have not been many works that address this issue. In [12], Barbot et al. utilise a timed automaton, that implements the input constraints, to generate meaningful words, and then they apply Monte Carlo sampling to produce input signals. In [13], Barbot et al. use a transformation technique so that they can sample in a hyper-box but obtain timed automaton traces that satisfy the input constraints. We also have a line of work solving this problem. In our work [63], we treat the specification violation and the input constraint satisfaction as two objectives, and apply a lexicographic method to highlight the importance of the satisfaction of the input constraints. In another work [64] of us, similar to [13], we tackle this problem via a method called search space transformation, where we map an unconstrained space to the desired space for constrained signals, and then apply the optimisation algorithms in the unconstrained one; we will elaborate on this work in Section 1.6.3. Sato et al. also have a line of works [51, 52] on constrained falsification, but their constraints are imposed on outputs rather than inputs as other works in this section do.

1.5.4 Confidence Estimation of Falsification

As a testing method, falsification has an intrinsic weakness—when a counterexample cannot be detected by a falsification algorithm, no guarantee is provided that the system does not violate the property. In other words, we do not know whether the specification is really not falsifiable, or the falsification algorithm did not explore the search space enough. Indeed, this is a major difference between verification and testing, and it yields another problem—how confident should we be on our falsification results.

In the traditional software testing techniques, people usually use coverage as a metric to measure how much the search space has been explored. Commonly-used metrics for program testing include statement coverage, branch coverage, function coverage, MC/DC, etc. The higher coverage is achieved, the more confidence can be obtained. However, these metrics cannot be straightforwardly adapted to hybrid system falsification, because they require the knowledge of system internal structures (recall that falsification usually assumes black-box systems, as mentioned in Section 1.3.1.1). New metrics or methodologies for estimating confidence are needed.

As this is a new research direction, only a few works [55, 62] have addressed this problem. In [62], we leverage supervised learning to estimate the falsification confidence. Essentially, our idea is to treat the simulation data in falsification as training data, and train a Gaussian process to approximate the function from inputs (signals) to outputs (robustness). Gaussian process is an extension of Gaussian distribution to continuous domains, and, therefore, Gaussian process is used to model the distribution of a continuous function. The benefit of using Gaussian process in [62] is that each point in the learned Gaussian process is a Gaussian distribution, so it naturally conveys how likely the point is distributed in the negative domain (i.e., it has a negative robustness). Therefore, [62] collects those points whose lower confidence bound is below 0, and computes a probability that there exists a negative value in their joint distribution. Another recent work [55] uses bounding boxes that contain the falsification samplings to characterize the input space covered by the samplings. The sizes of the bounding boxes are dependent on the robustness values of the samples, so a small observed robustness indicates a higher “suspiciousness” of an area, and thus requires more samplings to cover it. Consequently, this technique can also help us understand how much of the space has been covered by the falsification samples, and how much effort is still needed to cover the whole space.

1.6 A Hierarchical Optimisation Framework for Effective Falsification

In this section, we introduce a general hierarchical optimisation framework that can be instantiated to solve some of the problems presented in Section 1.5. The instantiated techniques introduced in the following sections improve the effectiveness of the classic falsification framework in Chapter 1.

The hierarchical optimisation framework is shown in Fig. 1.9. It firstly decomposes the problem into a set of sub-problems, and then uses a hierarchical methodology: the top layer makes a (discrete) decision on selecting one child problem as the next step to proceed, based on the information coming from the bottom layer; the bottom layer performs numerical optimisation on the sub-problem suggested by the top layer, and it returns feedback to the top layer. This process takes place iteratively, until the problem is solved. One feature of this framework is the interaction between the two layers: the top layer makes high-level decisions and advises the bottom layer; the bottom layer performs concrete numerical evaluation and gives feedback to the top layer to facilitate the future decisions.

1.6.1 Monte Carlo Tree Search for Search Space Exploration

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a popular technique in recent years due to its successful application in the computer Go game [53]. This technique is especially effective in handling discrete search problems with large search space. The key of MCTS is that it allocates more budget to the subspace where the search target is more likely to exist, and meanwhile it also explores the less visited areas to take a balance between exploration and exploitation.

In [65], we apply MCTS to solve the “local optima” issue in falsification. As shown in Fig. 1.10a, the search space is organised as a tree by time staging and space discretization.A key notion of MCTS is reward, which is an indicator of the quality of a subspace, and is used for deciding the budget allocation. We connect the definition of reward with robustness—the branches that have witnessed high robustness have low reward, and vice versa. The robustness values are obtained by running hill-climbing optimisation on the subspaces identified by the branches.

As a result, we combine MCTS and hill-climbing optimisation, and build a two-layered framework, as shown in Fig. 1.10b. On the top layer, MCTS decides which subspace to explore, based on the reward information provided by the low layer; on the low layer, hill-climbing optimisation exploits a specific subspace, and provides feedback to the top layer.

1.6.2 QB-Robustness for the Scale Problem

In this section, we introduce our works for solving the scale problem in the definitions of Boolean connectives (see Section 1.5.2). Our idea consists in exploring the discrete structures of STL formulas to avoid the value comparison between signals with different scales; and this idea, again, results in a two-layered hierarchical optimisation framework that follows Fig. 1.9.

We initiate an early attempt in [66], where we focus on safety properties with Boolean connectives only, namely the formulas in the forms of □(φ 1 ∧ φ 2 ) and □(φ1 ∨ φ2 ). We treat the two sub-formulas φ1 and φ2 as two “arms” in the Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem, so, during falsification, we can iteratively select one sub-formula by using MAB algorithms, and then try to falsify the selected sub-formula by hill-climbing optimisation. The MAB problem originally models the problem of how to maximise the rewards that a gambler can earn in front of a row of arms of slot machines. Existing research shows that balancing between exploration and exploitation of the machines is necessary to achieve the best rewards. In our work, we associate the “progressiveness” of the falsification process with the rewards of each arm (subformula)—the more progressively the optimisation falsifies a sub-formula, the larger rewards the sub-formula obtains. The selection of sub-formulas is decided by existing algorithms for MAB, such as UCB1, in the way as follows: we allocate more budget to the sub-formula with high reward, and less for the one with low reward. As a result, MAB algorithms work on the top layer, governing the hill-climbing optimisation running on the bottom layer.

The limitation on the target formulas of [66] motivates us to extend this idea to general STL formulas. In [67], we achieve that by formalizing QB-robustness and developing an MCTS-based approach. Differently from the classic robustness, QB-robustness introduces another parameter, that declares one of the sub-formulas, in the robustness computation, and gives the robustness value for Boolean connectives in a case-by-case manner. For instance, instead of having a real number [w, φ 1 ∧ φ 2]∈ R as the robustness of φ1 ∧ φ2 , QB-robustness introduces a parameter that either indicates φ1 or φ2 : if it is φ1 , then [w,φ1] will be the robustness; otherwise, [w,φ 2] will be.

Based on QB-robustness, we develop an MCTS-based algorithm for effective falsification. As shown in Fig. 1.11, we expand the syntax tree of the STL formula, and use MCTS to explore the structure. At each leaf, based on a syntax path, we can compute the QB-robustness, and perform hill-climbing optimisation to obtain the reward (similarly to the “progressiveness” in [66]) of each path. Again, this is a typical hierarchical optimisation framework: the high layer nodes select the best children based on the reward, and the leaf node performs hill-climbing optimisation on the selected child, and back propagates the reward information.

1.6.3 Search Space Transformation for Input Constraints

We have briefly introduced search space transformation in Section 1.5.3, as an approach to solving the input constraint problem in falsification. As illustrated in Fig. 1.12, it allows to sample a point x in a hyperbox Ξ, and then it maps x to a point y = T (x) in a constrained space Ωψ. The robustness ρ(y) of y can be computed by using the STL robust semantics, and then ρ(y) is assigned to r(x) as the fitness of the point x, so that an optimisation can be done that minimises r(x) in space Ξ. As a result, search space transformation turns the constrained optimisation problem into an unconstrained one, and when a counterexample x ∗ in Ξ is observed, its mapped point T (x ∗ ) in Ω ψ can be returned, which is guaranteed to satisfy the constraint.

The performance of this framework is subject to a hyperparameter that decides the map function T ; more specifically, the hyperparameter is a total order over the dimensions of the search space. In [64], we introduce an MAB-based method to achieve the best performance. The idea is, again, by building a hierarchical optimisation framework: on the top layer, the MAB algorithm selects a total order of dimensions and passes it to the bottom layer; on the bottom layer, the search space transformation applies the total order to falsify a specification with input constraints, and returns feedback to the top layer.

1.7 Conclusions

In this chapter, we give an overview of hybrid system falsification, a technique for quality assurance of CPS via searching for counterexample inputs. We introduce the basic methodologies, tools and applications, scientific challenges and recent advances in the technique. Notably, we present our contributions, i.e., a general hierarchical optimisation framework and its instantiations, that improve the falsification effectiveness.
