Chapter 2 Monitoring Temporal Specifications

Masaki Waga

Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan and National Institute of Informatics, Tokyo, Japan

Stefan Klikovits

Johannes Kepler University, Linz, Austria

Ichiro Hasuo

National Institute of Informatics and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

2.1 Introduction

2.1.1 What is Monitoring

Monitoring generally is an activity to observe system behaviour. It is essential to monitor the system for its development and maintenance. For example, in development, engineers modify the system to satisfy certain requirements. To decide the necessary modification, they must monitor the difference between the actual behaviour and the expected behaviour. In maintenance, engineers may have to replace the worn-out components in the system. This decision also requires monitoring because they must detect if the current behaviour deviates from the original behaviour.

The following two examples show concrete usage scenarios of monitoring.

 Example 1 (continuous monitoring of a deployed system) Consider a scenario in which a recently developed factory automation system is deployed. Initially, the system performs effectively, e.g., there is no overshoot, and the system behaves robustly. But with time, the system gradually becomes erroneous. For instance, wearing out of hardware may cause a slight overshoot, which ultimately could stop the system from functioning. Therefore, continuous monitoring of the system is needed to detect and deal with an issue as soon as possible.

Example 2 (monitoring as a test oracle) Consider a scenario in which a new engine is being developed from scratch, and there are several prototypes (either as a simulator or a hardware). Owing to the early stage of development, each prototype most likely contains issues, that must be detected by testing. In testing, an oracle is needed to decide if the behaviour of the system under test is erroneous or not; this is also monitoring.

2.1.2 Monitoring by a Human

One of the most primitive forms of monitoring is by humans: given a specification in a document, an engineer checks if the system observation meets the specification. Manual monitoring is ubiquitous in system development. For example, it is natural to check if the system under development satisfies the given requirement through manual trials.

Despite its ease of application and prevalence in system development, manual monitoring has poor scalability. There tends to be a huge number of observations in cyber-physical system (CPS) development, that requires high scalability of monitoring. For humans, it is extremely challenging to monitor such massive system observations. Manual monitoring is also usually expensive due to the cost of human resources.

2.1.3 Automated Monitoring by a Handcrafted Monitor

To overcome the scalability issue, monitoring can be automated by implementing a dedicated software or hardware. These automated monitors are necessary, especially for continuous monitoring of a running system, e.g., indicators of vehicles or airplanes. However, it is challenging to handcraft the correct monitor for a complicated specification. Developing a monitor that provides more information than just detecting a safety violation, like severity of a safety violation, is also very complex.

Moreover, such ad-hoc monitors are often developed from scratch and are rarely reused, increasing their development cost. If developed by novice developers their performance will also be suboptimal.

2.1.4 Monitoring Based on Formal Specifications

Specification-based monitoring is a monitoring method that uses logics. Given a formal specification (typically of an unsafe behaviour) expressed in some logical formalism, e.g., automata, temporal logic formalism, or regular expressions, specification-based monitoring observes a system execution and evaluates if the observation satisfies the specification. Research has shown that these logical specifications can be automatically turned into an efficient monitor. In other words, there is a specification-generic monitoring algorithm that instantiates to an efficient monitor for different events of interest and requires the user to only provide the formal specification of an event to the algorithm. Table 2.1 shows a comparison between the three monitoring methods. Human monitoring is highly flexible and informative, but its scalability is extremely limited. Ad-hoc automated monitoring is highly scalable, but its engineering cost is high, especially if the monitored specification is complicated. Moreover, ad-hoc automated monitoring is usually not very informative. The engineering cost of formal automated monitoring is much lower than that of ad-hoc automated monitoring because the user does not have to develop a dedicated program but must only provide a formal specification. As this monitoring is automatically executed, its scalability is high. Research has shown that formal automated monitoring can be more informative than only detecting safety violations, which is presented in the later part of this chapter. We remark that such additional information does not increase the engineering cost of formal automated monitoring because the specification-generic monitoring algorithms can still be used.

Table 2.1: Comparison of monitoring methods
Monitoring Method Flexibility Informativeness Scalability
Human monitoring very high very high very low
Ad-hoc automated monitoring low low high
Formal automated monitoring high high high

2.1.5 About This Chapter

Monitoring-based on formal specifications (also called as “runtime verification”) has attracted extensive research efforts, see e.g., [9, 10, 21]. The current chapter is too short to provide a systematic overview of the entire field. Instead, in this chapter, we will discuss several different problem settings of formal monitoring. We present algorithms and prototype tools for solving those problems—many of which are results of our own—and show that the problems are tractable. The problem formalizations and algorithms are all based on timed

automata [1], showing the impressive potential of the fundamental construct in theoretical computer science.

The problem settings differ in complexity and tractability—the more complex a setting is, the slower the algorithm. However, the additional complexity is the price for properties of monitoring that are highly desirable in its practical usage scenarios.

2.1.6 Organisation of This Chapter

In Section 2.2, we introduce timed pattern matching [22, 26] as the theoretical background of specification-based monitoring. In Sections 2.3 to 2.5, we show the extensions of timed pattern matching by parametric specifications (Section 2.3), events equipped with data (Section 2.4), and quantitative monitoring results (Section 2.5). These extensions endow timed pattern matching with extra flexibility, one that is often appreciated in real-world usage scenarios. In Section 2.6, we discuss the methodological difficulty in monitoring continuous behaviour with digital sampling where only discrete observations are available. To tackle this issue, we introduce model-bounded monitoring. The key idea is to exploit the prior knowledge of the system under monitoring to interpolate the behaviour between discrete samples. Finally, we conclude in Section 2.7.

2.2 Timed Pattern Matching

2.2.1 Motivation: Locating Unsafe Parts in an Execution Log

There have been various mathematical formulations of specification-based monitoring of CPSs, e.g., Boolean monitoring of discrete-time signals [16], Boolean monitoring of continuous-time signals [20], and quantitative monitoring of continuous-time and continuous-valued signals [13, 14]. Refer to [9] for an example of a survey of CPS monitoring.

The objective of most monitoring problems is to detect a safety violation, i.e., provide a Boolean value showing if the monitored system behaviour satisfies the given specification. This is useful in cases such as raising alarms on a safety violation. However, returning a Boolean value is not always informative enough. For example, when monitoring of a system for debugging, it is helpful to locate part of the log in which an unsafe behaviour is detected, to find which component requires a fix. In such a use case, locations of the erroneous part in the log will be needed rather than the Boolean satisfaction value.

2.2.2 Solution: Pattern Matching with the Specification

Timed pattern matching [22, 26] is a monitoring problem to locate the satisfaction of the specification in the given log. More precisely, given a system log w and a specification A, timed pattern matching provides the set of the intervals (t,t ′ ) for which the restriction w|(t,t ′ ) of the log w to the open interval (t,t ′ ) satisfies the specification A. Typically, the specification A represents an unsafe behaviour, e.g., the gear of a vehicle changing too frequently. In this case, timed pattern matching finds when such an unsafe behaviour occurs in the given log.

After the introduction in [22], the timed pattern matching problem has been studied in various settings with technical improvements (e.g., [22, 23, 26, 30]). In [26], the timed pattern matching problem is defined with timed words and timed automata (TAs) [1]. A timed word is a sequence of events with timestamps. A TA is a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) equipped with clock variables to represent timing constraints on the timed words.

Example 3 (gear changes of a vehicle) Consider the example in Fig. 2.1. The timed word w in Fig. 2.1a is the log of the gear changes of a vehicle. The objective of the monitoring with the TA A in Fig. 2.1b is to find too frequent gear changes. Roughly speaking, A matches if the gear changes from g4 to g1 within 1 time unit, which is too soon and undesirable. First, g4 is at 0.7 and g1 is at 1.6 in w, A matches around [0.7,1.6]. Next, g4 is at 2.0 and g1 is at 3.2 in w, A does not match around [2.0,3.2] because the time difference is longer than 1.0.

Formally, timed pattern matching returns the set of matching intervals {(t,t ′ ) | w|(t,t ′ ) ∈ L(A)} = {(t,t ′ ) | t ∈ [0.2,0.7),t ′ ∈ (1.6,2.0]}, which is the set of open intervals (t,t ′ ) such that the restriction w|(t,t ′ ) of the timed word w in (t,t ′ ) is accepted by the TA A. Here the notion “around [0.7,1.6]” is formalised as the open intervals containing [0.7, 1.6] but not including any other events, i.e., not including either 0.2 or 2.0. We note that $ in the TA A is the special terminal character representing the end of the matching.

2.2.3 Algorithms and Implementations

There are several algorithms proposed for the timed pattern matching problem, such as [8, 22, 23, 26, 30]. We discuss the one presented in [30].

In [30], we presented an automata-based algorithm for timed pattern matching. Roughly speaking, each event is fed in the given log to the timed automaton to check which subsequence of the given timed word is accepted by the timed automaton. Notably, an interval-based symbolic analysis is needed for the beginning and the end of the matching because the number of the matching is, in general, infinite, and is represented by intervals, as shown in Example 3. The algorithm in [30] is optimised using skipping [11, 17, 19] originally used for string search [15].

Using the algorithm shown in [30], a prototype tool MONAA [31] was implemented.1

Our experimental evaluation shows the efficiency of MONAA. For example, MONAA monitors approximately 250,000 entries per second for a realistic benchmark called Gear on MacBook Pro 2019 (2.8 GHz Quad-Core Intel Core i7, and 16GiB RAM). This is as big as the number of the search queries on Google per second and, for example, is fast enough to monitor controller area network (CAN) messages2

2.2.4 Summary

The problem of timed pattern matching, which is the most basic problem setting amongst the ones discussed in the current chapter, is considered in this section. Timed pattern matching is a monitoring problem locating all the unsafe behaviours in the given log. In [30], the problem is formulated with timed automata. There are efficient algorithms and tools for timed pattern matching such as MONAA [31]. Note that the above algorithm achieves “informativeness” in the following sense.

Informativeness All the unsafe behaviours in the monitored log can be located using timed pattern matching. This is more informative than the standard monitoring problem returning Boolean satisfaction, i.e., returning if the log satisfies the specification.

2.3 Parametric Timed Pattern Matching

2.3.1 Motivation: Specification with Unspecified Thresholds

All the occurrences of the unsafe behaviour in the monitored log can be located using timed pattern matching as discussed in Section 2.2. There is an algorithm that uses skipping to optimise this method. Also, the tool MONAA for timed pattern matching is highly scalable.

However, it is often practically challenging to fix a concrete specification. Notably, determining the exact threshold in the specification is challenging. For example, for an automatic transmission system of a vehicle, frequent gear changes are not desirable, and the following is a reasonable requirement: “the gear should not change too soon after the latest gear change”. While providing a specification in a TA, the concrete threshold, that determines what "too soon” means for a gear change, needs to be fixed. However, it is not easy to provide a suitable threshold (e.g., 1 s, 300 ms, and so on) as it highly depends on the domain and requires an in-depth domain knowledge of the developed system. This issue can be a significant obstacle to timed pattern matching.

2.3.2 Solution: Pattern Matching with Parametric Specifications

Our solution to the aforementioned issue is to use parameters for unspecified thresholds. More precisely, we use parametric timed automata (PTAs) [3] for parametric specifications. Figure 2.2 shows an example of a parametric timed automaton (PTA). A PTA is a TA that allows the use of parameters and the constant numbers in the timing constraints. For instance, using the parameter p for the unspecified threshold, one can represent “the gear should not change for p seconds after the latest gear change” in a PTA.

Parametric timed pattern matching [5] is a generalisation of timed pattern matching where the specification is given in a PTA A rather than a TA. Given a timed word w and a PTA A, it returns the part of the timed word w and the parameter valuation v, assigning a real-value to each parameter, the parametric specification represented by the PTA A is satisfied.

Example 4 (gear changes of a vehicle) Consider the timed word w in Fig. 2.1a and the PTA A in Fig. 2.2. Here, the PTA A matches if the gear changes from g4 to g1 within p time unit. As we have g4 at 0.7 and g1 at 1.6 in w, A matches around [0.7,1.6] for p > 0.9. As we have g4 at 2.0 and g1 at 3.2 in w, A matches around [2.0,3.2] for p > 1.2.

Formally, the output of parametric timed pattern matching is as follows, where (t,t ′ ) is a matching interval and v is one of the corresponding parameter valuations.

Example 5 (automated cleaning system) Consider an automated cleaning system as shown in Fig. 2.3. There are cameras in a public space, and once a camera finds trash, it notifies a robot cleaner to remove the trash. A reasonable specification is that the robot should remove the trash as soon as the camera finds it. However, it is hard to define the exact threshold determining if the robot is too late because it depends on various factors, e.g., the size of the public space, how crowded it is, and the number of the working robots.

By using a PTA, this specification can be expressed as in Fig. 2.4. By parametric timed pattern matching, for each trash, the time between detection and removal of trash can be obtained. A global constraint of the parameter p, to ignore the very short delay between the detection and the removal, can also be provided.

2.3.3 Algorithms and Implementations

Parametric timed pattern matching is a relatively new problem, and not many algorithms have been proposed. Here we discuss our algorithms, presented in [5, 27].

The two algorithms for parametric timed pattern matching have been proposed: an algorithm via model checking and a dedicated algorithm. Both methods are similar in the sense they utilise the finite abstraction of the clock and parameter valuations by polyhedra. The latter algorithm is optimised using skipping [17] that is originally from string matching. This optimisation is much like the algorithm for (non-parametric) timed pattern matching in [30].

The former algorithm is implemented with IMITATOR [4], which is a model checking tool for PTAs. Meanwhile, the latter is implemented in a prototype tool ParamMONAA.3

2.3.4 Summary

Parametric timed pattern matching is a parametric extension of timed pattern matching with parameters in timing constraints introduced in [5]. In [5], this problem is solved via model checking, and a more efficient algorithm is proposed in [28]. Note that the above algorithms achieve “flexibility” and “informativeness” in the following sense.

Flexibility Parameters allows the use of timing constraints with unspecified thresholds in the specification. This allows providing a specification without precisely defining timing constraints, which tends to be practically challenging.

Informativeness With parametric timed pattern matching, how robustly the timing constraints are satisfied (or violated) can be synthesised. This is more informative than returning Boolean satisfaction. The idea is to enlarge the timing constraints using parameters representing the robustness of the satisfaction. For example, by replacing the guard x 1 of Fig. 2.1b with x 1 + Px, where px is a parameter, the robust satisfaction degree of x 1 can be synthesised.

Figure 2.11: A PTDA to locate the interval [t, t'] in the log where the balance decreases by more than 100 in total with at least two transactions, where x is the clock variable for the global time, t and t’ are timing parameters, and sum is the variable to contain how much the balance decreases.

2.4 Symbolic Monitoring against Specifications Parametric in Time and Data

2.4.1 Motivation: Beyond Finite Domain Events

By parametric timed pattern matching in Section 2.3, monitoring can be conducted even if the timing constraints in the specification contain unspecified thresholds, represented by parameters. Its essence is the use of PTAs instead of TAs.

In parametric timed pattern matching, the monitored log is a timed word, which is the same as timed pattern matching. A timed word is a sequence of events with timestamps, where the events are from a finite domain. However, this finiteness of the events is often too restrictive to represent behaviour of a system with infinite or unbounded nature.

Example 6 (automated cleaning system) Consider again the scenario in Example 5. In Example 5, the observed actions are abstracted into two events: detection and removal. This abstraction is too coarse when there are multiple pairs of detection and removal. Consider the following observation.

  • The camera observed trash (say #1) at 0.7.
  • The camera observed another trash (say #2) at 2.5.
  • The cleaning robot removed #2 at 3.0.
  • The cleaning robot removed #1 at 3.5.

Figure 2.5a shows the timed word modelling this observation using the events in Example 5. The issue here is that the information on the correspondence between the detection and the removal is abstracted away, and it cannot be monitored in the preferred manner. One possible solution is to equip an identifying string for each event. However, the technical issue is that the number of such strings is unbounded owing to the unbounded number of observed trash.

Example 7 (bank account) Consider the transactions of a bank account shown in Fig. 2.6. It can be modelled as a timed word by abstracting each transaction to either withdraw or deposit. However, this abstraction is extremely coarse because the amount is essential in modelling the transactions; without the amount of deposit or withdrawal, it is not possible to monitor, e.g., the extreme decrease in the balance in a short period. The amount of each withdrawal or deposit is a number, which is obtained from an infinite domain.

Overall, timed words are often not expressive enough, and thus each event needs to be equipped with data from some infinite domain.

2.4.2 Solution: Symbolic Monitoring of Infinite Domain Data

To overcome the above issue of the expressive power of the timed words, symbolic monitoring of infinite domain data is introduced in [28]. In the formulation in [28], the log is provided by a timed data word, and the specification is provided by a parametric timed data automaton (PTDA).

A timed data word is a timed word such that each event is equipped with infinite domain data as well as a timestamp. For example, Fig. 2.5b shows an example of a timed data word for the automated clearing system; here, #1 and #2 are strings to identify each trash.

PTDA is an extension of PTA with infinite domain data. It can represent constraints on data using data variables, data guards, and variable updates. Parameters can be used for data as well as the timing constraints. For example, Fig. 2.7 shows an example of the PTDA for the automated clearing system with timing parameter p and data parameter idp. This PTDA accepts a timed data word containing a removal of trash that is more than p time units after the detection.

Given a timed data word and a PTDA, the symbolic monitoring algorithm in [28] returns the set of parameter valuations such that the PTDA accepts the timed data word.

Example 8 (automated cleaning system) Let us continue the scenario in Example 6. The observation in Example 6 contains two pairs of the detection and the removal of trash; the first trash (say #1) is detected at time 0.7 and removed at time 3.5; the second trash (say #2) is detected at time 2.5 and removed at time 3.0. The removal of the trash idp more than p time unit following the detection is alerted, where idp is the string-valued data parameter to identify the trash, and p is the timing parameter for the timing constraint. For the above observation, an alert exists for idp = #1 ∧ p < 2.8 and idp = #2 ∧ p < 0.5.

Formally, these observation and specification are represented by the timed data word w in Fig. 2.5b and the PTDA A in Fig. 2.7, respectively. The result of the symbolic monitoring for w and A is the following set of parameter valuations v, where v(idp ) is a string and v(p) is a rational number.


{v∣(v(pid),v(delay))=(#A,4.3)or(#B,11.8)}

Example 9 (vehicle platooning) Consider monitoring of a vehicle platooning [18] system. Vehicle platooning is a style of self-driving in which a group of vehicles drive in a line. Owing to the inter-vehicle communication, vehicle platooning can reduce the inter-vehicle distance and the brake usage, and thus, improve the efficiency of the road usage and the energy consumption.

The goal is to monitor a joining process to a platoon as shown in Fig. 2.8 and check if the acceptance of the joining request is too late. In the log in Fig. 2.9, it can be observed that the acceptance of the vehicle #B takes much longer time than #A. The PTDA A in Fig. 2.10 can be used to detect such delay in acceptance. The result of the symbolic monitoring is as follows.


{v∣v(idp)=#1,v(p)<2.8)}∪{v∣v(idp)=#2,v(p)<0.5)}

In principle, the symbolic monitoring problem as formulated in [28] does not answer where unsafe behaviour is detected, but it only answers the acceptance with the corresponding parameter valuations. However, it is possible to locate the part of the log in which the unsafe behaviour occurs, using timing parameters. In Example 10, a simpler pattern matching problem than (parametric) timed pattern matching is shown. See [28] for the encoding of parametric timed pattern matching with symbolic monitoring.

Example 10 (bank account) For the scenario in Example 7, the goal is to locate in which part of the log, the balance decreases by more than 100 in total. In the log in Fig. 2.6, it can be observed that such a decrease happens between 3.8 and 6.7 and between 3.8 and 8.9.

The PTDA A in Fig. 2.11 can be used to locate such a decrease. The PTDA A contains two timing parameters t and t ′ for the interval [t,t ′ ] where such a decrease happens. In A, the summation of the amount of the withdrawals and deposits between t and t ′ is considered. The result of the symbolic monitoring is as follows.


{v∣(v(t),v(t′))=(3.8,6.7)or(3.8,8.9)}

2.4.3 Algorithm and Implementation

In [28], we gave an algorithm to solve the symbolic monitoring problem with infinite domain data. Owing to the finite abstraction of the time and data valuations, e.g., by convex polyhedra for rational-valued data and an ad-hoc data structure based on a list for string-valued data, the main body of the algorithm is a breadth-first search.

SyMon4

2.4.4 Summary

The symbolic monitoring problem with infinite domain data [28] is a generalisation of parametric timed pattern matching with data from some infinite domain. In [28], the problem is formulated using timed data words and PTDAs. The experimental results in [28] show the efficacy of the algorithm. Note that the above algorithm achieves "genericity", "flexibility", and "informativeness" in the following sense.

Genericity The symbolic monitoring algorithm in [28] works for any “data” from a domain that offers suitable operations. For example, the algorithm works for both rationals and strings.

Flexibility Data and timing parameters introduced in Section 2.3 can be used. In this sense, the specification in symbolic monitoring is more flexible.

Informativeness Similar to Section 2.3, the safety degree can be synthesised using the parameters. Moreover, timing and data information can be extracted from the log. For example, in Example 10, by monitoring the log, the intervals of the withdrawal were extracted for each range of amounts.

2.5 Online Quantitative Timed Pattern Matching with Semiring-Valued Weighted Automata

2.5.1 Motivation: Online Algorithm for Quantitative Timed Pattern Matching

2.5.1.1 More Informative Timed Pattern Matching

Consider the monitoring of a driving record of an automated driving system (ADS). For example, the goal is to locate where in the driving record the acceleration is too sudden. More precisely, there should be an alert if the velocity v changes from v < 40 to v > 100 within 3 time units. For the signal of the velocity in Fig. 2.12, such a pattern appears in [0,2.5) and [6.0,8.7). Timed pattern matching in Section 2.2 locates such time intervals.

However, it can be observed that this result is not informative enough to provide the following information: the acceleration is more sudden in [0, 2.5) than in [6.0, 8.7); the acceleration in [3.3, 5.3) is more sudden than in [9.3, 10.8), even though both are not too sudden according to the specification. To provide a more fine-grained and informative answer, for each area, the degree of unsafety is required rather than the Boolean verdict of unsafety.

Quantitative timed pattern matching [7] is a quantitative extension of timed pattern matching, which returns quantitative semantics representing the satisfaction degree of the given specification rather than the Boolean satisfaction. For each subsignal, quantitative timed pattern matching returns how robustly the given specification is satisfied or violated. When the specification represents unsafe behaviour, the degree of unsafety for each subsignal is obtained.

Example 11 For the signal σ in Fig. 2.12, the quantitative semantics α(σ( [0,2.5))) for the subsignal σ( [0,2.5)) in [0,2.5) is 20 because the

inequality constraints (v < 40 and v > 100) are satisfied even if the signal values are shifted up or down, by a gap up to 20. Refer to Fig. 2.13 for illustration. As the quantitative semantics α( σ( [6.0,8.7))) for the subsignal σ( [6.0,8.7)) is 10, σ( [0,2.5)) satisfies the specification more robustly than σ( [6.0,8.7)) . As the specification represents unsafe behaviour, it can be concluded that σ is safer in [6.0,8.7) than in [0,2.5). Similarly, the quantitative semantics α( σ( [3.3,5.3))) and α( σ( [9.3,10.8))) for the subsignals

2.5.1.2 Issue: Online Monitoring Capability

In [7], an offline algorithm for quantitative timed pattern matching is introduced. This algorithm requires the entirety of the monitored signal to start monitoring. Such a monitoring algorithm is offline monitoring capable for a log of previous system execution, and it can compute the quantitative semantics for each subsignal. However, such a monitoring algorithm is not online monitoring capable for a stream of a log of the running system, and it cannot compute the quantitative semantics along with the system execution. This limitation is critical for certain usage scenarios. For example, an offline monitoring algorithm cannot give feedback to a running system using the monitoring result before the execution is complete. The introduction of an online algorithm is valuable because it expands the application area.

2.5.2 Solution: Quantitative Timed Pattern Matching with Weighted Automata

2.5.2.1 Online Algorithm with Automata

In [24], we introduced an online algorithm for quantitative timed pattern matching. The algorithm in [24] utilises weighted automata, which is a quantitative extension of NFAs. In general, the use of automata simplifies an online monitoring algorithm.

By combining the concepts from both timed automata and weighted automata, we introduced timed symbolic weighted automata (TSWAs). Fig. 2.14 shows an example of a TSWA. In a TSWA, each location has a constraint on the signal values. The other structure of TSWAs is the same as TAs.

Example 12 (velocity monitoring) Continuing with the scenario in Example 11, let σ be the signal shown in Fig. 2.12. The TSWA in Fig. 2.14 represents the specification “the velocity v changes from v < 40 to v > 100 within 3 time units”. Note that the constraints at locations l1 and l3 are true, and the associated signal values are ignored.

For the subsignal σ( [0,2.5)) of σ in [0,2.5), the quantitative semantics α( σ( [0,2.5))) is 20 because of Equation (2.1), where σ(0) and σ(1.7) are the signal values at 0 and 1.7, respectively, and 40 and 100 are the thresholds in the specification. This follows the intuition in Fig. 2.13.

(2.1)
α(σ([0, 2.5))) = min {(40−σ(0)),(σ(1.7)−100)} = min {(40−20),(120−100)} = 20

Quantitative timed pattern matching provides such a quantitative semantics for each subsignal. Fig. 2.15 illustrates the result of quantitative timed pattern matching, where the colour at point (t,t ′ ) shows the quantitative semantics α( σ( [t,t ′ ))) for the subsignal σ( [t,t ′ )).

2.5.2.2 Genericity via Semirings

The monitoring algorithm in [24] is not just an online algorithm for quantitative timed pattern matching but also generic for various quantitative semantics. We utilise an algebraic structure called semiring in our algorithm, and our algorithm works for various quantitative semantics, i.e., various choices of semirings. For example, the summation of the difference from the threshold, rather than the minimum value as in Equation (2.1), can be considered. Mathematically, this is

to use the semantics αsup -+ based on sup-plus semiring instead of the semantics α based on the sup-inf semiring.

The preference between these semantics depends on the usage scenario. For example, as shown in Example 13, when the quantitative semantics αsup -+ is used with the sup-plus semiring, the “safe” values compensate for the “unsafe” ones. This semantics may be an option, e.g., for cost or energy consumption, but not suitable, e.g., for physical distance, because while the debt can be covered with revenue, very long inter-vehicular distance cannot compensate for a collision of vehicles. See, for example [12] for an example usage of sup-plus semiring to capture the notion of cost. The quantitative semantics by the sup-inf semantics is useful in many settings owing to the intuition in Fig. 2.13.

Example 13 (quantitative semantics by summation) For the scenario in Example 12, the quantitative semantics αsup -+ defined by sup-plus semiring instead of sup-inf semiring is used. For the subsignals σ( [0,2.5)) , σ( [3.3,5.3)) , σ( [6.0,8.7)) , and σ( [9.3,10.8)) , the quantitative semantics are as follows.


$$\begin{array}{l} {\alpha_{sup - +}(\sigma(\lbrack 0,2.5))) = (40 - 20) + (120 - 100) = 40} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {\alpha_{sup - +}(\sigma(\lbrack 3.3,5.3)))} & {= (40 - 10) + (90 - 100) = 20} \\ {\alpha_{sup - +}(\sigma(\lbrack 6.0,8.7)))} & {= (40 - 30) + (110 - 100) = 20} \\ {\alpha_{sup - +}(\sigma(\lbrack 9.3,10.8)))} & {= (40 - 40) + (60 - 100) = - 40} \\ \end{array} \\ \end{array}$$

For the ( (quantitative )) semantics ( (defined by )) sup-plus semiring, we have α sup -+ σ [3.3,5.3) = αsup -+ σ [6.0,8.7) while for the quantitative semantics defined by sup-inf semiring, α( σ( [6.0,8.7))) is larger than α( σ( [3.3,5.3))) . This inconsistency is because, in the quantitative semantics αsup -+ by sup-plus semiring, small deviation from the specification by the velocity (v = 10) at the beginning of σ( [6.0,8.7)) affects the quantitative semantics, while in the quantitative semantics α by sup-inf semiring, large deviation by the velocity (v = 90) masks it.

2.5.3 Generic Algorithm and Implementation

In [24], we provided an online algorithm for quantitative timed pattern matching using the shortest distance over (semiring-valued) weighted graphs. It works for any semiring satisfying a certain condition. For example, it captures both quantitative semantics aforementioned. Polyhedra-based abstraction was used when reducing the size of the weighted graph to finite. In signal monitoring, there are continuously many possible timings of the switching in a temporal specification owing to the continuity of the signals. For example, there are continuously many possible durations to stay at l0 in the automaton in Fig. 2.14. Polyhedra was used to obtain finite abstraction of such possibilities and reduce the size of the weighted graph finite so that the existing shortest distance algorithm can be applied.

The implementation of the algorithm in [24] for online quantitative timed pattern matching is called QTPM. The experimental evaluation in [24] shows the efficiency of QTPM, especially when the specification has a time-bound, i.e., the length of each matching is bounded. For example, for a realistic benchmark called OVERSHOOT with time-bound of length 150 s, when the sampling interval is 10 s, QTPM monitors more than 3,000 entries, i.e., 30,000 s in the simulation time, per second on an Amazon EC2 c4.large instance (2.9 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2666 v3, 2 vCPUs, and 3.75 GiB RAM) that runs Ubuntu 18.04 LTS (64 bit). This assumption on the time-bound is not too restrictive because too long matching is usually not of interest. For instance, for the automaton in Fig. 2.14, although the length of the matching is unbounded, matching longer than 3 time unit is usually not of interest. This is because it is the maximum duration between v < 40 and v > 100. Therefore, it does not harm the practical usefulness to assume such a bound of the length of the matching.

In addition to the number of the monitored entries, we also measured the shortest feasible sampling interval of QTPM. In signal monitoring, the shortest feasible sampling interval is an important efficiency criterion. This is because by shortening the sampling interval, the monitoring result can be made more accurate. But it does make monitoring more computationally demanding because the algorithm must now handle more information in a certain length of time. For the aforementioned benchmark OVERSHOOT, the shortest feasible sampling interval of QTPM is approximately 450 ms on an Amazon EC2 c4.large instance (2.9 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2666 v3, 2 vCPUs, and 3.75 GiB RAM) that runs Ubuntu 18.04 LTS (64 bit). Although this is not fast enough to monitor the raw sensor values of sampling interval 100 ms, the bound of matching length (150 s) is much longer than the available sampling intervals, and the performance of QTPM may be enough for some applications.

2.5.4 Summary

Quantitative timed pattern matching is a quantitative extension of timed pattern matching, computing the quantitative semantics rather than the Boolean satisfaction. In [24], the quantitative timed pattern matching problem is formulated with TSWAs. The experimental results in [24] show the efficiency of QTPM, which is an implementation of the online algorithm in [24]. We used polyhedra-based symbolic analysis to obtain a finite abstraction of the weighted graph used in the algorithm. Note that the above algorithm achieves “genericity” and “informativeness” in the following sense.

Genericity The quantitative semantics is parameterised with a semiring. The algorithm works for different semirings provided they satisfy some conditions.

Informativeness For each subsignal, quantitative timed pattern matching computes the unsafe degree rather than deciding the Boolean satisfaction.

2.6 Model-Bounded Monitoring of Hybrid Systems

2.6.1 Motivation: Bounding Possible Signals between Samples

2.6.1.1 Signal Monitoring Requires Sampling and Interpolation

In the monitoring of CPSs, the monitored signal is thought of as the system behaviour. For example, in Section 2.5, monitoring the signal σ shown in Fig. 2.12, the quantitative semantics for each subsignal of σ is computed. However, in reality, what is observed is not a continuous signal but a series of discrete sampling points, which are interpreted as a continuous signal by interpolation. For example, in Fig. 2.12, the left end points of the constant pieces of a signal are observed, which are then interpreted as a signal by the piecewise-constant interpolation. Although, the piecewise-constant or piecewise-linear interpolations (see Fig. 2.16) are the commonly used, other interpolations, e.g., with spline curves, can also be used.

2.6.1.2 Issue: No Guarantee between Samples

In signal monitoring, due to the sampling and interpolation mechanism aforementioned, there is a methodological difficulty in guaranteeing the correctness of the analysis. Namely, the safety of the system between samples cannot be determined.

This issue can be ignored when the sampling intervals are short, implicitly assuming that the system state does not change a lot in a short period. However, this can be a big issue when the sampling interval is longer, which is often the case for an IoT-based monitoring system to reduce power consumption.

2.6.2 Solution: Model-Bounded Monitoring for Flexible Interpolation

2.6.2.1 Idea: Exploit the Knowledge of the Monitored System

Our solution is to bound the unknown behaviour between samples using the prior knowledge of the monitored system. The latter knowledge is expressed by what is called a bounding model, which is an abstraction of the monitored system. Utilising the bounding model, the behaviour between samples is bounded and it is determined if there is a possibility of unsafe behaviour between samples. This procedure is called model-bounded monitoring.

Linear hybrid automata (LHAs) is used as the formalism for bounding models. The use of LHAs is due to the following observations: While LHAs are expressive, e.g., it allows discrete switching as well as bounding the derivative by the Lipschitz constant; they form a limited subclass of hybrid automata, and their reachability analysis is tractable using convex polyhedra analysis.

Example 14 (thermostatic chamber) Consider the monitoring of a thermostatic chamber. The thermostatic chamber has two modes, on and off, and at each location, the rate of the temperature change satisfies Ṫ ∈ [2.0, 4.0] and Ṫ ∈ [−2.0, 0], respectively. The actual dynamics can be much more complicated, but it is assumed that these intervals bound the actual derivatives of the temperature under the current condition, e.g., the output of the heater, range of the temperature, amount of the water, and room temperature. The LHA in Fig. 2.17 models such a thermostatic chamber.

Figure 2.18 illustrates the model-bounded monitoring procedure. The goal is to alert if the temperature enters the unsafe areas, which are shown as red in Fig. 2.18. It is observed that all the samples (the black points x1 ,...,x4 ) are in the safe area. For each pair (xi−1 ,xi ) of samples, the reachable area (the blue areas) is computed and the temperature moves from the previous sample xi−1 to the next sample xi through this. The reachable area is represented by a finite union of convex polyhedra. Here, it is observed that the (blue) hatched and (red) dotted areas intersect in between x3 and x4 , implying that the unsafe area might be visited. Therefore, there is an alert about a potential safety violation, although no violation is observed in the samples.

Example 15 (automatic transmission system) Consider the monitoring of a vehicle. The vehicle has two gear modes, low and high, and at each location, the acceleration of the vehicle satisfies ˙v ∈ [−6,15] and ˙v ∈ [−6,7], respectively. At low and high gear modes, the velocity must be in v ∈ [0,90] and v ≥ 30, respectively. The gear can change from low to high and high to low when v ≥ 45 and v ≤ 50, respectively. There must be at least 2 time units between each gear change for the comfort. The LHA in Fig. 2.19 models such a vehicle.

Figure 2.20 illustrates the model-bounded monitoring procedure. The goal is to alert if the velocity is too high, i.e., v ≥ 120; the red dotted area in Fig. 2.20 shows the unsafe area. It is observed that the reachable area between v2 and v3 is non-convex. This is because the maximum acceleration is different between the low velocity and the high velocity. Nevertheless, the reachable area is represented by a finite union of convex polyhedra, and the symbolic analysis of LHAs with convex polyhedra can be used. Even though all the samples (the black points v1 ,...,v3 ) are in the safe area, it is alerted that there is a potential safety violation because an intersection of (red) dotted and (blue) hatched areas is observed between v2 and v3.

Example 16 (vehicle platooning) Consider a vehicle platooning scenario where two vehicles drive one after the other, with small distance between them. As mentioned in Example 9, such vehicle platooning attracts interest as a measure for enhanced road capacity as well as for fuel efficiency.

The vehicle platooning system has two modes, cruising and recovering. In the normal cruising mode, the relative distance has a drift and the inter-vehicle distance decreases. The recovering mode is used to increase the inter-vehicle distance. At each location, the velocity of each vehicle is ẋ1 ∈ [7.5,8.5] and ẋ2 ∈ [8.0,9.0]; and ẋ1 ∈ [11.0,13.0] and ẋ2 ∈ [9.0,11.0], respectively. The LHA in Fig. 2.21 models such a vehicle platooning system.

Figure 2.22 illustrates the model-bounded monitoring procedure. The goal is to alert if the two vehicles could potentially touch each other. Physical contact of the vehicles is not observed in Fig. 2.22, but the same cannot be assured between the sampling instants. The hatched areas show the reachable area i.e., the symbolic interpolation using the bounding model.

Here, in the first interpolation (the blue areas), there is no potential physical contact, whereas in the second interpolation (the red areas), there is a potential physical contact. Therefore, there is an alert about a potential safety violation, even though no violation is observed in the samples.

2.6.2.2 On the Usage of the Model

One might say that the application area of model-bounded monitoring is smaller than the other monitoring methods because it requires a model. It certainly requires an LHA as a bounding model, which is much like a system model for the exhaustive verification of hybrid systems [2]. It is usually challenging to obtain system models, and the use of these usually limits the application of the exhaustive verification.

However, in model-bounded monitoring, the model construction is not a big issue as in exhaustive verification because unlike the system model required for exhaustive verification, the bounding model need not be very precise. The analysis in exhaustive verification is global, and the modelling error accumulates over time; thus, even a small modelling error can cause a huge impact on the analysis. In contrast, the reachability analysis in model-bounded monitoring is local, and the modelling error is reset at each sample. For example, in Fig. 2.18, it is observed that the reachable area converges to one point at each sample.

2.6.3 Algorithms and Implementations

In [29], we presented two approaches to solve the model-bounded monitoring problem: by a reduction to reachability analysis and by a dedicated algorithm. The former approach is implemented with a model checker PHAVerLite, and the latter is implemented in a prototype tool HAMONI. Both approaches share the technical essence, namely the bounded-time reachability analysis of LHAs. The reachability analysis of PHAVerLite is optimised with recent techniques, while HAMONI is a simple prototype tool using Parma Polyhedra Library for convex polyhedra operations. The experimental results in [29] show the feasibility of model-bounded monitoring, especially by HAMONI. For example, for a benchmark on adaptive cruise control, HAMONI monitors 1,000 samples in about 12 seconds for dimension 5 on an Amazon EC2 c4.large instance (2.9 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2666 v3, 2 vCPUs, and 3.75 GiB RAM) that runs Ubuntu 18.04 LTS (64 bit). Refer to [29] for further experiment results, especially on the number of false alarms (the number was found to be permissible).

2.6.4 Summary

Model-bounded monitoring is a monitoring method guaranteed to detect every unsafe behaviour even if the signal is coarsely sampled. Although there may be false alarms, it is reducible using a more precise bounding model. In [29], the model-bounded monitoring problem is formulated using LHAs with two algorithms. The experimental evaluation suggests the feasibility of the model-bounded monitoring. Note that the above algorithm achieves “flexibility” and “informativeness” in the following sense.

Flexibility Model-bounded monitoring utilises a flexible interpolation of the sampled logs considering the prior knowledge of the system called bounding model. It is guaranteed to detect every unsafe behaviour even if the log is sampled sparsely.

Informativeness Since parametric LHAs is equivalent to LHAs, parameter valuations and unobserved signal values can be synthesised, similar to Sections 2.3 and 2.4. Refer to [25] for the detailed discussion on this point.

2.7 Conclusions

In this chapter, automata-based techniques for monitoring CPSs with formal specifications were reviewed. Formal automated monitoring is much more scalable than human monitoring. Formal automated monitoring is not only more informative but also the associated engineering costs are much lower, in comparison to ad-hoc monitoring. However, it must be noted that human monitoring and ad-hoc automated monitoring can still be viable options in some situations.

Among various techniques for formal automated monitoring, the focus of this chapter was on the timed pattern matching problem (in Section 2.2) and its parametric and quantitative extensions (in Sections 2.3 to 2.5). Timed pattern matching is the most basic and efficient problem as other complex problems take longer time. Nevertheless, the experimental results show that the complex problems, e.g., symbolic monitoring with infinite data domains (Section 2.4) and quantitative timed pattern matching (Section 2.5), are still efficient enough to monitor the values observed by sensors in real-time.

In these monitoring techniques, there is a methodological difficulty. Although the actual behaviour is continuous, the logs can only be observed in discrete time by digital sampling. This approximate observation does not matter if the sampling interval is short enough but can cause an issue when only a sparsely sampled log is available, e.g., due to a network limitation. In Section 2.6, we discussed model-bounded monitoring to flexibly interpolate the behaviour between the discrete samples utilising what is called a bounding model. Although model-bounded monitoring is highly complex, the experimental results show that it is still feasible and computationally tractable.

We believe that these formal techniques for system monitoring will play an essential role during the development and after the deployment of safety-critical cyber-physical systems.

Chapter 3 Formal Specification of Temporal Properties

Clovis Eberhart

National Institute of Informatics and JFLI, Tokyo, Japan

Jérémy Dubut

National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Tokyo, Japan

Ichiro Hasuo

National Institute of Informatics and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

3.1 Introduction to Formal Specifications

This chapter is a basis for many other chapters as it introduces so-called formal specifications. Formal specifications are necessary whenever one wants to automatically check whether a system behaves as expected on a given input. They are therefore necessary in many testing and verification methods. In particular, in this book, they will be used extensively in Chapter 1, which deals with falsification, an advanced testing technique. They can also be used in relation to monitoring, as explained in Chapter 2.

3.1.1 What is a Formal Specification?

In a nutshell, a formal specification is a description of a property of a system, written in a mathematical language. It is given an unambiguous and precise meaning, unlike specifications written in a natural language.

As such, formal specifications have the advantage that it is possible to reason about them and compute on them automatically, using computers. In particular, they can be used to design (or automatically generate) algorithms for problems such as model-checking, falsification, or monitoring. In such problems, researchers and engineers need to describe what is considered “interesting” without relying on human intervention. The specification therefore has to be completely formalised, hence the need for formal specifications.

On the other hand, they might be perceived as cumbersome to write by non-specialists, especially compared to sentences written in a natural language. The goal of this chapter is to make non-specialist readers familiar with formal specifications, and particularly specifications describing temporal properties.

3.1.2 Challenges for Practitioners

One of the main challenges for practitioners concerning specifications is to choose the right language to describe the particular property they are interested in. Choosing the right language is primarily about striking the right balance between the language’s expressiveness and how costly it is to run different algorithms on specifications written in the language. In this regard, the languages we introduce in this chapter are among the most expressive generalistic languages for temporal properties, that is, specifications that describe sequences of events occurring in time, such as eventually reaching a target, staying in a safe area forever, or not staying out of one’s work area forever, that possess rather computationally efficient algorithms.

Formal specifications can make things unnecessarily complicated in some cases, in particular when they are meant to be understood by humans. In such cases, natural languages offer better support, as they usually describe high-level concepts that can be subject to interpretation. For example, they are more naturally adapted to write laws, because they must be understood by most people and ambiguity can be broken by jurisprudence.

However, when digital systems, such as computers, are involved, it is necessary to write specifications in an abstract and unambiguous manner. For example, according to Mobileye’s Responsibility-Sensitive-Safety philosophy,

You must drive in such a way that you must not be responsible for any crash.

However, a computerised system cannot understand such a high-level concept, and must instead be given specifications such as the following:

When cruising on a straight line, the distance from the ego vehicle to the leading vehicle must be at least D, When changing lane between two vehicles, the distance between them must be at least D ′ ,

and so on, where D, D ′ are given by mathematical expressions depending on the speed of the other vehicles, the response time, the physics of the ego vehicle and so on.

For all these reasons, finding the proper language boils down to balancing intuitive understanding, expressivity, unambiguity, and computational tractability.

3.1.3 Goal of this Chapter

The main goal of this chapter is to introduce the reader to formal specifications, as well as basic mathematical notions needed for them. Numerous examples will be given throughout the chapter to give intuitions on all the concepts, but the reader is encouraged to come up with their own to check their understanding: the end goal is for the reader to be able to write their own specifications, either in the proposed frameworks or in their own framework, adapted to their own problems.

This chapter will serve as a basis for other chapters, particularly Chapter 1 on falsification and Chapter 2 on monitoring, whose problems and algorithms heavily rely on formal specifications, with particular emphasis on temporal specifications.

The progression will be as follows. Starting from the basic examples of arithmetic and regular expressions, we will introduce the concepts of syntax and semantics (Section 3.2). The goal of this section is for the reader to understand the distinction between what is written (the syntax), and what is meant (the semantics), but also to understand basic inductive definitions. We will then introduce a syntax and semantics for basic temporal specifications of discrete-time systems: linear temporal logic (LTL) (Section 3.3). The goal for the chapter at this point is to (1) understand basic temporal operators such as until, next, and globally; (2) be able to come up with formal specifications adapted to their own problems; (3) understand the meaning of “a system satisfies a specification” in terms of execution traces. Based on what has been learnt with linear temporal logic (LTL), we will next introduce a more complex framework for temporal specifications of continuous-time systems this time: signal temporal logic (STL) (Section 3.4). The goal in this section is still to be able to write formal specifications, but also to be able to handle a complex, quantitative semantics that answers the question “by how much does a system satisfy a specification?”

3.2  Introduction to Syntax and Semantics

Syntax and semantics are key notions in computer science, formal logic, and elsewhere. Syntax is what allows us to properly write programs, specifications, and sentences by giving symbols to depict notions and rules to structure them, while semantics is what gives a meaning to these objects.

In this section, we will gradually introduce syntax and semantics by examples with arithmetic expressions (Section 3.2.3) and regular expressions (Section 3.2.4), but first, we will explain the intuition (Section 3.2.1) and the purpose of introducing these concepts for formal specifications (Section 3.2.2).

3.2.1 What are Syntax and Semantics?

A syntax is a collection of symbols that can be combined in a structured manner. A typical example is the syntax of a programming language. This consists in keywords (such as “if”, “then”, “while” and so on), symbols (such as “+”, “=”, “;”), variable names, and so on, that can be written sequentially following some fixed structural rules (such as typing rules). Another example is the syntax of a natural language consisting of words and punctuation symbols structured by grammar rules. A phrase written using the symbols of the syntax, following the structural rules is called a term.

The key is that syntax is not interpreted yet: these symbols bear no meaning in themselves. This meaning is given by a semantics, which consists in a domain and an interpretation. The domain describes the possible meanings of a given syntax. In the case of a programming language, this domain can be the collection of mathematical functions of a given type, or the collection of assembler functions of a given architecture. The interpretation then associates any valid term of the syntax with an element of the domain. For example, a compiler can be seen as an interpretation of the syntax of a programming language into machine language. It gives a meaning to symbols which are understandable by a machine.

Syntax and semantics fulfil two complementary purposes. The syntax is for describing: it is usually compositional and easy to write, that is, you can write it by block, but its rigidity makes it hard to reason about. Complementarily, it is usually hard to describe the semantics of a given object as it often is infinite by nature (infinite executions traces, functions on integers, and so on), but its mathematical nature makes it easy to formally reason about.

3.2.2 How are They Related to Formal Specifications?

In what follows, we introduce some syntaxes and semantics to describe and give a precise meaning to specifications.

The syntax will be given by formulas composed of basic blocks (here called operators) that would describe specifications with logical connectives (such as conjunctions, implications), and temporal properties (such as the happening of an event at a given time in the future). The domain of the semantics of those formulas will be given by runs (or executions) of a system.

In the remainder of this section, we will give concrete examples of syntaxes and semantics not directly related to specifications. The purpose is to kindly introduce crucial concepts, necessary for the description and the understanding of syntax and semantics on basic examples.

3.2.3 Example: Arithmetic Expressions

Let us start with the example of integer arithmetic. In this example, the syntax is given by the usual symbols for addition, multiplication as well as constant integers. The domain of its semantics is then given by the set of integers and the interpretation by the result of the computation.

3.2.3.1 Syntax

It is usual to describe the syntax by a grammar. In the case of the integer arithmetic, the grammar is the following:

(3.1)
E ::=0|1|−E|E+E|E*E.

This means that terms of this syntax are all the object you can inductively write using symbols in {0, 1,−,+,∗} following the rules that you must have exactly one expression after a symbol −, and exactly one before and one after a symbol + or ∗. Here, inductively means that you can iterate the process to construct more and more complex terms. Precisely, it means the following:

  • 0 and 1 are arithmetic expressions. They are the basic blocks of the construction of an arithmetic expression.
  • If E is an arithmetic expression that one has already constructed, then one can obtain another expression by appending a − symbol in front of E. Namely, −E is another expression.
  • If E and F are two already constructed arithmetic expressions, then one can obtain two other expressions by appending a + or a ∗ symbol in- between. Namely, E + F and E ∗ F are two other expressions.

Example 17 It is for example possible to write


1 + 0

as an arithmetic expression. Indeed, 0 and 1 are arithmetic expressions as basic blocks. Then 1+0 is obtained by appending a + symbol between the expressions

1 and 0. It should be understood that, at this point, the expression 1 + 0 is not equal to the expression 1. Indeed, no meaning has been given to the symbols of the syntax. Consequently, 1 + 0 is just a different sequence of symbols than 1. Later, after introducing the semantics, 1 + 0 and 1 will have the same semantics, namely, they will both be interpreted (or computed in this case) as the integer 1. Likewise, 1 + 1 is an arithmetic expression obtained by appending a + symbol between two copies of the expression 1. Confusingly enough, it is usual to denote this expression by 2. At this point, this only means that the symbol 2 is a shorthand for the expression 1 + 1. This process of adding symbols to the syntax to represent bigger terms is usual: it allows to describe a term by blocks which makes the syntax modular. Such shorthands are called syntactic sugar. In a similar, manner we can write 3 for the expression


(1+1) + 1

(which is the same as the expression 2 + 1), obtained by appending a + symbol between the expressions 1 + 1 and 1; 4 for the expression ((1 + 1) + 1) + 1; and so on.

Observe that, in those few last expressions, we added parentheses ( and ). In this book, those symbols are not part of the syntax, they just help to delimit the scope of each symbol: for example, writing 1 + 1 ∗ 0 would be ambiguous between (1+1)∗0 and 1+(1∗0). Another syntactic sugar is given by E , which is a shorthand for the expression E ∗ E for any expression E. Using all those pieces, we can write bigger expressions, such as,


1 + (3*22)

which is a shorthand for the expression


1+(((1+1)+1) *((1+1) *(1+1))) .

Remark that the latter is much harder to read than the former, which explains the interest of using syntactic sugar.

3.2.3.2 Semantics

As said, the domain of the semantics of arithmetic expressions is the set ℤ of integers. The interpretation of an expression is then the integer obtained after unfolding the computation. For example, the semantics of the expression 1 + 0 is the integer 1 (that is the integer 1 in Z, not to be confused with the expression 1, that is an expression E built inductively by the grammar (3.1)). Precisely, the semantics of a term is defined by induction on its construction, that is, all symbols of the syntax are assigned a meaning, and the meaning of a term is obtained by unfolding its definition, using the meaning of each encountered symbol. We denote by 〚E〛 the semantics of an expression.

In the case of integer arithmetic, the interpretation is defined as follows.

  • The semantics 〚0〛 of the expression 0 is the integer 0 (again, not to be confused with the expression 0).
  • The semantics 〚1〛 of the expression 1 is the integer 1.

  • The semantics of an expression of the form −E is obtained by taking the opposite of the semantic of E, namely,


    〚 − E〛 =  − 〚E〛.

    In this equality above, both − are different. The left one is just a symbol without meaning, while the one on the right is the function from ℤ to ℤ mapping an integer n to −n.

  • The semantics of an expression of the form E + F is given by the sum of the semantics of E and F, that is,


    〚E + F〛 = 〚E〛 + 〚F〛.

  • The semantics of an expression of the form E ∗ F is given by the product of the semantics of E and F, that is,


    〚E * F〛 = 〚E〛 * 〚F〛.

Example 18 Unfolding this process, we can explicitly give the semantics of expressions given in Example 17.


  • 〚1 + 0〛 = 〚1〛 + 〚0〛 = 1 + 0 = 1 = 〚1〛;


  • 〚2〛 = 〚1 + 1〛 = 〚1〛 + 〚1〛 = 1 + 1 = 2;


  • 〚3〛 = 〚1 + 2〛 = 〚1〛 + 〚2〛 = 1 + 2 + 3;


  • 〚E2〛 = 〚E * E〛 = 〚E〛 * 〚E〛 = 〚E〛2;


  • 〚1 + (3 * 22)〛 = 〚1〛 = 〚3 * 22〛 = 1 + (〚3〛*〚22〛) = 1 + (3+22) = 8.

Again, the reader must be careful in understanding that what is inside the 〚〛 is different from elements of the domain, even though they are written in the same way. This confusion where a symbol and its meaning are written the same way is useful in practice, as this allows us to avoid introducing new symbols. However, this is only a peculiarity of arithmetic expressions, and we will see another example next where this is not the case.

3.2.4 Example: Regular Expressions

In this section, let us overview another example of syntax and semantics for regular expressions, such as in the POSIX standard. Note that the regular expressions presented here are a theoretical notion, and that they are simpler than the regular expressions of the POSIX standard.

3.2.4.1 Syntax

The syntax describes some patterns, using basic constructors such as concatenation or Kleene star, that describe some sets of words. It is given by the following grammar:

(3.2)
R::=⌀|ε|a|R⋅R|R+R∣R*.

Here a ranges over a fixed set Σ called the alphabet. In the case of the POSIX standard, Σ contains alphanumeric characters, punctuation signs, spaces, digits, and so on. The other symbols are · the concatenation, + the alternation, and ∗ the Kleene star.

Similarly to the case of arithmetic expressions, this means that regular expressions can be constructed as follows. For each symbol, we also provide the intention behind them in terms of pattern recognition (again, no meaning is given to the symbols at this point).

  • Every symbol a in the alphabet Σ is a regular expression. This is a basic block of regular expressions. The intention is to match every character a in a string.
  • The symbols ∅ and ε are regular expressions. These two items are also basic blocks of regular expressions. The intention of the former is to match no strings, while the latter matches only the (zero-length) string with no character.
  • If R and S are two regular expressions, then R · S and R + S are two other regular expressions. The former intends to match every string that is formed as a string matched by R followed by a string matched by S. The intention of the latter is to match strings that are matched by R or by S.
  • If R is a regular expression, then R ∗ is another regular expression. The intention here is to match all the strings that are obtained by concatenating a finite (possibly empty) sequence of strings matched by R.

Example 19 In Example 17, we described some arithmetic expressions in a bottom-up manner, that is, we started from basic blocks and combined them to construct bigger and bigger expressions. Here, let us use a top-down manner, namely, starting from the outermost symbol, we dig deeper into the expression until we reach the basic blocks. Let us look at the following regular expression:


((a + c) ⋅ b)*,

where a, b, and c are symbols in Σ, and let us analyse how it is generated using the grammar. The outermost symbol of this expression is a Kleene star ∗, applied to (a + c) · b, so the expression is of the form R∗ (again, the parentheses are not part of the syntax and are just for disambiguation). The outermost symbol

of the inner part of this expression is a concatenation ·, separating a + c and b. Consequently, the term is of the form (R · R) ∗. Next, the left-hand side of the expression is a + c whose outermost symbol is an alternation, so the expression is of the form ((R + R) · R) ∗ , and so on. Pictorially, we can write


$$\begin{array}{l} \left. R\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad R^{*}\rightsquigarrow{(R \cdot R)}^{*}\rightsquigarrow{((R + R) \cdot R)}^{*}\rightsquigarrow{((a + R) \cdot R)}^{*} \right. \\ \left. \rightsquigarrow\quad{((a + c) \cdot R)}^{*}\rightsquigarrow\quad{((a + c) \cdot b)}^{*} \right. \\ \end{array}$$

to describe the previous explanation, where ⇝ represents one step of replacing a missing part of the expression using some rule of the grammar.

In practice, it is usual to use both bottom-up and top-down manners at the same time while writing an expression: it often is clear what basic blocks to use (which is important for bottom-up) but also what outermost symbol to use (which is good for top-down), and the difficulty is to bridge the gap. The importance of outermost symbols will be further illustrated in Section 3.3.2.5.

As for arithmetic expressions, the POSIX standard has a variety of syntactic sugar, of which we introduce some pieces now, together with their intended meanings.

  • [A − Z] is a shorthand for the expression A + (B + (...(Y + Z))). The intention of this syntactic sugar is to match all capitalised alphabetic letters.
  • R+ is a shorthand for R · R ∗. This expression is called the Kleene plus and its intention is the same as the Kleene star, except that the empty sequence is forbidden.
  • R? is a shorthand for ε + R. This is called the question mark and its intention is to match all the strings matched by R or empty. A typical usage is to match British and American English spellings at the same time. For example, behavio · u? · r matches both “behavior” and “behaviour”.

3.2.4.2 Semantics

Regular expressions are used to describe patterns of words that one would like to detect in a text for example. Consequently, their meaning can naturally be described in terms of sets of words. Precisely, we call a word any finite sequence of symbols in the alphabet Σ. We denote the set of words by Σ ∗. The semantics 〚R〛 of a regular expression will then be a set of words, that is, 〚R〛 ⊆ Σ ∗. As for the case of arithmetic expressions, the semantics of regular expressions is given by induction on the construction of the expression, as follows.

  • The semantics 〚∅ 〛 of the expression ∅ is the empty set of words


    〚⌀〛 = ⌀.

  • The semantics 〚ε〛 of the expression ε is the set consisting of exactly one element, which is the empty word (usually also denoted by ε)


    〚ε〛 = {ε}.

  • For a given symbol a of the alphabet Σ, the semantics of 〚a〛 of the expression a is the set consisting of exactly one element, which is the 1-letter word a


    〚a〛 = {a}.

  • If R and S are two regular expressions whose semantics are 〚R〛 and 〚S〛 respectively, then the semantics 〚R · S〛 of their concatenation is the set of words consisting of concatenations uv of a word u in 〚R〛 followed by a word v in 〚S〛. Concretely,


    〚R ⋅ S〛 = {uv u∈.〚R〛 and v ∈ 〚S〛}.

  • If R and S are two regular expressions whose semantics are 〚R〛 and 〚S〛 respectively, then the semantics 〚R + S〛 of their alternation is the union of their semantics, that is,


    〚R + S〛 = 〚R〛  ∪ 〚S〛.

  • If R is a regular expression whose semantics is 〚R〛, then the semantics 〚R ∗〛 of its Kleene star is the set of words that are formed by concatenating a finite number of words in 〚R〛, which means


    〚R〛 = {w∣there is n≥0 and w1,…,wn∈ 〚R〛 such that w=w1…wn}.

Example 20 Let us continue Example 19 by unfolding the definition of its semantics.


$$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{ll} {{〚{((a + c) \cdot b)}^{\ast}〛} = \left\{ {w_{1}\ldots w_{n} \mid w_{1},\ldots,w_{n} \in {〚{(a + c) \cdot b}〛}} \right\}} & {(semantics\ of \ast )} \\ \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {= \left\{ {u_{1}v_{1}\ldots u_{n}v_{n} \mid u_{1},\ldots,u_{n} \in {〚{a + c}〛}\,\, and\, v_{1},\ldots,v_{n} \in {〚b〛}} \right\}} & \\ \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{ll} & {(semantics\ of \cdot )} \\ \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {= \left\{ u_{1}b\ldots \middle| u_{n}b \middle| u_{1},\ldots,u_{n} \in {〚{a + c}〛} \right\}} & {(semantics\ of\, b)} \\ \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {= \left\{ {u_{1}b\ldots u_{n}b \mid u_{1},\ldots,u_{n} \in {〚a〛} \cup {〚c〛}} \right\}} & {(semantics\ of\, + )} \\ \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{ll} {= \left\{ u_{1}b\ldots u_{n}b \mid for\ all\, i.u_{i} \in \left\{ a,c \right\} \right\}} & \text{(semantics~of~a~and~c)} \\ \end{array} \\ \end{array}$$

Concretely, ((a+c) · b) ∗ represents the set of words obtained by taking any finite sequence of a’s and c’s, appending the letter b after each symbol. For example, the empty word ε, ab, and cbab are in this set, while a, bc, aba, and cbb are not.

Remark 3.1 The semantics we just gave is useful to give precise meaning to functions such as UNIX’s grep command-line: the command shows the lines in a text such that part of the line matches the pattern given by the regular expression, that is, this part belongs to the set of words given by the regular expression’s semantics. This type of semantics (which is the only type we are considering in this chapter), which interprets the syntax purely mathematically, is called denotational semantics. In contrast, there exist other types of semantics that are more targeted at computation: they are called operational semantics. The domain of those semantics are often given by a set of abstract machines that compute the meaning of the syntax. Such an example for regular expressions is given by finite automata, which can computationally check whether a given word is matched by a given regular expression. A reader interested in the rich world of semantics may check [21], and [20] if interested in the connection between regular expressions and automata.

3.3 Linear Temporal Logic

In this section, we define LTL, study its properties, and illustrate its usefulness on some examples. In Section 3.3.2 we define LTL’s syntax, which is necessary for readers who want to learn to write their own specifications. In Section 3.3.3, we discuss LTL’s semantics, which makes formal the intuitions about formulas and can help check whether a specification has the intended meaning. Section 3.3.4 is dedicated to existing tools based on LTL, and Section 3.3.5 to references for readers who want to learn more about LTL.

3.3.1 Introduction to Linear Temporal Logic

Linear temporal logic (LTL) is a logic that describes temporal properties of discrete-time systems. Let us explain the different words in the previous sentence. Since LTL is a logic, its main ingredient is formulas, which are formal objects (the syntax) that represent specifications, together with what these formulas mean (their semantics). LTL describes temporal properties, by which we mean properties that refer to a system’s evolution over time. For example, if we are considering ADSs, properties such as

the ego vehicle will never crash,

the ego vehicle will eventually reach its destination, or

the taxi will arrive at destination after picking up its passenger

are temporal properties, since they deal with the different states of the system over time. LTL specifying properties of discrete-time systems means that the behaviours it can specify have been discretised: either because the system itself works in discrete time (such as synchronous software systems), or because systems that work in continuous time are simplified through their modelling as discrete-time systems. Finally, LTL describes linear temporal properties, which means that the properties it describes consider each execution of the system separately (as a single linear execution in time), rather than all the possible executions together (which have a tree or graph structure).

LTL is a rather simple logic among temporal logics and therefore a lot of interesting problems are decidable for it. In particular, the model-checking problem, which consists in answering whether a (finite-state) system satisfies a given specification, is decidable: there exist algorithms that answer true when a system verifies a given specification, and can give a counter-example otherwise. This approach, known as verification, is complementary to testing, and used extensively for example in security-critical software systems. While we do not discuss it in this book, the interested reader will find more in the references in Section 3.3.5.

The main goal of this section is to bring the reader to a level of familiarity with LTL high enough that they will be able to come up with LTL formulas that represent simple specifications on their own. The reader should become familiar enough with temporal logic in general that the definitions and examples of signal temporal logic (STL) in the next section will seem natural to them.

3.3.2 Syntax

In this section, following the basic examples of Sections 3.2.3.1 (for arithmetic expressions) and 3.2.4.1 (for regular expressions), we introduce the syntax of LTL. We define the syntax of LTL formulas in Section 3.3.2.1 and give intuitive meanings to the different constructs in Section 3.3.2.2. These are necessary to be able to understand specifications written in LTL and come up with one’s own formal specifications. We define syntactic sugar for common constructions in Section 3.3.2.3 and explain how to extend the modalities with timing constraints in Section 3.3.2.4, both of which are useful shorthands when manipulating LTL specifications. Finally, Section 3.3.2.5 describes several classes of usual specifications expressible in LTL, which will help the reader come up with their own specifications more easily by following predefined templates.

3.3.2.1 Grammar

We fix a set P of atomic propositions, that is, a set of basic properties of interest for the system under study. Let us give a few examples of such atomic propositions that are relevant for ADSs. A first property of interest is whether the ego vehicle’s left blinker is on, which can be denoted by an atomic proposition leftBlinker. We may want to be more precise than whether a component is on or off by asking whether that component is in a certain mode, for example whether the vehicle is in third gear, which can be denoted by the atomic proposition gearEq3. Finally, we may also be interested in the value of a particular physical quantity by comparing it to a given value, for example that the vehicle’s speed is greater than 20m/s, which can be written as speedGt20.

Definition 3.1 (LTL formulas) The set of LTL formulas is generated by the following grammar:

(3.3)
 φ    ::=    p|⊤|¬φ|φ∧φ|◯φ∣φ𝒰φ,

where p is an atomic proposition in P.

Example 21 Given atomic propositions leftBlinker and steeringGt0.2, it is possible to write the following example:

(3.4)
¬(⊤𝒰((¬ leftBlinker )∧ steeringGt0.2 )),

which is generated in a top-down manner by the grammar as follows:


$$\begin{matrix} \left. \,\varphi\,\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}\varphi\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}(\varphi\mathcal{U}\varphi)\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}(\top\mathcal{U}\varphi)\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}(\top\mathcal{U}(\varphi \land \varphi)) \right. \\ \left. \,\,\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}(\top\mathcal{U}((\text{¬}\varphi) \land \varphi))\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}(\top\mathcal{U}((\text{¬}~leftBlinker~) \land \varphi)) \right. \\ \left. \,\,\rightsquigarrow\text{¬}(\top\mathcal{U}((\text{¬}~leftBlinker~) \land ~steeringGt~0.2)). \right. \\ \end{matrix}$$

Throughout the rest of this chapter, we will use formula and specification interchangeably. From a formal point of view, both terms have the same meaning, but formula is more appropriate when discussing syntax and semantics, while specification is more natural when discussing desired properties of systems.

3.3.2.2 Intuitive Explanation of the Formulas

The intuitive meaning of the constructors of LTL formulas is as follows.

  • An atomic proposition is a basic property that can be either true or false at a given time. Typical examples are whether the velocity of a vehicle is above some threshold (as in speedGt20) or whether it is in a particular gear (as in gearEq3). For more details, see the beginning of Section 3.3.2.1 above.
  • The truth ⊤ represents a property that is true at all times.
  • The negation ¬φ represents the property that is true whenever φ is false. For example, if leftBlinker represents a proposition that is true whenever the left blinker is on, then ¬leftBlinker is true whenever the left blinker is off.
  • The conjunction φ ∧ ψ is a property that is true whenever both φ and ψ are true. For example, if gearEql and speedGt30 have their intuitive meaning, then gearEq1 ∧ speedGt30 is true whenever the vehicle is in gear 1 and its speed is greater than 30m/s at the same time.
  • The next ○ φ represents the property that is true whenever φ is true at the next time step. The formula ○ gearEq3 is true at some point in time if the vehicle is in third gear at the next time step.
