  • The until φ U ψ represents the property that is true whenever ψ becomes true at some point in time, and φ has stayed true at all times until then. For example, the formula speedLt25 U gearEq4 is true if the vehicle is in fourth gear at some point in time, and its speed has stayed under 25m/s until then.

These intuitions will be made precise when we describe the semantics of these formulas.

Example 22 Combining those intuitions, the formula (3.4) represents the property that is true whenever there is no time in the future where the steering angle is bigger than 0.2 radians (i.e., the vehicle is turning left) and the left blinker is not on. This can be rephrased as “whenever the vehicle turns left, its left blinker is on”. Notice that the part of the intuition of the until about all intermediate times can be dropped because it is applied on the truth T, which is true at all times.

3.3.2.3 Syntactic Sugar

It is often convenient to add some notations to usually used formula constructs.

Definition 3.2 Here are some notations that will be used in the rest of this chapter.

  • We will denote the falsehood ¬⊤ by ⊥. Following the intuitive explanation above, this is an expression representing the property that is true whenever the truth ⊤ is false, that is, ⊥ represents the property that is always false.
  • We will denote the disjunction ¬(¬φ ∧ ¬ψ) by φ ∨ ψ. This represents the property that is true whenever at least one of φ or ψ is true.
  • We will denote the implication ¬φ ∨ ψ by φ → ψ. This represents the property that is true whenever ψ is true or φ is false (this is the usual notion of implication in classical logic).
  • We will denote the finally (also called eventually) ⊤ U φ by ◊ φ. This formula represents the property that is true if there is a time in the future when φ is true.
  • Lastly, we will denote the globally (also called always) − (◊ ¬φ) by □ φ. It represents the property that is true if at all times in the future φ is true.

Note also that a double negation ¬¬φ represents the same property as φ. This fact will be made formal with the semantics: ¬¬φ and φ have the same semantics. Since we are interested in the specifications represented by the formulas, i.e., in the semantics rather than the syntax, it is sometimes useful to replace a formula with another one with the same semantics to make the semantics clearer from the syntax, as illustrated by the example below.

Example 23 Using this syntactic sugar and the previous remark, we can shorten the formula (3.4). First, we can observe ⊤ U φ which can be shortened as ◊ φ. The formula then becomes ¬(◊(¬leftBlinker) ∧ steeringGt0.2). Using the syntactic sugar □ together with the double negation, the formula can be rewritten as □ ¬((¬leftBlinker) ∧ steeringGt0.2). Introducing a disjunction, this becomes □ (leftBlinker ∨ ¬steeringGt0.2). Finally, recognising an implication, the formula is shortened as

(3.5)
( steeringGt0.2 → leftBlinker) .

Remark that the intuition ofthis formula following the explanation ofthis section is slightly different than the one from Section 3.3.2.2: this formula represents the property that is true whenever for all times in the future if the vehicle is turning left then it must have its left blinker on. However, those two formulations are semantically equivalent.

There exist other syntactic sugar notations that are commonly used in LTL, but which we will not use throughout this book. We list them here nonetheless, as they can be useful to the reader to express some specifications.

Definition 3.3 The following notations are common syntactic sugar for LTL.

  • The weak until φ W ψ denotes the formula (φ U ψ) ∨ □ φ. It is true whenever φ stays true untilφbecomes true, butφhas to stay true at all times if ψ does not hold true at any point in time. For example, if systemSafe and protocolEnd are atomic propositions that respectively describe that the system is safe and that a protocol has reached its end, then systemSafe W protocolEnd describes the fact that the system is safe until the end of the protocol. Note that this is different from systemSafe U protocolEnd because the latter states that the protocol will end at some point (which may or may not be desired in the specification).
  • The release φ R ψ denotes the formula ψ W (φ ∧ ψ). It is true whenever φ is true at some point, and ψ has stayed true at all times until then (including the point in time when φ is true), or if ψ stays true at all points in time. While the meaning is essentially the same as weak until, its intended meaning is closer to the intuition that ψ turning true releases the constraint on φ to stay true.

3.3.2.4 Adding Timing Constraints

The operators described until now - except for the Next operator ○ - do not give any precise information on the time an event occurs. For example, the Finally operator ◊ states that there is a time in the future when a property is true, without giving any explicit information on this time. We can overcome this problem by iterating the Next operator. Let us define some syntactic sugar ○i φ by induction on i ≥ 0:

  • if i = 0, ○0 φ is a notation for φ itself,
  • if i = 0, ○0 φ is a shorthand for ○ (○i−1 φ).

The intuition is that ○i φ is true whenever φ is true in i time steps in the future.

Using this syntactic sugar, we can define a timed finally ◊[a,b] φ (where 0 ≤ a ≤ b) as a shorthand for


$$\underset{i = a}{\overset{b}{\vee}}◯^{i}\varphi = ◯^{a}\varphi \vee ◯^{a + 1}\varphi \vee \ldots \vee ◯^{b}\varphi.$$

The intuition is still that ◊[a,b] φ is true whenever there is a time in the future where φ is true, but furthermore this time is required to be between a and b. Similarly, we can define a timed globally □[a,b] φ as


$$\underset{i = a}{\overset{b}{\land}}◯^{i}\varphi = ◯^{a}\varphi \land ◯^{a + 1}\varphi \land \ldots \land ◯^{b}\varphi$$

that is true whenever φ is true at all time in the future between a and b, and a timed until φ U[a,b] ψ as


$$\underset{i = a}{\overset{b}{\vee}}\left( {◯^{i}\psi \land \underset{k = 0}{\overset{i - 1}{\land}}◯^{k}\varphi} \right)$$

that is true whenever there is a time in the future between a and b when ψ is true and φ is true at all times before that.

3.3.2.5 Examples of Classes of Property

Here, we describe some recipes to express common specifications using the syntax above.

Safety is a class of properties describing that the system does not show any undesirable behaviours, such as bugs, crashes, dangerous driving, data race, etc. This can be described using LTL syntax in the following equivalent ways: ¬◊somethingBadHappens (there is no time in the future when something bad happens) or □¬somethingBadHappens (at all time in the future, something bad does not happen). Here somethingBadHappens is a formula formally describing what it means for the system to do something bad. An example can be given by an atomic proposition longDistUnsafe which would be true whenever the longitudinal distance of the ego vehicle with another vehicle is smaller than a certain safe distance.

Guarantee is a class of properties that ensures that some fixed event must happen at some point of the execution, e.g., reaching a target, the end of a protocol, etc. It can simply be described as a finally ◊desiredEvent, where desiredEvent is a formal description as an LTL formula of the event we want to guarantee. For example, if a system satisfies ◊(speedEq0 ∧ targetReached), then it is guaranteed that it will reach its target and stop there at some point, if speedEq0 and targetReached have their intuitive meanings.

Readiness is a class of properties describing that the system is doing some action only when it is ready. This can be formulated as


 ▫ (somethingHappens → isReady), 

where somethingHappens and isReady are formulas. For example, if the former is an atomic proposition steeringGt0.2 that is true when the vehicle is turning left, and if the latter is another atomic proposition leftBlinker that is true the left blinker is on, then the readiness formula means that the vehicle will only ever turn left when the left blinker is on (note that this is formula (3.5)).

Fairness is a class of properties describing that if all the conditions for an event to happen are satisfied, then this event must happen in the future. This can be described as □ (conditions → ◊eventHappens). For example, if the condition formula is given by the conjunction lowSpeedLaneEmpty ∧ speedLt25 where lowSpeedLaneEmpty and speedLt25 are atomic proposition, and if eventHappens is given by the atomic proposition takeover, then fairness means that if the low-speed lane is empty and if the vehicle has a low speed, then it must change to the low-speed lane at some point in the future, in compliance with driving laws.

Liveness is a class of properties guaranteeing that the system never gets blocked. This can be expressed as □OsomethingHappens. For example, if greenLight is an atomic proposition that is true whenever a given traffic light is green, then □◊greenLight is true if the traffic light is green at infinitely many times in the future. Note that this is equivalent to saying that there is no point in the future when the light will never be green again. This will be made formal when discussing semantics, since □◊greenLight will have the same semantics as ¬◊□¬greenLight (by double negation).

Finally, it is also useful to note that these classes of properties can be combined to obtain richer specifications. For example, the formula


▫((▫⋄ greenLight )→⋄ targetReached )

combines fairness (about traffic lights), guarantee (about reaching the target), and readiness (the overall structure of the formula) properties to obtain a specification that describes the fact that, at any point in time, if the traffic light turns green infinitely often in the future, then the ego vehicle will reach its target at some point, which is a realistic specification.

3.3.3 Semantics

In this section, following the basic examples of Sections 3.2.3.2 (for arithmetic expressions) and 3.2.4.2 (for regular expressions), we introduce the semantics of LTL. The section is organised as follows. We link the semantics of LTL formulas to system executions through the notion of trace (Sections 3.3.3.1), inductively define the semantics of LTL formulas (Section 3.3.3.2), and describe how to derive the semantics of the syntactic sugar (Section 3.3.3.3).

3.3.3.1 Systems and Execution Traces

An execution trace represents what can be observed of the execution of a system. More precisely, the system state changes over time throughout its execution, and the trace of that execution represents which atomic propositions are true at each point in time. For example, an ADS contains both software and hardware, and we may only be interested in the physical position and velocity of the hardware, while the software variables are of no interest to us. In that case, the system state at some point in time comprises both the physical values of interest to us, and the value of all variables in the software, which we do not care about. On the other hand, since we are only interested in the position and velocity of the vehicle, the execution trace of the system would only contain boolean values derived from those quantities.

Definition 3.4 (traces) An execution trace of a system is an infinite sequence of sets of atomic propositions, that is, a sequence of the form S0,Sn,... where each Sn is a subset of P and is the set of the atomic propositions that are true at time i. More generally, we call trace (or execution trace) any sequence as above where all Sn’s are subsets of P, even if it does not stem from the execution of a system.

For example, if we are only interested in the two atomic propositions turnLeft and turnRight (which describe that the ego vehicle is turning left and right respectively), then the following is a trace:


S0 = { turnLeft }, S1 = { turnLeft , turnRight }, S2 = ⌀, …, Sn = ⌀, …,

even though this does not correspond to the execution of a system, since S1 does not make sense (a vehicle cannot be turning left and right at the same time). We denote by T the set of all traces.

Both the semantics of an LTL formula and that of a system are given by a subset of T: the semantics 〚φ〛 of a formula φ is the set of traces that satisfy the specification represented by the formula; the semantics 〚S〛 of a system S is the set of all possible execution traces of the system.

This correspondence allows us to formally compare a system with a specification. We say that a system. S satisfies a specification φ if


〚S〛 ⊆ 〚φ〛.

The model-checking problem is then to decide whether a given system satisfies a given specification.

3.3.3.2 Inductive Definition of the Semantics

As explained above in Section 3.3.3.1, the semantics of a formula 9 is the set of execution traces that satisfy that formula. This is made formal by the following definition.

Definition 3.5 (LTL semantics) The semantics of a given LTL formula φ, denoted by 〚φ〛, is a set of execution traces defined by induction on the definition of the formula.

  • When φ is an atomic proposition p, its semantics is given by the set of execution traces of the form S0, S1, with p ∈ S0:


    〚p〛 = {S0,S1,…∣p∈S0}.

  • When φ is the basic formula ⊤, its semantics is given by the set of all possible traces:


    〚⊤〛 = T.

  • When φ is formed as a negation ¬ψ, its semantics is given by the set of execution traces that are not in the semantics of ψ, that is, 〚¬ψ〛 is the complement of 〚ψ〛:


    〚¬ψ〛 = 𝕋 ∖ 〚ψ〛.

  • When φ is formed as a conjunction ψ1ψ2, its semantics is given by the set of execution traces that are both in the semantics of ψ1 and ψ2, that is, 〚ψ1 ∧ ψ2〛 is the intersection of 〚ψ1〛 and 〚ψ2〛:


    〚ψ1 ∧ ψ2〛 = 〚ψ1〛 ∩ 〚ψ2〛.

  • When φ is formed as a next ○ ψ, its semantics is given by the set of execution traces of the form S0, S1where S1, S2, … is in the semantics of ψ and S0 is arbitrary:


    〚◯ψ〛 = {S0,S1,…∣S1,S2,…∈ 〚ψ〛  and S0⊆ℙ}.

  • When φ is formed as an until ψ1 U ψ2, its semantics is given by the set of execution traces S0, S1 such that there exists a time i ≥ 0 where
  • Si, Si+1 is in the semantics of ψ2 and

  • for every 0 ≤ k < i, Sk, Sk+ i,... is in the semantics of ψ1.


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\psi_{1}\mathcal{U}\psi_{2}}〛}\,\, = \,\,\,\left\{ {S_{0},S_{1},\ldots \mid \exists i \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in \,{〚\psi_{2}〛}\,} \right.\, and~} \\ {\forall 0 \leq k < i.S_{k},S_{k + 1},\ldots\left. {\in \,{〚\psi_{2}〛}} \right\}} \\ \end{array}$$

In Section 3.3.2.3, we argued that the double negation ¬¬φ represents the same property as φ. This can be made formal using the semantics:


〚¬¬φ〛  = 𝕋 ∖ 〚¬φ〛  = 𝕋 ∖ (𝕋∖〚φ〛 ) = 〚φ〛 .

Example 24 Let us unfold this inductive definition on the formula (3.4).


$$\begin{array}{l} {〚{\text{¬}(\top\mathcal{U}((\text{¬}~leftBlinker~) \land ~steeringGt~0.2))}〛} \\ {= \mathbb{T} \smallsetminus {〚{\top\mathcal{U}((\text{¬}~leftBlinker~) \land ~steeringGt~0.2)}〛}\,\,~(semantics\ of~\text{¬}~)~} \\ {= \mathbb{T} \smallsetminus \left\{ {S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in \,\,\,{〚{(\text{¬}~leftBlinker~) \land ~steeringGt~0.2}〛}\,~and} \right.} \\ {\left. {\forall 0 \leq k < i.S_{k},S_{k + 1},\ldots \in {〚\top〛}} \right\}\,(~semantics\ of~\mathcal{U})} \\ {= \mathbb{T} \smallsetminus \left\{ {S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in \,\,\,{〚{(\text{¬}~leftBlinker~) \land ~steeringGt~0.2}〛}} \right\}\,} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(~semantics\ of~\top)~} \\ {= \mathbb{T} \smallsetminus \left\{ {S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in \,\,\,{〚{\text{¬}~leftBlinker~}〛}\,\, and} \right.} \\ {\left. {S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in \,\,\,{〚{steeringGt~0.2}〛}} \right\}\,\,~(semantics\ of~ \land )} \\ {= \mathbb{T} \smallsetminus \left\{ {S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \notin \,\,\,{〚{~leftBlinker~}〛}\,\, and} \right.} \\ {\left. {S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in \,\,\,{〚{steeringGt~0.2}〛}} \right\}\,\,~(semantics\ of~\neg)} \\ {= \mathbb{T} \smallsetminus \left\{ {S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i \geq 0.\, leftBlinker\, \notin \, S_{i}\, and\, steeringGt~0.2 \in S_{i}} \right\}} \\ \end{array}$$

(semantics for atomic proposition)

As claimed in Example 22, the semantics of this formula can be described as the set of traces such that there is no time in the future where the steering angle is bigger than 0.2 radians (i.e., the vehicle is turning left) and the left blinker is not on.

Furthermore, using basic set theory, this set can also be written as

{S0, Sn,... | ∀i ≥ 0. if steeringGt0.2 ∈ Si then leftBlinker ∈ Si},

which support the intuition of Example 23 that this formulation is equivalent to the fact that for all times in the future if the vehicle is turning left then it must have its left blinker on.

3.3.3.3 Semantics of Syntactic Sugar

In Section 3.3.2.3, we described shorthands for useful pieces of formulas. In this section, we unfold the inductive definition of the semantics on these constructs.

  • For the falsehood,


    〚⊥〛 = 〚¬⊤〛 = 𝕋 ∖ 〚⊤〛 = 𝕋 ∖ 𝕋 = ⌀,

    that is, its semantics is the empty set, meaning that no traces satisfy the falsehood.

  • For the disjunction,


    〚φ ∨ ψ〛 = 〚¬(¬φ ∧ ¬ψ)〛 = 𝕋 ∖ ((𝕋 ∖ 〚φ〛)∩(𝕋 ∖ 〚ψ〛 = 〚φ〛∪〚ψ〛,

    that is, the semantics of the disjunction is the union of the semantics.

  • For the implication,


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚\left. \varphi\rightarrow\psi \right.〛} = {〚{\psi \land \text{¬}\varphi)}〛} = {〚\psi〛} \cup \left( {\mathbb{T} \smallsetminus {〚\psi〛}} \right)} \\ {= \left\{ S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid if\, S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \in {〚\varphi〛}, \right.} \\ {\left. then\,\, S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \in \,{〚\psi〛} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • For the finally,


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\lozenge\,\varphi}〛} = {〚{\top\, U\varphi\,}〛}} \\ {= \left\{ S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i\, \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in {〚\varphi〛}\, and \right.} \\ \left. {\forall 0 \leq k < i.S_{k},S_{k + 1},\ldots \in {〚\top〛}} \right\} \\ {\left\{ S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i\, \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in {〚\varphi〛}\, \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • For the globally,


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\square\,\varphi}〛} = {〚{\neg\,▱\neg\varphi\,}〛}} \\ {= T\backslash\left\{ {S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \exists i\, \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in {〚\varphi〛}} \right\}\,} \\ {\left\{ S_{0},\ldots,S_{n},\ldots \mid \forall i\, \geq 0.S_{i},S_{i + 1},\ldots \in {〚\varphi〛}\, \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Example 25 In Example 23, we argued that formula (3.5) is a shorthand for formula (3.4). Unfolding the semantics of the syntactic sugar, we obtain that the semantics of the former is

{S0, . . . , Sn, . . . | ∀i ≥ 0. if steeringGt0.2 ∈ S then leftBlinker ∈ Si}.

As said in Example 24, this is an equivalent formulation of the semantics of formula (3.4). Consequently, both formulas represent the same property.

3.3.4 Tools

Recall from Section 3.3.3.1 that the model-checking problem is, for a given system S and specification φ, to decide whether 〚S〛 ⊆ 〚φ〛, i.e., whether all execution traces produced by S satisfy φ.

A strong point of LTL is that the model-checking problem is decidable for a large class of systems. Standard algorithms can be derived using automata-theoretic approaches: an LTL formula can effectively be described by an automaton (precisely, by a Büchi automaton), in the sense that the set of traces composing the semantics of an LTL formula can be recognised by such an automaton. Consequently, whenever a system can also be described by such an automaton, the model-checking problem is decidable by checking trace inclusion of Büchi automata. This decidability is used in several tools that we introduce here.

3.3.4.1 Spin

Spin [13] is an open-source verification tool originally developed by the NOKIA Bell Labs. Its target is the study of multi-threaded software, described in a high level language called PROMELA. It can check deadlocks, race conditions, as well as any correctness properties expressed in LTL, and is particularly adapted to basic safety and liveness. This tool has been successfully used in domain such as telecommunications, space missions, automobile industry, and medical devices.

3.3.4.2 Spot

Spot is a C++ library for the model-checking problem of LTL and automata-theoretic manipulations developed at EPITA. Its main purpose is to enrich the class of systems that can be dealt with. It also comes with Python bindings, such as Jupyter, which makes it a good candidate as an introductory tool to modelchecking.

3.3.4.3 NuSMV

NuSMV is an open-source symbolic model-checker jointly developed by FBK- IRST, Carnegie Mellon, Genova, and Trento Universities. This tool has been used as a cornerstone for several academic and industrial projects, including static analysers, a tool-kit for human-machine interfaces, and a language for embedded software engineering.

3.3.5 References

The literature on LTL is rich, as it is the base of formal verification. The textbooks [5, 11, 14] provide an exhaustive and accessible overview of it. The original work by Pnueli can be found in [19]. In the coming section, we will introduce a continuous-time extension of LTL, but the logic can be extended in many directions. To go further, one can check [7] (branching extension), [17] (extension with fixpoint operators), [12] (probabilistic extension), and [6] (parametric extension) for example.

3.4 Signal Temporal Logic

Building on the section on LTL, we define signal temporal logic (STL), study its properties, and illustrate its usefulness on examples. In Section 3.4.2 we define STL’s syntax, in Section 3.4.3 its boolean semantics, and in Section 3.4.4 its robust semantics. Finally, Section 3.4.5 is dedicated to existing tools that use STL and Section 3.4.6 to references.

3.4.1 Introduction to Signal Temporal Logic

STL is inspired by LTL, but with two significant differences: it aims at modelling systems that evolve both in continuous time and in some continuous space. Properties of these systems are harder to prove, since continuous spaces are typically harder to handle than discrete ones. Notably, the model-checking problem, which is decidable for LTL, is undecidable for STL. On the other hand, the continuous nature of space allows us to define a quantitative (or robust) semantics, which proves helpful to solve other problems, such as falsification, explained in detail in Chapter 1.

Our first goal in this section is to familiarise the reader with specifications written in STL, so that they can understand written specifications and come up with their own. Our second goal is for the reader to understand the notion of robust semantics, which is the main addition compared to LTL, and how it can be helpful in quantising “how much” a signal satisfies a formula.

3.4.2 Syntax

We define STL’s syntax and commonly used syntactic sugar constructs, mainly emphasising the differences with LTL.

3.4.2.1 Grammar

Definition 3.6 (STL syntax) The set of STL formulas is generated by the following grammar:

(3.6)
φ::=f(x1,…,xn)>0|⊤|¬φ|φ∧φ|φ𝒰Iφ,

where x1,...,xn are variables, and I is an interval of the form [a, b] or [a, + ∞) (technically, intervals of the form [a, + ∞) are not in the original syntax of STL, but we include them here for their expressiveness).

Let us note the differences with LTL, on which we will elaborate later. First, there is no next operator, which corresponds to the fact that there is no “next” instant in continuous time. Secondly, in STL, the until operator comes equipped with an interval that specifies bounds on when its subformulas have to hold. This is crucial to express timed properties of real systems, since we can specify behaviours such as “the vehicle should brake before 1s”, rather than “the vehicle should brake at some point”. Finally, propositional variables p have been replaced by comparisons of the form f(x1,...,xn) > 0. The variables x1,..., xn represent the observed values of the signals we are interested in, and f: X1 × ... × Xn → ℝ is a function that evaluates “how true” the proposition is, with positive values meaning the proposition is true and negative ones meaning it is false.

Example 26 Let us look at a few examples of atomic propositions.

As a first example, we want to define an atomic proposition that expresses whether the ego vehicle’s speed v is greater than some threshold, say 25m/ s. Obviously, we need v to be one of the variables xi, i.e., one of the variables of interest of our system, so we will assume it is the case. /n LTL, we would need to define a new atomic proposition, but here, we can simply define it as v – 25 > 0. Formally, we consider the function f1 (x1,...,xn) = v – 25 (which can be done because v ∈ {x1,..., xn}), and the corresponding atomic proposition f1(x1,..., xn) > 0. Notice that the function f1 returns a positive value exactly when the speed is above the threshold, which is exactly what we wanted to model. We will see when we define syntactic sugar (Section 3.4.2.2) that this can simply be written v > 25, which is even simpler and closer to our intuition. We can do the exact same thing for discrete values, such as gears.

A powerful aspect of STL’s atomic propositions is that many important properties of systems can be encoded without having to define new atomic propositions, but simply by considering other functions. For example, let us say we are interested in whether a vehicle is not too far away from its initial position (0,0) (say at most 100m). Assuming the coordinates x and y of the vehicle are among the variables of interest {x1,...,xn}, we can use function $f_{2}\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) = 100 - \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ and consider f2(x1,..., xn) > 0.

We can also model boolean values. Say we are interested in whether the left blinker of our vehicle is on, and we have a signal leftBlinker that is mapped to 1 when the blinker is on and to 0 otherwise. We can use the function f3(x1,...,xn) = 2leftBlinker − 1 and consider the atomic proposition f3(x1,...,xn) > 0. Note that we could use the simpler function (x1xn) = leftBlinker, but when the blinker is off, f̅3(x1,..., xn) = 0, while f3(x1,..., xn) < 0. The latter property (f3(x1,..., xn) begin strictly negative) will be important when we define the robust semantics.

Example 27 Recall Example 3.4, in which we write an LTL formula stating that the vehicle should never turn left unless its left blinker is on. We can write a similar formula in STL. First, we need leftBlinker and steering to be among the propositions of interest to us, and let us assume that leftBlinker is 0 when the left blinker is off, and 1 when it is on, and steering is the steering angle. Then we can write

(3.7)
¬(⊤𝒰[0,  + ∞)((¬(2 leftBlinker −1>0))∧( steering −0.2>0))).

Note that, contrary to LTL, we do not need a specific atomic proposition to check that steering is above a given threshold, so the formula can be written more naturally.

3.4.2.2 Syntactic Sugar

STL admits similar syntactic constructs as LTL. First, we can define constructs that correspond to usual (propositional) logic: ⊥, φ ∨ ψ, and φ → ψ, which are defined exactly as in LTL. We can also define syntactic sugar for temporal operators, again as in LTL: the eventually operator ◊Iφ, defined as ⊤ UI φ, and the globally operator □Iφ, defined as ◊I ¬φ. We also use the shorthands φ U ψ for φ U[0, +∞) ψ, ◊ φ for ◊[0,+ ∞) φ and □ φ for □[0,+ ∞) φ.

We can also define the following syntactic sugar for atomic propositions: f(x1,...,xn) > λ stands for f(x1,...,xn) – λ 0, f(x1,...,xn) < 0 for – f (x1,...,xn) > 0, f (x1,...,xn) ≥ 0 for − (f (x1,...,xn) < 0), etc.

Example 28 As in the case of LTL, we can rewrite the formula (3.7) as

(3.8)
▫  (( steering >0.2)→(2 leftBlinker >1)),

making use both of STL’s intuitive syntax and of syntactic sugar.

3.4.2.3 Differences from Linear Temporal Logic

Let us come back to the differences between STL and LTL. The absence of the next operator is self-explanatory, as there is no “next” instant in continuous time.

Equipping the until operator with an interval gives us more expressivity than LTL’s until operator. A similar operator can be encoded in LTL by


$$\begin{matrix} {\,\varphi\mathcal{U}_{\lbrack n,m\rbrack}\psi\, \equiv \underset{i = n}{\overset{m}{\vee}}\left( {\left( {\underset{j = 0}{\overset{i - 1}{\land}}◯^{j}\varphi} \right) \land ◯^{i}\psi} \right)} \\ {\,\varphi\mathcal{U}_{\lbrack n, + \infty)}\psi\, \equiv \left( {\underset{i = 0}{\overset{n - 1}{\land}}◯^{i}\varphi} \right) \land ◯^{n}(\varphi\mathcal{U}\psi).} \\ \end{matrix}$$

The first one can be read as “At some instant i between n and m, ψ will hold, and ψ will hold at all points until then”. The second one can be read as “For the next n steps, φ will hold, and it will keep holding after that, until ψ holds”. There are however two drawbacks to these encodings. First, they cannot be written in STL so they do not have a robust semantics. Moreover, discrete time only reflects continuous time in synchronous systems (in presence of a global clock), so this encoding does not correspond to a fixed amount of time in general.

In LTL, atomic propositions are either true or false in each state. In STL, they are given by functions, which should be designed so that f (x1xn) > 0 where the proposition holds true, and f (x1xn) ≤ 0 where it does not. In general, if the zone where the proposition holds true is X, f (x1xn) can be defined as

  • the distance to X’s border if (x1,xn) is inside X,
  • minus the distance to X’s border if it is outside.

Therefore, the propositions are larger (which we think of as “more true”), the further inside X they are. Note that this is how the functions f1 and f2 are defined in Example 27.

3.4.3 Boolean Semantics

STL can be equipped with two semantics: a boolean semantics that returns whether a formula is true or false, and a robust semantics that returns “how true” the formula is. In this section, we define the first semantics, which is very close to LTL’s semantics, before we explore the robust semantics in Section 3.4.4.

3.4.3.1 Signals

Remember from Section 3.3.3.1 that the semantics of an LTL formula is a set of traces S0, . . . , Sn, . . . Similarly, the boolean semantics of an STL formula is a set of signals. Therefore, before defining any form of semantics, we need to define signals.

A signal represents what is observed from an execution of a system. A signal maps all execution times to specific values for the variables of interest (which may be position, velocity, but also control state, etc.).

Definition 3.7 (signal) If the variables we observe are x1,...,xn, a signal is a function a : {x1,..., xn} × ℝ≥0 → ℝ such that σ(xi, t) is the value of variable xi at time t.

Note that, just like for LTL, STL formulas do not work directly on systems, but rather on what is observed of a system execution. This is a useful feature when studying complex systems, since it means that we can apply STL to blackbox systems too.

One difficulty when working with signals in continuous time is to know their values at all points in time. Input signals are usually defined by the user, so they can be defined in a format that makes them finitely representable. Let us list some of the most commonly used classes of input signals:

  • piecewise constant signals, which are defined by their values at a finite number of points in time t0,tn and is constant on [ti, ti+1),
  • piecewise linear signals (sometimes called piecewise linear continuous signals), which are similarly defined by their values at t0,..., tn and is linear on [ti, ti+1), in such a way that the whole signal is continuous,
  • more generally, piecewise polynomial signals (called splines), with constraints on smoothness at time points ti.

Example signals from these three classes are illustrated in Fig. 3.1.

On the other hand, output signals do not belong to a class of signals fixed in advance. Still, in practice, output signals are sampled and their values interpolated as if they belonged to one of these classes (for example piecewise linear). While this is enough for most applications in practice, it is inherently limited, as it can give both false positives and false negatives.

3.4.3.2 Definition

While we could define the boolean semantics of an STL formula as a set of signals (like the semantics of LTL), we choose to define it as a function that takes a signal and returns a boolean. This is completely equivalent: given a set X, the corresponding function returns ⊤ on x if and only x is in X. Moreover, this approach will be more natural when we introduce the robust semantics later.

The boolean semantics of an STL formula φ is a function that takes a signal σ and answers whether σ satisfies φ.

Definition 3.8 (STL boolean semantics) STL’s boolean semantics is a function 〚—〛 that takes as input an STL formula φ and a signal σ, and returns a boolean 〚φ〛 (σ) ∈ {⊤, ⊥}. It is defined inductively as follows:


$$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) > 0}〛}(\sigma) = \begin{cases} \top & {~if~f\left( {\sigma\left( {x_{1},0} \right),\ldots,\sigma\left( {x_{n},0} \right)} \right) > 0} \\ \bot & {~otherwise~} \\ \end{cases}} \\ {{〚\top〛}(\sigma) = \top} \\ {{〚{\text{¬}\varphi}〛}(\sigma) = \text{¬}{〚\varphi〛}(\sigma)} \\ {{〚{\varphi \land \psi}〛}(\sigma) = {〚\varphi〛}(\sigma) \land {〚\psi〛}(\sigma)} \\ {\left. {{〚{\varphi\mathcal{U}_{I}\psi}〛}(\sigma) = \underset{t^{\prime} \in I}{\vee}\left( {\left( \underset{t^{''} \in t^{\prime}}{\land} \right){〚\varphi〛}\left( \sigma \middle| t^{''} \right)} \right) \land {〚\psi〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime}} \right)} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$

where σ|t is the signal σ shifted by t defined as σ|t (xi, t') = σ(xi, t + t′).

The definition of the semantics uses operators on booleans, which is the set {⊤, ⊥} ordered ⊥ < ⊤. The first operator is ∨ (the logical or operator) which takes the maximum of its arguments, and the second one is ∧ (the logical and operator) which takes the minimum of its arguments. The first operator generalises to ∨x∈Xbx, which takes the maximum of all bx’s (for all x in X). Similarly, the second operator generalises to ∧x∈Xbx, which takes the minimum of all bx's (for all x in X).

This is very similar to LTL, so we only emphasise the differences. First, for atomic propositions, we use the signal values at time t = 0 (rather than fixed atomic propositions for each state) to compute the value of f and check whether this value is positive. For example, if f(x1,...,xn) = v − 50 is supposed to represent whether the vehicle speed is above 50m/s, then 〚f (x1,...,xn) > 0〛 (σ) is ⊤ if and only if σ(v, 0) > 50, i.e., if the initial value of v for signal σ is greater than 50. In essence, this is the same as LTL, but using signal values instead of atomic propositions linked to states.

Secondly, the semantics for the until operator is different, due to the continuous nature of time, and the fact that until is bounded in STL. In order for the semantics 〚φ U ψ〛 to hold, there must exist a time t′ ∈ I where ψ holds, and φ must hold at all time instants until t′. Again, this is in essence the same as the semantics of until in LTL, except for boundedness.

3.4.3.3 Boolean Semantics of Syntactic Sugar

Let us compute the boolean semantics of the different syntactic sugar constructions.

  • For propositional constructs, such as φ ∨ ψ and φ → ψ, this is computed as in the case of LTL, and we get


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\varphi \land \psi}〛}(\sigma) = \left( {{〚\varphi〛}(\sigma) \land {〚\psi〛}(\sigma)} \right)} \\ {{〚\left. \varphi\rightarrow\psi \right.〛}(\sigma) = \left( {〚\varphi〛}(\sigma)\rightarrow{〚\psi〛}(\sigma) \right),} \\ \end{array}$$

    where, on the right-hand sides of the equations above, ∨ and → are operators on booleans (with b → b′ defined as ¬b ∨ b′),

  • for f (x1,...,xn) > λ, we have


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) > 0}〛}(\sigma) = {〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) - \lambda > 0}〛}\left( \sigma \right)} \\ {= \begin{cases} \top & {~if~f\left( {\sigma\left( {x_{1},0} \right),\ldots,\sigma\left( {x_{n},0} \right)} \right) - \lambda > 0} \\ \bot & {~otherwise~} \\ \end{cases}} \\ {= \begin{cases} \top & {~if~f\left( {\sigma\left( {x_{1},0} \right),\ldots,\sigma\left( {x_{n},0} \right)} \right) > \lambda} \\ \bot & {~otherwise,~} \\ \end{cases}} \\ \end{array}$$

    which means that f (x1 ,..., xn) > λ holds for some signal σ if f applied to the value of σ at time t = 0 is greater than λ, which is indeed the intended meaning,

  • for f (x1 ,..., xn) < 0, f (x1 ,..., xn) ≥ 0, etc., we get the intended semantics by a similar computation,

  • for ◊I φ, we have


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\diamond_{I}\varphi}〛}(\sigma) = {〚{\top\mathcal{U}_{I}\varphi}〛}(\sigma) = \underset{t \in I}{\vee}\left( {\underset{t^{\prime} < t}{\land}{〚\top〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime}} \right) \land {〚\varphi〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right)} \\ {= \underset{t \in I}{\vee}\left( {{〚\varphi〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right)~(because~{〚\top〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime}} \right) = \top~for\ any~t^{\prime}),} \\ \end{array}$$

    which means that ◊I/ φ holds for σ at time t = 0 if φ holds for σ|t (or equivalently that φ holds for σ at time t) for some t in I, which is the intended semantics,

  • for □I φ, we have


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\square_{I}\varphi}〛}(\sigma) = {〚{\neg \diamond_{I}\neg\varphi}〛}(\sigma) = \neg{〚{\diamond_{I}\neg\varphi}〛}\left( \sigma \right) = \neg\underset{t \in I}{\vee}\left( {{〚{\neg\varphi}〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right)} \\ {= \neg\underset{t \in I}{\vee}{〚{\neg\varphi}〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right) = \underset{t \in I}{\land}\left( {{〚\varphi〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$

    which is also the intended semantics.

Example 29 Let us compute the boolean semantics of formula (28) on some given signals. Let us assume that the signal for steering and leftBlinker is as shown in Fig. 3.2. If we call this signal σ, then for example σ (steering, 6) = 0.2 and σ (leftBlinker, 6) = 0. We adapt the formula to finite signals by changing □ to □[0,20] and compute its boolean semantics as follows:


$$\begin{array}{l} {{〚\left. \square_{\lbrack 0,20\rbrack}(~steering~ > 0.2)\rightarrow 2~leftBlinker~ > 1 \right.〛}(\sigma)} \\ \begin{array}{l} {= \underset{t \in \lbrack 0,20\rbrack}{\land}\left( {\left. {\text{¬}\left( {\left. \sigma \right|_{t}(~steering~,0) > 0.2} \right) \vee 2\sigma} \right|_{t}(~leftBlinker,~0) > 1} \right)} \\ {= \underset{t \in \lbrack 0,20\rbrack}{\land}(\text{¬}(\sigma(~steering~,t) > 0.2) \vee 2\sigma(~leftBlinker~,t) > 1)} \\ {= \underset{t \in \lbrack 4,12\rbrack \cup^{}\lbrack 18,20\rbrack}{\land}\text{¬}(\sigma(~steering~,t) > 0.2)} \\ {= \bot,} \\ \end{array} \\ \end{array}$$

where the first step is by inductive definition and the second one by definition of σ|t. The last two steps are where the semantics is computed, which is done by considering each t in [0,20] separately.

  • In the third step, we take the value of σ (leftBlinker, t ) into account: if t is in [0,4] or [12, 18], then a (leftBlinker, t ) = 1, so 2σ (leftBlinker, t ) = 2 > 1, and the disjunct is true. For other values oft, a (leftBlinker, t ) = 0, so 2σ (leftBlinker, t ) = 0 ≮ 1, and the disjunct is true if and only if the other branch is.
  • In the fourth step, we take the value of σ (steering, t ) into account: ift is in [0,6] or in [13, 20], then σ (steering, t ) ≤ 0.2, so ¬(σ (steering, t ) > 0.2) is true, and so is the disjunct. However this fails for other values oft. For example, if t = 9, then σ (steering, 9) = 0.3 > 0.2, so the negation is false. Therefore, the semantics of the whole formula is false.

3.4.4 Robust Semantics

In this section, we first motivate the definition of a robust semantics of STL (Section 3.4.4.1) before defining it (Section 3.4.4.2) and mentioning some challenges in its design (Section 3.4.4.3).

3.4.4.1 Qualitative and Quantitative Semantics

The boolean semantics defined in the previous section tells us whether a specification holds or not, which is necessary for basically any application. However, we may sometimes want to know more than just whether a specification holds. For example, in falsification, in order to efficiently search for counterexamples to some specification, it is necessary to know which signals look “more promising” for the search, that is, which signals are “closer” to not satisfying the specification. STL’s robust semantics is a quantitative semantics that can be used for this purpose. That is, unlike a qualitative semantics that answers either true or false, evaluating the robust semantics of a signal yields a number that evaluates “how true” the specification is.

Since STL’s boolean semantics is on signals that have real values (rather than boolean ones, as in the case of LTL), we can use these values to give a quantitative semantics: if our specification is for a certain quantity x to be positive at time t, then a signal σ such that σ (x, t) = 100 is said to be more robust than one such that σ (x, t) = 0.01, even though they both satisfy the specification.

Formally, the robust semantics is a function 〚—〛r (or simply 〚—〛 if there is no ambiguity with the boolean semantics) that takes an STL formula φ and a signal σ, and returns a real number 〚φ〛r(σ) that can be interpreted as follows:

  • if 〚φ〛r(σ) > 0, then σ satisfies φ; the bigger 〚φ〛r(σ) is, the further σ is from violating φ, and the smaller it is, the closer σ is to violating φ,
  • conversely, if 〚φ〛r(σ) < 0, then σ does not satisfy φ; the smaller 〚φ〛r(σ) is (i.e., the bigger it is in absolute value), the further σ is from satisfying φ, and the bigger it is, the closer σ is to satisfying φ,
  • finally, if 〚φ〛r(σ) = 0, nothing can be said about whether σ satisfies φ, but it is infinitely close to both satisfying and violating it.

3.4.4.2 Definition

The robust semantics of STL is defined as follows:

Definition 3.9 (STL robust semantics) STL’s robust semantics is a function 〚—〛r that takes as input an STL formula φ and a signal σ, and returns a real number 〚φ〛r(σ) ∈ ℝ (or an extended real, that is a value in ℝ ∪ {+ ∞, − ∞}). It is defined inductively as


$$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) > 0}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = f\left( {\sigma\left( {x_{1},0} \right),\ldots,\sigma\left( {x_{n},0} \right)} \right)} \\ {{〚\top〛}_{r}(\sigma) = v} \\ {{〚{\text{¬}\varphi}〛}(\sigma) = - {〚{\text{¬}\varphi}〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \\ {{〚{\varphi \land \psi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = \min\left( {\,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}(\sigma),\,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \right)} \\ {{〚{\varphi\mathcal{U}_{I}\psi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = \sup\limits_{t^{\prime} \in I}\,\min\left( {\left( {\,\inf\limits_{t^{\prime\prime} < t^{\prime}}{〚\varphi〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime\prime}} \right)\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime\prime}} \right)} \right),\,\,{〚\psi〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime}} \right)} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$

where v > 0 is some arbitrary threshold decided in advance (in the rest of this section, we consider v = + ∞ in the computations).

These formulas use the notions of suprema and infima. Readers who are unfamiliar with these notions can think of them as maxima and minima respectively.

This is just a quantitative version of the boolean semantics from the previous section. This is obvious for atomic propositions, since 〚φ〛(σ) can be defined as 〚φ〛r(σ) > 0, which respects the intuition that truth corresponds to the robust semantics being positive. The same is true for ⊤. For φ ∧ ψ and φ UI ψ, notice that the formulas for robust semantics are the same as those for boolean semantics, where conjunction has been replaced with minimum and disjunction with maximum. This also reflects intuition, since

  • x and y are both positive exactly when min(x, y) is,
  • at least one of x and y is positive exactly when max(x, y) is.

Using this remark, we get a correspondence between the boolean semantics and the robust one.

Lemma 3.1

For all formulas φ and signals σ,

  • if 〚φ〛r(σ) > 0, then 〚φ〛 (σ) = ⊤,
  • if 〚φ〛r(σ) < 0, then 〚φ〛 (σ) = ⊥

Note that this lemma does not tell us anything if 〚φ〛r(σ) = 0, in which case 〚φ〛(σ) may either be ⊤ or ⊥ (but this rarely happens in practice when computing the robust semantics of physical systems).

We can also compute the robust semantics of the different syntactic sugar constructions.

  • For disjunction, the semantics is computed as follows:


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\varphi \land \psi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = {〚{\neg\left( {\neg\varphi \land \neg\psi} \right)}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = \min\left( {\,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}(\sigma), - \,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \right)} \\ {= \max\left( {\,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}(\sigma), - \,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$

    Similarly, for implication, we get


    〚φ ∧ ψ〛r(σ) = 〚¬φ ∧ ¬ψ〛r(σ) = max ( 〚φ〛r(σ),− 〚ψ〛r(σ)).

  • For f (x1,...,xn) > λ, we have


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) > \lambda}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = {〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) - \lambda > 0}〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \\ {= f\left( {\sigma\left( {x_{1},0} \right),\ldots,\sigma\left( {x_{n},0} \right)} \right) - \lambda.} \\ \end{array}$$

    We get similar expressions for f (x1,..., xn) < 0, f (x1,..., xn) ≥ 0, etc.

  • For ◊I φ, we have


    $$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\diamond_{I}\varphi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = {〚{\top\mathcal{U}_{I}\varphi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = \sup\limits_{t \in I}\,\left( {\min\left( {\inf\limits_{t^{\prime} < t}{〚\top〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime}} \right),{〚\varphi〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right)} \right)} \\ {= \sup\limits_{t \in I}\,\left( {{〚\varphi〛}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right)~because~{〚\top〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t^{\prime}} \right) = + \infty~for\ any~t^{\prime}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • For □I φ, we have


    $${〚{\square_{I}\varphi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = {〚{\neg \diamond_{I}\neg\varphi}〛}_{r}(\sigma) = \sup\limits_{t \in I}\,{〚\varphi〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right) = \inf\limits_{t \in I}\,\left( {{〚\varphi〛}_{r}\left( \left. \sigma \right|_{t} \right)} \right).$$

Example 30 Let us compute the robust semantics of the formula of Example 28 on the signals of Example 29.


$$\begin{array}{l} {{〚\left. \square_{\lbrack 0,20\rbrack}~(steering~ > 0.2\,\,\rightarrow 2~leftBlinker~ > 1 \right.〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \\ {= \inf\limits_{t \in \lbrack 0,20\rbrack}\max\left( {- \left( {\left. \sigma \right|_{t}(~steering~,0) - 0.2} \right),\left. {2\sigma} \right|_{t}(~leftBlinker,~0) - 1} \right)} \\ {= \inf\limits_{t \in \lbrack 0,20\rbrack}\max(0.2 - \sigma(~steering~,t),2\sigma(~leftBlinker~,t) - 1).} \\ \end{array}$$

This expression only depends on the values of the signals, and can be computed easily. In this particular case, we get that the infimum is reached att = 9, where the robust semantics is −0.1, which implies that the boolean semantics is false by Lemma 3.1.

We invite the reader to compute the robust semantics for other signals and check that the robust semantics behaves as intended: signals that are “further away” from matching the specification (in this case, where the value of steering is always larger, and that of leftBlinker always smaller than those in this example) have a smaller robust semantics, and those that are “closer" to it have a larger robust semantics, until it becomes larger than 0, in which case the boolean semantics becomes true.

3.4.4.3 Challenges

Let us discuss a few challenges that arise in the definition of STL’s robust semantics that the reader may encounter in practice. First, while there is a way to define equality of values in STL’s syntax as (f(x1,...,xn) ≥ λ) ∧ (f(x1,...,xn) ≤ λ), its robust semantics can never be positive:


$$\begin{array}{l} {{〚{\left( {f\left( {x_{1},. \mid ,x_{n}} \right) \geq \lambda} \right) \land \left( {f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) \leq \lambda} \right)}〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \\ {= \min\left( {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) \geq \lambda}〛}_{r}(\sigma),{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right) \leq \lambda}〛}_{r}(\sigma)} \right)} \\ {= \min\left( {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right)}〛}_{r} - \lambda, - \left( {{〚{f\left( {x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}} \right)}〛}_{r} - \lambda} \right)} \right)\,\, \leq 0.} \\ \end{array}$$

Therefore, in practice, instead of writing equalities, one should rather specify a small error margin ε and specify the two values are not more than ε apart, as f(x1,..., xn) ≥ λ – ε ) ∧ f(x1,..., xn) ≥ λ + ε).

Secondly, the variables involved in a formula may have different scales, which makes some variables more influential in the computation of the robust semantics. For example, consider the formula φ = (x > 1000) ∨ (v < 10), where x (measured in meters) can grow up to thousands, while v (measured in meters by second) can grow up to a few dozens. Its robust semantics is 〚φ〛r = max(x − 1000, v − 10), and x − 1000 can grow up to thousands, while v − 10 can only grow up to a few dozens. Therefore, v − 10 is nearly never the maximal term, which may cause troubles for some algorithms. A particular case is when one of the variables is discrete or ⊤ appears in the formula (usually in ◊ or □), then the robust semantics can be “blocked” at some fixed value, which is known as the threshold problem. The robust semantics may have two forms:

  • min(v, f (x1, …, xn)) for some threshold v, in which case the threshold has to be greater than other values for the robust semantics not to be constant (otherwise optimisation algorithms cannot perform well),
  • max(v, f (x1, …, xn)), in which case v has to be smaller than other quantities for the same reasons.

Therefore, it is advised to use threshold values for truth and discrete variables that have the same order of magnitude as other quantities used in the formula. (See Chapter 1 for other methods that deal with a similar problem, called the scale problem.)

3.4.5 Tools

We list some tools that make use of STL. One of the strong points of having a robust semantics (rather than a boolean one) is that it is a function into the reals, which can thus be optimised. That is the principle of falsification (elaborated upon in Chapter 1), whose goal is to find a counter-example to some property φ by finding a control signal σ that minimises 〚φ〛r (σ): if 〚φ〛r (σ) < 0, then σ is a counter-example. Some of the tools listed here are falsification tools.

3.4.5.1 STLInspector

STLInspector is a tool to check STL specifications. The user specifies an informal specification in natural language and an STL formula that they think reflects the specification. The tool then automatically generates signals using mutation testing and asks whether they satisfy the intended specification. If at least one signal is wrongly classified by the user, then they can rework their STL specification. If all signals are classified correctly, then the user can have some confidence that their specification is correct (although it does not guarantee that the formal specification corresponds to the informal one).

3.4.5.2 S-TaLiRo

S-TaLiRo is a Matlab toolbox for falsification. The user provides a description of the system, either as a Simulink / Stateflow diagram, or as a user-defined function. They also provide a specification, in the form of an metric temporal logic (MTL) formula. MTL is a simpler version of STL, where atomic propositions return a boolean, rather than a real. The tool then tries to find system inputs that minimise the robust semantics of the specification using stochastic optimisation algorithms, such as Monte-Carlo methods or ant colony optimisation. See Chapter 1 for further description of the tool.

3.4.5.3 python-monitors

This is a python package that monitors STL specifications, as well as properties expressed in other formalisms (for example regular expressions). It works on discrete sequences (like LTL), rather than in continuous time (like STL). Given a signal σ and a specification φ, monitoring is the problem of knowing for which times t, 〚φ〛(σ|t) is true (this problem is discussed in more details in Chapter 2). The user provides a discrete sequence of atomic propositions (for example given by some system execution) and a specification to monitor, and the tool returns the set of times at which the specification holds.

Several monitoring algorithms are discussed in Chapter 2. The form of specifications these algorithms accept are timed automata, which STL formulas translate to.

3.4.5.4 Breach

Breach is a Matlab toolbox that can serve multiple purposes: writing informal requirements as formal specifications, monitoring temporal properties, and generating tests. For the latter, if the system is given as a Simulink model, then the tool can use falsification to generate inputs with low robust semantics, in order to find counter-examples to the specification. See Chapter 1 for further description of the tool.

3.4.6 Conclusion

Logics of real-time systems have been studied for decades, see [3] for a survey. Apart from LTL, STL was inspired by a few logics, notably MTL [16] and metric interval temporal logic (MITL) [2]. STL itself was introduced in [18]. The idea of robust semantics was first introduced in [10] for MITL, and later adapted to STL. STL is a relatively specific topic, and there are no general textbooks or surveys about it. However, [15] is a general survey of methods used in cyberphysical system (CPS) development, and it contains a part on STL. The interested reader can also look at extensions of STL, such as a parametric extension [4], or an extension with frequency analysis [9]. Moreover, the robust semantics we introduced in this section is the most standard, but not necessarily the best-suited for every purpose, for example [8] defines a robust semantics that takes time into account, while [1] extends the expressivity of STL to give a robust semantics that takes both space and time into account.
