Chapter 4 Testing for Machine Learning-Based Systems

Xiao-Yi Zhang

University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, China

Fuyuki Ishikawa

National Institute of Informatics, The University of Electro-Communications and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

Paolo Arcaini

National Institute of Informatics, Tokyo, Japan

4.1 Introduction

Testing is an “activity in which a system or component is executed under specified conditions, the results are observed or recorded, and an evaluation is made of some aspect of the system or component” (defined in ISO/IEC/IEEE 26153). Testing has been one of the key activities for quality assurance in software-intensive systems.

The recent advance of machine learning (ML) techniques, especially deep learning, has led to active investigation towards their industrial applications. Beforehand, ML techniques were target of laboratory research and the primary concern was on the prediction performance. As the prediction performance has evolved rapidly, increasing demand is put more on the dependability and quality of the ML applications.

With the aforementioned trend, it is natural to see increasing attention on testing for ML components and systems [13, 20]. We here refer to ML components/systems as those that were constructed with ML techniques to provide prediction functions. In the ML terminology, such components are called models that reflect mathematical relations between inputs and outputs. Examples of such functions include detection of pedestrian in images obtained by car cameras. On the other hand, ML components have different characteristics from traditional software components (programs) as their behaviors are inductively derived from training data, not by direct human design. This point is especially critical when we use deep neural networks that consist of millions or more parameters and the behavior is too complex to interpret.

This chapter describes the key principles in testing of ML components and ML-based systems. We first focus on difference from testing traditional programs. We then introduce how automated testing techniques have evolved starting from techniques for traditional programs.

4.2 Preliminary: Machine Learning and Deep Neural Networks

Machine learning (ML) refers to techniques to build functionality of prediction by experience or data. The current trend from late 2010s for applications of ML techniques primarily focuses on supervised learning. In supervised learning, training data is given that contains input-output pairs so that the relationship between them can be learnt via training. Practical application of supervised learning has been actively investigated as its role is often clear: supervised learning allows to build software components by deriving their behaviors from training data even if we cannot rigorously specify the behaviors.

Other types of ML techniques include unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. Unsupervised learning allows for extracting mathematical relations from given data. An example of unsupervised learning techniques is clustering, which divides the given data into multiple clusters by some similarity metric. Unsupervised learning is considered as data analysis activities rather than software system development. Reinforcement learning allows us to build agents that take proper actions in an evolving environment. Here what is learnt is the value of each action in each state or what action should be taken in each state. Although there have been active efforts on reinforcement learning, it is still in an early stage before discussing practical testing activities or quality assurance in industrial use.

In this chapter, we use the term ML to refer to supervised learning and focus on testing activities of components (models) constructed by supervised learning and systems including such components.

We illustrate the use of ML techniques, i.e., supervised learning, in Fig. 4.1. The mathematical structures to capture the prediction functionality are called models. In a simple case, models can have the form of y = ax+b to predict y from the input value of x. Values of the parameters a,b are derived through the training process: typically to minimize the mean prediction error to the given points in the training data. We sometimes distinguish the models whose parameter values are determined as trained models. The model is represented as a program object and integrated into the whole system.

This use of the term model is different from that for software engineering where we consider human-designed models to capture the essence of the target system at different abstraction levels. In this chapter, we explicitly use the word ML components as the same meaning as trained models in the ML context.

There are many different models, together with the learning mechanisms. The previous example of y = ax + b, called linear regression, was simplistic. More sophisticated model structures are often used such as Support Vector Machine and Random Forest to capture more complex relationships.

The trend on ML was driven by technical advance in Deep Learning. Deep Learning uses the model structure called Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Fig. 4.2 illustrates the structure. A DNN contains multiple layers and each layer consists of multiple neurons as shown in the left side of the figure. Each neuron collects output values from the neurons x i,1, x i,2, ··· in the previous i-th layer. Then, the output values are aggregated by using weight parameters w i and the result is passed to an activation function

4.3 Testing of ML Components: Viewpoint from Prediction Performance and Data

4.3.1 Foundation for Quality Evaluation of ML Components

The baseline for quality evaluation of ML components is to measure the prediction performance by using metrics such as accuracy. Specifically, we prepare a test dataset, which must be independent of training data so that we can evaluate the generalization ability. The test dataset contains input-output pairs and we compare the output from the ML component under test for each input with the expected output.

Let us consider the case of anomaly detection for products in a factory by using images from cameras. The input-output pair consists of a camera image and a binary label that tells us whether the product has anomaly or not (positive or negative). This example thus is a binary classification task.

Suppose we had 500 of test input-output pairs and the ML component could make correct outputs for 465 of them. The det ailed counts were shown below.

ML Output Positive (total 45) Negative (total 455)
Positive in ground truth (total 20) 15 5
Negative in ground truth (total 480) 30 450

Then, we say the accuracy is (15 + 450)/500 = 93% by counting the correct outputs, i.e., true-positive and true-negative cases. We usually want to investigate more detail of the performance by distinguishing wrong detection (false-positive, 30 cases) and oversight (false-negative, 5 cases). Specifically, first we count the number of outputs correctly said as positive (anomaly) among all the outputs of positive. This metric is called precision: 15/45 = 33%. Second, we count the number of outputs correctly said as positive (anomaly) among all the really positive products. This metric is called recall: 15/20 = 75%. It depends on the stakeholders which metrics are significant while there is trade-off between precision and recall. A typical way of thinking is to put higher priority in recall so that possibly anomaly products are reported with little oversight and then human experts can check false-positives or non-anomaly products.

We will not introduce many other essential concepts in evaluation of ML components such as overfitting and ROC curve, or evaluation criteria for other types of tasks, e.g., regression tasks to predict continuous output values. Foundation of machine learning can be found in books such as [10].

What should be noted here is that in this way the performance evaluation is relative to the test dataset. It is essential to explicitly argue what are included or not in the 500 images of the test dataset. For example, do we cover different anomaly patterns expected to appear in the operation? Are the photographic conditions unified or diverse as expected in the operation such as camera position and lighting? The validity and impact of evaluation thus depends on the data quality.

4.3.2 Quality Guidelines

As practical application of ML systems is intensively investigated, more focus has been put on quality or dependability of such systems. In Japan, two guidelines called QA4AI [6]

Both of the guidelines clarify the targets of evaluation. QA4AI defines five targets of evaluation as data, model, system, process, and customer expectation. Data and model are the core deliverables in ML development as described in Section 4.3.1. Quality of the whole system should be argued including other components, possibly those that complement incompleteness of the ML components such as filters of improper outputs from the ML components. Process quality is significant specifically in terms of agility as ML imposes various types of uncertainty, e.g., it is impossible to precisely estimate beforehand what level of accuracy will be achieved, inputs in the operation may have an unknown different distribution from the one in training and test datasets. It is therefore significant to have agility to continuously iterate experiments and improvements. Finally, as quality investigated by the developer side should match with the customer expectation, we should explicitly evaluate it, e.g., how much the customers can accept unavoidable failures or how much the customers require assertive explanations.

AIQM defines three external quality characteristics, observable from user, as AI performance, safety, and fairness. AI performance refers to the traditional ML quality aspect shown in Section 4.3.1. Although average performance of prediction over the dataset is high as AI performance, occurrences of highly severe hazards are not accepted in some applications, e.g., automated driving. Safety deals with this aspect by evaluating the risks. Fairness refers to a lack of undesirable bias over sensitive features such as gender and race.

AIQM also defines eight internal quality characteristics handled by engineers to achieve the three external characteristics. These internal characteristics start with requirements coverage to explicitly consider case decomposition of originally fuzzy target of prediction. This is exactly the same point discussed in Section 4.3.1. Then, we can think of data design, data amount, and model performance.

In both of the guidelines, the essence lies in intensive analysis of requirements in the form of case decomposition so that we can argue the quality of data and model not only on the whole dataset but with more fine-grained viewpoints.

4.4 Focus of This Chapter

As demonstrated in QA4AI and AIQM, evaluation approaches for data and model performance have been discussed well and established to some extent. In this chapter, we further discuss application of traditional testing techniques for program code. We assume data collection based on requirements has been done to some extent but cannot be perfect due to the fuzzy nature of the target as well as the heavy cost of data collection and preprocessing such as labelling. Traditional testing techniques can enhance quality investigation by aiming at effective tests in terms of diversity or capability to discover potential problems.

4.5 Automated Testing for Traditional Programs

The ultimate goal of testing is to detect bugs (defects) effectively and efficiently and ensure quality of the target product or service. On the other hand, it is impossible to test all the possible execution scenarios or to certainly expose unknown bugs. Various testing techniques have been investigated under these limitations to efficiently reach bug-exposing scenarios or realize a certain level of completeness.

Coverage criteria in white-box testing are one representative of testing techniques. Coverage criteria allow for evaluating a test suite TS (a set of test cases) by measuring how much of the “elements” in the target program are covered by executing the test suite. For example, suppose there is a conditional branch such as if (A or B) then ... else .... In this case, we can think of coverage criteria such as:

  • Decision coverage (Branch coverage) We should prepare test cases in the test suite TS that cover both of the two branches as true and false, i.e., ∰t ∈ TS: (t ⊨ (A or B)), and ∰t ∈ TS: (t ⊨ not(A or B)).
  • Condition coverage We should prepare test cases in the test suite TS that cover different values for each of the two conditions A and B, i.e., ∰t ∈ TS: (t ⊨ A), ∰t ∈ TS: (t ⊨ not A), ∰t ∈ TS: (t ⊨ B), and ∰t E TS: (t ⊨ not B).
  • Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC) A condition value is said to be covered for MC/DC only when it makes “impact” on the decision, i.e., flipping its value also flips the value of the decision (it turns it from true to false, or from false to true); note that a condition is required to impact the decision in both directions. For example, test t = (true, true) is not useful for MC/DC, as flipping any of the two conditions does not affect the overall decision (which remains true). The test t = (true, false), instead, covers A in one direction, i.e., flipping its value makes the decision false.

By designing tests with high coverage values, we expect to detect hidden bugs by executing relevant part of the code. We also have a certain level of confidence when we don’t find any bugs after executing high-coverage tests.

We can say coverage criteria are examples of adequacy criteria that serve as the test objectives. We aim at obtaining a test suite that meets the adequacy criteria as much as possible by human design or automated test generation. In this chapter, we are specifically interested in automated input generation methods as an advanced approach to testing. By applying such methods, we generate test inputs that achieve high scores of the adequacy criteria.

The above two aspects are used to derive inputs of test cases. We also need to define the way to judge success or failure of test execution, called test oracle.

For traditional programs an enormous amount of work has been conducted for automated test generation. One line of such work is Search-based Testing described in Chapter 10. For example, EvoSuite is a tool for Java unit testing with the following characteristics [5].

  • Adequacy criteria: common coverage criteria such as statement coverage and branch coverage
  • Oracle: optional application of mutation-based search to identify assertions
  • Input generation method: metaheuristic optimization that searches for best suites by iterative improvement

Another direction of automated test generation is Concolic testing [15], which combines the concrete approach such as random input values with the symbolic approach such as use of solvers to find input values that meet a certain set of conditions.

In this chapter, we discuss testing techniques for ML components and systems with the same scheme of the three characteristics.

4.6 Challenges and Approaches in Testing of ML Components and Systems

We need to be aware of how different characteristics of ML components affect the existing principles and techniques for testing of traditional software programs. Although there have been many discussions on this point, e.g., [20], we focus on the three aspects discussed in the previous section for automated test generation.

Adequacy criteria for ML components and systems have been investigated actively as traditional code coverage criteria do not work effectively. For example in deep neural networks, there is no essential conditional branch and computation just goes straightforwardly. Instead, the results of complex, interconnected numerical computation decide the output from the component.

The oracle problem is often critical in testing of ML components and systems as in many cases they are non-testable [19]. That is, it is too costly or even impossible to prepare the expected output for every possible input value. For example, for testing image recognition model, we need to give a label to each input image, which is costly and cannot be done for many images. There is no absolutely right answer for some applications such as salary prediction. Sometimes we apply ML because we humans cannot find answers from the enormous data, e.g., book recommendations.

Finally, the input generation method may be changed according to characteristics of the target, the components or systems under test and the adequacy criteria.

We review the key studies for testing of ML components and systems though this area is still evolving at the time of writing.

4.7 Automated Testing Methods for ML Components

There have been intensive studies on automated testing for ML components, specifically, deep neural networks (DNNs). Below we review initial key studies in the evolving area.

4.7.1 Initial Studies: DeepXplore and DeepTest

DeepXplore is a key study that has invoked active investigation of testing methods for DNNs [12]. It was applied for testing of image classification models and its approach is characterized as below.

  • Adequacy criteria DeepXplore adopts a new concept called “neuron coverage”. This criterion measures how many of the neurons have been activated
  • Oracle DeepXplore adopts N-version testing, that is, use of other implementations of the same functionality. This is pseudo-oracle as different DNNs cannot always have exactly same outputs. However, use of pseudo-oracle helps identify potential problems of the target DNN.
  • Input generation method DeepXplore adopts a gradient-based search method. Input images are generated by adding perturbations to the original ones. The generation is guided by gradients to increase both of the neuron coverage and distances of outputs from the pseudo-oracles. Constraints are defined by domain knowledge to limit the perturbations so that they are not too destructive and unrealistic.

DeepXplore is said as the first whitebox-testing method for DNN for its use of neuron coverage.

DeepTest is the successor from the same research group [17]. The essential idea is similar but DeepTest adopts so-called “metamorphic testing” for the oracle. DeepTest was applied to a DNN that outputs a steering control value from an input traffic image. The output is considered “problematic” for a perturbed input image if the output is too different from the output for the original input image. We thus do not need different implementations in the case of DeepTest, or even the expected right answer for each input image. This is because we compare two outputs for two inputs rather than checking one output for one input. We will discuss this idea of metamorphic testing later in this chapter.

In the following sections, we will review other key studies that followed DeepXplore and DeepTest. Although each study has different design choices on the three aspects (and others) but we will pick up only specific part of the individual studies.

4.7.2 Input Generation Methods

We showed that DeepXplore adopts a gradient-based search method to generate input images by adding perturbations to the original ones. Below are examples of other notable approaches.

4.7.2.1 DeepRoad

Perturbed images do not essentially extend the space of input images used for testing as they only apply limit types of small changes such as scaling to the original images. The work called DeepRoad used Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to convert input images to have features of specific weather [21]. GANs learn distributions of natural images and can generate new images from the distributions. The state-of-the-art GANs also allow for specifying or transferring “styles” of images and image features for different weather conditions are transferred in the case of DeepRoad.

4.7.2.2 DeepConcolic

In testing of traditional software programs, Concolic testing has been one of key approaches for input generation [15]. Concolic testing combines the concrete approach such as random input values with the symbolic approach such as use of solvers to find input values that meet a certain set of conditions. Concolic testing thus has advantages of the two approaches: efficient computation for easy cases and targeted generation of rare or corner cases that cannot be easily reached.

The work called DeepConcolic applies the same way of thinking to input generation for DNNs [16]. Here, the symbolic approach is Linear Programming to solve optimization problems defined by different types of adequacy criteria. We will review different criteria used by DeepConcolic in the following discussion on the adequacy criteria.

4.7.3 Test Adequacy Criteria

DeepXplore defined the new concept of a neuron coverage that evaluates whether each neuron has been activated by the test suite or not. The following studies investigated such criteria in depth.

4.7.3.1 DeepGauge

DeepGauge [9] investigated more fine-grained coverage criteria for deep neural networks. The original neuron coverage only checked whether each neuron has been activated or not by the test suite execution. This is simplistic as continuous values of neuron outputs are captured in a binary way and relationships between neurons are not considered. DeepGauge defined various coverage criteria such as one about how diverse values were covered for each neuron output, e.g., how many of four output areas of [0, 0.25), [0.25, 0.5), [0.5, 0.75), [0.75, 1] were covered. Another example is which different combinations of neurons were activated in each layer (a unit including many neurons), e.g., neurons [0, 4, 10] were activated together, but [0, 1, 3] were not.

4.7.3.2 DeepConcolic

DeepConcolic [16] we described for input generation methods used different types of adequacy criteria, including the neuron coverage. Another adequacy criterion adopted by DeepConcolic is based on Lipschitz Continuity. Lipschitz Continuity intuitively says that input changes do not lead to radical output changes, which is judged by a threshold c. An adequacy criterion was defined to count how many test instances were found that prove Lipschitz Continuity does not hold for a certain value of c.

4.7.3.3 Surprise Adequacy

The key aspect of test inputs is how they differ from the distribution of training data. It is expected that the trained models (DNNs) cannot make proper inference if the inputs are far from the training data. Surprise adequacy is a adequacy criterion that tries to capture this aspect [8]. Not simply looking at the distances from training data in the input space, it tries to capture differences of neuron activations of the target DNN. It thus aims to measure differences of how the input data are perceived by the target DNN.

4.7.4 Oracle

DeepXplore used N-version testing or other implementations of the same functionality. DeepTest used metamorphic testing to check output changes are within a certain range given variations of inputs. The latter approach has been used also by many other studies as metamorphic testing only requires the definition of the checked properties (not other implementations). Below we discuss different directions to define the test oracle, that is, what are problems we want to detect.

4.7.4.1 Metamorphic Testing

As discussed in Section 4.6, it is often difficult or impossible to prepare the expected right answer for each individual test input. Metamorphic testing is a technique used for such situations [14]. Instead of checking individual outputs, we check certain relationships, called metamorphic relations (MRs) hold between two test cases. Specifically, we consider a relationship in the form “if we change the input this way, the output should change in that way”.

The simple case is shown in Fig. 4.3. Suppose we obtained output y for a certain input x with the function under test f. We apply a certain transformation Min to the input x and obtain another input xfollow and then the output yfollow = f(xfollow) as the follow-up test case. We define Min so that we can expect a relation or constraint holds between these values as a metamorphic relation and use this relation as a criterion to check the function f.

A simple example is shown for the sin function:


y=sin(x)⇒yfollow =f(xfollow )=y where xfollow =π−x

We can also have:


y=sin(x)⇒yfollow =f(xfollow )=−y where xfollow =−x

If such conditions do not hold, we can expect there is some problem, bug or sometimes other types of reasons such as misunderstanding of the specification. We can execute this pair of test cases even if we don’t have the way to calculate the right sin value for any individual input.

4.7.4.2 Fairness

There have been many other studies that focus on the oracle, or requirements specific to ML. One example of such oracle with increasing attention is fairness. As ML sometimes has large impact on organizational or social decision making, specific types of bias are not acceptable, e.g., bias based on gender or race. There are several ways to define as concrete, measurable criteria for fairness [2]. Sometimes fairness is argued by comparing individuals. For example, in salary prediction or loan approval decision, for a woman with very similar attributes (career etc.) to a certain man, the system should make similar outputs. Otherwise, the output for the woman is considered as undesirable. For such a definition of individual fairness, testing is suitable to detect undesirable cases as studied in [18].

4.8 Methods for Different Testing Targets

We have discussed active studies for testing ML components, especially DNNs. Below we discuss testing of other targets such as the whole system including ML components as well as the training pipeline to build ML components.

4.8.1 Testing of Whole System including ML Components

Some systems include many functional components other than those built with ML techniques. For example, automated driving systems may use ML only for part of the perception functionality, specifically, for image recognition on obstacle objects, signals, and lanes. In such systems, failures of ML components do not always lead to failures of the whole system. Other sensors may detect objects even if image recognition with cameras fails. Failures in recognizing objects far away from the ego-vehicle may not lead to any problem. It is therefore significant to test ML components from the viewpoint of the system-level requirements or hazards. This direction is significant also because it is an endless activity to improve ML components that cannot have 100% accuracy.

There have been studies in this direction primarily targeting automated driving systems. Below we describe two key studies in this direction.

The work in [1] considered the testing of a braking system with an ML-based perception component. Various environmental conditions are considered as the input space such as levels of snow, rain, or fog as well as road topology. Conditions that led to critical situations were discovered by the search-based approach, i.e., use of an evolutionary algorithm. Specifically, the work builds a decision tree to model how much critical situations tend to occur in what conditions.

Another work used uses formal analysis to identify positions of the preceding car such that recognition failure of the car leads to the failure of driving requirements (crash or near-crash). Then, physical conditions can be mapped to constraints on the images, e.g., the position of the preceding car, especially if we use computer-graphic images rather than natural images [3].

4.8.2 Metamorphic Testing for Various Testing Targets

Metamorphic testing described in Section 4.7.4.1 is a generic approach not limited to testing of ML components. It has been used for many applications such as mathematical computations. We can use it to test the training pipeline used for building ML components, including the training data and the code for running the training task.

The work in [4] investigated the effectiveness of metamorphic testing for training pipeline implementations. An example of the metamorphic relations is given as follows:

  1. Prepare a certain training dataset. This is the input to the training pipeline, and then a ML component is built. Finally, prediction results are also made by using the component. Suppose for example the object in image0 is judged as a dog.
  2. Then, apply a certain conversion on each image in the training dataset, such as shuffling RGB channels or rotating orthogonally. Then, this modified input is given to the training pipeline to built another ML component. The image0 is modified to image0 ′ and passed to the second ML component. Then, it is expected image0 ′ (color-shuffled or rotated object) should be judged as a dog.

We do not need to assume the object in image0 is really a dog, as we are only checking the metamorphic relation. It was reported [4] that these kinds of tests could reveal many implementation bugs experimentally embedded in the training pipeline code.

4.9 Concluding Remarks

In this chapter, we have discussed emerging techniques of automated test generation for ML components and systems. We have focused on automated input generation methods primarily for image classification tasks and discussed how the concepts for testing of programs have been evolved for ML components and systems, especially, DNNs.

On the other hand, practical effectiveness of these testing techniques is still under investigation. For example, there are several studies that checked effectiveness of the neuron coverage or similar structural coverage criteria [7].

Although more empirical studies are required, investigation on ML testing is further accelerating. We hope the content of this chapter provides readers the foundation for tackling the challenges in ML testing. We envision effective disciplines and techniques will be established soon thorough academia-industry collaboration.

Chapter 5 Safety Standards and Safety Assurance Framework for ADS

Kenji Taguchi

Underwriters Laboratories, Tokyo, Japan

Fuyuki Ishikawa

National Institute of Informatics, The University of Electro-Communications and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

Tsutomu Kobayashi

Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), Tsukuba, Japan

Ichiro Hasuo

National Institute of Informatics and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) systems greatly impact the current safety regulatory framework, including domestic/international standards and guidelines on safety critical systems such as automobiles, railways and aeroplanes. In this chapter, we will briefly explore the current safety standards and guidelines around AI/ML-related systems, especially for automated driving systems (ADS).

The chapter is organised as follows. Current safety standards and guidelines for ADS are reviewed in Section 5.1, and safety assurance for ADS based on safety cases is discussed in Section 5.2. In particular, in Section 5.2.2, we compare the safety case framework from Uber ATG [9] and the ANSI/UL 4600 [4], based on our results in [25].

5.1 Safety Standards and Guidelines for ADS

Traditional safety standards for safety critical systems focus on the functional safety of the target systems. Functional safety standards such as ISO 26262 [6] for automotive electric and electronic (E/E) systems have dealt with systematic failures and random hardware failures found in E/E systems. They also mandate the system life-cycle to reduce risks involved in those failures. However, AI/ML systems introduce unexpected behaviours that threaten those systems’ safety. In this section, we will explain some standards by ISO, ANSI/UL and an industrial consortium and discusses how they address safety issues in ADS.

5.1.1 ANSI/UL 4600

ANSI/UL 4600 [4] is a safety standard for autonomous products standardised by Underwriters Laboratories (UL). This standard has several unique characteristics compared with other safety standards. One of the main characteristics is to rely on the safety case as the primary safety assurance framework, and its use is carefully and meticulously specified in the standard. We will explain the history of the notion of safety case and its applications to ADS in later sections including Section 5.2.1. The contents of a safety assurance requirement (which is a clause in the standard) are classified into the following categories:

  • General: General description of the requirement.
  • Mandatory: More detailed description of the requirement. Addressed by the safety case. No deviation is permitted.
  • Required: Addressed by the safety case. The deviation is only permitted in some particular cases.
  • Highly Recommended: Best practices, which should be followed. May be omitted in case of low-risk items.
  • Recommended: Optional. Good practices and/or suggestions for helpful techniques.
  • Conformance Conformance measure for the requirement via self-audit and independent assessment following Chapter 17 in the standard.

The category choice for an assurance requirement depends on the evaluated level of risks. For instance, a Mandatory requirement should be faithfully followed and addressed in a safety case. On the other hand, a Recommended requirement can be omitted if the level of risk is low.

Assurance requirements stated in ANSI/UL 4600 range from Safety Case (in Chapter 5) to (Risk) Assessment (in Chapter 17).

  1. Safety Case and Arguments
  2. Risk Assessment
  3. Interaction with Humans and Road Users
  4. Autonomy Functions and Support
  5. Software and System Engineering Processes
  6. Dependability
  7. Data and Networking
  8. Verification, Validation, and Test
  9. Tool Qualification, COTS, and Legacy Components
  10. Lifecycle Concerns
  11. Maintenance
  12. Metrics and Safety Performance Indicators (SPIs)
  13. Assessment

We briefly explain Chapters 5 and 8 of ANSI/UL 4600. Chapter 5 discusses a safety case format and a style, such as the use of Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) [7], avoidance of argument defects by using a checklist of logical fallacies and the use of epistemic defeaters. It also deals with risk acceptance, such as an acceptable level of risk by acceptance criteria, and more general issues on safety management, such as safety culture throughout the development activities. Chapter 8 deals with hazards related to the pipeline (sensing, perception, planning, etc.) of autonomy functions and safety constraints, e.g., coverage of relevant environment information on the Operational Design Domain (ODD), acceptable robustness on machine learning and AI techniques. Even though this standard does not aim solely at ADS, it discusses how to map assurance requirements in the standard to ISO 26262.

5.1.2 SOTIF: ISO 21448

ISO 21448 [5] is a safety standard referred to as the Safety of Intended Functionality (SOTIF), which deals with the absence of unreasonable risk due to hazards resulting from functional insufficiencies of the intended functionality or by reasonably foreseeable misuse by persons. On the other hand, functional safety deals with the malfunctioning behaviour of the electric/electronic systems.

The basic approach of the SOTIF is to argue the system’s safety based on the scenarios which take interactions between the system and its surrounding environment into account. The scenarios are classified into the four areas in Fig. 5.1. These four areas are combinations of Known/Unknown and Hazardous/Not Hazardous in which Not hazardous scenarios represented by Areas 1 and 4 can be excluded since they do not impose any risk. The SOTIF aims to reduce the probability of scenarios in Areas 2 and 3, which would confine hazardous behaviour to an acceptable level of risk.

5.1.3 SaFAD: Safety First for Autonomous Driving

The Safety First for Autonomous Driving (SaFAD) [2] is an industrial consortium-based guideline for safety principles, design methods, validation, and verification of ADS. The design focuses on Fail-Safe (FS) capabilities (e.g., FS-1: Determine the location, which uses perception information from the environment, map data and motion data of an ego vehicle to ensure that the automated driving systems operate within ODD) and Fail-Degraded (FD) capabilities (e.g., FD-3: Detect when degraded performance is not available, which continuously check the availability of the degraded mode), and lists the following twelve principles for the development for ADS.

  • Safe Operation (Degradation and fail-operation)
  • Operational Design Domain (ODD determination)
  • Vehicle Operator-Initiated Handover (Interaction for engaging and disengaging)
  • Security (Protection from security threats)
  • User Responsibility (Clarification of driver’s responsibility)
  • Vehicle-Initiated Handover (Minimal risk condition, takeover requests)
  • Interdependency between the Vehicle Operator and the ADS (Fail-operation)
  • Safety Assessment (V&V to ensure that the safety goals are met)
  • Data Recording (Recording the relevant data and compliance with data privacy laws)
  • Passive Safety (Crash scenarios)
  • Behavior in Traffic (Manners on the road)
  • Safe Layer (Recognition of system limits)

The essence of the safety design is represented by how Fail-Safe and Fail-Degrade capabilities are mapped to the logical architecture of ADS. A case study demonstrates how this architecture works.

SaFAD proposes a lifecycle and an assurance pipeline to collect safety (assurance) artefacts to build the safety case for DNN (Deep Neural Net). See Fig. 5.2.

SaFAD was issued as ISO TR 4804 [20] and is further developed as a new ISO standard ISO/AWI TS 5083 [19].

5.2 Safety Assurance for ADS

How safe is safe enough? is the perennial question we ask about the safety of ADS. We are now witnessing a new technology trend where safety cases are being adopted as the primary safety assurance framework for ADS. We will explain its historical background, related research projects, and an experimental conformance evaluation of a safety case for ADS by Uber ATG (currently Aurora Innovation).

5.2.1 Safety Case for ADS

The safety case concept was introduced after the Piper Alpha (an offshore oil platform in the North Sea) incident occurred in 1988. It killed 167 people and cost approximately 1.8 billion pounds in financial losses. The incident report by Lord Cullen [13] emphasised the importance of the goal-based regulatory approach as opposed to the traditional prescriptive approach to ensuring safety. In recent years, the goal-based regulatory approach (the so-called safety case regime) has been introduced in various industrial sectors such as automotive (ISO 26262 and ISO 21448), railway (IEC 62425), avionics (ICAO guidance for a safety case [18]) and medical devices (FDA infusion pump safety case). This has not been welcomed without any criticism. The most notable criticism of the safety case-based approach comes from N. Leveson [21], who pointed out that a safety argument can be misguided by psychological biases (e.g., confirmation bias) and logical fallacies, which would jeopardise the legitimacy of the safety case as a safety assurance framework. As discussed in the previous section, some new safety case-based standards, such as ANSI/UL 4600, take this criticism seriously and provide strict guidelines for properly using safety cases.

A safety case can take several forms, but most often, it is a structured document that can be supported by a graphical notation such as Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) [7]. Using a notation such as GSN helps present a safety case in a concise and structured manner that is easy for reviewers and assessors to understand and review.

The use of safety cases is also adopted in various safety assurance frameworks for ADS, such as Pegasus and Uber ATG’s Safety Case Framework [9].

To construct a safety argument for ADS, we need to address the following structural issues when designing a safety argument structure:

  • Macro argument structure

    • the top-level argument structure, which reflects the fundamental principles for safety assurance

  • Micro argument structures

    • Sub-argument structures that address specific issues, e.g., safety assurance of ML components, systems engineering process specifics, etc. Connection argument structure

  • Connection argument structure

    • Connecting micro-argument structures that address different safety issues based on some consideration of harmonising cross-cutting concerns

The Safety Case Framework by Uber ATG in Section 5.2.1.2 presents an example of the macro argument structure. A macro argument structure should be carefully designed to cover the entire safety assurance framework consistently and comprehensively. An example of a micro argument is given in the SOTIF argument structure, which should be integrated into the macro argument structure later in a complete safety case. To connect each micro-argument structure, it is necessary to harmonise cross-cutting concerns that may be addressed independently in multiple micro-argument structures. For example, suppose we consider functional safety and cybersecurity in separate micro argument structures. In that case, some interference between hazards and threats should be captured in some way to connect multiple argument structures. This type of interference and the resulting argument structure is discussed in [26].

5.2.1.1 Pegasus

The Pegasus (Project for the Establishment of Generally Accepted quality criteria, tools and methods as well as Scenarios and Situations for the release of HAD functions) [1] is a research project for the safety assurance of Highly Automated Driving (HAD) functions for ADS. It has developed the scenario description language OpenScenario [8] and a safety assurance framework, among other research results. The safety assurance framework for HAD proposed by Pegasus is the Pegasus Safety Argumentation, which is a conceptual framework to support tight integration of its process and associated pipeline for assurance artefacts production, representing how they support the safety argumentation. The Pegasus safety argumentation is a layered approach which consists of four layers (layer 1: ADS acceptance model (technology (social) acceptance of the HDS functions), layer 2: Logical structure of the safety argument (in GSN), layer 3: Methods and tools (e.g., V&V) and layer 4: Evidence (results from the application of layer 3). Fig. 5.3 shows the process where evidence to support safety argumentation is generated [22].

5.2.1.2 The Safety Case Framework (Uber ATG)

The Safety Case Framework (SCF) is a safety case for ADS developed by then Uber ATG (currently Aurora Innovation). It was a detailed yet publicly available safety case modelled in GSN. Unfortunately, the SCF we used for our study on conformance evaluation against ANSI/UL 4600 in [25] and explained in Section 5.2.2 is no longer available on the internet, and the current version by Aurora Innovation [11] does not provide the whole argument structure including evidence as solutions. In what follows, we will refer to the SCF by Uber ATG, not by Aurora Innovation.

Figure 5.4 shows the top-level argument structure of the SCF. Its ultimate goal is to establish that “our self-driving vehicles are acceptably safe to operate on public roads.” This goal is further broken down into the following sub-goals G1 to G5:

  • G1: Proficient The Self-Driving Vehicle is acceptably safe during nominal operation,
  • G2: Fail-Safe The Self-Driving Vehicle is acceptable safe in presence of faults and failures,
  • G3: Continuously improving Any anomaly that could affect the safety of the Self-Driving Vehicle is identified, evaluated, and resolved with appropriate corrective and preventative actions,
  • G4: Resilient The Self-Driving Vehicle is acceptably safe in case of reasonable foreseeable misuse and unavoidable events,
  • G5: Trustworthy The Self-Driving Enterprise is trustworthy.

The argument structure under G1 is devoted to systems engineering and SOTIF, including autonomy functions. G2 is for functional safety, i.e., handling safety functions under faults and failures. G3 deals with any risks involved in the operational process and their mitigation measures, G4 is for the system’s dependability, and G5 is for satisfying regulatory requirements.

This macro argument structure is very reasonably presented because it covers all the necessary safety principles required to assure the entire safety of an ADS. An attractive characteristic of this structure is that it faithfully follows the safety principles in Uber ATG’s safety report [10], which is submitted to NHTSA (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration) as a Voluntary Safety Self-Assessment Report (VSSA) for ADS [23]. Maintaining consistency between a safety case and a safety report is beneficial for an automotive manufacturer since these two documents/artefacts are essential to claim its ADS’s safety without reworking.

5.2.1.3 SOTIF Argument Structure

Annex A (General Guidance on SOTIF) of ISO 21448 [5] provides two examples of SOTIF-related safety arguments in GSN. They are very generic and avoid system-specific features, which helps one build their safety argument. We will explain the first example in Fig. 5.5.

The top goal is SOTIF is achieved and upheld for the AD (Automated Driving)/DA (Driver Assistant) functionality, which is placed in the context of Context C1-G-SOTIF and Context C2-G-SOTIF. The former context refers to the function and system specification produced as WP (Work Product) 5.5 and WP 8.5, and the latter to ODD and associated WP 5.5 and WP 8.5. Referring to some specific work products helps to understand which part of the standard is related to the argument.

The top goal is decomposed into two subsequent sub-goals. One is G-Dev; it claims that the development activities carried out faithfully follow the SOTIF-related assurance requirements. The other is G-field, which claims that if any safety issues arise in the field operation (e.g., trial runs), suitable measures are taken to keep the AD/DA functionality free from unreasonable risk. The latter sub-goal has an assumption A1-G-Field, which states that new risks referred to in the G-Field sub-goal are either scaling effects or changes in the ODD. Each goal has further decompositions referred to as Figs. A.2 and A.10 in the subsequent pages; we do not discuss them here.

SOTIF micro argument structure needs to be built in the macro argument structure, which covers the whole safety argument for ADS without causing any inconsistencies in an argument.

5.2.2 Conformance Evaluation on the SCF against ANSI/UL 4600

We review our results in [25] that experimentally assess whether the SCF conforms to ANSI/UL 4600. The main reasons for this exercise are that we would like to develop and establish a methodology for assessing a safety case to comply with a certain standard and an analysis method on the structural characteristics of that safety case. To our knowledge, there are no well-established criteria to assess a given safety case compliant with a certain standard or analysis methods to support it.

We must emphasise that ANSI/UL 4600 we used for this study is the first edition published in 2020 [3] (currently, the third edition [4] is available).

We analysed assurance requirements specified as General (the most general assurance requirement) and Mandatory (more general assurance condition than the General and no deviation is permitted) from Chapter 5 to Chapter 17 in ANSI/UL 4600. We compared them with goals and solutions in the SCF. As was stated previously, the choice of categories of assurance requirements depends on the risk assessment result of the item. Still, it is unavailable from the SCF, so we chose the most mandatory part of the assurance requirements.

5.2.2.1 Evaluation

The SCF was not developed in conformance with ANSI/UL 4600 per se. We must emphasise that our preliminary aim of this exercise is not for a judgement of its conformance to 4600 but to get insights into the construction method of a safety case for the ADS as a whole and to establish an assessment method for a safety case in compliance with a certain safety standard and a guideline.

Some general difficulties we encountered while analysing the SCF are as follows:

  1. Interpretation of a standard is inherently ambiguous. Generally, a newly issued standard such as ANSI/UL 4600 needs several years to establish a common understanding among engineers and assessors. We had difficulties understanding some safety requirements in the standard.
  2. The SCF represented in GSN only provides an argument structure without any evidence, such as V&V results and with some reference to substantial evidence, such as test results, etc., so that we can only judge whether statements expressed as goals conform to some assurance requirements in the standard (we may call our approach the black-box assessment).

We used the format shown in Table 5.1 for assessment, where the content of the first column is an assurance requirement in ANSI/UL 4600, the second column for identified goal(s) and solution(s) from the SCF, which we judged being complied with the assurance requirement, and the third column for our verdict (Conformed or Nonconformed).

Table 5.1: Assessment format
ANSI/UL 4600 Safety Case Framework Verdict
Assurance requirement in ANSI/UL 4600 solution(s), if any Conformed or Nonconformed (with some remarks)

We present some cases to show how we analysed and judged the conformance.

Table 5.2 shows the straightforward conformance relation between the assurance requirement 7.3.3 in ANSI/UL 4600 with a goal G2.1.3.1.1.6 in the SCF, even though slightly different terms human-settable item parameters and human adjustable parameters are used. This type of mismatch in terminology occurs in several places, but we did not take a stringent policy to interpret the terms.

Table 5.2: Example of assessment result #1
ANSI/UL 4600 Safety Case Framework Verdict
7.3.3 Hazards which can be contributed to by human-settable item parameters shall be acceptably mitigated. G2.1.3.1.1.6 Hazards and risks due to human adjustable parameters have been mitigated. Conformed

Table 5.3 shows the lack of supporting argument relevant to the assurance requirement 8.3.3 for sensor fusion and redundancy management techniques with relation to the ODD. Our judgement, shown in the third column, is that even though a goal G1.2.2.1.2.12 and a solution Sn1.2.2.1.2.12 are relevant to the assurance requirement 8.3.3, they are not sufficiently argued to comply with it.

Table 5.3: Example of assessment result #2
ANSI/UL 4600 Safety Case Framework Result
8.3.3 Sensor fusion and redundancy management techniques shall be used as necessary to result in acceptable sensor ODD. Unconfirmed (No clearly defined goals for sensor fusion, but the relevant argument we found is a goal G1.2.2.1.2.12 Perception system has sufficient availability and coverage to detect objects in the ODD appropriately and a solution Sn1.2.2.1.2.12.5 Perception fusion architecture.)

Table 5.4 shows that the standard has a wider scope than ADS, which might be useful for autonomous products in general but not necessarily compliant with the SCF. A Minimum Equipment List (MEL) is a list for the operation of aircraft and neither this notion nor associated assurance requirements are found in safety standards for automotive systems.

Table 5.4: Example of assessment result #3
ANSI/UL 4600 Safety Case Framework Result
10.3.5 A Minimum Equipment each autonomous operational mode. Unconfirmed (No argument on MEL)

ANSI/UL 4600 introduces new safety metrics called the Safety Performance Indicator (SPI), which can be defined for various properties/components to quantify safety performance. SPIs play an important role in validating a safety argument, and its definition is elaborated in edition 3. Table 5.5 shows that our judgement is done with a goal and its associated solutions (evidence).

Table 5.5: Example of assessment result #4
ANSI/UL 4600 Safety Case Framework Result
16.3.1 Date for each defined SPI shall be collected. G3.2.5.2 Safety performance indicator data measurements are valid, Sn3.2.5.2.3 SPI data collection tools, Sn3.2.5.2.4 SPI data collection justification of robustness Confirmed (Date collection related to SPIs can be judged as conforming indirectly from a combination of a goal and associated solutions)

As can be seen from the sample analysis results, the verdict for conformance is straightforward in some cases and difficult to judge in others.

This table can be interpreted horizontally and vertically. The horizontal interpretation shows which chapter in ANSI/UL 4600 deals with which sub-goal of the SCF. The vertical interpretation shows which sub-argument structure addresses issues specified in corresponding chapters in ANSI/UL 4600.

Some observations from the horizontal analyses are listed below:

  1. H-1 Chapter 5. Safety case: Goals are spread across almost all sub-argument structures since the fundamental mechanism for safety assurance is based on the safety case.
  2. H-2 Chapter 6. Risk Assessment: It is covered by G2: Fail-Safe and G3: Continuously Improvement. This is plausible since risk assessment is mainly carried out by Fail-Safe operations and operational processes addressed in G2 and G3.
  3. H-3 Chapter 8. Autonomy Functions and Support: It is mainly covered in G1: Proficient, which is plausible for its intention.
  4. H-4 Chapter 9. Software and System Engineering Process: It is mostly covered by G1: Proficient. We cannot judge its plausibility, but there is no reason against it.
  5. H-5 Chapter 10. Dependability: It is either safety-related (G2: Fail-Safe) or resilient (G4: Resilient), which results from the very nature of dependability.
  6. H-6 Chapter 16. Metrics and SPIs: It is entirely covered by G3: Continuously Improving. It is plausible since SPIs are used for risk assessment in the operation phase.
  7. H-7 Chapter 17. Assessment: It is only covered by G5: Trustworthy due to its role in assessment.

According to this analysis, we can conclude that the distribution of intended use of assurance requirements is very plausible.

Likewise, some observations on the vertical analyses are listed below:

  1. V-1 G1: Proficient: It covers almost all Chapters 8, 9 and 12 since it intends to cover systems engineering development as a whole and autonomy,
  2. V-2 G2: Fail-Safe: It covers almost all chapters since safety analysis is carried out in almost all activities,
  3. V-3 G3: Continuously Improving: It covers a part of Chapter 6 and all of Chapter 16, which matches its intention,
  4. V-4 G4: Resilient: It mostly covers Chapter 10, which can be predictable from its main role,
  5. V-5 G5: Trustworthy: It covers Chapters 5 and 17. Particularly why G5 covers Chap 17 is based on the same reason as H-7.

These vertical analyses show that each sub-goal and its argument structure fulfils its intention.

5.2.2.3 Related Work

A few research works address the issues we pursued in our evaluation in Section 5.2.2. The closest is that by Graydon et. al [17], which discusses issues on conformance to software assurance standards and presents a conformance arguments structure in which how a part of an argument is linked to objectives in software safety standard in avionics DO-178B [24]. This approach appears useful since assessing compliance with a given safety argument is time-consuming for assessors. This approach would help them understand the intent of the safety argument and its relation with assurance requirements/objectives in the standard.

Submission of a safety case is mandated in several safety standards, as was stated previously. Many research works propose their methods of constructing a safety case for a certain standard. For instance, Dargar et. al [14, 15] focuses on a safety case for ISO 26262, but it does not deal with conformance criteria for the standard. This kind of research result assumes that conformance to a standard is built into its approach and does not provide any explicit criteria for how the approach assures conformance with a standard.

The safety case approach to assure the safety of AI/ML systems is carried out by several authors. For instance, Gauerhof [16] focused on the inherent nature of functional inefficiencies which could be caused by AI/ML systems and provided a safety argument structure that covers their root causes. As was explained in a previous chapter, the Pegasus is a European research project on autonomous driving and developed the safety argumentation framework for Highly Automated Driving Functions. Its presentation material [22] includes reference to standards, e.g., ISO 26262, ISO 21448 and NHTSA guidelines. Still, it does not detail how the framework can conform to those standards and guidelines.

5.2.2.4 Final Remarks

To obtain more objective judgement on our evaluation results in Section 5.2.2, we consulted various industry experts (OEMs, suppliers and tool vendors) in functional safety, SOTIF, and ADS on our evaluation results by providing them with the check sheet (Table 5.1). Their overall response was positive due to our detailed analyses on the conformance relation between ANSI/UL 4600 and the SCF, which they think would help to understand ANSI/UL 4600 and the role of a safety case for documents for future certification of their ADS. They found difficulty assessing the results due to terminology mismatches between the two and the lack of deep understanding of ANSI/UL 4600. Still, they provided helpful comments to improve our results.

Here are our observations from the survey on related work and our experience with this experimental evaluation on the SCF in Section 5.2.2.

  • Safety principles affecting the top-level argument structure may vary from one company to another. There remains a question of whether there would be a generic and one-fit-all top-level argument structure.
  • Micro-argument patterns adopted in the SCF are very traditional, as seen in many existing works, e.g., papers and guidelines. There are several proposals for micro-argument structures for machine learning and SOTIF so that these results could be used as micro-argument patterns.
  • Safety case approaches in the Pegasus project and SaFAD could be useful to connect the assurance artefact production pipeline (simulation results, etc) with the argument structure.
  • Interrelations between functional safety, SOTIF, and cybersecurity are not presented in the SCF. Security-informed safety case [12] type of approach or argument patterns for safety and security [26] could be used as micro-argument patterns.

6.1 Introduction

There have been intensive discussion on uncertainty in software engineering as more and more systems operate deeply in the real world [1]. In the context of software engineering, uncertainty refers to aspects that make it impossible to fix everything at development time. There has been various classifications of uncertainty, 26 types of uncertainty were discussed in [5] in the context of dynamically adaptive systems. One example of uncertainty type is unpredictable environment where events and conditions relevant with the state transition cannot be fully predicted and fixed beforehand. This chapter presents an approach to explicitly handle the uncertain aspects through the development process from requirement models to executable tests.

Uncertainty is fairly common in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) due to their nature. Thus, various types of uncertainties in the CPS development must be identified, understood, and properly handled to eliminate (if possible) any safety and security issues during their operation. Figure 6.1 shows a typical CPS together with various places at which different uncertainties may occur in the CPS. A CPS consists of a set of physical units that communicate with each other, e.g., via information networks (e.g., 4G or directly wired connections). Each physical unit itself may consist of dedicated hardware with deployed software or could be a simple sensor reading data from the environment.

Uncertainties may appear at various situations in a CPS. First, uncertainties may be introduced by agents, e.g., humans, animals, or other systems that interact with a CPS. A typical example is humans interacting with the CPS in an unexpected manner. Second, uncertainties may occur in physical units such as in software, or hardware, or both. Examples include software and hardware errors leading to uncertain behaviors of a CPS. Third, uncertainties may occur in the information network used by the physical units to communicate with each other, such as due to packet loss or slow internet connection. Fourth, uncertainties may happen in the physical environment of a CPS, such as unexpected high temperatures. Fifth, uncertainties can occur due to interactions of more than one of the uncertainties described in the first four points.

6.2 Running Example

To explain our approach from the beginning to the end in a unified manner, we will use a running example of Safe Home which is inspired by a case study from Pressman [4]. This case study is about smart features implemented in a sensor-based smart home. In particular, we will focus on functionalities related to ensuring the safety and security of the system. Examples of such functionalities include detecting intrusion and other disasters such as fire or water leaks based on specialized sensors. For the sake of simplicity, we only focus on one such functionality, i.e., related to intrusion detection. This functionality aims at detecting the intrusion at home with continuous monitoring via dedicated motion sensors installed on windows and doors of the home. If a motion is detected, the home owner is notified and an alarm is enabled. If it is a false alarm, the home owner can simply enter her/his secret code and stop the alarm. If the secret code is entered wrong more than three times, a notification is sent to the police automatically. If the home owner is away and the alarm keeps ringing for more than the configured number of minutes (e.g., 5 minutes), a notification is also sent to the police automatically. A use case diagram corresponding to this functionality is shown in Fig. 6.2.

A use case diagram corresponding to this functionality is shown in Fig. 6.2. It has four actors, i.e., Home Owner, Control Panel, Alarm, and Sensor. In addition, it has two use cases Monitor Windows and Doors and Configure Monitoring Area. Home Owner can configure the monitoring area through a dedicated control panel via the Configure Monitoring Area use case. This use case is included by the Monitor Windows and Doors use case, which in turn detects an intrusion via dedicated sensors, consequently activates the alarm and notifies the home owner or the police, in case an intrusion is detected. Additionally, Home Owner can enable/disable the detection via Control Panel.

6.3 Overview of Uncertainty-wise Testing Approaches

This chapter focuses on testing CPSs under uncertainties, which is composed of a series of methodologies from specifying and modeling uncertainties, and all the way down to test generation and test execution. An overview of these methodologies and their relationships are shown in Fig. 6.3. The figure shows that the overall process has four main methodologies, which were proposed based on an uncertainty conceptual model (see Section 6.4 for more details).

The uncertainty conceptual model is called U-Model and it conceptualizes uncertainties in the context of developing and testing CPSs [14]. U-Model was specifically designed to identify various uncertainties in CPSs at a higher level of abstraction for the purpose facilitating common understanding of various uncertainty related concepts. Later on, U-Model was used as the basis to support the development of specialized uncertainty identification, definition, and classification mechanisms tailored for developing and testing CPSs of different domains and for achieving various purposes such as model-based testing (MBT) of CPSs under uncertainty and uncertainty-wise requirements verification and validation. In this chapter, we will demonstrate its application to support MBT of CPSs under uncertainty. Concretely, first, we will discuss a methodology for specifying uncertainty-related testing requirements in Section 6.5. Second, we will present an uncertainty-wise test design to develop test ready models using specified uncertainty testing requirements in Section 6.6. Finally, test generation (including test optimization) based on defined test ready models, and test execution will be discussed together in Section 6.7.

6.4 Conceptual Understanding of Uncertainty

This section describes conceptual understanding of uncertainty in the context of CPSs. Given the complexity of the topic, it is important to conceptually understand various concepts related to uncertainty at a higher-level of abstraction. We present detail of U-Model in Section 6.4.1 to support conceptual modeling and understanding.

6.4.1 U-Model—The Conceptual Model for Uncertainty

U-Model was proposed with the aim to take the subjective perspective of understanding uncertainties; thus, it was built around the concept of Belief. Thus, at a high-level, U-Model consists of BeliefModel, which is imported by MeasureModel and UncertaintyModel, as shown in Fig. 6.4. BeliefModel describes necessary concepts and their relationships related to belief. UncertaintyModel focuses on concepts and their relationships concerning uncertainty. Finally, MeasureModel formulates concepts related to measurements that can be associated with beliefs and uncertainties. In the following subsections, we will describe each of these models and illustrate them with the running example (Section 6.2).

6.4.1.1 Belief Model

The various concepts and relationships among them from BeliefModel are shown in Fig. 6.6, whereas their definitions are provided in Table 6.1. Note that these definitions are reused from the original paper [14]. Since U-Model takes the subjective perspective when defining uncertainties in the context of the development and testing of CPSs, U-Model defines BeliefAgent (see B2 in Table 6.1). For example, in our context, a belief agent can be a tester who wants to test SafeHome. The tester wants to test her/his Belief (see B1 in Table 6.1) about SafeHome, e.g., whether motion sensor on windows can detect intrusion. As shown in the figure, Belief is an abstract concept and it has to be concertized as BeliefStatement (see B3 in Table 6.1). A belief statement could be a simple statement in English or a complex model (e.g., a UML state machine). An example of such a statement is: Tester believes that “the system can detect the intrusion with 99% probability.”(see Fig. 6.5) and tester can state that she/he is highly confidence (i.e., a measurement of the belief) about her/his statement. The belief may be supported by Evidence (see B4 in Table 6.1). For example, the evidence for the statement could be logs of previous versions of the product. The belief statement has a source, because of which a belief agent has Uncertainty (see U1 in Table 6.2) in her/his statement, i.e., IndeterminacySource (see B5 in Table 6.1). In this example, the source of the uncertainty might be related to the sensors or the communication between the sensors and the system. Both IndeterminacySource and Uncertainty can have associated Measurement (see B6 in Table 6.1), of a particular Measure (see Fig. 6.8). With this statement, the measurement of the uncertainty (i.e., “the system can detect intrusion”) is 99%.

Table 6.1: Definition of the belief model.
Concept# Name Definition

B1

Belief

“A belief is an implicit subjective explanation or description of some phenomena or notions that is held by a BeliefAgent”

B2

Belief Agent

“BeliefAgent represents an individual, a community of individuals sharing the same set of beliefs, or a technology, such as a software system, with built-in beliefs.”

B3

Belief Statement

“A BeliefStatement is an explicit specification of some Belief about a possible phenomenon or notions belonging to a given subject area.”

B4

Belief Evidence

“Evidence is either the observation of or record of a real-world event occurrence or, alternatively, the conclusion of some formalized chain of logical inference, which provides information that may contribute to determining the validity (i.e., truthfulness) of a BeliefStatement.”

B5

Indeterminacy Source

“IndeterminacySource represents a situation whereby the information required to ascertain the validity of a BeliefStatement is indeterminate in some way, resulting in uncertainty being associated with that statement.”

B6

Measurement

“Measurement represents the optional quantification (or qualification) that specifies the degree of Belief/ Uncertainty/IndeterminacySource.”
Table 6.2 Definition of the uncertainty model
Concept# Name Definition

U1

Uncertainty

“Uncertainty (lack of confidence) represents a state of affairs whereby a BeliefAgent does not have full confidence in a Belief that it holds.”

U2

Occurrence

“Occurrence represents a situation whereby a BeliefAgent lacks confidence in occurrence existing in a BeliefStatement.”

U3

Content

“Content represents a situation whereby a BeliefAgent lacks confidence in content existing in a BeliefStatement.”

U4

Time

“Time represents a situation whereby a BeliefAgent lacks confidence in time existing in a BeliefStatement.”

U5

Environment

“Environment represents a situation whereby a BeliefAgent lacks confidence in environment existing in a BeliefStatement.”

U6

Geographical Location

“GeographicalLocation represents a situation whereby a BeliefAgent lacks confidence in geographical location existing in a BeliefStatement.”

U7

Pattern

“Pattern represents an intelligible way in which an Uncertainty appears.”

U8

Lifetime

“Lifetime represents the duration of time for which an Uncertainty remains active.”

U9

Locality

“A particular place or a position where Uncertainty occurs in the BeliefStatement.”

U10

Risk

“Risk measures the risk associated with Uncertainty.”

U11

Effect

“Effect represents the result of Uncertainty in the BeliefStatement.”

6.4.1.2 Uncertainty Model

UncertaintyModel in Fig. 6.7 shows various concepts and relationships among them. An uncertainty can be of any of the following types: Occurrence (see U2 in Table 6.1), Content (see U3 in Table 6.1), Time (see U4 in Table 6.1), Environment (see U5 in Table 6.1), and Geographical Location (see B2 in Table 6.1). In the belief statement, the tester holds that the system has uncertainty about the detection of intrusion; thus, the uncertainty type is Occurrence. In addition, an uncertainty can have several other properties, i.e., Pattern, Lifetime, Locality, Risk, and Effect (see definitions U7–U11 in Table 6.2). For this uncertainty (i.e., detect the intrusion successfully), its Effect is none and the probability of the occurrence uncertainty is 99%, thus the Risk would be Low. But for its alternative (i.e., fail to detect the intrusion), its Effect is extreme and the probability is low (1%), thus the Risk would be High.

6.4.1.3 Measure Model

MeasureModel of U-Model is shown in Fig. 6.8. Measure can be of many different types; however, at a high level, these can be classified into Probability, Ambiguity, and Vagueness. These measures are standard textbook concepts and can be consulted here [2, 3, 6, 12]. In this example, the measure is Probability and the measurement is 99%.

6.5 Uncertainty Requirements

U-Model defines concepts at a high level for the purpose of facilitating the understanding of uncertainty from the subjective perspective. However, we need to instantiate the conceptual model such that more detailed and concrete uncertainty specifications can be achieved. To this end, Uncertainty-wise Restricted Use Case Modeling (U-RUCM) was developed [15]. U-RUCM is an extension of (RUCM) [10], which is a restricted language-based use case specification language, aiming to reduce ambiguity of natural language and facilitate automated generation of other software development artifacts such as UML analysis models [11] and test cases [9]. RUCM has been demonstrated to be successful in many areas. Interested readers may check [7, 8 and 9].

The architecture of U-RUCM is shown in Fig. 6.9. U-RUCM is based on UML’s use case notation. Key features of U-RUCM are formalized as Belief-UCMeta—a metamodel for formalizing U-RUCM’s concepts and their relationships. Belief-UCMeta imports UCMeta [10] and U-Model (Section 6.4.1). UCMeta is the underlying metamodel that formalizes RUCM. UCMeta consists of four main packages: (1) UCTemplate implementing the RUCM template with various fields, e.g., use case name and description (see an example in Fig. 6.11); (2) SentenceStructure defining sentence constructs from the English linguistic perspective, e.g., noun phrases and subjects of sentences; (3) SentenceSemantics focusing on providing semantics of sentences in terms of their roles in flows of events, e.g., the sentence describing a system validation with given data; and (4) SentencePattern distinguishing sentences in terms of their structures such as sentences with the structure of subject-verb-direct object.

U-RUCM extends RUCM by providing two additional templates to specify Belief Use Case Specifications (BUCS) and uncertainties by implementing concepts from U-Model. Examples include indeterminacy sources, risk, and belief degree. A BUCS is the result of an instantiation of Belief-UCMeta.

At a high-level, U-RUCM consists of a use case diagram, for instance, the one shown in Fig. 6.2 for Safe Home. Corresponding to each use case in the use case diagram, e.g., Monitor Windows and Doors, one can define a detailed use case specification based on a template defined in [10] and extended in [15] to specify uncertainty requirements. The template includes a well-defined structure, a set of keywords, and restrictions such that various automation can be supported, such as the automated generation of UML diagrams and tests.

The templates for specifying use case specifications and uncertainties are shown in Fig. 6.10, which are composed of the basic fields such as use case name, description, actors, and relationships. In addition, the template for use case specifications describes the key fields for specifying uncertainty related information such as belief agent, time points and duration, and indeterminacy source, i.e., the implementation of the concepts defined in U-Model. The template for uncertainty also shows specific structures that are related to the specification of uncertainty (see the bottom of the figure). Note that Fig. 6.10 describes the purpose of each field.

Figure 6.10: U-RUCM templates.
The template for specifying a BUCS

Use Case Name

The name of the use case. It usually starts with a verb.

Brief Description

Summarizes the use case in a short paragraph.

Primary Actor

The actor who initiates the use case.

Secondary Actor(s)

Other actors the system relies on to accomplish the services of the use case.

Dependency

Generalization

Generalization relationships to other use cases.

Belief Agent(s)

One or more agents who hold belief about this BUCS.

Time Point and Duration

The time point when the BUCS is specified and the duration in which the belief agent{s)'s belief on the BUCS holds.

Belief Degree

The degree to which the belief agent(s) believe the BUCS.

Indeterminacy Source(s)

The set of indeterminacy sources related to the BUCS (REF is used).

Evidence

Evidence to support the BUCS, and its contained belief and uncertainty elements (REF is used).

Belief Precondition

Belief agent(s)' belief on the precondition of the BUCS, which describes what should be true before the use case is executed.

Belief Basic Flow (Belief degree)

Specifies the main successful path, also called “happy path”.

Steps (numbered)

A set of ordered belief sentences.

Belief Postcondition

Belief agent(s)' belief on what should be true after the basic flow executes.

Belief Specific Alternative Flow (Belief degree)

Applies to one specific step of the reference flow.

URFS

The reference flow step where the belief agent(s) believe there are uncertainties.

Alternative Step

An alternative to the reference flow step.

Steps (numbered)

A set of ordered belief sentences.

Belief Postcondition

Belief agent(s)' belief on what should be true after the specific alternative flow executes.

Belief Bounded Alternative Flow (Belief degree)

Applies to more than one step of the reference flow, but not all of them.

URFS

A list of reference flow steps where the belief agent(s) believe there are uncertainties.

Alternative Steps

A set of alternatives to the reference flow steps.

Steps (numbered)

A set of ordered belief sentences.

Belief Postcondition

Belief agent(s)' belief on what should be true after the bounded alternative flow executes.

Belief Global Alternative Flow (Belief degree)

Applies to all the steps of the reference flow.

Belief Branching Condition

Belief agent(s)' belief on the condition, which describes what should be true when branching from any of the steps of the reference flow.

Steps (numbered)

The set of ordered beliefs sentences.

Belief Postcondition

Belief agent(s)' belief on what should be true after the global flow executes.

The template of specifying a belief sentence (BS) with one and more Uncertainties

Belief Degree

Indeterminacy Source(s)

Evidence

Uncertainty Details
