For our running example Safe Home, we show the uncertainty requirements specification corresponding to the “Monitor Windows and Doors” in Fig. 6.11, Fig. 6.12, and Fig. 6.14.

Figure 6.11 describes the basic fields of the use case and uncertainty related information. For example, it describes that this use case includes Configure Monitoring Area use case, as also shown in Fig. 6.2. It also shows the uncertainty related information such as a tester being the belief agent and various indeterminacy sources such as Broken Control Panel (Button or Screen), due to which uncertainty may occur when monitoring windows and doors.

In addition, Fig. 6.11 shows a Belief Basic Flow named as BB, that is, a set of “happy day” scenarios. In total, it has 13 steps and a postcondition. A set of keywords are highlighted in different colors such as VALIDATES THAT, which checks a condition performed by the system or the testing framework. For example, in Step 6, the system checks whether the system is monitoring the home. If the check fails, then the flow is transferred to SAlt1 Specific Alternate Flow shown in Fig. 6.12. Similarly, there is another check at Step 10, if it fails then the flow branches to SAlt1 Specific Alternate Flow shown in Fig. 6.12.

In RUCM, alternative flows should be branched with specific conditions. For instance, Fig. 6.12 shows a Specific Alternative Flow named SAlt1 which branches from a condition check (i.e., VALIDATE THAT) referring to Step 6 of BB using keyword RFS (i.e., RFS BB 6). In this example, Step 6 is to check whether the status of the system is updated to Monitoring after the system invokes a method to enable the monitoring function (see Step 5 in BB). If the condition check is evaluated as false (i.e., the status is not updated improperly), the steps in SAlt1 will be executed. Considering that the result of the condition check is uncertain (but it is determined), an occurrence of executing SAlt1 could be regarded as an uncertainty that relies on the referred steps (see rfsSentence in Fig. 6.12). As shown in Fig. 6.13, the uncertainty might be due to improper implementation of the system (i.e., IndeterminacySource) and the probability of its occurrence could be 5%.

Figure 6.14 shows more constructs of U-RUCM. First, it shows another example of Belief Specific Alternative Flow, i.e., BSAlt1 capturing alternative steps which might replace the referred step(s), i.e., SAlt2 Step 2 in Fig. 6.12. As one can see from SAlt2, Step 1 describes a condition: the windows and doors are open, which can be referred as an intrusion. Step 2 is to a system check on whether the Sensor detects the intrusion. However, due to some unknown reasons, the Sensor might fail to detect the intrusion. Thus, the Step 2 in SAlt2 can be replaced by the Steps A1–A2 in BSAlt1 in Fig. 6.14, then the flow will resume to Step 8 of BB. Note that, in the view of the system, there is no any error since the Sensor gives the incorrect signal to the system. To specify this situation, U-RUCM defines URFS, and it can be used to specify alternative steps referring to behaviors which are scope of the system (e.g., Control Panel (BBAlt1 in Fig. 6.12), Sensor (BSAlt1 in Fig. 6.14)). Regarding RFS, it typically refers to the check performed by the system, e.g., the system Status should be Monitoring once the monitoring function is invoked (see SAlt1 in Fig. 6.12).

In U-RUCM, each step in the flows can have associated uncertainty which can be characterized with the specific template shown in Fig. 6.10. For example, the associated specification with Step A1 is shown in Fig. 6.15. The specification describes a possible uncertainty in Step A1 in BSAlt1, which is related to the inability of the system to identify the intrusion. The details of the uncertainty include: (1) information about associated indeterminacy sources, i.e., Broken Sensor, (2) belief degree, e.g., 1% in this example, and (3) risk, e.g., High. Figure 6.14 also shows two Belief Global Alternative Flows (i.e., BGAlt1 and BGAlt2). These can be invoked from any step of the belief basic flow presented in Fig. 6.11.

6.6 Uncertainty Modeling

Uncertainty-wise Test Modeling (UncerTum) is a model-based testing approach to support testing CPSs under uncertainty. UncerTum supports creating test ready models in UML that explicitly specify uncertainty. UncerTum can be applied as a follow-up of the uncertainty specification in U-RUCM or one can start creating test ready models directly with UncerTum.

UncerTum implements a UML profile for uncertainty specification, called the UML Uncertainty Profile (UUP). Just like U-RUCM, UUP implements U-Model described in Section 6.4.1. As shown in Fig. 6.16, UUP has four UML profiles corresponding to Belief, Measurement, Uncertainty, and Indeterminacy based on U-Model. In addition, UncerTum includes a set of model libraries to allow test modelers to quantify uncertainties with various uncertainty measures such as ambiguity, probability, and vagueness from U-Model. However, in U-Model, these concepts are abstract, but UncerTum implements them with concrete measures from the literature, or reuse some from the UML profile for Modeling and Analysis of Real-Time and Embedded Systems (MARTE).

To explain how to create test ready models with UncerTum, we will use the running example presented in Section 6.2. To use UncerTum, one needs to create a set of UML class diagrams and state machines with stereotypes from UUP. Figure 6.17 and Fig. 6.19 show the example class diagram and state machine respectively, which correspond to the intrusion detection feature belonging to the Security System of Safe Home.

To implement intrusion detection, the security system needs sensors and an alarm, shown as the composition relationships between SecuritySystem and Sensor, and SecuritySystem and Alarm, respectively. Both Sensor and Alarm are stereotyped as «InfrastructureElement» for being hardware components, whereas SecuritySystem is stereotyped as «IntegrationElement» since it integrates elements from different levels. SecuritySystem is also composed of a ControlPanel with a dedicated interface IControlPanel that can be accessed by home owner to configure the security system. IControlPanel is stereotyped as «ApplicationElement» since it is related to the application use of the system. The class diagram also shows two indeterminacy sources associated with ControlPanel and Sensor annotated with the «IndeterminacySource» stereotype. The indeterminacy source related to ControlPanel is about whether the buttons on the control panel are broken or not. The indeterminacy source related to Sensor is about whether or not the sensor can detect intrusion correctly. To evaluate the occurrence of such indeterminacy sources, we define constraints specified with OCL representing specifications of the occurrences annotated with the «IndeterminacySpecification» stereotype. For instance, Sensor could have two possible statuses defined with The sensor is normal constraint and The sensor is out of the order constraint, respectively. Here, Sensor has two operation stereotyped with «IndeterminacySourceInput» (i.e., deactivateDetection() and activateDectection()) represents methods that can introduce indeterminacy sources when testing CPSs. The methods could be implemented in the testing environment for testing CPS under various environmental configurations. Figure 6.18 shows the specification of The sensor is out of the order in detail. As shown in the figure, the specification is not an expected status (see the value for the Is Expected property in the Properties window); the status could occur with 1% probability (see the value for the Measurement property); the status can be manipulated by deactivateDetection() for triggering the occurrence of the indeterminacy source (see value for the Triggered By property) and activateDectection() for releasing its occurrence (see the value of the Released By property).

To specify the behavior, an example UML state machine is shown in Fig. 6.19 with stereotypes from UUP. The state machine starts from the S1: Idle state, from where it leaves from two transitions. The first transition is related to the inability of the system to enable monitoring and leading the system to the S3: Failed to enable monitoring state. The second transition is related to the monitoring being enabled successfully. In this case, the system transits to the S2: Monitoring state. From S2, when an intrusion is triggered via the T3: IntrusionOccurred() signal, there are two possible transitions. First, due to a system failure, the warning is not issued and the system transits to the S7: Not Warning state. Otherwise, the system activates the alarm (the activateAlarm() effect on T3), notifies the home owner with the notifyHomeOwner() effect, and transits to the S5: Waiting for resolving warning state. If the home owner resolves the warning via the secret code, the system transits via the exit1 point to the S2 state, and continues the monitoring. If the warning is not cleared by the home owner, then the police is notified after 5 minutes and the system transits to the S6: Police notified state. Moreover, if the secret code entered is wrong for more than three times, the police is notified.

Note that various states and transitions are stereotyped «BeliefElement» from UUP. Corresponding to each belief element, we can specify various information such as belief degree and indeterminacy source. Figure 6.20 shows detailed information of state S4: Intrusion Warning and Alarm Ringing stereotyped with «BeliefElement». The element contains a Measurement and an Uncertainty. As properties of the Uncertainty shown in the figure, the uncertainty is specified with the Low risk and of type Occurrence. In addition, the uncertainty is caused by transition T3: IntrusionOccurred() (see Referred Cause, led by the indeterminacy source referring to ControlPanel (see Referred Indeterminacy Source). The corresponding specification of the source is The sensor is normal (see Related Ind Specs). Enable Pattern, Find Position and Select Specification are used to specify how to introduce the indeterminacy source in order to enable the occurrence of the uncertainty. As shown in the figure, the Specified indeterminacy source is Always introduced at a position where is Just_Previous of this uncertainty, i.e., T3.

6.7 Uncertainty Testing

The UML class diagram and state machines developed as test ready models with UncerTum shall be used to generate test cases with suitable testing strategies. To this end, UncerTest was proposed in [13], which consists of uncertainty-wise test case generation and test case minimization approaches as shown in Fig. 6.21. UncerTest has four steps. As shown in the figure, the creation of test ready models is step 1 of UncerTest. A test ready model is an abstract representation of the CPS under test, with a particular focus on modeling the expected behavior of the CPS under various uncertainties. Step 2 generates abstract test cases, whereas Step 3 converts the generated abstract test cases into executable test cases. Finally Step 4 executes test cases on CPS being tested. Step 1 was discussed in Section 6.6, whereas Step 3 is about simply converting abstract test cases into executable test cases with a software. The rest of the subsections explain Uncertainty-wise Test Case Generation and Uncertainty-wise Test Case Minimization from Step 2 and test case execution details of Step 4.

6.7.1 Uncertainty-wise Test Case Generation

The second step of UncerTest generates a set of abstract test cases with uncertainty-wise test case generation consisting of two coverage criteria.

Abstract test cases are those that do not have concrete data and are independent of implementation details. For the abstract test case generation, we defined two coverage criteria on UML state machines (i.e., Belief State Machines (BSMs)) developed with UncerTum: (1) the All Simple Belief Paths coverage (ASiBP), which generates all simple paths in a BSM containing unique states and transitions. By simple, we mean there is no loop. An example is shown in Fig. 6.22; and (2) the All Specified Length Belief Paths coverage (ASlBP), which generates all paths in a BSM. Given that the number of all paths in a BSM can be very large, one need to specify the maximum length. For both of the coverage, a path is one abstract test case.

Figure 6.24 represents an example of a test (generated by UncerTest) based on the state machine shown in Fig. 6.19. The left represents a path of the state machine which is regarded as a test. It starts from an initial state IS1 and ends with the final state FS1. The right side represents a snippet of the executable test case corresponding to the sub-path, i.e., S2 (lines 1–3) $\overset{\text{~T3(lines~}7 - 12)}{\rightarrow}S4$ S4 (lines 13–41). Lines 4–6 introduce the specified indeterminacy activateDetection() (see Fig. 6.20). To evaluate the occurrence of the uncertainty specified in S4, lines 14–22 first report whether the specified uncertainty is occurred with the related indeterminacy source specification. Since the uncertainty might not always occur, it is necessary to report the occurrence of its alternative. In this example, an alternative of this uncertainty is $S2\overset{T3}{\rightarrow}S3,$ and its occurrence is reported at lines 23–32. Next, lines 33–34 record the current state of the SUT. Then, lines 36–41 are to check whether the uncertainty is occurred as expected.

6.7.2 Uncertainty-wise Test Case Minimization

To minimize the number of abstract test cases to be concertized and executed, we devised multi-objective search-based approaches. In particular, the four approaches were developed. All the four approaches shared two objectives, i.e., minimizing the number of test cases to be executed and maximizing the transition coverage. However, the approaches differ in terms of the four uncertainty-related objectives to be maximized as follows.

Average number of uncertainties Cover more uncertainties by each test case.

Uncertainty space coverage Cover more combinations by the whole test suite.

Uncertainty measurement Increase confidence on normal execution by more likely test runs.

Coverage of unique uncertainties Cover more unique uncertainties by the whole test suite.

The NSGA-II search algorithm was employed for test case minimization. Depending on the preferences of a user, one or more of these minimization techniques can be employed.

6.7.3 Test Case Execution

When test cases are executed, one needs to determine the pass and fail of the test cases and determine whether uncertainties are discovered. To test CPS under uncertainty, we introduce indeterminacy sources (see Fig. 6.24) and determine whether expected uncertainties occurred due to the introduced indeterminacy sources. UncerTest focuses on evaluating known uncertainties and identifying unknown uncertainties and possible indeterminacy sources.

In particular, we defined the following types of uncertainty verdicts:

  • Known uncertainty occurred with known indeterminacy source introduced;
  • Known uncertainty occurred without introduction of known indeterminacy source;
  • Known uncertainty not occurred with the introduction of known indeterminacy source;
  • Known uncertainty not occurred without the introduction of indeterminacy source;
  • Known uncertainty occurred with unknown indeterminacy source;
  • Known uncertainty not occurred with unknown indeterminacy source; and ■ Unknown uncertainty occurred.

Figure 6.25 represents results of the occurrence of an uncertainty (in the test case shown in Fig. 6.21) specified with such a verdict. As shown in the figure, the uncertainty and related indeterminacy source occurred as expected (see lines 3 and 19), and none of the alternative uncertainties occurred. Thus, for the uncertainty, its results is “KnOccurred-With-In” (i.e., known uncertainty occurred with known indeterminacy source introduced).

In addition, we implemented the following test case verdicts by further considering occurrences of the uncertainties in test cases: Known uncertainty occurred, Unknown uncertainty occurred, Not occurred, Passed, Failed, Error, Inconclusive, and None.

6.8 Conclusions

This chapter presented uncertainty-wise testing approaches that were designed for automated and systematic testing of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) under various uncertainties. The complete solution starts with specifying uncertainty test requirements in a restricted natural language-based approach, called U-RUCM. Then, followed by test requirement specifications, a tester can design test ready models with a dedicated uncertainty-wise test modeling solution, called UncerTum, using the requirements specified with U-RUCM. Once we have test ready models, the accompanying model-based testing tool can generate test cases from test ready models and further minimize them, if required. Finally, the test cases (with or without optimization) are concertized to be executed on CPSs for testing.

Chapter 7 Decision Making for Automated Driving

Sasinee Pruekprasert

National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Tokyo, Japan

Ahmet Cetinkaya

Shibaura Institute of Technology, Tokyo, Japan

Ichiro Hasuo

National Institute of Informatics and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

7.1 Introduction

In the last few decades, we have witnessed the increasing popularity and rapid development of automated driving systems (ADSs). New sensing, perception, planning, and control techniques are being introduced, and as a result, vehicles are becoming increasingly more capable to achieve automated driving tasks.

In this chapter, we discuss decision making components in ADS, which provide guidance on the driving behavior of vehicles. In our discussion, we focus our attention to safety, as it is one of the major concerns for decision making. This issue is emphasised in standards such as ANSI/UL 4600 [67], which addresses safety requirements during the operation of ADSs, and ISO/DIS 21448 [35], which identifies measures to be taken to achieve the safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) in ADSs.

We start by introducing the decision-making hierarchy of a contemporary ADS. Then, we focus on the motion planning component, which is responsible for computing feasible trajectories for the vehicle. Designing motion planners is challenging because the computed trajectory must be dynamically feasible for the vehicle and comfortable for the passenger. In addition, trajectories must avoid collisions with obstacles detected by sensors, which may be subject to uncertainties. As a result, motion planning for ADSs is a large research area with a variety of approaches. In this chapter, we discuss optimisation-based, model predictive, game theory-based, and machine learning-based motion planning approaches.

next, we discuss formal verification techniques that can be combined with decision-making components to ensure the safety of the ADS. We discuss two reachability analysis techniques, a set-based one and a probabilistic one, that can be used to compute road occupancy of all road participants subject to uncertainties such as sensor noise and environmental disturbances. Based on this information, we can verify the safety of the vehicle for some future time interval if the vehicle’s road occupancy area does not intersect with that of other road participants.

Finally, we discuss a recent rule-based approach to the safety of ADSs, namely the responsibility-sensitive safety (RSS) framework. RSS introduces a set of mathematically defined safety rules, each of which is adapted to an individual driving scenario. In general, there is a big gap between driving safely and arguing that vehicles can do so—a gap that is currently hindering the public acceptance of automated driving. Rule-based safety arguments, such as those enabled by RSS, bridge the gap and thus play a crucial role in the deployment of automated driving in the real world.

7.2 Hierarchy of Decision Making

As depicted in Fig. 7.1, the decision making of a ADS mainly consists of four hierarchical components: a route planner, a behavioral planner, a motion planner, and a local feedback controller.

7.2.1 Route Planner

A route planner is at the highest level of the decision-making hierarchy. The role of this component is to plan a static route through the road network toward a given target destination, which is represented as a directed graph with weighted edges, where a weight can represent the travel time or the cost of taking a particular road. Therefore, a route planning problem can be formulated as finding a path with minimum cost in a directed graph. Since a road network graph may contain millions of nodes and edges, the application of route-planner is an important driving force behind the research on speedup techniques for shortest path algorithms [8]. Efficient route planning algorithms are up to three million times faster than Dijkstra’s algorithm [18], and are capable of computing an optimal route on continent-scale benchmark instances in milliseconds [8]. We invite an interested reader to see [8, 18] for comprehensive surveys of practical route-planning algorithms.

7.2.2 Behavioral Planner (Maneuver Planner)

Given a sequence of road segments of the planned static route, the task of a behavioral planner is to plan appropriate driving maneuvers (e.g., cruise-in-lane, change-lane, parking) based on perceived information of other traffic participants, obstacles, road conditions, and signals from infrastructure. For instance, at an intersection, the behavioral planner of the ego vehicle needs to decide between “passing” and “yielding” maneuvers based on its perceived behaviors and predicted intentions of other traffic participants [34]. Several techniques for intention prediction and future trajectories estimation of other road participants have been studied, e.g., learning-based techniques [29, 41] and probabilistic planning formalisms [10, 34].

7.2.3 Motion Planner

After the behavioral layer decides the driving maneuver of the ego vehicle, a motion planner is responsible for computing a path or a trajectory, where a trajectory is a path with a prescribed velocity profile along the path. The computed path or trajectory must be dynamically feasible for the vehicle model, comfortable for the passenger, and avoid collisions with obstacles and other traffic participants. The motion planning problems are generally formulated as optimisation problems, whose exact solutions are mostly computationally intractable. Therefore, numerical approximation and heuristic methods are typically used in practice. We will discuss the motion planning layer in more detail in Section 7.3.

7.2.4 Feedback Controller

A feedback controller’s task is to select appropriate actuator inputs that execute the reference path or trajectory computed by the motion planner. The controller needs to execute the planned motion while dealing with tracking errors due to the inaccuracies of the vehicle model used by the motion planner and other road participants’ trajectories prediction errors. A survey of effective feedback controllers is discussed in [53].

7.3 Motion Planning

In this chapter, we focus on the motion planning layer, in which various challenges of an ADS are the most manifest. There are many motion planning techniques designed for various driving scenarios such as highway driving, parking, and urban driving in cities with intersections and roundabouts (see [27] and the references therein). In what follows, we start with an overview of some optimisation-based and model-predictive motion planning techniques. Then we discuss game theory-based and other planning approaches.

7.3.1 Optimisation-Based Approaches

We provide an overview of optimisation-based trajectory planning approaches for ADSs. Specifically, we explain some techniques introduced by the earlier works [71] and [48], and provide a discussion on the more recent literature that employ related techniques. In the literature, planned trajectories are commonly described by using Frenet frames. Moreover, Frenet frames are also used for characterising lattice-based discretisations of the road. For this reason, we start our exposition with an explanation of Frenet frames defined for smooth planar curves [42].

7.3.1.1 Planar Curves and Frenet Frames

Many trajectory planning algorithms use smooth planar curves to represent possible paths on a road. Such curves can also be used for characterising the roads themselves (see, e.g., [12]). Let p: [0,L] → ℝ2 be a smooth planar curve of length L < 0. We use s ∈ [0,L] to denote the arc length along this curve and e1 : [0,L] → R2 to denote the tangential vector that satisfies

(7.1)
e1⊤(s)e1(s) = 1,

(7.2)
$$\frac{\text{d}p(s)}{\text{d}s} = e_{1}(s),$$

where (·)⊺ denotes transpose. now, let e2 : [0,L] → R2 be given by

(7.3)
$$e_{2}(s) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & {- 1} \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}e_{1}(s).$$

The vector e2(s) is called the normal vector at arc length s and the pair (e1(s),e2(s)) is referred as the Frenet frame [42]. An illustration of the Frenet frame is given in Fig. 7.2.

It follows respectively from (7.1) and (7.3) that we have $e_{1}^{\text{T}}(s)\frac{\text{d}e_{1}(s)}{\text{d}s} = 0$ and e1(s)e2(s) = 0. As a consequence, for each arc length s, there exists a unique scalar κ(s) ∈ ℝ such that


$$\frac{\text{d}e_{1}(s)}{\text{d}s} = \kappa(s)e_{2}(s).$$

Here, κ : [0,L] → ℝ is called the curvature. Using the curvature, we can obtains as, the orientation θ ∈ ℝ of the curve at arc length s as θ(s) = θ0 + ∫0sκ(τ)dτ, where θ0 is the initial orientation.

In the following, we first look at a trajectory generation approach where the goal is to find the optimal movements along the axes of the Frenet frame.

7.3.1.2 Optimal Trajectory Generation Using Frenet Frames

The work [71] uses planar curves and Frenet frames for generating optimal trajectories for a vehicle on a highway. In particular, a planar curve p is used as an ideal path along a given road. This ideal path is also referred as the center line. Frenet frames along the curve p are then used for representing locations of points on generated trajectories.

Consider a trajectory x: [0,T] → ℝ2 parameterised with time t ∈ [0,T]. The location of a point on this trajectory at any given time t can be represented using the Frenet frames that move along p. Specifically, x(t) can be given by


x(t)=p(s(t))+d(t) e_2(s(t)),

where s(t) denotes the arc length at time t, and d(t) is the lateral offset from p at that time, as shown in Fig. 7.3. notice that given the ideal path p, the point x(t) ∈ ℝ2 can be represented equivalently with the pair (d(t),s(t)).

The key idea in [71] is to separately design the lateral offset d and the arc length s as functions of time t. The design is based on an optimisation framework with different parameters for different on-road tasks such as velocity keeping, following, and stopping.

The first step in the optimisation framework of [71] is to find d: [t0,t1] → ℝ and s: [t0,t1] → ℝ that minimise certain cost functions over a given time interval [t0,t1] The parameters and the structure of the cost functions differ for each different task. For instance, the cost for the lateral offset in the case of high speed lane keeping task can be written as


$$C_{d} = k_{1}{\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}{\overset{¨}{d}}^{2}}(\tau)\text{d}\tau + k_{2}\left( {t_{1} - t_{0}} \right) + k_{3}d^{2}\left( t_{1} \right),$$

where k1,k2,k3 > 0 are the weight coefficients that characterise the contribution of different cost terms. The first cost term ${\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}{\dddot{d}}^{2}}(\tau)\text{d}\tau$ is the integral of the lateral jerk (time-derivative of the acceleration) and is related to the passenger comfort, the second term t1 — t0 is the total time length, and the last term d2 (t1) is the squared lateral deviation from the path at the final time t1.

Given the initial time to and the initial offset d(t0) as well as its derivatives d(t0), d(t0), the algorithm of [71] first prepares a set of different candidate time intervals Tj (representing t1 — t0) and candidate final lateral offsets dj (representing d(t1)), where j denotes the candidate index. For each candidate j, the integral cost ${\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{0} + T_{j}}{\dddot{d}}^{2}}(\tau)\text{d}\tau$ is minimised by considering the boundary conditions


$$d(t_{0} + T_{j}) = d_{j},\overset{˙}{d}(t_{0} + T_{j}) = 0,\overset{¨}{d}(t_{0} + T_{j}) = 0.$$

For each j, the minimisation yields d(t) as a quintic polynomial over t ∈[t0,t0+ Tj]. Then, the total cost $C_{d,j} = k_{1}{\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{0} + T_{j}}{\dddot{d}}^{2}}(\tau)\text{d}\tau + k_{2}T_{j} + k_{3}d_{j}$ is computed to evaluate the performance of the associated trajectory.

An important point of the algorithm is that certain candidate trajectories can be discarded if they fail validity checks. Valid trajectories are the ones that avoid collision and stay within the drivable road areas. noting that a similar optimisation approach (with different cost structure and parameters) is used for designing the arc length s as a function of time, validity checks can be conducted for the candidate pairs (d, s). The algorithm picks the valid trajectories for both d and s that yield the lowest costs.

Repeated Trajectory Optimisation

The trajectory optimisation for d and s is repeated frequently to take account of potential variations in the road environment. The duration of the planned trajectories can be longer than the time period between two consecutive optimisations. An important point of the algorithm of [71] is that the end times of the candidate trajectories in any optimisation overlap with the end times of candidate trajectories of previous optimisations. This ensures “temporal consistency”, meaning that a computed optimal trajectory is followed without any modification if the environment does not change. A related goal is to ensure that the vehicle’s acceleration does not face instantaneous jumps between two motion planning cycles. This is achieved if the end-point acceleration values of sequentially planned trajectories are equal. The work [78] proposes a re-planning scheme to achieve this. The scheme proposed in that work also accounts for the processing time needed for trajectory optimisation.

Practical Issues

Optimisation-based approaches with the Frenet frame representation can handle static/dynamic obstacles as well as stop signs, speed limits, and traffic lights commonly faced in the urban traffic [20]. For instance, it is mentioned in [20] that a red traffic light can be represented as an obstacle that is present for a certain time period, and furthermore, speed limits and stop signs can be considered as velocity constraints. Moreover, the work [22] discusses how a Frenet frame-based trajectory planner can be equipped in an autonomous driving system with sensing and control components.

It is discussed in [46] that Frenet frame-based planning approaches may have performance issues on roads with large curvatures (representing sharp turns). There, a new optimisation-based approach is proposed to conduct trajectory planning in the Cartesian frame.

7.3.1.3 Spatiotemporal Lattices

We next look at the motion planning framework introduced by [48]. This framework uses both state lattices and spatiotemporal lattices in construction of a search space with finitely many elements representing potential trajectories of an on-road vehicle for several seconds. Similarly to the approach of [71], this framework can generate maneuvers around the center line of a road lane that avoid hitting static/dynamic obstacles. One of the key features of the framework of [48] is that it takes account of the kinematic constraints of a vehicle. This allows generation of trajectories that the vehicle can follow exactly. In addition, the lattice structures proposed in [48] also enable expressing relatively complex maneuvers.

State lattices were used previously in planning problems in different settings (see, e.g., [54]). The lattice-based framework of [48] is different from those of the previous works in that it is designed to be used in a structured environment such as highways with moving traffic.

State Lattices

We start with a short description of the state lattices considered in [48]. Similarly to [71], first, the center line of a lane is considered as a curve that is parameterized with arc length. Cartesian coordinates, orientation, and curvature of the center line at arc length s are represented respectively by x(s),y(s), θ(s), κ(s). Any arbitrary point on the road that is not on the center line can be characterized similarly. In particular, a point at arc length s and at lateral offset d has the Cartesian coordinates

(7.4)
x(s, d) = x(s) + dcos (θ(s)),

(7.5)
y(s, d) = y(s) + dsin (θ(s)),

the orientation

(7.6)
θ(s, d) = θ(s),

and the curvature

(7.7)
κ(s, d) = (κ − 1(s) + d) − 1.

Construction of the state lattice is based on discretisation of the arc length and lateral offset. More specifically, the lattice is composed of vertices at uniformly-separated increasing arc lengths s0, s1 ,… , sn-1 and uniformly-separated increasing lateral offsets d0,d1,2026 , dM-1. Each vertex in the lattice corresponds to a different pair of arc length and lateral offset. The Cartesian coordinates of each vertex are obtained by using (7.4) and (7.5), and moreover, the orientation and the curvature are obtained through (7.6) and (7.7). An illustration of the state lattice is given in Fig. 7.4.

The work [48] generates a path between two vertices in the state lattice by designing the curvature as a function of the arc length along the path. Each curvature function is defined as a cubic polynomial, and the coefficients of this polynomial are identified by considering the kinematic model of a vehicle. Given the known initial position (first vertex) and the desired final position (second vertex), the coefficients are obtained by solving equations with end-point constraints. The utility of this approach is that a vehicle with the considered model is guaranteed to be able to follow the generated path.

The works [14, 16] also take into account the constraints induced by the kinematic model of a vehicle. In [14], clothoids are used for representing potential paths of a vehicle, and moreover, probabilistic risk assessment methods are utilised for characterising the cost terms that are related to the safety of those paths. In [16], the authors tackle the problem of motion planning on general road networks composed of lanes, intersections, and roundabouts.

Spatiotemporal Lattices and Trajectories

Paths between the vertices of the state lattice do not contain any timing or velocity information, as the curvatures are characterized as functions of arc length instead of time. The work [48] supplements each generated path with time and velocity components. In particular, given a starting time, a starting velocity, and a constant acceleration value, the velocity profile of a vehicle moving on a path can be identified uniquely. Based on this observation, [48] extends the state lattice to a spatiotemporal lattice. Vertices in the spatiotemporal lattice contains not only the information of Cartesian coordinates, orientation, and curvature (x,y, θ, κ), but also time and velocity (t, v). Connecting a pair of vertices in the spatiotemporal lattice corresponds to a trajectory. Figure 7.5 illustrates an example spatiotemporal lattice, where a trajectory is indicated by two vertices with different spatial and temporal components.

Costs Assigned to Paths and Trajectories

Once the spatiotemporal lattice is constructed, the framework of [48] assigns costs to pairs of vertices in the lattice. Then the sequence of vertices with the minimum sum of costs can be chosen as the best motion plan. The costs can penalize lateral acceleration to promote comfort, and moreover, they can penalize foreseen collisions with static/dynamic obstacles to ensure safety. An important aspect of the approach of [48] is that multiple trajectories can use the same path. To avoid repeated computations, the cost terms that depend only on position and curvature (but not time and velocity) are evaluated only once using the path information. These costs are often associated with efficiency, comfort, or safety. Physical interpretations and impacts of many different cost terms are provided in [73]. Moreover, a variety of common cost functions used in motion planning benchmarks are also discussed in [5].

Computational Issues

As a spatiotemporal lattice can have many vertices, direct search within the lattice can be slow. However, spatiotemporal lattices of [48] allow efficient re-parametrisations, which makes motion planning fast. The approach presented there is reported to be capable of repetitively planning the motion of a vehicle at every 0.1 seconds on a standard computer.

7.3.1.4 Trajectory Optimisation in Different Architectures

So far we have looked at works that propose motion planning techniques with the goal of finding trajectories that are optimal with respect to certain criteria. There are a few works where trajectory optimisation is combined with other concerns. For instance, [47] aims to ensure fail-safe operation. According to the architecture proposed in that work, in each planning cycle, the vehicle applies either the optimal trajectory or a certain collision-free emergency maneuver. The optimal trajectory is selected only if that trajectory guarantees existence of an emergency maneuver in future planning cycles. Otherwise, the vehicle executes the emergency maneuver. Typically, optimisation-based motion planners are considered to be separate components that interact with sensing, prediction, and local control components. However, we also note that there are approaches where sensing, prediction, planning, and control tasks are combined in a single component to enable the so-called end-to-end self-driving (see, e.g., [9, 60]).

7.3.2 Model Predictive Control Approach

Optimisation-based approaches discussed in Section 7.3.1 generate optimal trajectories as motion plans and pass them to local controllers. The role of a local controller is to provide control commands (e.g., steering angle and acceleration) to the vehicle so that the trajectories can be followed closely. The model predictive control (MPC) approach proposed in [50] provides combined trajectory generation and local control. In what follows, we present a short overview of this approach.

First, we describe the framework developed in [50] for generating optimal paths and trajectories to help a vehicle to move from an initial position to a desired destination in an environment with obstacles.

7.3.2.1 Visibility Graphs and Optimal Paths

The initial step for the path generation approach of [50] is to create a visibility graph. The nodes in a visibility graph are the initial position of the vehicle, the desired destination of the vehicle, and the corners of the polygons representing obstacles. The edges correspond to visibility lines between the nodes (see Fig. 7.6).

The edges in the visibility graph are assigned positive weights [50]. The weights of the edges that are not connected to the initial position or the destination are proportional to the physical distance between the connected nodes. On the other hand, the edges that are connected to either the initial position or the destination are assigned weights based on both the physical distances and the so-called orientation gaps. To compute an orientation gap, one needs the information of the initial orientation of the vehicle and its required final orientation at the destination. Orientation gap for an edge connected to the initial position is the angle between the orientation of the edge and the initial orientation. Orientation gaps for the edges connected to the destination are computed similarly.

Once all edges are assigned weights, one can use a search algorithm (e.g., A*) to find the path with minimum total weight that connects the initial position to the destination [50].

7.3.2.2 Reference Trajectory

The obtained optimal path is then used for generating a reference trajectory. This is done by assigning a velocity profile that describes the velocity of the vehicle at different positions on the path. The trajectory is represented with the sequence r(0), r(1), , r(T —1) ∈ ℝ2, where r(0) is the initial position of the vehicle, and r(t) represents the position at time tΔ, where Δ is the sampling and the control input update period of the vehicle.

7.3.2.3 MPC Approach to Follow the Reference Trajectory

The goal of the model predictive control approach in [50] is to make the vehicle follow the reference trajectory closely. This is achieved by minimising a cost (related to the distance from the trajectory) in a rolling horizon fashion. In a simplified setting, the objective can be set to minimise

(7.8)
$$\left. \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{h} \right\|\left. p(t + i \mid t) - r(t + i) \right\|^{2},$$

at each time t, where h is a positive integer denoting the optimisation horizon, r (t + i) ∈ ℝ2 is the desired position on the reference trajectory at time t + i, and p(t +i|t) ∈ ℝ2 is the prediction regarding the position of the vehicle at time t + i. The prediction is obtained at time t by using the vehicle dynamics


$$\begin{array}{l} {�x(t + i + 1 \mid t) = f(x(t + i \mid t),u(t + i)),����i \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots h - 1 \right\},�} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, p(t + i \mid t) = g(x(t + i \mid t)),} \\ \end{array}$$

where x(t + i|t) ∈ℝn is the state variable with x(t|t) = x(t) denoting the state measurement at time t, u(t + i) ∈ ℝm is the control input, f : ℝn × ℝm →ℝn describes the evolution of the state over one time step, and g: ℝn → ℝ2 is a function that maps the vehicle’s state variable to vehicle position.

The cost in (7.8) is minimised with respect to the control inputs u(t), u(t + 1), . , u(t + h — 1). The optimisation problem in [50] incorporates multiple weighted cost terms and it also includes constraints on p(t + i|t) and u(t + i) so as to keep a certain distance from the obstacles and to satisfy actuation constraints (e.g., maximum acceleration).

The framework of [50] uses the MPC approach. The key idea in MPC is to solve the optimisation problem at time t, find optimal control inputs for the entire horizon (from t to t +h— 1), and apply the first control input to the system (see, e.g., [11, 58] for more detailed discussions). The optimisation problem is solved again at the next time step t + 1. This idea is illustrated in Fig. 7.7.

The utility of the MPC approach is that the optimisation problem is solved repeatedly with updated information about the system states. Uncertainties in the system and the environment as well as constraints on the inputs and the states can be explicitly taken into account [11, 58]. In particular, nonlinear model predictive control can be used for handling the planning and control needs when nonlinear vehicle models are considered (see, e.g., [28, 70]). In addition, robust MPC methods can be employed for operation under uncertainty. For instance, a robust tube-based MPC approach was developed in [39] to tackle scenarios where the obstacle information available to the ego-vehicle is subject to uncertainties. MPC-based approaches can also handle more complicated objectives involving passenger comfort and lane keeping performance (see [30, 44]).

MPC-based approaches are also used in other domains. For instance, [7] uses MPC in trajectory generation for robotic arms, and moreover, [76] uses an MPC- based approach to find optimal routes and schedules for a group of vehicles in mobility-on-demand systems.

7.3.3 Game Theory-Based Approaches

Let us consider the road situation in Fig. 7.8. While driving on the highway, we notice a vehicle trying to cut closely in front of us. In this situation, we can safely avoid the collision if we apply a sudden brake and let the other vehicle cut in. However, if we accelerate, we may force the other vehicle to decelerate and move to our lane behind us so that we could avoid the accident without a sudden brake.

A game theory-based decision-making approach can naturally model the above inter-vehicle interactions in a human-like manner [61, 75]. Game theory-based approaches model the vehicles as players of the game, where the reward functions are designed based on several criteria such as the speed of the ego vehicle, the distance between vehicles, and the jerk-based smoothness of our movement. Then, the players decide their actions by optimizing their reward in response to the actions of others.

In this section, we focus on game theory-based approaches that model the vehicle interactions as a Stackelberg (or leader-follower) dynamic game [23, 55, 57, 61]. We first introduce the framework in [55, 57]. Let us consider n vehicles, where the state (e.g., information of position and speed of the vehicle) of each vehicle i ∈ {1, ,n} at time t ≥ 0 is represented by xi (t). Then, we assume that the dynamics of the vehicle i is


xi(t + Δ) = fθi(xi(t), ui(t)),

where fθ, is the discrete-time dynamics function, Δ is the duration between discrete time steps, and ui is the control input of the decision-maker of vehicle i. We assume that the dynamics function fθi, is dependent on a set θi of parameters such as the navigation path, target region, aggressiveness, and priority to the right of way. The parameters θj of the other vehicles j ≠i are unknown to i.

The high-level overview of the algorithms in [55, 57] is depicted in Fig. 7.9. First, the decision-maker of the ego vehicle i observes the states of each nearby vehicle j(step-1). Based on the observation, the ego vehicle i initiates the parameters in θj,i, which is the estimation of θj (step-2). Then, the ego vehicle computes an optimal control input based on fθ̂j,i (step-3). In the next time step, the ego vehicle observes the other vehicles and updates the parameters in and repeats the process.

We compute the optimal control input in step-3 by computing an equilibrium of a Stackelberg (or leader-follower) game: a strategic game in which the leader player makes her decision first and then the follower player decides her action sequentially. For simplicity, we consider a two-player Stackelberg game played between two players: l and f, which are the leader and follower, respectively. Let the reward of player i ∈ {l,f} at each time step t be given by Ri(ui(t),ui(t)), where j ≠i is the other player and Ri is a reward function of i computed using xi(t), (t), fθ, and fθ̂j,i The reward function can be designed based on several criteria such as the ego vehicle’s speed, the distance between vehicles, and the smoothness of the movement.

Algorithm 1 Algorithm for a two-player Stackelberg game equilibrium.
1 ul∗ ← an arbitrary control input of the leader.

2

for each control input ul of the leader do

3

uf∗(ul) ← an arbitrary control input of the follower.

4

for each control input uf of the follower do

5

if Rf (ul,uf) > Rf (ul,uf∗ (ul)) then

6

ul∗(ul) ←uf

7

if Rl(ul,uf∗ (ul)) > Rl(ul∗,uf∗ (ul∗)) or uf∗ (ul∗) is undefined then

8

(u∗l,uf∗) ← (ul,uf∗ (ul))

9

Then, at each time step, a Stackelberg equilibrium (ul∗>,uf∗) is computed as in Algorithm 1. Figure 7.10 shows the decision tree corresponding to Algorithm 1 for the example situation in Fig. 7.8. notice that the leader makes the decision first, then the follower selects the best control input based on the leader’s decision. Figure 7.10 shows possible decisions of the players in terms of the control inputs associated with acceleration and braking actions. As the leader usually has the advantage, the computed equilibrium depends on which player is the leader. The leader and the follower of the game can either be fixed for all time steps [23, 61] or decided adaptively based on the observations at previous time steps [55, 57].

The main advantages of game theory-based decision-making approaches are that (1) they can model rational vehicle interactions in a human-like manner, and (2) they do not require previous training data as they are adaptive to changes (based on observation). However, as shown in Algorithm 1, the approaches require the control input set to be finite. Moreover, the complexity of the algorithms can be high if we consider a large set of actions and a game with many players [55].

7.3.4 Other Approaches

In this section, we looked at optimisation-based, model predictive control, and game theory-based motion planning approaches that are well-suited for autonomous vehicles. There are motion planning approaches such as sampling-based motion planning, which was originally designed for robots but can be applied to certain driving scenarios. Regardless of the state space and dynamic constraints, the sampling-based methods explore the state space and find an optimal path using random sampling. Examples of well-known sampling-based motion planning methods are Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM) [38], Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT) [45], and RRT* [37]. We refer interested readers to [40, 53] for the surveys of sampling-based motion planning approaches.

In recent years, machine learning techniques have had a significant impact on autonomous driving. Several machine learning paradigms, such as deep learning and reinforcement learning, have shown their efficiency both in academia and industry and have been continuously developed [29, 41]. However, one crucial issue of the learning-based approaches is the lack of formal guarantees and valid explanations for their reasoning. Although Explainable Artificial Intelligence has been widely studied, it is arguable whether the existing methods are adequate to provide trust in the decision-making for autonomous vehicles [26].

In the following sections, we introduce some formal verification techniques to ensure the safety of autonomous vehicles. We first introduce online verification techniques using reachability analysis methods, where the goal is to compute potential road occupancy areas of the ego vehicle and other road participants in Section 7.4. Then, in Section 7.5 we discuss the Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS) framework: a framework that derives logical safety rules from the traffic regulations and common senses.

7.4 Online Verification Using Reachability Analysis

Formal verification can be combined with behavior and motion planners to ensure the safety of the autonomous vehicle. The safety of the vehicle is guaranteed for some future time interval if the vehicle’s road occupancy area does not intersect with that of other road participants during the time interval. In order to verify the safety online, we can apply reachability analysis to predict all possible road occupancies of all road participants by considering all possible uncertainties such as sensor noise and environmental disturbances. In this section, we introduce two approaches for safety verification: the set-based and the probabilistic approaches.

7.4.1 Set-Based Reachability Analysis for Safety Verification

Set-based approaches verify the safety of autonomous vehicles by computing a set that contains all possible road occupancy areas of all road participants during a considered future time interval. In this section, we briefly introduce an approach to overapproximate the reachable set of the autonomous vehicle that is proposed in [3, 4]. Let X, R(0), and U be the state space, the bounded set of initial states, and the bounded set of inputs, respectively. The dynamics of the vehicle is given by a nonlinear function ẋ = f(x,u), where x(t) ∈ X is the state vector and u(t) is the input vector at time t. The solution of this system at time t is denoted by χ(t,xin,u), where xin is the initial state vector. The reachable set during time interval tf is


ℛe([0, tf]) = {χ(t,xin,u)∣t∈[0,tf],xin∈ℛ(0),u(t)∈𝒰}.

The reachable set Re([0,tf]) cannot be exactly computed in general. We, therefore, compute its overapproximation R([0,tf]) ⊇ Re([0,tf]), which is a compact convex set that can be represented by a polytope or a zonotope. The overapproximated reachable set is computed by considering each time interval [tk, tk+1], where tk+1 - tk is constant for all time step k = 0. The set R([tk, tk+1]) is then computed from a linear system obtained by linearising the original nonlinear dynamics using a first-order Taylor expansion, then the linearisation errors are overapproximated using the Lagrange remainders. We consider a linearisation point z∗ = [x∗,u∗]⊺, where x∗ and u∗ are points of state and input, respectively. One possible choice for z∗ is the center of R([tk−1, tk]) and U. then, using the first-order Taylor expansion around the point z∗, the original differential equation of the ith coordinate is enclosed by

(7.9)
$$\left. \forall t \in \lbrack t_{k},t_{k + 1}\rbrack,{\overset{˙}{x}}_{i}(t) \in f_{i}(z^{\ast},u^{\ast}) + \frac{\partial f_{i}(z,u^{\ast})}{\partial z} \middle| {}_{z = z^{\ast}}(z - z^{\ast}) \oplus \mathcal{L}_{i}(\lbrack t_{k},t_{k + 1}\rbrack), \right.$$

where ⊕ is the Minkowski addition and ℒ is the Lagrange remainder that covers all possible linearisation errors, which can be computed using interval arithmetic [4, 36]. Then, the overapproximated convex reachable sets are computed using the linearised system (7.9).

The set-based reachability analysis is an efficient methodology for the safety verification of autonomous vehicles. The approach has been demonstrated by test drives with an autonomous vehicle [4].

7.4.2 Probabilistic Approach Through Moment Propagation

Another approach to guarantee the safety of the autonomous vehicle is to use probabilistic verification. We focus on the method proposed in [56], which approximates the moments of a discrete-time polynomial stochastic system. These approximate moments are used to compute probability bounds for the state to be outside of given regions.

We consider a finite-dimensional discrete-time stochastic polynomial system

(7.10)
$$x(t + 1) = \sum\limits_{i = 0}^{d_{s}}F_{i}(t)x^{\lbrack i\rbrack}(t),\,\,\,\,\, t \in {\mathbb{N}},$$

where x(0) = xin is a given initial state, x(t)i∈ ℝn is the state vector, x[i] is the ith Kronecker power of x, and Fi(t) ∈ ℝn×ni are randomly-varying coefficient matrices for all i ∈ {0,1, . . .,dS}. We assume that the vector xin and the matricesF(t), t ∈ ℕ, are all independent. Moreover, F(t), t ∈ℕ, are identically distributed.

We use Carleman linearisation to obtain an infinite-dimensional linear system that describes the evolution of the Kronecker powers of the state vector x(t). By defining


$$F(t) = \lbrack\begin{matrix} {F_{0}(t)} & {F_{1}(t)} & {F_{2}(t)} & \cdots & {F_{d_{s}}(t)} \\ \end{matrix}\rbrack$$

and


$$y(k,t) = {\lbrack\begin{matrix} 1 & {x{(t)}^{\top}} & {x^{\lbrack 2\rbrack}{(t)}^{\top}} & \cdots & {x^{\lbrack k\rbrack}{(t)}^{\top}} \\ \end{matrix}\rbrack}^{\top},$$

the dynamical system (7.10) can be rewritten as


x(t + 1) = F(t)y(dS, t).

By using the mixed-product property of the Kronecker product, we obtain


$$\begin{array}{l} {x^{\lbrack j\rbrack}(t + 1)\,\, = F^{\lbrack j\rbrack}(t)y^{\lbrack j\rbrack}(d_{S},t)} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = \sum\limits_{k = 0}^{jd_{S}}(\sum\limits_{{(i_{l})}_{l \leq j} \in H_{j,k}}F_{i_{1}}(t) \otimes \cdots \otimes F_{i_{j}}(t))x^{\lbrack k\rbrack}(t),} \\ \end{array}$$

for j ∈ ℕ, where


$$H_{j,k} = \left\{ {\left( i_{l} \right)_{l \leq j}\left| {\underset{j}{\overset{l = 1}{\sum^{}}}i_{l} = k~and~i_{l} \leq d_{S}} \right.} \right\}.$$

In order to give a simpler description of the system, we introduce the matrices


$$A_{j,k}(t) = \underset{{(i_{i})}_{l \leq j} \in H_{j,k}}{\sum^{}}F_{i_{1}}(t) \otimes \cdots \otimes F_{i_{j}}(t),$$

and


$$A(t;n,M) = \begin{bmatrix} {A_{0,0}(t)} & \cdots & {A_{0,M}(t)} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ {A_{n,0}(t)} & \cdots & {A_{n,M}(t)} \\ \end{bmatrix}.$$

Then, for any k ∈ ℕ, we have

(7.11)
$$\begin{array}{l} {y(k,t + 1) = {\lbrack\begin{array}{llll} 1 & {x^{\lbrack 1\rbrack}{(t + 1)}^{\top}} & \cdots & {x^{\lbrack k\rbrack}{(t + 1)}^{\top}} \\ \end{array}\rbrack}^{\top}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = A(t;k,kd_{S}){\lbrack\begin{array}{llll} 1 & {x^{\lbrack 1\rbrack}{(t)}^{\top}} & \cdots & {x^{\lbrack kd_{S}\rbrack}{(t)}^{\top}} \\ \end{array}\rbrack}^{\top}} \\ {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = A(t;k,kd_{S})y(kd_{S},t).} \\ \end{array}$$

note that the vector y(k,t) contains all Kronecker powers x[0](t),x[1](t),...x[k](t) of the state x(t). We now derive the deterministic system that describes the evolution of the moments of x(t) by taking expectation in (7.11). This gives


$$\mathbb{E}\lbrack\begin{matrix} 1 & {x^{\lbrack 1\rbrack}{(t)}^{\top}} & \cdots & {x^{\lbrack k\rbrack}{(t)}^{\top}\rbrack = \mathbb{E}\lbrack y(k,t + 1)\rbrack = E(k,kd_{S})\mathbb{E}\lbrack y(kd_{S},t)\rbrack,} \\ \end{matrix}$$

where E(k,kdS) is the expectation of A(t;k,kdS), which is independent of t thanks to the assumption that the matrices F(t),t ∈ ℕ, are all independent and identically distributed.

Using the first and second moments, E[x(t)] and E[x[2](t)], at a given time t, we can compute probability bounds for the state vector x(t) using Chebyshev’s inequality. However, to compute the second moment E[x[2](t)], we need the knowledge of matrices E(2,2dS), E(2ds,2dS2), ..., E(2dSt−1,2dSt) of exponentially increasing dimensions. As a result, the exact computation for the moments becomes infeasible when t is large. Therefore, we need an efficient approach to approximate the moments at a given time t. The approach in [56] considers the truncated system with a fixed truncation limit. We nT ∈ ℕ and define x̃i(t) ∈ ℝni, i ∈ 1, . . ., nT, by


$${\lbrack\begin{matrix} 1 & {{\widetilde{x}}_{1}{(t)}^{\top}} & \cdots & {{\widetilde{x}}_{n_{T}}{(t)}^{\top}} \\ \end{matrix}\rbrack}^{\top} = E{(n_{T},n_{T})}^{t}{\lbrack\begin{matrix} 1 & {\mathbb{E}\lbrack x_{in}} \\ \end{matrix}\rbrack}^{\top}\,\,\ldots\,\,\mathbb{E}{\lbrack x_{in}^{\lbrack n_{T}\rbrack}\rbrack}^{\top}\rbrack^{\top}.$$

The vector x̃i(t) represents an approximation of the moment E[x[i](t)] that is computed using only our knowledge of the first nT moments of xin. The truncated system allows us to iteratively compute approximations of the moments of x(t) at consecutive time instants. The approach only requires an offline computation of the matrix E(nT,nT )t . Efficient ways to compute the upper bounds of the truncation error are proposed in [56]. Figure 7.11 shows the over-approximated road occupancy with probability 0.9, which is computed using Chebyshev’s inequality, of an autonomous vehicle modeled using kinematic bicycle model in [56].

7.5 Responsibility-Sensitive Safety

7.5.1 What is RSS?

Responsibility-sensitive safety (RSS) is an approach to the ADS safety that attracts growing attention. Safety is a central theme in every aspect of the ADS research, including the approaches we discussed earlier in this chapter. RSS is unique among these approaches in that it provides safety rules that are rigorously formulated in mathematical terms. Unlike the algorithms and techniques we discussed earlier, RSS is not so much about how to drive safely as about breaking down the ultimate goal (namely safety) into concrete and instantly-checkable conditions. The goal of RSS is that those safety rules guarantee the ADS safety in the rigorous form of mathematical proofs. How far RSS has gone so far towards this ultimate goal of ADS safety proofs, and what are still needed for the ultimate goal, are questions that we will discuss later in Section 7.5.6.

The methodology and basic techniques of RSS are first introduced by researchers at Mobileye/Intel [64], The safety rules derived in RSS have a variety of possible usages (as we will discuss in Section 7.5.5), giving RSS a multifaceted character. Moreover, its presentation to non-expert audience such as Mobileye/hitel’s webpage5

Remark 7.1 (RSS terminologies) Although there are already a number of research works on RSS as well as practical works (including the efforts to use it in international standards), comprehensive technical accounts on RSS are scarce. In particular, terminologies for the core concepts in RSS do not seem to be fixed in the literature.

In this section, we will use the terminologies listed in Table 7.1. note that they may differ from the terminologies used in the literature (which vary from a paper to another). The notions in the table will be introduced in due course. Their correspondence to those used in the original paper [64] is also shown in the table.

Table 7.1: RSS terminologies
In this section in [64] Meaning

RSS safety rule

(no explicit name)

A pair of an RSS safety condition and a proper response

RSS safety condition

Safe distance

An instantly-checkable condition that guarantees safety henceforth. Often stated in terms of a safety distance

Proper response

Proper response

A control strategy that realises safety
