9.1.1 Interactive Theorem Proving

In interactive theorem proving, a proof is written by a human prover. The difference from the usual pen-and-paper mathematical proofs is that they are written in a piece of software called a proof assistant. A proof assistant can help a human prover with many functionalities, the most important of which being proof check (checking if each logical reasoning step in a proof is valid). For example, checking the validity of a 1,000-page pen-and-paper proof is unrealistic; in contrast, a big proof in a proof assistant can be validated mechanically.

Therefore, interactive theorem proving is really about manual theorem proving. It is called interactive since proofs are written in the interaction between a human prover and a proof assistant.

In this chapter, after reviewing the landscape of different proof assistants (Section 9.3.1), we review a well-known proof assistant called Isabelle/HOL (Section 9.3.2).

9.1.2 Automated Theorem Proving

Interactive theorem proving is costly—it is not uncommon that a single proof takes months or years to complete. Therefore automation of proof search has been actively sought. There are some no-go results for automated theorem proving—the most famous one being Gödel’s incompleteness theorem—and in general proof search is an expensive computational task. Nevertheless, the rise of SAT and SMT solvers is making automated theorem proving an attractive approach to many real-world problems.

SAT solvers prove propositional formulas (cf. Section 9.2) and they are complete (they can prove every formula that is semantically true). While the worst-case complexity is not good (NP-complete), it has been observed that modern SAT solvers can efficiently handle big formulas in real-world problems. We review SAT solvers in Section 9.4.2.

SMT solvers prove first-order formulas (cf. Section 9.2) and they are usually incomplete (they may not prove every formula that is semantically true). Still, their enhanced expressivity—they can prove formulas about real numbers, for example—is a great advantage and it has opened up many new applications. SMT solvers are reviewed in Section 9.4.3.

9.1.3 Accommodation of Continuous and Hybrid Dynamics

Accommodation of continuous and hybrid dynamics—where hybrid means the combination of discrete/digital and continuous/physical—may not sound easy for theorem proving approaches, since the latter are traditionally developed for safety assurance of (pure) software. However, the study of hybrid systems theorem-proving initiated in 2000s has identified many commonalities in software science and control theory—a scientific field that traditionally studies continuous dynamics. Thanks to its findings, we now see multiple approaches and tools that can efficiently prove theorems about continuous or hybrid dynamics.

In Section 9.5.1, we review one such tool called KeYmaera X. It is an interactive proof assistant in principle, but comes with many automation techniques, especially around the use of symbolic computer algebra engines.

9.1.4 Model Refinement

A big burden for theorem proving in practice is the problem of modelling. In mathematics, to state a theorem and prove it, one has to define all the notions used in the theorem. In safety assurance of automotive and other systems by theorem proving, therefore, one has to define what the target system is, describing all its behaviours and the principles behind them. This amounts to mathematical modelling of the target system.

Such modelling is especially hard for automotive systems: (1) they have complex physical components; (2) they typically come with third-party components whose internal working is not known; (3) modern ADAS and ADVs include machine-learning components (such as neural networks for object recognition) whose behaviours are hard to define; and so on. Note that Simulink models—“mathematical models” commonly used in automotive industry—are usually not fit for theorem proving. Simulink models, and also other digital twins, are principally constructed for the purpose of numeric simulation and not for the logical analysis in theorem proving.

As a countermeasure to this problem of modelling, in Section 9.6, we review a modelling and theorem-proving framework called Event-B. Its most notable feature is model refinement: one can start with a coarse-grained model of the target system and prove its safety; for stronger assurance, one can refine the model to include more details about the system and prove its safety. Moreover, the safety proof for the refined model can be done in an incremental manner, in the sense that the safety proofs for previous (coarser-grained) models play the role of key lemmas.

A mathematical proof obtained this way can be seen as a top-down one (cf. Table 9.1). The conventional direction of constructing proofs is bottom-up, in that unquestionable facts get composed to derive more complex facts, all the way towards the ultimate claim. In Event-B, in contrast, one decomposes the ultimate claim gradually into simpler claims, using increasingly detailed system models.

The problem of modelling is a general one in the application of software science methods to automotive systems. Model refinement by Event-B is one answer. Another answer, in the specific problem of safety of automated driving vehicles, is the methodology of RSS [53]. It addresses the problem of modelling by letting RSS rules cut a clear line between what should be modelled and what should not. See Section 7.5, and also recent papers [19, 32, 33].

9.2 Formal Logic

In this section, we review the common foundation of the theorem proving approaches we describe later, namely formal logic.

To ensure some correctness property of a system, an ultimate means is a mathematical proof. It is the record of a series of reasoning steps from the assumptions (such as system requirements, a system model, environmental contracts, etc.) all the way to the conclusion (namely the desired correctness property). Being a mathematical proof, there should not be any gap in the course of these reasoning steps, giving a very strong degree of guarantee. A mathematical proof offers a high level of explainability, too, explicating why the correctness property should hold in the course of its reasoning steps.

Such use of mathematical proofs, however, is easier said than done. The most common form of mathematical proofs are the pen-and-paper one. Checking the validity of such pen-and-paper “proof candidates” incurs the following challenges.

  • Written in a natural language, the check must rely on human efforts. But human checkers—much like human provers—are never free from mistakes and oversights.
  • Mathematical proofs of system correctness are very often of the least interesting and the most tedious kind. They are typically painfully long. Moreover, their technical substance is not so much in enlightening mathematical insights as in massive case distinctions. Humans easily get bored of such unexciting proofs, leading to mistakes.

Formal logic, which is almost synonymous with symbolic logic, is a scientific discipline that offers a solution. Formal logic provides a formal language in which mathematical proofs are written; more specifically, this formal language defines: (1) what symbolic expressions can be used for proofs, and (2) what symbolic proof rules, that tell which reasoning steps are valid, can be used. In this way, formal logic enables mechanical and automated solution of our problem of checking the validity of proof candidates: symbolic expressions can be processed by software; and the validity of proof candidates, amounting to the compliance with symbolic proof rules, can be effectively checked by an algorithm.

In the rest of Section 9.2, we describe two basic examples of such formal languages for writing proofs, namely propositional logic and first-order logic. Our exposition is brief and its emphasis is more on intuition than on mathematical precision. Interested readers are referred to classic textbooks such as [55, 57] as well as online lecture notes such as [31].

9.2.1 Propositional Logic

Our first example is propositional logic, one of the most basic logical languages that is about what true statements can be formed using common logical connectives such as ∧ (“and”), ∨ (“or”), → (“implies”), and ¬ (“not”).

The first component of propositional logic is a formal syntax in which statements of our interest—those which are composed using the aforementioned logical connectives and the truth of which we want to prove—are expressed. These statements, expressed symbolically, are called (well-formed) formulas.

Here is a formal definition. We fix a set of atomic propositions; its elements are denoted by p,q,... in what follows. The set of propositional formulas is defined by the following BNF notation:

(9.1)
ϕ::=p|⊤|⊥|¬ϕ|ϕ∧ϕ|ϕ∨ϕ|ϕ→ϕ

where p ranges over atomic propositions. BNF notations such as (9.1) describe inductive definitions of syntax: the one in (9.1), for example, can be read as (1) each atomic proposition p is a propositional formula, (2) ⊤ and ⊥ are both propositional formulas, and (3) combinations of propositional formulas with the connectives ∧,∨,→,¬ are also propositional formulas. Although ϕ ∧ ϕ in (9.1) uses the same symbol ϕ twice, they do not have to be instantiated by the same propositional formula. See the example below.

Example 31 Let p and q be atomic propositions. Then p and q are propositional formulas, too, by the first case of (9.1). By the last case of (9.1), p → q is a propositional formula, too; so is p ∧ (p → q) by the fifth case. Using the last case again, (p ∧ (p → q)) → q is a propositional formula.

The second component of propositional logic is a set of symbolic proof rules that one can use to derive propositional formulas in reasoning steps inside a proof. There are different styles of proof rules: the Hilbert style, natural deduction, sequent calculus, etc. The one presented here follows the natural deduction style. See [55].

Our proof rules for propositional logic derive judgments

(9.2)
ϕ1, …, ϕn ⊢ ψ

instead of propositional formulas themselves. This use of judgments is for syntactic convenience. In a judgment such as (9.2), the sequence ϕ1 ,..., ϕn of assumption propositional formulas is followed by a consequent propositional formula ψ, delimited by a special symbol ⊢. Carrying assumptions around explicitly, in this manner, is useful when we formulate proof rules. In what follows, sequences ϕ1 ,..., ϕn of propositional formulas are often denoted by Γ, ∆, etc.

Let us now introduce proof rules for propositional logic. A proof rule consists of zero or more judgments Γ1 ⊢ ϕ1, ...,Γn ⊢ ϕn called premises, and a judgment ∆ ⊢ ψ called the conclusion, and is often written in the following form, where NAME is the name of the rule:


$$\frac{\text{Γ}_{1} \vdash \phi_{1}\,\,\ldots\,\,\text{Γ}_{n} \vdash \phi_{n}}{\text{Δ} \vdash \psi}N_{AME}$$

The rule is such that if all premise judgments Γ1 ⊢ ϕ1 ,...,Γn ⊢ ϕn have been already derived, then one can further derive the conclusion judgment ∆ ⊢ ψ. Table 9.2 shows some of the proof rules of propositional logic.

Table 9.2: Some proof rules for propositional logic
Proof rule Informal description

 


$$\frac{}{\Gamma,\,\phi,\,\Delta\, \vdash \phi}\text{As}$$

Assuming ϕ, one can infer ϕ

 


$$\frac{}{\text{Γ} \vdash \top}\top\text{I}$$

One can always infer ⊤ (⊤-introduction)

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \bot}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi}\bot\text{E}$$

If one has contradiction (⊥), then one can infer anything (ϕ) (⊥-elimination)

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{Γ} \vdash \psi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi \land \psi} \land \text{I}$$

If one has both ϕ and ψ, then one can infer ϕ ∧ ψ

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi \land \psi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi} \land \text{E}1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi \land \psi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \psi} \land \text{E}2$$

If one has ϕ ∧ ψ, then one can infer both φ and ψ

 


$$\left. \frac{\text{Γ},\phi \vdash \psi}{\left. \text{Γ} \vdash \phi\rightarrow\psi \right.}\rightarrow\text{I} \right.$$

If assuming ϕ one has ψ, then on can infer ϕ → ψ

 


$$\left. \frac{\left. \text{Γ} \vdash \phi\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{Γ} \vdash \phi\rightarrow\psi \right.}{\text{Γ} \vdash \psi}\rightarrow\text{E} \right.$$

If one has both φ and φ → ψ, then one can infer ψ

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi \vee \psi} \vee I1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \psi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi \vee \psi} \vee \text{I}2$$

If one has either ϕ or ψ, then one can infer ϕ ∨ ψ

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi \vee \psi\,\,\,\,\,\text{Γ},\phi \vdash \rho\,\,\,\,\,\text{Γ},\psi \vdash \rho}{\text{Γ} \vdash \rho}\, \vee \text{E}$$

If one has ϕ ∨ ψ, and assuming either ϕ or ψ has ρ, then one can infer ρ

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ},\phi \vdash \bot}{\text{Γ} \vdash \text{¬}\phi}\text{¬I}$$

If assuming ϕ one has ⊥, then one can infer ¬ϕ

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \text{¬¬}\phi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi}\text{¬¬E}$$

Double negation elimination

Formal proofs are built by stacking appropriate proof rules.

Definition 9.1 A formal proof is a tree whose nodes are judgments, such that for each node, there is an instance of a proof rule whose conclusion is the node itself and whose premises are the children of the node. A formula ϕ is said to be a theorem if there is a formal proof whose root is the judgment ⊢ ϕ.

Example 32 The formula (p ∧(p → q)) → q is a theorem in propositional logic. It is witnessed by the following formal proof.


$$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ \right.\_\,\,\,\,\,\text{As}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_}\,\,\,\text{As}} \\ {\,\frac{\left. p \land (p\rightarrow q) \vdash p \land (p\rightarrow q) \right.}{\left. p \land (p\rightarrow q) \vdash p \right.} \land \text{E}1\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\frac{\left. p \land (p\rightarrow q) \vdash p \land (p\rightarrow q) \right.}{\left. p \land (p\rightarrow q) \vdash p\rightarrow q \right.} \land \text{E}2} \\ \left. \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\rightarrow\text{E} \right. \\ \left. \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\frac{\left. p \land (p\rightarrow q) \vdash q \right.}{\left. \vdash (p \land (p\rightarrow q))\rightarrow q \right.}\rightarrow\text{I} \right. \\ \end{array}$$

It is emphasised that the proof rules we have introduced are purely symbolic entities. A major benefit of being so is that their application can be mechanised: for example, in the application of the ∧I rule, what we have to check are (1) if the two premises and the conclusion have the same assumptions Γ, and (2) if the consequent of the conclusion is the ∧-combination of those of the two premises. This symbolic check can be done without thinking of any meanings such as those in the “informal description” column of Table 9.2.

Here arise questions about the relationship between the symbolic machinery of proof rules and the “truth” of propositional formulas. Specifically,

  • Do the proof rules derive only true formulas?
  • Conversely, is every true formula derivable using the proof rules?

The first property is called soundness of proof rules, while the latter is called their completeness. To answer these questions, we need to be first able to talk about the truth (or the meaning) of propositional formulas; the theory of formal logic about doing so is called semantics. In contrast, the symbolic machinery that we have described belongs to syntax. See, e.g. [31].

As for propositional logic, the semantics of formulas is commonly defined in terms of two truth values (true and false). Our proof rules in Table 9.2 enjoy both soundness and completeness.

9.2.2 First-Order Logic

Our second example is first-order logic, which additionally accommodates quantifiers, namely ∀ (“for all”) and ∃ (“there exists”). This requires the extension of the syntax by terms: terms represent objects, while (first-order) formulas represent statements about properties of such objects.

We first fix sets of variable symbols (denoted by x, y, . . . ), constant/function symbols (such as 0, 1, 2, . . . , +, −, ×, . . . ), and predicate symbols (such as =,

<, ≤, . . . ). For the latter two kinds of symbols, each comes with its arity, which is the number of arguments it expects. For example, the function symbols +,× as well as the predicate symbols =,< all have arity 2; constant symbols such as 0,1 have arity 0.

The set of (first-order) terms is defined by the BNF notation


t :  :  = x ∣ f(t, …, t)

where x is a variable symbol and f is a function symbol. We require that the number of argument terms t in f (t,...,t) is the arity of f .

Now the set of (first-order) formulas is given by the BNF notation


ϕ::=P(t,…,t)|⊤|⊥|ϕ∧ϕ|ϕ∨ϕ|¬ϕ|ϕ→ϕ|∀x.ϕ|∃x.ϕ

where P is a predicate symbol, the number of argument terms t in P(t,...,t) is the arity of P, and x is a variable.

The set of proof rules for first-order logic extends that for propositional logic, with the proof rules presented in Table 9.3. In the table, ϕ(x) represents a formula with a variable x, and ϕ(s) denotes the formula where the occurrences of x are replaced7

Table 9.3: Additional proof rules for first-order logic.
Proof rules Informal description

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi(x)}{\text{Γ} \vdash \forall x.\phi(x)}\forall\text{I}$$

where Γ does not mention x

If one has ϕ(x) without assuming anything on x, then one can infer ∀x. ϕ(x)

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \forall x \cdot \phi(x)}{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi(s)}\forall\text{E}$$

If one has ∀x. ϕ(x), then one can infer ϕ(s) for any term s

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \phi(s)}{\text{Γ} \vdash \exists x.\phi(x)}\exists\text{I}$$

If one has ϕ(s) for some term s, then one can infer ∃x. φ(x)

 


$$\frac{\text{Γ} \vdash \exists x.\phi(x)\text{Γ},\phi(x) \vdash \psi}{\text{Γ} \vdash \psi}\exists\text{E}\,$$

where Γ and ψ do not mention x

If one has ∃x. ϕ(x), and by assuming ϕ(x) has ψ, then one can infer ψ

Much like in propositional logic, our proof rules for first-order logic are known to be sound and complete, although completeness requires some remarks. Completeness for first-order logic is proved in famous Gödel’s completeness theorem, which states that formulas that are true in any possible semantics are also symbolically derivable using the rules. This variety of semantics, however, can include those which are not intended. For example, for the famous grammar of Peano arithmetic for natural numbers, besides the standard model that interprets variables over natural numbers in the intended manner, there are other non-standard models. When we focus on the truth in this standard model (instead of any possible semantics), Gödel’s incompleteness theorem states that there is no set of mechanisable proof rules that is complete.

For practitioners who wish to use formal logic for system correctness guarantee, completeness of proof rules is usually not very important: even if the proof rules are complete, the complexity for proof search can be so big that a proof may not be found (although its existence is theoretically guaranteed). In contrast, soundness of proof rules is of utmost importance: without it, the theorem “proved” by the proof rules may be semantically false, offering little value to the goal of ensuring system correctness.

9.3 Interactive Theorem Proving

Formal logic enables one to mechanically and automatically check the validity of formal proofs (or candidates for formal proofs, to be more precise). These proof candidates must be fed to computers, either manually or automatically. The manual approach, where a human work on a computer to write a proof candidate, is called interactive theorem proving. Software for doing so is called proof assistants. In contrast, the automatic approach is called automated theorem proving, where a proof candidate is searched by some algorithm.

9.3.1 (Incomplete) History of Proof Assistants

The earliest known attempt to mechanically verify mathematics is Automath (automating mathematics) developed by de Bruijn in 1968 [16].

The early 1970s saw the births of several proof assistants whose descendants are still in use today. The Boyer–Moore theorem prover NQTHM, developed in 1972, is based on the first-order logic and implemented using Common LISP [13]. Its successor ACL2 has gained wide use in industry, including the verification of processor units of, e.g., AMD [41], IBM [49], Centaur [34], Rockwell Collins [59].

Mizar, initiated by Trybulec in 1973, is now based on the Tarski—Grothendieck set theory and has focus on human-readable proofs [42]. One reason that makes Mizar stand out among other ITP systems is The Mizar Mathematical Library, also known as the Journal of Formalized Mathematics in a publication form, consisting of 1290 articles (as of 2018) contributed by the worldwide user base of the Mizar system [5].

The LCF (logic of computable functions) [27] family initiated by Milner in 1973 implements inferences on Scott’s formal logic for functional programming (written in 1969 but published only in 1993 [51]). LCF had focus on verifying

functional programs. Probably the most well-known spin-off of LCF is the ML programming languages including Standard ML [45] and OCaml [39], but LCF also evolved into various major proof assistants of broader scope.

Gordon evolved LCF to HOL in 1986, shifting the base formal logic into the higher-order logic [28]. Among the well-known applications of the HOL family are the formalisation of IEEE floating-point operations in HOL Light [30], and the formal proof of the Kepler Conjecture (in combination of Isabelle/HOL and HOL Light) [29],

Paulson developed Isabelle in 1983 as a generic inference engine from LCF, but mostly known for it’s HOL instance, Isabelle/HOL, emerged in 1991 [46]. Isabelle is still actively maintained and a large body of mathematical libraries, the Archive of Formal Proofs, are publicly available.

Coq [8], developed by Huet and Coquand in 1984, is based on the formal logic called the Calculus of (Inductive) Constructions. Coq is among the most actively used theorem provers of today, probably best known for the formal proof of the four-colour theorem [26] and the formally verified C compiler [38].

9.3.2 Isabelle/HOL

We demonstrate the use of proof assistants by employing Isabelle/HOL as an example. A file collecting Isabelle proofs is called a theory file. An example theory file TheoremProvingChapter. thy would start like this:

  1. theory TheoremProvingChapter
  2. imports Main
  3. begin

The second line of the file directs Isabelle to import the standard theory file HOL/Main. thy, which declares basic axioms of (a dialect of) the formal logic HOL and natural numbers, and then definitions and lemmas for derived notions, such as sets, lists, and integers. A vast amount of further notions are available in the standard library and external Archive of Formal Proofs.

After importing basic concepts, we begin our own definitions, claims and proofs on top of them. As a quick example, let us define a predicate my_sorted, which takes a list of integers (represented by type int list) and tells if the list is sorted.

  1. definition my_sorted : : “int list ⇒ bool” where
  2. "my_sorted xs =
  3. (∀ i j . i < j → j < length xs → xs! i ≤ xs ! j )"

The definition would look like the usual mathematical definition, except that in Isabelle (and the LCF family), function application is written “fx” instead of “f(x)”. Hence xs is the argument of predicate my_sorted. The function length

gives the length of the list, and infix ! operator takes the ith element of the list. These functions, as well as other symbols, are defined in Main.

To conveniently use my_sorted afterwards, let us prove a (trivial) lemma.

  1. lemma my_sortedI:
  2. assumes my_asmml: "∀ i j . i < j → j < length xs → xs ! i ≤ xs!j"
  3. shows “my_sorted xs”

In Isabelle, lemmas can be used as inference rules. In notation of Section 9.2, the above lemma can be used as the inference rule

after it is proved. Proving the lemma means proving the judgment

where Γ represents the all available facts, that is, axioms, definitions, lemmas, and theorems. To prove this goal, we would like to unfold the definition of my_sorted. Instead of applying primitive inference rules, Isabelle provides a convenient way of unfolding equations:

  1. unfolding my_sorted_def

where my_sorted_def refers to the equation of line 5 (put in Γ). Now the goal my_sorted xs (the right-hand side of ⊢) is replaced by

which is precisely in the premise (the left-hand side of ⊢). Thus the assumption would conclude the proof, but Γ, the collection of all known facts, is so big that one should specify which fact one uses. There are several ways to do this, among which we use the following:

  1. by (rule my_asm)

where my_asm refers to the formula of line 8 as the name is explicitly given there. At this point the proof of the lemma my_sortedI is done.

Now let us prove the following easy statement:

  1. theorem my_sorted_123: “my_sorted [1,2,3]"

It would look trivial to human readers, but unfortunately it is not to Isabelle. We first tell Isabelle to apply my_sortedI as an inference rule to this goal as follows.

  1. apply (rule my_sortedI)

This yields the following new goal:


∀ij.i<j→j< length [1,2,3]→[1,2,3] ! i ≤[1,2,3] ! j 

Proving this requires to consider all possibilities of i and j and requires many proof steps if one is restricted to primitive application of inference rules. Luckily, most proof assistants have automatic proof methods that build a proof tree following some strategies. For Isabelle, we need to guide it to do case splitting according to j < length [1,2,3], that is, j is either 0, 1, or 2. It needs some training to find how, but this is achievable by the following equation less_Suc_eq available in Γ:


(m < Sucn) = (m < n∨ m = n)

Here, Sue is the internal representation of the successor of natural numbers (i.e., Suc n represents n + 1). We conclude the proof by instructing Isabelle’s automatic proof procedure to add less_Suc_eq in simplification rules:

  1. by (auto simp: less_Suc_eq)

9.4 Automated Theorem Proving

As we have seen in the previous section, building a formal proof purely in the manner of interactive theorem proving needs some training and is often tedious. There is another line of research directed towards automating the theorem proving task: automated theorem proving (ATP).

9.4.1 General-Purpose ATP

The history of automated theorem proving (ATP) is longer than that of interactive theorem proving (ITP); the earliest ATP system (over propositional logic) is The Logic Theory Machine (LT) [43] developed by Newell and Simon in 1956, way before the dawn of ITP. Afterwards several ATP systems appeared (see, e.g. [9] for early history), leading to The CADE ATP System Competitions [54] held since 1996 to evaluate general-purpose ATP systems on the first-order and higher-order logics. Only a few of remarkable participants of the competitions are: Prover9 (in a lineage since the early 1960s [35]), the E Prover [50], and Vampire [48].

To do justice to ITP, the level of trust ATP offers should be said lower than ITP. This is because the correctness of an ATP tool relies on the implementation of the entire proof search algorithms, while ITP relies only on the implementation of small number of inference rules. In fact, one of the specialities of Isabelle/HOL is Sledgehammer [12], a command to delegate proof obligations to automated theorem provers (ATPs), see Fig. 9.2. ATPs are seen as untrusted black-boxes that suggest proofs, and Isabelle tries to reconstruct fully formal proofs following the suggestions.

9.4.2 SAT Solving

It is not expected that a general-purpose ATP system will solve a real-world problem fully automatically. One way of making full ATP possible is to restrict the logic to those for which an efficient way of solving is known. A well-known example of this line is SAT (satisfiability) solvers.

Satisfiability of a formula in a formal logic asks if it is possible to instantiate variables in the formula so that the resulting formula evaluates to true (⊤) in the logic. For example, in propositional logic, the formula p ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q) is satisfiable, since by instantiating p ↦ ⊤ and q ↦ ⊥ yields ⊤ ∧ (⊥ ∨ ⊤), which is simplified into ⊤. In contrast, p ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) is unsatisfiable, since the formula is false under any assignment on p and q. Satisfiability is closely related to theorem proving: ϕ is a theorem if and only if ¬ϕ is unsatisfiable.8

SAT solvers are concerned with solving satisfiability in propositional logic. Propositional logic is very restrictive, in the sense that the value of each variable has only two choices (either ⊤ or ⊥). It is however well suited for verifying electronic circuits [20], where each wire must have either high (⊤) or low (⊥) voltage. Typical SAT solvers further restrict formulas to conjunctive normal forms (CNFs), but there is an efficient transformation of any propositional formula into CNF with the same satisfiability [56]. Moreover, any problem with finite search space can be encoded into a SAT problem, and often solved faster by reducing to SAT solving than other means [11], thanks to the impressive performance of recent fine-tuned SAT solvers.

Example 33 A typical class of faults in electronic circuit manufacturing is the stuck-at faults. For instance, consider a good, fault-free circuit in Fig. 9.3a and a faulty one in Fig. 9.3b. Notice that in the faulty circuit, the second input to the AND gate in the center is stuck at ⊥. To detect such a fault by testing, one wants to find an input such that the outputs of the good and faulty circuits differ.

A propositional formula encoding the good circuit is as follows, where each wire is represented by a propositional variable of the same name:

(9.3)
$$\begin{array}{l} {\left( i_{1} \oplus i_{2}\leftrightarrow m_{1} \right) \land \left( m_{1} \land \underset{¯}{i_{3}}\leftrightarrow m_{2} \right) \land \left( i_{2} \land i_{3}\leftrightarrow m_{3} \right) \land} \\ {\left( m_{1} \oplus i_{3}\leftrightarrow o_{1} \right) \land \left( m_{2} \vee m_{3}\leftrightarrow o_{2} \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

where x ⊕ y represents the exclusive or: (x ∧ ¬y) ∨ (¬x ∧ y). Similarly, the faulty circuit is encoded as follows:

(9.4)
$$\begin{array}{l} {\left( i_{1} \oplus i_{2}\leftrightarrow m_{1}^{\prime} \right) \land \left( m_{1}^{\prime} \land \bot\leftrightarrow m_{2}^{\prime} \right) \land \left( i_{2} \land i_{3}\leftrightarrow m_{3}^{\prime} \right) \land} \\ {\left( m_{1}^{\prime} \oplus i_{3}\leftrightarrow o_{1}^{\prime} \right) \land \left( m_{2}^{\prime} \vee m_{3}^{\prime}\leftrightarrow o_{2}^{\prime} \right)} \\ \end{array}$$

In order to detect such faulty circuits by testing, we want an assignment on the input {i1, i2, i3} such that the output {o1, o2} of the good circuit and {o′1, o′2} of the faulty one differ. This requirement is expressed as a propositional formula as follows:


(9.3) ∧ (9.4) ∧ (o1⊕o1′∨o2⊕o2′)

After CNF translation, any reasonable SAT solver will immediately provide a solution to the formula; for instance the SAT solver lingeling [10] finds the following solution (also called a model):

i1 ↦ ⊤

i2 ↦ ⊥

i3 ↦ ⊥

m1 ↦ ⊤

m2 ↦ ⊥

m3 ↦ ⊥

o1 ↦ ⊤

o2 ↦ ⊥

m′1 ↦ ⊤

m′2 ↦ ⊤

m′3 ↦ ⊥

o′1 ↦ ⊤

o′2 ↦ ⊤

The first line indicates the desired test pattern for detecting such a stuck-at fault.

There are a large number of SAT solvers and they are evaluated annually in the SAT competitions [23]. As the participants and winners dynamically change by years, interested readers are invited to check recent competition results.

9.4.3 Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT)

Propositional logic is not the only logic for which efficient mathematical techniques are known. Other examples include integer and real arithmetics and regular expressions. Moreover, other formal logics, such as bit-vector arithmetics or arrays, are highly useful when verifying software.

Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers [7] are tools that decide whether a formula is satisfiable in such a formal logic other than propositional logic.

Example 34 Consider the following C program that computes the gravity at time t between two particles A and B, initially at position (9,4) and (3,14) and moving with velocity (0.4,0.8) and (0.7,0.3), respectively:

I

double gravity_between_A_and_B(double t) {

2

double Ax, Ay, Bx, By, x, y;

3

Ax = 9.0 + 0.4 * t; Ay = 4.0 + 0.8 * t;

4

Bx = 3.0 + 0.7 * t; By = 14.0 + 0.3 * t;

5

x = Ax - Bx; y = Ay - By;

6

X = X * x; y = y * y;

7

return 1.0 / (x + y);

8

}

The program is not safe: it can cause a division-by-zero error. However, finding the error by testing is not a trivial task.

One can find such errors by encoding the problem of finding an erroneous input as an SMT problem. The problem can be encoded as follows:


$$\begin{array}{l} {Ax = 9.0 + 0.4t \land Ay = 4.0 + 0.8t \land} \\ {Bx = 3.0 + 0.7t \land By = 14.0 + 0.3t \land} \\ {x_{1} = Ax - Bx \land y_{1} = Ay - By \land} \\ {x_{2} = x_{1}^{2} \land y_{2} = y_{1}^{2} \land} \\ {\text{x\_2+y\_2=0}\text{.0}} \\ \end{array}$$

where all but last lines correspond to lines 3-6 of the program, and the last line represents the situation where the denominator of the division is 0. The SMT solver Z3 [17] solves the problem, with the following solution:

t ↦ 20.0

Ax ↦ 17.0

Ay ↦ 20.0

Bx ↦ 17.0

By ↦ 20.0

xi ↦ 0.0

x2 ↦ 0.0

y1 ↦ 0.0

y2 ↦ 0.0

Besides the aforementioned Z3 [17] developed by Microsoft, various academic SMT solvers compete in the annual SMT competitions [58], most notably the CVC family [6] and Yices [18].

9.4.4 Discussion: Limit of Automation

Full automation is successful for restricted logic such as propositional logic or (linear) arithmetics. In many other logics, whether a statement is provable or not is undecidable (as in nonlinear integer arithmetic), or decidable but in intractable complexity (as in nonlinear real arithmetic). In the next section we aim at verifying cyber-physical systems (CPSs), which requires more involving formal logic that can deal with differential equations. It should be clear that full automation on such a logic is far beyond our reach. Therefore we will step slightly back towards interactive theorem proving, but still a high degree of automation is achieved by the domain-specific knowledge of differential equations.

9.5 Theorem Proving for Continuous and Hybrid Dynamics

Given their nature, CPSs such as automotive systems require the verification that a system’s software, physical components, and their interactions are all correct. This section discusses the theorem proving of such systems by modelling and verifying them as hybrid(-dynamical) systems, that combine discrete and continuous dynamics which represent software (or “cyber”) and physical components, respectively. Theorem proving for CPS deserves special attention as it requires reasoning about hybrid dynamics, that is continuous evolutions combined with discrete mode switches. As a result—and in contrast to discrete approaches (e.g., SAT solving)—complete proof automation cannot be expected. Nonetheless, by restricting our attention to hybrid system models, we significantly facilitate their proofs and also enable partial automation.

9.5.1 KeYmaera X: An Interactive Theorem Prover

A well-known tool providing such support is KeYmaera X [24], a specialised interactive theorem prover (IT?) for hybrid systems. Its specialisation enables significant proof automation, a convenient user interface (UI), and a readable modelling language. Despite the emphasis on user-friendliness, KeYmaera X is based on formal logic, providing proofs and confidence in CPS correctness.

9.5.1.1 Hybrid Systems Modelling

Hybrid systems (HSs) is a common modelling formalism, which we use as a stepping stone to expressing CPS in KeYmaera X. HSs enable the precise expression of a system’s behaviour and enable reasoning about its evolution in an unambiguous way.

In KeYmaera X, HSs are modelled as hybrid programs (HPs), consisting of executable statements representing the CPS’s continuous and discrete evolutions. Note that HPs relate closely to hybrid automata (HAs) [4], a common and expressivity-wise equivalent modelling formalism. HPs thereby add a textual syntax that is well-suited for verification and closely resembles theorem proving intuitions.

The rest of this section uses a one-dimensional vehicle example to discuss CPS theorem proving and HPs. The HP is presented in Fig. 9.4 and an equivalent HA is presented in Fig. 9.5 for the sake of comparison. The example vehicle’s aim is to safely drive up towards a stop sign and brake to a complete halt at the sign. As the controller is time-triggered, the time between its executions is at most some reaction time react. Furthermore, the maximum acceleration A and fixed brake rate B restrict potential evolution, such that the actual acceleration acc is in [—B,A]. The controller stops, once the velocity v is zero or below. Figure 9.4 shows this behaviour as a HP.

Note how the controller features separate modes for accelerating and braking, whose switching is decided by staySafe. The condition staySafe is true if and only if, even when the maximum acceleration A is maintained until the next time the controller runs (react), the vehicle could still safely brake to a stop (at rate —B) without reaching the stop sign (position sign). Formally, staySafe follows from the standard equations for Newtonian motion:


$$\left. staySafe\ \leftrightarrow\frac{\left( {vel + A \cdot react} \right)^{2}}{2 \cdot B} \leq sign - \left( {\ pos\ + \ vel\ \cdot \ react\ + A \cdot \frac{react^{2}}{2}} \right) \right.$$

The left-hand side of the comparison < represents the distance needed to brake (after the worst-case acceleration). The right-hand side represents the available distance between the stop sign and vehicle (after the worst-case acceleration).

In Fig. 9.4, if the check of staySafe succeeds, the vehicle accelerates at any rate (acc := *) subject to the condition acc ∈ [—B,A]. Otherwise, it brakes at the maximum rate. We express this behaviour as HP in Fig. 9.4, such that the while loop repeats while the vehicle is moving (vel > 0). Variable vel represents the 1-dimensional velocity of the vehicle, where positive values of vel mean forward motion and negative values mean reverse motion. The velocity vel and all other variables in the HP are real-valued R. The if statement models the mode switching, as described above. The rest of the HP code models the physical model (i.e., the “plant”) and initialises the timer for the time-based trigger, and the system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs).

ODEs are the characteristic feature of hybrid programs, which distinguish them from discrete programs. Every ODE statement contains a comma-separated list of equations and optionally contains a formula called an evolution domain constraint, which is separated from the equations by an ampersand (&). The evolution domain constraint determines how long the ODE evolves. Specifically, the duration of the ODEs is non-deterministic, but it can only be used until the evolution domain constraint (ever) becomes false. In the example, the equations mean that the derivative of position is velocity, the derivative of velocity is acceleration, and the derivative of the timer is, by convention, 1. In the example, the evolution domain constraint means that the timer must never exceed the reaction time and the velocity must never be negative. It is important that the ODE ends by react, because the control condition staySafe is only designed to guarantee safety if the vehicle accelerates for time react and is allowed to brake afterwards if needed.

Figure 9.4 Time-triggered HP of the 1D vehicle.

car ≡

while (vel > 0){

if (staySafe)

{acc := *;?acc ∈ [—B,A];}

else

{ace := —B;}

timer := 0;

{pos′ = vel, vel′ = acc, time′ =1

&(timer≤react ∧ vel>0)};

}

Based on this vehicle model, we use differential dynamic logic (dL) [47] to state a theorem that we prove in KeYmaera X. Using dL it is possible to define that one or all executions of a (possibly non-deterministic) HP are valid. For instance, in the above example, acc:= * can take arbitrary values in [—B,A]. Thus, to ensure safety, we want to express that given some starting conditions, all executions lead to safe postconditions. By specifying [car]safe, we define that the car always satisfies a postcondition safe. The standard safety result for our vehicle is that, under appropriate initial conditions, it does not drive through the stop sign, i.e., pre → [car] (pos < sign) where pre is shorthand for a safe initial condition. Next, we discuss the proof UI.

9.5.1.2 Strong Logical Foundations

The design and implementation of KeYmaera X are based on the rigorous underlying theory of dL to increase our trust in the tool. KeYmaera X is in fact sound, meaning that if the tool labels a formula as true, the formula is in fact true. Specifically, if a safety formula is true according to the KeYmaera X tool, it is also true according to the theory of dL, in which case we call it valid.

The theory of dL defines the truth of formulas by formalising the notion of runs from Section 9.5.1.1. Proof techniques are formalised using inference rules which assume that premises are true and conclude that a conclusion is true. The inference rules are shown to be sound, meaning that only true conclusions are proved. As shown in Fig. 9.6, proof rules necessarily perform small proof steps, so that their soundness can be justified more easily. One of KeYmaera X’s major contributions is that it builds complex automation from the soundness of these small steps.


$$\begin{array}{l} {\lbrack\text{if}\rbrack\frac{\left. Q\rightarrow\lbrack\alpha\rbrack P\quad\neg Q\rightarrow\lbrack\beta\rbrack P \right.}{\lbrack{if}(Q)\left\{ \alpha \right\}\text{else}\left\{ \beta \right\}\rbrack P}\,\,\,\lbrack;\rbrack\frac{\lbrack\alpha\rbrack\lbrack\beta\rbrack P}{\lbrack\alpha;\beta\rbrack P}\,\,\,\,\,_{\lbrack?\rbrack}\frac{\left. Q\rightarrow P \right.}{\lbrack?Q\rbrack P}} \\ {\text{DI}\frac{P\,\,\text{[}x^{\prime} = f\text{\&}Q\text{]}{(P)}^{\prime}}{\text{[}x^{\prime} = f\text{~\&}Q\text{]}P}\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{DC}\frac{\text{[}x^{\prime} = f\text{~\&}Q\text{]}C\,\,\text{[}x^{\prime} = f\text{~\&}Q \land C\text{]}P}{\text{[}x^{\prime} = f\text{~\&}Q\text{]}P}} \\ \end{array}$$

As shown in the first row of example proof rules in Fig. 9.6, many HP statements can be proved by unfolding their structure, as automated by KeYmaera X. The [if ] -rule is proved by considering each branch. Sequential statements (rule [; ]) require consideration of each statement in a sequence and tests (rule [?]) are inferred by assuming the test condition and showing the postcondition.

The second row shows that greater insight is often required for invariant-style proofs, in this case about ODEs. In rule dl, formula P is proved to be an invariant by showing that it holds initially and that its differential formula (P)′ holds throughout. Although (P)′ can be automatically determined [47], rule dI still produces two premises which must be proved. Rule dC requires more insight: the user chooses a differential cut formula C, proves that it holds throughout the ODE, then adds it to the domain constraint to help prove the postcondition P.

In summary, the automation provided by KeYmaera X both helps automate simple steps (first row) even when hard steps (bottom) are performed manually and provides best-effort automatic proof attempts for hard steps (bottom row).

9.5.1.3 High-Level Proof UI

KeYmaera X offers an intuitive and interactive browser-based UI, depicted in Fig. 9.7. For space reasons, we only discuss key aspects here and refer to the literature [40] for additional details. As mentioned above, some dL proofs cannot be fully automated, traditionally requiring significant user input and steep learning curves. Thus, KeYmaera X’s UI focuses on the crucial reduction of these efforts.

The tool thus encourages iterative development, and even allows reuse of proof attempts on initial (typically incomplete or faulty) models for later, corrected versions of those models. Further, the undo feature helps correcting proof attempt mistakes without the need to restart from scratch. Finally, even though full automation is infeasible, KeYmaera X supports partial automation of significant portions of the proof, so that the user may focus on the actually tricky parts, while the rest is handled by the tool. For instance, a user might have to identify invariant formulas for loops or ODEs, then use automation to attempt remaining proof tasks, avoiding unnecessary manual proof effort.

KeYmaera X supports novice users by providing proof suggestions, helping identify proof mistakes and automatically identifying which rules are currently relevant. This reduces the learning effort of both the tool and theorem proving in general. Finally, for both new and expert users, it is often unclear how to proceed when a proof attempt fails. KeYmaera X provides additional insight by searching for counter examples, i.e., showing specific configurations where the formula is false.

9.5.2 Related Work

Next to KeYmaera X, various other tools and approaches can be used for CPS verification. These “competitor methods” can be organised in terms of the fundamental tradeoff between expressive power and automation. In general, verification of “more powerful” properties will require more manual effort by the user. We compare approaches along this spectrum.

  • Given their general-purpose nature, many ITPs such as Isabelle/HOL [44] aim to cover many problems and domains. However, given the lack of HS automation, CPS proofs require significant manual effort. Recent efforts try to add such automation after-the-fact, though. See [21].
  • Hybrid systems model checkers such as SpaceEx [22] and Flow* [14] automatically explore all configurations of a HS to prove or falsify a property, usually a safety property. Even though specific features vary according to their expressive power, common limitations restrict the classes of supported ODEs, impose finite time horizons for safety guarantees, or safety on restricted (compact) sets of configurations. These limitations however enable that model checkers achieve a high degree of automation, sometimes with a high degree of scalability.
  • dReach [37] deserves mentioning as it is a special HS model checker. Though restricted to bounded model-checking, its dReal [25] SMT solver-basis simplifies checking of real-number formulas using 5-robustness, i.e., allowing for small perturbations. dReal excels at automating difficult arithmetic functions, but it shares the limitations of other SMT solvers.
  • Simulations, such as those provided in Stateflow/Simulink [1], provide strong automation and scalability, but typically only consider individual starting configurations, or small sets thereof. The inherent problems of e.g., naive floating-point arithmetics and numerical solvers result in lacks of soundness.

In summary, KeYmaera X excels at proving general-case correctness properties about hybrid systems, which are expressive models of CPS s such as automotive systems. The tradeoff is that many KeYmaera X proofs are interactive and that interactive proving takes time to learn. Thus, KeYmaera X is appropriate when general-case correctness is desired, but more automatic tools are appropriate when automation is more important than generality.

9.6 Theorem Proving with Model Refinement

The theorem proving approaches described in Sections 9.3-9.5 are bottom-up: they assume a formal description of the target system at the bottom and build up correctness proofs on top of it. However, realistic systems often have black-box components or overwhelming complexity that prevent us from providing formal descriptions, i.e., they have uncertainties.

In this section, we introduce a top-down approach: we start from the requirements of the target system at the top, and gradually design details of the system so that they satisfy the requirements. This approach is a powerful countermeasure against the challenge of uncertainties — uncertainties are gradually confined or eliminated one by one as we gradually provide design details.

In the rest of this section, we introduce Event-B [2],9

9.6.1 Top-Down Theorem Proving in Event-B

Event-B has a mechanism called stepwise refinement that enables top-down theorem proving. Using the mechanism, we start with constructing a model of abstract aspects of the target system, such as safety requirements, and gradually evolve the model to include concrete aspects, such as behavioural details.

In each step of stepwise refinement, we add a new component called machine to a model. A machine presents the target system as a state transition system. The primary interest in a refinement step is whether the behaviour of the machine introduced in model version n conforms with that of the machine introduced in model version n— 1. We call them a concrete machine and an abstract machine, respectively.

A machine refers to the following constructs:

  • a variable: A variable whose value is changed by the system’s behaviour.
  • an invariant: A property that must always hold (a safety property).
  • an event: A set of state transitions regarding the system’s behaviour.

When we check the conformance of the concrete machine’s behaviour with the abstract machine’s. we use terms such as abstract events and concrete events in the same manner as machines.

For instance, a train system with a controller can be gradually modelled as shown in Fig. 9.8. In version 0 of the model, we construct a machine Mo, which focuses on the modelling of the physical safety of the train without going into details of the controller. In version 1, we add a machine M1, which describes details of the safety and behaviour of the controller’s architecture in addition to M0’s focuses. In version 2, we add a machine M2, which describes details of the concrete behaviour of controller modules in addition to M1’s focuses.

The safety of the final system is proved in a stepwise manner. For example, the train system is verified as follows:

  1. We prove that M0’s behaviour satisfies M0’s invariants. The latter express the train’s physical safety.
  2. We prove that M1’s behaviour satisfies M1’s invariants. The latter express desirable properties that are specific to the structures additionally introduced in M1. For example, they are about the controller’s architecture; they do not refer to the train’s physical safety since it is already covered by M0’s invariants.
  3. We prove that M1’s behaviour conforms with that of M0.
  4. We prove that M2’s behaviour satisfies M2’s invariants. Much like for M2’s invariants are concerned about desired properties of M2 which are not yet covered in M1.
  5. We prove that M2’s behaviour conforms with that of M1.

In what follows, we demonstrate how an Event-B model is gradually constructed while verified, by using the train system (Fig. 9.8) as an example.10

9.6.2 Constructing and Verifying Abstract Event-B Machine

In this section, we explain how the most abstract machine can be constructed and verified using the abstract machine Mo of the train system as an example.

9.6.2.1 Requirements of Abstract Machine M0

Typically, we first construct a machine that focuses on what should be satisfied (basic requirements) and abstracts away how the system satisfies those requirements.

For instance, assume that the train system has the following requirement for the train’s physical safety (Fig. 9.9):

SAF-0 The train must always be able to stop before reaching the destination xdst by activating the emergency brake (deceleration rate: b.). Formally, the following must always hold:


x + stopDist(v) ≤ xdst,

where stopDist(v) = v2/2bmax is the stopping distance, bmax is the emergency brake rate, and xdst is the position of the destination.

There is another requirement regarding a physical constraint on the train hardware:

EQP-0 The train’s maximum acceleration rate is amax.

9.6.2.2 Specifying M0

In the most abstract machine Mo, we focus on the requirement SAF-0. The specification of the controller’s behaviour simply says it somehow satisfies the requirement; the detailed behaviour such as how the architecture and controller modules work to satisfy the requirements are deferred to concrete machines.

We assume that the controller works once in a cycle.

The machine M0 is as follows:

machine M0

variables x, v

invariants @inv_stop: x stopDist(v) ≤ xdst

events

event run

where @grd_whenever: true

then @act_xv: x, v: x′ + stopDist(v′) ≤ xdst

∧x′ < nextMaxX (x, v) ∧ v′ ≤ nextMaxV (v)

end

end

Variables x and v denote the position and velocity of the train. Invariant @inv_stop expresses requirement SAF-0. Event run describes the behaviour of the train controller in a cycle.

An event is composed of guards specified in the where clause, which define when the event is allowed to occur, and actions specified in the then clause, which describe state transitions due to the event.

The event rim can occur in any situation (guard Ogrd_whenever). The action @act_xv updates the values of variables x and v so that their new values (x′ and v′) satisfy the formula specified in the then clause:


$$\begin{array}{l} {x^{\prime} + stopDist\left( v^{\prime} \right) \leq x_{dst}} \\ {\land \, x^{\prime} \leq nextMaxX(x,v) \land v^{\prime} \leq nextMaxV(v),} \\ \end{array}$$

Some readers may be interested in definitions of nextMaxX(x,v) and nextMaxV (v). They denote the maximum possible position and velocity at the next cycle following EQP-0, respectively, i.e., the position and velocity if the train accelerates with amax for a cycle:


$$\begin{array}{l} {nextMaxX(x,v) = x + {\int_{t = 0}^{1}\left( {v + a_{\max}t} \right)}dt,} \\ {nextMaxV(v) = v + {\int_{t = 0}^{1}a_{\max}}dt.} \\ \end{array}$$

9.6.2.3 Verifying Safety of M0

After constructing a machine, we need to verify that invariants are satisfied after any possible events, given that they are satisfied beforehand. We call this property invariant preservation.

The following judgment expresses the invariant preservation in M0.

x+ stopDist(v) ≤ xdst,

(@inv_stop with old values)

true,

(@grd_whenever)

x′ + stopDist (v′) ≤ xdst ∧

x′ ≤ nextMaxX (x, v) ∧ v’ ≤ nextMaxV(v)

(@act_xv)

x′ + stopDist (v′) ≤ xdst

(@inv_stop with new values)

This judgment is trivially true, since the conclusion x′ + stopDist(v′) < xdst itself appears as part of the assumption. Note here that the occurrence of x′ + stopDist(v′) < xdst in the consequent part (i.e., on the right of h) comes from the invariant @inv_stop (we have to preserve it), while its occurrence in the assumption (i.e., on the left of ⊢) comes from @act_xv. Indeed, in the definition of @act_xv, it is specified that the controller somehow manages to ensure x′ + stopDist(v′) < xdst after the event.

Rodin platform [3], a modelling environment for Event-B, provides support in verifying machines. It generates judgments such as the above after we construct a machine. We call such judgments proof obligations (POs). Rodin also has automatic provers (including SMT solvers) that help prove generated POs. As we construct M0 in Rodin, it generates and proves the PO above.

9.6.3 Constructing and Verifying Concrete Event-B Machines

In this section, we explain how concrete machines can be constructed and verified, using the intermediate machine M1 and the concrete machine M2 of the train system as examples.

9.6.3.1 Requirements of Intermediate Machine M1

We assume that the train has a black-box controller (e.g., one based on machine learning). Since it is black-box, we cannot formally guarantee that the train can stop before the destination (SAF-0).

To guarantee SAF-0 while using the black-box controller, in M1, we adopt the Simplex architecture [52] for the train controller, which is shown in Fig. 9.10.

In the Simplex architecture, we refer to the black-box controller as advanced controller (AC). We provide two additional modules: baseline controller (BC) whose behaviour can be formally specified (e.g., rule-based controller) and thus verifiable; and decision module (DM), which switches the active controller between AC and BC according to the current situation.

The architecture is expected to satisfy the following requirements:

SAF-1 AC is used only when SAF-0 (stoppability) will be guaranteed after a cycle (i.e., the worst-case situation after a cycle (of acceleration with rate amax) is safe).

FUN-1 DM switches from BC to AC if SAF-0 is far from being violated (values of x and v are small enough to be able to use AC at the next cycle) when using BC. Let ACNext(x,v) denote this condition. In contrast, DM switches from AC to BC if SAF-0 is about to be violated (¬ACNext(x,v)) when using AC.

We need to define appropriate ACNext(x,v). This is not a trivial task, because the definition of ACNext(x,v) needs to take into account the switching delay — DM should select BC if the current state (current values of x and v) indicates that the next state (values of x and v at the next cycle) may violate SAF-0, even if the current state satisfies it.

9.6.3.2 Specifying M1

In M1, we specify how DM switches between AC and BC according to FUN-1. We also specify that SAF-1 should be satisfied by DM’s behaviour. Details of BC’s control rules are deferred to M2.

The overview of M1 is as follows:

machine M1 refines M0

variables x,v, ctrl

invariants Oinv_ctri: ctrl ∈ {AC, BC}

@inv_AC:

ctrl = AC ⇒ nextMaxX (x, v) + stopDist(nextMaxV(v)) < xdst

events

…

end

The new variable ctrl says which of AC and BC is activated. SAF-1 is specified as invariant @inv_AC using nextMaxX(x,v) and nextMaxV(v) defined in Section 9.6.2.2. There are four events AC->AC, AC->BC, BC->AC, and BC->BC, for specifying all switching cases.

We elaborate on events AC->BC and BC->BC below.

event AC->BC refines run

where @grd_AC: ctrl = AC

@grd_BCNext: ¬ACNext(x,v)

then @act_xv : x,v :| x′ + stopDist( v′) ≤ xdst

∧ x′ ≤ nextMaxX(x,v) ∧ v′ < nextMaxV(v)

@act_ctrl: ctrl : | ctrl′ = BC

end

event BC->BC refines run

where @grd_BC: ctrl = BC

@grd_BCNext : ¬ACNext(x, v)

then @act_xv: x,v :| x′ + stopDist(v′) < xdst

∧ x′≤ nextMaxX(x, v) ∧ v′ ≤ nextMaxV(v)

@act_ctrl: ctrl : | ctrl′ = BC

end

They inherit the guard and action from the rim event of machine M0. Newly introduced guards and actions are as follows: In event AC->BC, guard @grd_AC expresses that the event is for the case where the currently active controller is AC; guard @grd_BCNext expresses requirement FUN-1; and @act_ctrl expresses that BC will be used from the next cycle. Event BC->BC is the same as AC- >BC except that the event is for the case where BC is currently activated (guard @grd_BC).

An important point about M1 is that its invariants do not explicitly assert the system level safety, that is, that the train does not overrun (SAF-0). We can establish the safety of M1, however, by showing that: (1) M1’s behaviour conforms with M0’s, and (2) M0 is safe.

9.6.3.3 Verifying M1

The invariant preservation PO of M1 is generated much like that of M0. The key to proving it is defining an appropriate ACNext(x,v). We do not present an explicit formula here, but it essentially says @inv_stop is satisfied by a large enough margin. Guided by the PO, we can even derive the definition so that it makes PO provable.

In addition, we need to prove that the behaviour of the concrete machine conforms with that of the abstract machine. PO In particular, we need to prove the following two properties.

  • Guard strengthening: Concrete guards should be stronger than abstract guards. This guarantees that if the concrete event is enabled, then the abstract event is also enabled.
  • Action simulation: Predicates written in concrete actions should imply those of abstract actions. This guarantees that the concrete state transition is not contradictory to the abstract one.

For example, the following PO is generated for AC- >BC:

…

(Mo’s invariants with old values)

ctrl ≤ {AC,BC},

(@inv_ctrl with old values)

ctrl = AC ⇒

nextMaxX(x,v) +

stopDist(nextMaxV (v)) ≤ xdst,

(@inv_AC with old values)

ctrl = AC,

(@grd_AC)

¬ACNext(x,v),

(@grd_BCNext)

x′ + stopDist(v′) ≤ xcist ∧

x′ ≤ nextMaxX(x,v) ∧ v′ ≤ nextMaxV(v),

(@act_xv)

ctrl′ = BC,

(@act_ctrl)

⊢

true ∧ x’ + stopDist (v′) ≤ xdst ∧

(@grd_whenever and @act_xv

x’ ≤ nextMaxX(x,v) ∧ v′ ≤ nextMaxV (v)

of run in M0)

The assumption of this PO is constructed in the same manner as the invariant preservation, while the consequent part has the abstract guard (@grd_whenever) and the abstract action (@act_xv) in M0’s run event.

Since AC->BC inherits the guard and the action of the abstract event run, Rodin can easily prove this PO.

9.6.3.4 Requirements of Concrete Machine M2

In M2, we specify the deterministic control of BC. BC can be any rule-based controller such that we can guarantee its safety; in this example, it simply brakes with a fixed deceleration rate until it stops.

The following are functional requirements of BC’s control:

  1. Fun-2-1 When switching from AC to BC happens, BC calculates Tbrake, which is how long it should keep braking as follows:


    Tbrake  = v/bmax.

  2. Fun-2-2 BC keeps activating the brake with deceleration rate bmax for the duration Tbrake.
  3. Fun-2-3 After Tbrake, BC releases the brake.

By verifying the conformance of M2’s events with M1’s, we show that the deterministic control of BC satisfies the requirements specified in M0 and M1.

9.6.3.5 Specifying M2

In M2, we specify BC’s control by following FUN-2-1 – FUN-2-3. Since the control changes with time (FUN-2-2 and FUN-2-3), we take care of the remaining time (number of cycles) required for braking.

The overview of machine M2 is as follows:

machine M2 refines M1

variables x,v,ctrl, tbrake

invariants @inv_BC_v: ctrl = BC ⇒ bmaxtbrake

events

event AC ->AC refines AC ->AC

(same as M1)

end

event AC ->BC_brake refines AC ->BC

…

end

event BC_brake ->AC refines BC ->AC

…

end

event BC_brake ->BC_brake refines BC ->BC

…

end

end

The new variable tbrake is the remaining time required for braking. Invariant @inv_BC_v states that the remaining braking time tbrake should be the same as the time required for braking to stop. There are four events, each of which is declared as a refined version of an event of M1. All events except AC->AC are different from M1’s.

Among the four events, we elaborate on AC->BC_brake and BC_brake->BC_brake below.

Event AC->BC_brake inherits predicates of AC->BC but it has additional actions for requirement FUN-2-1; in action Oact_v_tBrake, the value of tbrake is updated with the duration needed to stop (Tbrake = v′/bmax).

event AC ->BC_brake refines AC ->BC

where (same guard as M1)

then @act _x : x : | x′ = x + ∫t = 0min (1, tbrake )(v−bmaxt)dt

Oact_v_tBrake : v,tbrake : | $\begin{array}{l} {v^{\prime} = b_{\max\ }t_{brake\ }^{\prime} \land} \\ {v^{\prime} = v - {\int_{t = 0}^{\min{({1,t_{brake\ }})}}b_{\max}}dt} \\ \end{array}$

end

In event BC_brake->BC_brake, actions are not inherited from its abstract event BC->BC. In particular, actions of updating values x and v (@act_x and @act_v) are deterministically specified — recall that they are non-deterministic in BC->BC of M1 (@act_xv). The event also has action @act_tBrake to update the remaining braking time.

event BC_brake ->BC_brake refines BC->BC

where @grd_BC: ctrl = BC

@grd_BCNext : ¬ACNext(x,v)

@grd_br : 0 < tbrake

then @act_x : x : | x′ = x + ∫t = 0min (1, tbrake )(v−bmaxt)dt

@act_v: v : | v′ = v − ∫t = 0min (1, tbrake )bmaxdt

@act_ctrl: ctrl : | ctrl′ = BC

@act_tBrake : tbrake : | t′brake = max(0, tbrake − 1)

end

9.6.3.6 Verifying M2

The interesting POs of M2 are about action simulations between M1’s events and M2’s. They guarantee that the deterministic control specified in M2 satisfies the requirements specified in M1.

For instance, the PO of action simulation between BC_brake->AC and BC->AC is as follows:

x+ stopDist(v) ≤ xdst,

(@inv_stop)

…

(M0’s and M1’s other invariants)

…

(M2’s invariants)

x′ = x + ∫t = 0min (1, tbrake )(v−bmaxt)dt,

(@act_x)

v′ = v − ∫t = 0min (1, tbrake )bmaxdt,

(@act_v)

…

(other concrete guards/actions)

⊢

x′ + stopDist(v′) ≤ xdst ∧

x′ ≤ nextMaxX(x,v) ∧ v’ ≤ nextMaxV(v)

(@act_xv of BC->AC in M1)

For proving the PO, we need to guide Rodin using its interactive proof interface a little (e.g., for case analysis regarding min(1,tbrake)), but we can mostly rely on Rodin’s automatic provers.

9.6.4 Refinement Strategy

As described in the previous sections, the refinement in Event-B is done in a posit-and-prove style; we construct a machine that is declared as a candidate of a concrete machine of another, and then we verify that its behaviour really conforms with that of the abstract machine.

Therefore, planning which elements of the target system are introduced in each refinement step (refinement strategy) is not a trivial task. In fact, engineers often find it difficult.

There is not the “correct” refinement strategy, but good practices of refinement strategies including the following are shared:

In abstract machines In concrete machines
abstract concepts concrete concepts
whole system details of subsystems
requirements means to satisfy the requirements
what we observe as results how the system works

Also, our empirical study [36] indicated that the following practices can reduce the complexity of modelling and proving with the stepwise refinement mechanism.

  • Having more refinement steps, while trying to introduce, in the same refinement step, those variables which tend to occur together.
  • Introducing variables that often appear in invariants early.

9.7 Conclusions

In this chapter, we reviewed about technologies for theorem proving—writing mathematical proofs in a formalised, i.e., machine-assisted manner. After reviewing the basics of formal logic (Section 9.2), we covered some general techniques such as interactive theorem proving in a highly expressive logic (Isabelle/HOL, Section 9.3) and fully automated theorem proving in languages with restricted expressivity (SAT/SMT solvers, Section 9.4). We also reviewed two specific lines of development towards automotive applications, namely accommodation of continuous/hybrid dynamics (Section 9.5) and gradual model refinement (Section 9.6). The approaches we covered in this chapter are summarised in Table 9.1.

In general, theorem proving is a methodology that needs careful and strategic planning before its application.

  • When it is successfully applied, its benefits are enormous: safety claims as its conclusions come with absolute guarantees in the form of mathematical proofs; moreover, the logical reasoning steps explicated in those proofs serve as explanations why the conclusions must be true. These benefits should be especially favoured in the automotive domain that is safety critical (strong guarantees are desired in the face of potential loss of human lives) and socially accepted (car manufacturers are under a big pressure for social explainability and accountability).

  • However, the cost for these benefits can be enormous as well. The first kind of cost is modelling cost: proofs in theorem proving must be established on rigorous system models (i.e., the mathematical definitions of target systems, cf. Section 9.1.4). A detailed modelling of a single component of a car can easily take several person month. A comprehensive modelling of a car as a whole requires a fundamental reformation of development processes and decades of time—this is what is being pursued in the aerospace industry. In the automotive industry where the development processes are always under the pressure from competition and short model cycles, such a fundamental reformation is hardly feasible.

    The second kind of cost is the cost of proving. Automated theorem proving approaches such as SMT solvers only apply to problems that can be expressed in a restricted language; interactive theorem proving, in contrast, requires a lot of human effort. A single proof costing several person year is not uncommon.

Therefore, theorem proving is in general a high-cost high-return methodology. One has to choose a problem setting very carefully and strategically in order to find a good balance between cost and benefit.

One seeming example of such a good balance identified in the automotive domain is the methodology of RSS (mentioned in Section 9.1.4; more details in Section 7.5 and [19, 32, 33, 53]). In RSS, the “frontier” of mathematical modelling is chosen to be some behavioural safety rules imposed on each vehicle, and the theorem proving efforts never go into the internal working of vehicles. This makes the modelling efforts (each vehicle can be a black-box) and the proof efforts (proofs are essentially massive case distinctions over high-school physics) feasible. Indeed, in the recent paper [32], a logic similar to the one in Section 9.5 is used to express safety rules and prove their safety. These safety rules play the role of traffic laws in the automated driving ecosystem, ensuring the social and industrial relevance of these rules and their safety proofs.

We believe that more targets of theorem proving should be found in the automotive domain. In the coming years where V2V communication is more common, the correctness, security, and privacy of the V2V networks can be a good target of automated theorem proving (Section 9.4), much like the current widespread use of SAT/SMT solvers for the quality assurance of cloud systems [15]. In the quality assurance efforts by automotive manufacturers—e.g. to ensure that their products indeed comply with the safety rules in RSS—theorem proving by iterative model refinement (Section 9.1.4) can serve as a method to decompose system-level requirements into component-level requirements, where the latter can be further passed on to part manufacturers.
