Chapter 10 Search-Based Analysis and Engineering

Paolo Arcaini

National Institute of Informatics, Tokyo, Japan

Fuyuki Ishikawa

National Institute of Informatics, The University of Electro-Communications and SOKENDAI, Tokyo, Japan

10.1 Introduction

Many problems in Software Engineering (SE) can be translated to optimisation problems [31]. In software testing, for example, typical problems are the maximization of the coverage achieved by a test suite, or the minimization of the test suite size. In requirements engineering, a classical problem consists of maximizing the satisfaction of the requirements, and minimizing the software development costs. Very often, these problems have multiple objectives that are conflicting with each other; for example, still considering software testing, it is often desirable to maximize coverage and minimize test suite size at the same time. It is clear that the two objectives are conflicting, as, in order to obtain more coverage, one needs to add more tests.

Since the early 2000s,

Most of the works in SBSE are related to testing problems, and this area is known as Search-Based Testing (SBT) [29, 55, 56]. Works have been proposed for test generation [6, 24], test case prioritization [7, 67], mutation testing [68], combinatorial testing [76], etc. Also falsification (presented in Chapter 1) is an instance of SBT in which the objective function is given by the robustness of a formal specification written in some temporal logic.

Due to its ability to handle large and complex search spaces, SBT has been applied also to testing complex systems, such as machine learning systems [14, 63], quantum programs [72, 73 and 74], control systems [20], and automated driving systems (ADSs) [5, 11, 13, 15, 16, 41, 47, 53]. In this chapter, we are interested in the application of SBT to ADSs, in particular for scenario generation.

We first provide a minimal background on multi-objective optimisation in Section 10.2. Then, in Section 10.3, we present a general framework for SBT of ADSs. The different components of the framework are elaborated in Sections 10.4 to 10.8. Section 10.9 concludes the chapter.

10.2 Preliminaries

In SBSE, software engineering problems are cast as search problems of one or more objectives. In the following, we provide background on multi-objective optimisation; single-objective problems are considered a special case of these.

10.2.1 Multi-Objective Optimisation

A multi-objective optimisation problem is given by a set of m objectives that need to be either maximized or minimized; in the following, without loss of generality, we consider minimization problems.

A solution is an element of X. Optimization problems can also define constraints that must be satisfied by solutions; in this case, they are called constrained optimisation problems. We define the space of feasible solutions as Ω ⊆ X.

Given two feasible solutions A, B ∈ Ω, we say that A dominates B (A ≻ B) if,


(∀i∈{1,…,m}⋅fi(A)≤fi(B)) ∧ (∃j∈{1,…,m}⋅fj(A)<fj(B))

i.e., A is never worse than B for any objective, and it is better for at least one.

For simplicity, one can also consider the solutions in the objective space, i.e., A = (fl (x), …, fin (x)) with x ∈ Ω

A search algorithm explores the search space Ω trying to optimise all the objective functions. The algorithm evaluates some possible solutions S, and returns as output a Pareto front, i.e., the subset of S of non-dominated solutions:


PF(S) = {si∈S∣(∄sj∈S.sj≻si)}

Different algorithms have been proposed to solve optimisation problems, mostly based on evolutionary computation. Notable examples are NSGA-II [21], MOCe11 [59], SMPSO [58], SPEA2 [85], PAES [39], and Ce11DE [22].

10.2.2 Quality Indicators

In practical contexts, one often needs to choose the best among different Pareto fronts computed by the same algorithm or by different algorithms. However, this task is not trivial, as Pareto fronts are not directly comparable. Therefore, different quality indicators have been proposed. A quality indicator assigns a numerical value to a Pareto front, by considering how well the Pareto front achieves quality aspects such as uniformity, spread, convergence, or cardinality. In this way, different Pareto fronts can be compared using their quality indicator assessments.

Hypervolume (HV), for example, is a popular quality indicator that measures the volume of the objective space covered by a Pareto front PF [66] w.r.t. a reference point w (i.e., the worst possible solution). It is defined as:


$$HV(PF) = \ volume\ \left( {{\underset{s_{i} \in PF}{\cup}h}c\left( s_{i} \right)} \right)$$

where hc(si) is the hypercube defined between diagonal corners si and w. Figure 10.1 shows a visual representation of the hypervolume of the Pareto front computed for a two-objective problem (the gray area).

In literature, several quality indicators have been proposed that consider different quality aspects; please refer to [48] for a complete survey. Given this large set of indicators (100 indicators are surveyed in [48]), SBSE practitioners may have problems in selecting a proper quality indicator for evaluating the solutions produced by the used search algorithm. Therefore, guidelines have been developed that assist the user in selecting a quality indicator (or a set of quality indicators) that is most suitable for the used search algorithm [2]; namely, the guide suggests the minimum set of quality indicators that are representative of the “opinions” of different indicators. In other contexts, instead, the user may know which quality indicator to use (because it reflects some desired properties), but does not know which search algorithm to use; the guide in [3, 77] helps in doing such a selection: given a quality indicator, it suggests the search algorithm that most likely provides solutions that are good for it.

10.3 Search-Based Testing for Autonomous Driving Systems

ADSs can potentially transform the transportation domain, and bring several advantages, such as fewer accidents, and reduced congestion [79]. Being complex and safety-critical systems, the throughout testing of ADSs is mandatory for their acceptance [70]. One type of ADS testing consists of doing on-road driving of the autonomous vehicle. Although such testing is ultimately necessary and it is employed for different industrial ADSs such as Voyage.auto [71] and Waymo [75], it has several limits. First of all, it is costly as the final autonomous vehicle must have been produced, and also potentially very dangerous in case failures occur during testing. Moreover, it has been shown that such testing provides limited guarantees, and it requires to consider a huge amount of driving data; namely, 11 billion miles of drives can provide 95% confidence that the autonomous vehicle has a failure rate lower than that of a human driver [33, 54].

A more feasible and pursued approach is simulation-based testing, in which the ADS is run in a simulated environment [10, 84]. A simulator usually allows to specify the environment in which the ADS is run, in terms of road map, regulatory elements (e.g., traffic lights, traffic signals, etc.), initial position of the autonomous vehicle, initial position and behaviour of other traffic participants (i.e., other vehicles and pedestrians), etc. A tester can specify different test scenarios to exercise the ADS under different driving conditions. Given a test scenario, the ADS is simulated and simulation data is collected. This data can be then analysed to check whether the ADS behaves as expected.

Although simulation-based testing is more flexible than on-road testing, it still presents some issues. The main problem is related to the selection of the test scenarios to execute. One may think to use scenarios derived from real test drives or to re-use scenarios developed for other systems. However, Hauer et al. [32] have shown that such an approach is not effective, as these scenarios do not properly challenge the ADS under test, and so some faulty behaviours may not be triggered. They [32], instead, provided evidence that test scenarios should be generated for the specific ADS under test.

Assuming that some test goals have been specified, generating test scenarios that cover these goals is challenging. First of all, the search space for scenarios is infinite; moreover, logical approaches such as concolic testing are not applicable to generate such complex inputs. SBT is a promising technique that has demonstrated to be suitable to tackle these issues. Figure 10.2 shows an overview of SBT for ADSs.

One of the main components of the approach is the definition of the objective functions, which are implemented as fitness functions. These define the test goals (or test requirements) of the testing technique. Test requirements can be specified in different ways. Some approaches [11, 13, 15, 16, 47] focus on particular performance metrics, such as degree of safety, or comfort, and aim at finding scenarios that minimize them. Other approaches, instead, define specific coverage criterion, such as covering the parameters of the ADS [41], covering different types of driving manoeuvres [5], or covering different combinations of requirements violations [53]. We will review different approaches in Section 10.4.

Another component of the approach is the definition of the search space, i.e., where to search for scenarios that cover the test goals. Search spaces can be defined over different elements of a scenario, such as the behaviour of the traffic participants, the road structure, the weather conditions, etc. Some search approaches also search for different configurations of the ADS that can provide a better driving in some particular situations. An overview of different approaches to specify the search space will be given in Section 10.5.

The computation of the fitness functions requires the simulation of the ADS over the selected scenario, and the collection of the simulation data; Fig. 10.2 shows two examples of ADS simulators: the simulator of an industrial path planner, and WiseSIM [4], the simulator for the Autonomoose ADS [60]. Starting from the simulation data, the values of the fitness functions are computed. There are two main issues in this phase. First of all, running an ADS simulator is computationally expensive, with simulations that can take up to several minutes and more; in order to tackle this problem, some approaches (discussed in Section 10.7) have been proposed to approximate the computation of the fitness function using surrogate models that do not need ADS simulations. The second issue of this phase is that ADS simulations may not be completely deterministic, and so the simulation data is not completely reliable for the computation of the fitness values; some recent approaches, discussed in Section 10.8, have been proposed to tackle this problem.

As the final step of the SBT approach, the user receives as output a set of optimal scenarios. In case of single-objective search, only one scenario is provided. In case of multi-objective search, instead, the output is given by a Pareto front of scenarios, i.e., the scenarios that are not strictly dominated by other scenarios.

In the next sections, we will review research works regarding the different phases of the framework as summarised in Table 10.1.

Table 10.1: Research topics in search-based testing for autonomous driving systems
Definition of the search objectives Definition of the search space Oracle problem Scalability Noisy simulations
Section 10.4 Section 10.5 Section 10.6 Section 10.7 Section 10.8

10.4 Search Objectives

In a search-based approach, the search objectives specify the characteristics that the generated scenarios should have. Search objectives can be defined in different ways, depending on which aspects of the ADS need to be tested. We here identify two main categories of search objectives.

Metric-based search objectives aim at finding scenarios that optimise a given metric defined on the simulation of the ADS over the test scenario, such as Euclidean distance to the other vehicles, comfort (measured by, e.g., maximum acceleration), etc. We will review some of these approaches in Section 10.4.1.

Metric-based objectives are useful to generate particular scenarios possibly showing that the ADS can fail in a given way; however, they do not provide any type of guarantee regarding what ADS behaviours are observed in the generated test scenarios, i.e., they are not interested in the diversity of the ADS behaviours. In testing for classical programs, coverage criteria are used to characterize different aspects of the system under test that need to be covered by a test suite; coverage-based search objectives follow this approach and, starting from coverage criteria specified for ADSs, use objective functions that aim to obtain full coverage. We will review these approaches in Section 10.4.2. A summary of all the approaches is given in Table 10.2.

Table 10.2: Different types of search objectives in search-based testing for autonomous driving systems
Metric-based search objectives Coverage-based search objectives
Time to collision [12] (Section 10.4.1.1) Parameter coverage [40] (Section 10.4.2.1)
Safety distance [47] (Section 10.4.1.2) Patterns of driving characteristics [5] (Section 10.4.2.2)
Feature interactions [13] (Section 10.4.1.3) Patterns of requirements violations [53] (Section 10.4.2.3)

10.4.1 Metric-Based Search Objectives

We classify in the metric-based category all the approaches that aim at maximizing or minimizing a specific metric defined over the ADS simulation. Usually, the goal is to worsen the metric (e.g., minimizing the minimum Euclidean distance between the ego vehicle and the other vehicles) in order to find specific ADS failures.

Several approaches test the ADS for safety and the typical goal of these approaches is to find dangerous situations in which the autonomous vehicle collides or is close to a collision. We here review some of them.

10.4.1.1 Time to Collision

Ben Abdessalem et al. [12] tested an Automated Emergency Braking (AEB), that is a common component in ADSs. An AEB operates as follows: its senses through sensors the position and speed of other traffic participants (pedestrians, vehicles, etc.) in a given field of view in front of the ego vehicle; if an object is perceived, the time to collision (TTC) is computed; if TTC is below a given threshold, the vision component is informed, and this tries to recognize the type of object; on the basis of the recognized object, the system decides whether to apply an emergency braking. AEB can be tested in the PreScan simulator that allowed it to specify different scenarios. The authors propose an SBT approach for finding critical test scenarios in which the autonomous vehicle interacts with a pedestrian who is trying to cross the street; specifically, the approach tries to find scenarios in which the autonomous vehicle collides at high speed with the pedestrian. This test goal is specified using two fitness functions:

  • One requiring it to minimize the distance between the pedestrian and the vehicle.
  • The other one requiring it to maximize the collision speed.

Note that the approach provides a Pareto front of solutions as output, each one showing a different way to satisfy the test goal.

10.4.1.2 Safety Distance

Li et al. [47] propose AV-FUZZER, an SBT approach combined with fuzzing, that has the goal of finding safety violations of an ADS implemented in the Apollo

10.4.1.3 Feature Interactions

Ben Abdessalem et al. [13] target the safety violations due to feature interactions. An ADS is composed of different units of functionality (also called features), such as the Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), the Automated Emergency Braking (AEB), the Traffic Sign Recognition (TSR), etc. Even if these features work correctly in isolation, they may lead to failures when combined together, in particular if they provide commands to the same actuators: for example, ACC and AEB both provide commands to the vehicle brakes. A feature interaction could occur when the command provided by a feature is overridden by a command of another feature, e.g., the command of the AEB to stop is overridden by the command of ACC to maintain the speed. The authors propose FITEST (Feature Interaction TESTing), an SBT approach to discover harmful feature interactions; the approach solves a many-objective problem, i.e., a problem with more than three objectives. Specifically, for each branch of the code involved in a feature interaction, the approach specifies an objective that aims at covering the branch and, at the same time, violating a safety requirement; in total, there are k × n objectives, being k the number of branches in the code and n the number of safety requirements. FITEST implements a type of search algorithm, called MOSA [61], that aims at solving each objective individually, rather than trying to optimise all the objectives together.

10.4.2 Coverage-Based Search Objectives

In testing, a coverage criterion defines what needs to be covered by the test suite in order to consider the system under test sufficiently tested. Specifically, a coverage criterion defines a set of test goals (also called test requirements); in order for the criterion to be completely fulfilled, each test goal must be covered in at least one test. SBT is an effective technique to generate tests satisfying particular test goals; the satisfaction of a test goal is embedded in the fitness function used to drive the search.

Most of the criteria proposed for ADS testing are black box: they are required to cover different types of scenarios in which the ADS may operate, or to observe different types of behaviours (i.e., different types of manoeuvres) of the ADS. For classical programs, different white box (also called structural) coverage criteria (e.g., statement coverage, branch coverage, MC/DC, etc.) have been proposed and are actively used. However, in [42], we have shown that this type of coverage is rather weak for ADSs, as very simple scenarios can achieve very high structural coverage: this is a problem, as it means that scenarios are not able to discriminate between the execution of different parts of the code and, hence, of possibly different types of ADS behaviours. Recently, some approaches have been proposed that still aim at covering the ADS implementation, but, in order to tackle the problems we identified in [42], they target the specific way ADSs are implemented. In the following, we review these criteria.

10.4.2.1 Parameter Coverage

In [40, 41], we proposed a coverage criterion specific for testing the path planner component of the ADS of our industrial partner.

The next short-term path is decided using an optimisation algorithm. A cost function is used to assign a cost value to all the possible short-term paths: the cost function considers aspects such as safety of driving, compliance to traffic regulations, and comfort. The least costly short-term path is selected to be followed. A more detailed description of the selection of a short-term path is given in Algorithm 2. Given a short-term path stp:

  • it evaluates the driving characteristics that are required in order to follow stp. Namely, given a characteristic dc, it checks whether the amount of dc is non-negligible, using a specific threshold (line 6). The intuition is that, over a given threshold, the driving characteristic dc affects some aspect of the drive, such as the safety, comfort, and compliance to traffic rules;
  • in case the driving characteristic dc is over the threshold, a parameter pdc is aggregated (either summed, or multiplied with some other quantity) to the cost of the path (line 7). Table 10.3 reports some of the driving characteristics of the path planner with their corresponding parameter.
Table 10.3: Path planner – driving characteristics and corresponding parameters
Driving characteristic Parameter
forward acceleration paccMax
lateral acceleration platg
speed Pspd
deceleration pdecMax
safety distance psafeDist
curvature pcurvature

The short-term path with the smallest cost is then followed (line 9).

Algorithm 2 Path planner — selection of the short-term path

1:

ShortTermPaths ← retrieveSTPs()

2:

STP costs ← ∅

3:

for stp ∈ ShortTermPaths do

4:

coststp ← 0

5:

for dc ∈ { accMax, …, safeDist} do

6:

if evaluateDC(stp, dc) then

7:

coststp ← aggregateCost(coststp, pdc)

8:

STPcosts ← STPcosts U {(stp, coststp)}

9:

return getMinCostShortTermPath(STPcosts)

In [40], we observed that, in order to thoroughly test the path planner, all the possible decisions that can be taken by the path planner should be observed in at least one test. This is particularly challenging, as there is no proper characterization of the path planner’s decisions: given two paths computed by the path planner, it is difficult to judge whether they have been taken for the same reason (i.e., the type of decision is the same), or they have been determined for different reasons.

To tackle this issue, we proposed to exploit the definition of the path planner’s cost function. We claimed that a minimal condition for testing the path planner is that each parameter is shown to be “relevant” in at least one decision in one test; in this case, we will say that the parameter is covered. The relevance, and thus the coverage, of a parameter is assessed as follows. A parameter pi is covered by a scenario S if the path planner configured with a different parameter value p′i would have selected a path different from the one computed by the original path planner; the intuition is that, if changing the parameter does not lead to a change in followed path, it means that the parameter is irrelevant in the decision taken by the path planner in that scenario.

Since checking all the possible alternative parameter values p′i is not feasible, we only check a fixed number of values k · pi, with k ∈ {0, 0.5, 0.9, 1.1, 1.5, 2}; we call this approximation of the criterion as mutation-based parameter coverage and the values k as mutation levels.

In [41], we proposed a search-based approach to generate scenarios achieving parameter coverage. We proposed two approaches:

  • Single-parameter approach: given a parameter pi , the approach searches for a scenario S that achieves mutation-based parameter coverage for pi. Specifically, the fitness function prefers the scenarios that achieve the coverage with the smallest mutation level: indeed, if the simulation changes by only slightly changing the parameter pi , it means that the decisions taken by the path planner in S are highly influenced by pi. Obviously, the fitness penalizes the scenarios that do not achieve any coverage. Moreover, the fitness also penalizes scenarios in which the vehicle collides (regardless of their coverage) as these are extreme scenarios that do not allow us to properly observe the influence of the parameter in the normal driving condition; such types of scenarios should be considered with other testing approaches, as those presented in Section 10.4.1.

  • Multi-parameter approach: the single-parameter approach is very effective, as it allows us to find scenarios that cover the parameters with the minimum mutation level. However, it could create test suites that are unnecessarily big, in particular when there are several parameters. Therefore, we proposed a variation of the approach that aims at covering as many parameters as possible with the same scenario. We provided two versions of this approach:

    • Multiple objectives: in this version, for each parameter pi , we specify a fitness function as defined in the single-parameter approach. This version of the approach is therefore multi-objective.
    • Combined multi-objective: this version, instead, is single-objective, and all the fitness values for the coverage of the different parameters are aggregated into a single value. The aggregation of the single fitness values for the different parameters follows two principles: (i) covering more parameters is preferred to covering less parameters; (ii) a solution that covers a parameter with mutation level i is worse than a solution in which all the parameters are covered with mutation levels j < i.

10.4.2.2 Coverage of Patterns of Driving Characteristics

Parameter coverage simply checks whether some parameter pi influences the decision of the path planner at some point in time during the execution of scenario S, but it does not impose any constraint on the duration of its influence. It could be that the parameter is relevant for a very short period of time during the scenario execution, making the usefulness of the scenario limited. Therefore, parameter coverage may not guarantee the chance to observe all the possible driving manoeuvres that can be done by the autonomous vehicle.

In [5], we tackled this problem by considering the driving characteristics (such as forward acceleration, later acceleration, curvature, etc.; see Table 10.3) that are implemented in a path. During simulation, at each time point, the path planner simulator reports which driving characteristics have been implemented in the path with a non-negligible value (over a given threshold, as shown in Algorithm 2). Our idea is that a driving characteristic is more “relevant” in a scenario execution if it is implemented for a longer period of time. For example, safety distance is more relevant if it is violated for a long period, as it may indicate a safety problem. In the same way, if lateral acceleration is applied during a turn, it is more relevant if it is applied for the whole turn rather than for few moments, as it may indicate an abrupt manoeuvre that should be inspected by ADS engineers. In some driving situations, two (or more) driving characteristics could be relevant simultaneously; observing such cases is important as well, as they may show some undesired interactions between the driving characteristics.

To capture these intuitions, in [5], we defined the notion of patterns of occurrence for single and pairs of driving characteristics. Namely, given the simulation of the path planner over a scenario S, we define:

  • activation interval of a given driving characteristic dc i as the consecutive time points in which dc i was applied; in Fig. 10.4a, for example, there are three activation intervals for dc i , and the one between t4 and t7 is the most relevant one, as it is the longest one;

  • pairs of activation intervals of two driving characteristics dc i and dc j ; the relevance of the pair is determined according to these criteria:

    • overlapping intervals in which the two characteristics are applied together for some time are more relevant than non-overlapping intervals; for example, the pairs of overlapping intervals in Fig. 10.4a are more relevant than the non-overlapping ones in Fig. 10.4b;
    • given different overlapping intervals, those in which the overlapping area is larger are more relevant; for example, in Fig. 10.4a, the pair of intervals between time points t9 and t12 are more relevant because they have the largest overlapping region;
    • given different non-overlapping intervals, those in which the intervals are closer are preferred. For example, in Fig. 10.4b, the pair between time points t3 and t8 is preferred, as it is distant of only one time interval.

      In [5], we proposed a search-based approach to generate scenarios containing given patterns of driving characteristics. Specifically, we proposed two versions of the approach:

      • Single Driving Characteristic approach (SDC): given a driving characteristic dc i , it searches for scenarios in which the relevance of dc i is maximized. The problem is multi-objective. The first objective aims at maximizing the length of the longest activation interval of dc i. The second objective, instead, aims at minimizing the likelihood of collisions; without this objective, the search could find very dangerous scenarios, for which assessing whether the ADS is implementing the correct driving manoeuvres is difficult; the minimization of the objective allows to find the minimum level of danger necessary to obtain the desired driving pattern.
      • Pair Driving Characteristics approach (PDCs): given a pair of driving characteristics dc i and dc j , it searches for scenarios in which their interaction is maximized. The problem is still multi-objective. The first objective aims at maximizing the overlapping of the activation intervals of dc i and dc j and, if this is not possible, it tries to minimize their distance. As for SDC, the second objective aims at minimizing the likelihood of collisions.

      Figure 10.5 shows an example of a scenario (snapshots of its simulation) generated for covering the pair of driving characteristics dec and latg. while the ego vehicle is turning, it must suddenly brake to avoid vehicle c2 crossing the intersection from top. Figure 10.5a is the simulation moment in which the two driving characteristic related to lateral acceleration (due to the turning) and deceleration start overlapping. Figure 10.5b shows the moment when the ego vehicle does not brake any more, and so the overlapping of the two driving characteristics finishes. You can observe that finding this type of scenario is far from trivial: the search approach managed to find the driving situation in which the ego vehicle decides to turn before vehicle c3 crosses from right, but then needs to break to let vehicle c2 pass.

      In some cases, finding the overlapping of two driving characteristics is not possible, but it still interesting to find a scenario in which they are activated closely. Figure 10.6 shows such a type of scenario found for acc and dec (that, by definition, can not be activated simultaneously). The ego vehicle first decelerates for to let vehicle c3 pass (Fig. 10.6a). Then, as soon as c3 is passed, it accelerates to do the turn (Fig. 10.6b): there is no time interval between the end of deceleration and the start of acceleration, meaning that the search managed to optimise the coverage of the pair as much as possible. The ego vehicle stops accelerating at the end of the curve, as shown in Fig. 10.6c.

10.4.2.3 Coverage of Patterns of Requirements Violations

The test generation approaches reviewed in Section 10.4.1 usually aimed at worsening a given metric related to some system requirement in order to violate it; examples are the minimization of the minimum Euclidean distance between the ego vehicle and the other vehicles to violate safety requirements, or the maximization of acceleration to violate comfort requirements.

However, in order to properly test the ADS, the satisfaction/violation of the different requirements should be considered together. Indeed, in some cases, the ADS can not satisfy all the requirements at the same time, and the ADS must trade-off among requirements. We call requirement violation pattern a specific combination of satisfied/violated requirements.

From a testing perspective, observing different requirement violation patterns is highly interesting, as this allows to judge whether the ADS gave a correct priority to the different requirements, i.e., it prioritized the satisfaction of the most critical requirements.

Moreover, in case of failure (e.g., accident), different requirement violation patterns could provide different explanations for the failure: the situation in which the ego vehicle collides and runs the red light is different from the one in which the collision happens while the ego vehicle is doing an unsafe lane change.

In [53], we proposed an SBT approach for covering as many requirement violation patterns as possible. Since the number of patterns is very large, trying to cover all of them is not feasible. Therefore, we identify two principles that must be followed: (i) the most critical patterns should be prioritized in the search; (ii) if a pattern is impossible to occur, it should not be searched. The proposed approach EM00D, based on the previous two principles, is shown in Fig. 10.7.

The central component of the approach is an Evolutionary Many-Objective Optimization (EMOO) that, given a pattern V taken as input, searches a scenario covering it; namely, for each requirement in V that needs to be satisfied, an object function is specified that maximizes the requirement satisfaction; instead, for each requirement that must be violated, the corresponding objective function minimizes its satisfaction.

The whole approach works as follows:

  1. The Initial Prioritization phase (IP) sorts all the possible requirements violation patterns in Vc according to their criticality, as shown in Fig. 10.8;

  2. EMOO is executed using the most critical pattern Vc[0] as input;
  3. Dynamic Prioritization (DP) sorts the patterns in Vt based on the likelihood of their occurrence. To do this, it uses the information on the patterns that have been previously searched and not found and those that have never been searched;
  4. EMOO is executed using as input the most critical pattern Vt[0] that is likely to occur;
  5. If the search budget is not exhausted, the approach performs another iteration starting from Item 3.

10.5 Definition of the Search Space

ADS simulators accept, as input, scenarios that describe the environment in which the autonomous vehicle is driving; such scenarios are usually specified using some DSL, such as OpenSCENARIO [8], GeoScenario [64], or Scenic [25]. Depending on the type of simulator, they allow us to specify different elements such as the road structure, the number and behaviour of other traffic participants (i.e., other vehicles and pedestrians), regulatory elements (e.g., traffic lights, traffic signs, etc.), weather conditions (e.g., fog, rain, etc.), and so on.

SBT approaches for ADSs (as those described in the previous sections) usually search for scenarios in which some specific test goals are satisfied. Deciding which scenarios to search for is a difficult task. Indeed, the possible ADS scenarios are infinite and so the search space must be restricted to some particular class of scenarios. A common technique followed by different SBT approaches [5, 11, 13, 15, 16, 41, 53] consists of identifying a particular road structure, a given number of traffic participants, and some regulatory elements, that define an abstract scenario; some elements of this initial abstract scenario are parametrized and they constitute the search space of the SBT approach: each individual of the search provides concrete values for the abstract scenario parameters and so identifies a concrete scenario.

However, for some particular test goals, the shape of the road could be particularly important; for example, testing the lane keeping component of an ADS requires us to test different types of roads. So, some recent works have proposed road generation. Gambi et al. [27] use procedural content generation (a technique used in video games) to generate an initial set of roads that are then evolved using a genetic algorithm, with the aim of finding a road in which the ego vehicle drives off the road.

The generation of roads has been recognized as a particular difficult problem, and so it has been proposed as a challenge in a competition on SBT for ADS at the 14th and 15th International Workshop on Search-Based Software Testing (SBST 2021 and SBST 2022).

One of the best approaches of the first edition of the competition was our approach Frenetic [18], that adopts a curvature-based representation for roads. The approach was further improved for the second edition of the competition with FreneticV [19], that adopts particular mechanism to generate valid roads (e.g., not self-intersecting); also FreneticV obtained good results in the competition. The two tools are integrated in the library Frentic-lib [36]. In both Frenetic and FreneticV, a road is represented by an array of N curvature values κ0,…,κN-1 ∈ ℝ. Please refer to Chapter 7 for a complete description of the theoretical framework; we here provide the intuition by means of an example. Figure 10.9a shows the curvature values of a road generated by the approach. A positive value requires a turn to the left, while a negative value requires a turn to the right; given a value κi, the higher its absolute value, the sharper the curvature. The value κi identifies the curvature between points i + 1 and i + 2. Figure 10.9b shows the corresponding generated road. The first two points are fixed, and independent of the concrete κ values; this allows the vehicle to start in a straight segment. Then, between points y1 and y3, the road turns left because of the first two positive curvature values κ0 and κ1. Then, the three negative values κ2 , κ3 , and κ4 make the road turn to the right between points y3 and y6. Then, since κ5 is 0, the road goes straight between the generated points y6 and y7. The road construction continues in this way for the remaining κ values.

Other testing works use different road representations. For example, Riccio and Tonella [65] use Catmull-Rom splines, Klück et al. [38] use Bézier curves, and Gambi et al. [27] use parametric straight and curved road segments to construct road networks. Given all these possible representations, one may wonder which is the best representation for their problem. In [17], we performed an empirical study to investigate which is the influence of the road representation on the effectiveness of SBT for ADS. In the study, we considered six road representations: (i) Catmull-Rom splines with Cartesian control nodes, (ii) Bézier curves with Cartesian control nodes, (iii) curvature-based representation, (iv) curvature-based representation with varying segment lengths, (v) orientation-based representation, (vi) orientation-based representation with varying segment lengths. These were used to represent individuals in an SBT approach that searches for failures of an ADS lane-keeping component. The study investigated the following questions: (1) Which representation allows to find more failures? (2) Which representation produces the most number of different roads? (3) Which is the impact of the mutation and crossover operations of the search algorithm on the different representations?

Results of the study show that: (i) curvature-based road representations trigger more failures and generate more diverse roads; (ii) mutation on different positions of an individual have different impacts depending on the adopted representation; (iii) the impact of the crossover operator is similar in the different representations.

10.6 Oracle Problem

One of the main challenges in software testing is the oracle problem [9]. It consists of specifying which is the expected output of each test execution and, therefore, deciding whether the test passes or fails. If complete system requirements are available, the oracle problem can be addressed. However, for complex systems, in some cases it is not clear which should be the expected behaviour. This is particularly true for ADSs. As an example, consider the case in which the autonomous vehicle collides with a fast vehicle that does not give the right of way, although it should: in this case, not only the autonomous vehicle is not responsible for the collision, but also it could be that it has no way to avoid it, i.e., the collision could be effectively unavoidable. Specifying whether this is a failure or not is challenging.

Most of the SBT approaches proposed for finding collisions overlook this problem; since their fitness functions aim at maximizing the probability of collisions (e.g., by minimizing the time to collision), they may find collisions that are so severe that they are actually unavoidable. From a testing point of view, these collisions are not interesting, as they do not manifest a failure of the ADS.

Starting from these observations, in [15], we tackled the oracle problem for the path planner of our industry partner. We provided the notion of avoidable collision as a collision that could have been avoided by performing some different driving manoeuvre. The core of the idea is that the path planner is configurable with some parameters that affect its decision process, as described in Section 10.4.2; changing the value of these parameters can lead the path planner to take different decisions in some particular scenarios. Starting from this observation, we identify an avoidable collision as the pair ⟨S, p′ ⟩, such that:

  • the original path planner PPp̅ (i.e., path planner configured with original parameter values p̅o ) leads to a collision if executed over the scenario S;
  • the modified path planner PPp̄ ′ (i.e., path planner configured with modified parameter values p̅′ ) does not lead to a collision when executed over S.

In [15], we also proposed a search-based approach to find avoidable collisions. The search space is given by scenarios and by alternative values for the path planner; so an individual of the search is a pair ⟨S, p̅′ ⟩.

The problem is multi-objective. The first objective requires us to find an avoidable collision. It is based on the function danger(S,p̅′ ) that specifies the danger of the simulation of scenario S using the path planner PPp̅′:

  • if there is no collision, it specifies how far the ego vehicle was from colliding;
  • in case of collision, it specifies the impact of the collision as relative collision speed.

The first objective, that needs to be minimized, is defined as:


$$f_{d}\left( \left\langle {S,{\overline{p}}^{\prime}} \right\rangle \right) = \left( {D_{{\overline{p}}^{\prime}} - D_{{\overline{p}}^{o}}} \right) + {penalty}\left( \left\langle {S,{\overline{p}}^{\prime}} \right\rangle \right)$$

where Dp̅o = danger(S,p̅o ) is the danger of the simulation with the original path planner, and Dp̅′ = danger(S,p̅′ ) the danger of the simulation with the modified path planner. The difference between danger values specifies that we want to find scenarios in which the danger of the original path planner is much higher than that of the modified path planner. However, this term of the sum is not sufficient to specify that we want to find cases in which the original path planner leads to a collision while the modified one does not. To this aim, the second term of the sum (i.e., penalty) is used to discriminate among different types of scenarios in which collisions occur or not using the two versions of the path planner:


$${penalty}\left( \left\langle {S,{\overline{p}}^{\prime}} \right\rangle \right) = \begin{cases} 0 & {\text{~if~}C_{{\overline{p}}^{o}} \land \neg C_{{\overline{p}}^{\prime}},} \\ 1000 & {\text{~if~}C_{{\overline{p}}^{o}} \land C_{{\overline{p}}^{\prime}} \vee \neg C_{{\overline{p}}^{o}} \land \neg C_{{\overline{p}}^{\prime}},} \\ 2000 & {\text{~if~}\neg C_{{\overline{p}}^{o}} \land C_{{\overline{p}}^{\prime}}.} \\ \end{cases}$$

where Cp̅′o and Cp̅′ specify whether a collision occurred, respectively, using the original and the modified path planner. The intuition is that the most preferred case (i.e., penalty 0) is when there is a collision with the original path planner and not with the modified one, as this is the exact definition of avoidable collision. The second best preferred case (penalty 1000) is when both the original and the modified path planners both lead or do not lead to a collision. The least preferred case (penalty 2000) is when the modified path planner leads to a collision but the original one does not.

The second objective requires that the alternative parameter values are not too different from the original ones, i.e.,


$$f_{p}\left( \left\langle {S,{\overline{p}}^{\prime}} \right\rangle \right) = \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( \frac{p_{i} - p_{i}^{\prime}}{d_{i}^{U} - d_{i}^{L}} \right)^{2}}$$

where [diL,diU] is the search interval of ith parameter, and p̅o = [p1 , …, pn ] and p̅′ = [p1 , …, pn ] are the original and the modified parameter values. The motivation is that changing the parameters too much could lead the ADS to behave strangely, e.g., standing still when encountering other vehicles. Moreover, the original parameter values p̅o have already been extensively tested and, therefore, it makes sense to try not to change them too much.

Figure 10.10 shows an example of avoidable collision found by the approach. The ego vehicle (i.e., the red vehicle) is approaching the crossroad with the aim of turning right. Meanwhile, a vehicle is approaching the intersection from north, and another one from east. Figure 10.10a shows snapshots of the simulation obtained using the original path planner: the ego vehicle stops to give the right of way to the vehicle coming from north, but then collides with the vehicle coming from east, as it does not have time to accelerate to avoid the collision. Figure 10.10b shows the behaviour of the alternative path planner: the ego vehicle enters the intersection while giving the right of way to the other vehicle; in this way, it can start turning as soon as the vehicle passes. By looking at the alternative parameter values p̅′ found by the search, we observe that high lateral acceleration and high curvature have lower penalties: this allows the path planner to select this more sharp manoeuvre that is needed to avoid the collision.

Experimental results in [15] show that the approach is able to find different types of avoidable collisions and that these require different alternative parameters values in order to be avoided. Such information can be used to do fault localization and debugging [80, 81] (see Chapter 11).

However, re-engineering the path planner starting from these test results is not easy, as it is not clear which parameter values to use. One solution is to build a path planner that at runtime decides which parameter values to use on the basis of the current driving situation; we pursued this approach in [51], where we built a path planner that recognizes whether a driving situation is similar to one observed during testing, and changes the parameter values to those that in testing turned out to lead to safer driving.

A different approach tries to find alternative parameter values that solve different types of collisions. In [16], we extended the approach in [15] by searching different types of collision that are all solved by the same alternative parameter values.

10.7 Scalability

The fitness computation in SBT for ADS requires us to run the generated scenario with the ADS simulator, collect the simulation log, and compute the fitness function from it. The ADS simulation can be computationally very expensive, taking from several seconds to few minutes; for example, all the simulations performed with the industrial path planner described before, take from one to two minutes. This limits the scalability of the approach. In optimisation problems, a typical way to tackle this issue is to use surrogate models that approximate the fitness function and so avoid its expensive execution. We refer to [69] for an extensive survey on surrogate models for search approaches.

For example, Ben Abdessalem et al. [11] use surrogate models to accelerate the testing of a Pedestrian Detection Vision (PeVi) system. The system perceives the front of the vehicle with a CCD camera, and uses image processing and object recognition algorithms to decide whether to warn the driver of the presence of pedestrians, in particular when the visibility is reduced due to bad weather conditions. The system can be simulated in the simulator PreScan that allows to simulate the driving environment, including the behaviour of pedestrians. A search-based approach has been implemented to find failures of PeVi; the approach has three objective functions:

  • minimization of the distance between the vehicle and the pedestrian;
  • minimization of the distance between the pedestrian and the most critical area in front of the vehicle;
  • minimization of time to collision.

Since simulating the PreScan simulator is expensive, the authors propose to use surrogate models to speed up the search. Specifically, for each fitness function, a surrogate model using a neural network is created, starting from training data of previous simulations. The evaluation of a scenario S using a surrogate model provides a predicted value F (S) and a confidence value Fcl (S) , being c/ the desired confidence level. The approach also computes the most optimistic value as F (S) — Fcl(S), and the most pessimistic value as F (S) + Fcl(5). Then, the NSGA-II search algorithm is modified as follows:

  • the fitness values of all individuals are computed using the surrogate models; for each fitness, the approach computes the most optimistic and the most pessimistic value;
  • it ranks all the individuals in three ways: in rank using the approximated fitness values, in rank— using the optimistic fitness values, and in rank+ using the pessimistic fitness values;
  • then, the approach assumes that the real fitness value of an individual is included between its optimistic and pessimistic approximated value. Starting from this assumption, it identifies all the individuals whose position in the real ranking would be unchanged (w.r.t. the position in rank) if they take any value between its optimistic and pessimistic value;
  • for all the individuals identified in the previous step, the computed approximated fitness values are good enough for search purposes (i.e., they do not affect the real ranking). The other individuals, instead, are simulated with the PreScan simulator in order to have precise fitness values.

10.8 Noisy Simulations

The ADS simulators used for executing the generated scenarios can be affected by some noise, i.e., repeated executions of the same scenario may not lead to the exact same simulation results. This is particularly true for simulators based on the Robotic Operating System (ROS), such as WiseSim [4], the simulator of the Autonomoose ADS [60]. Figure 10.11 visualizes the issue. Figure 10.11a shows the template of a scenario for WiseSim in which the ego vehicle must cross the intersection while there is vehicle V1 approaching the intersection from right. By modifying the parameters of this template, we can possibly find concrete scenarios in which the two vehicles collide. As an experiment, we modified the V ‘s initial position in the range [-70, —35], and we simulated each scenario 30 times. For each simulation, we computed the minimum Euclidean distance between the two vehicles along the whole simulation, as shown in Fig. 10.11b. We observe that for all the scenarios, the computed metric can vary greatly; for some scenarios, the different repetitions can lead both to collision (red crosses) and non-collision (green circles).

The non-determinism of ROS has been recognized as one of the issues in testing ROS-based systems [1]. Such issue is exacerbated in search-based scenario generation; indeed, noisy simulation values can mislead the search towards solutions that only apparently look good.

A simple solution to tackle the problem is to repeat each scenario several times and compute the fitness value as average of the metric along all the repetitions [23]. Although this approach is very precise, it is also very costly and does not scale for computational expensive systems such as ADSs. Therefore, in [35, 37], we have proposed a more scalable approach to handle noise in multi-objective optimisation; the approach has then been applied to SBT for Autonomoose in [34]. The main idea of the approach is to use the historical data of previous fitness evaluations to compute the fitness of a new individual. Figure 10.12 visualizes the approach. The left side shows the individual in the search space, while the right side shows their computed fitness values in the objective space. Given an individual whose fitness must be computed (e.g., the central point in the circle in the left plot), the approach selects its k nearest neighbours in the history of previously evaluated individuals; only neighbours that are within a given distance are selected. The fitness of the current individual is computed as the mean of the fitness values of the selected neighbours.

10.9 Conclusions

Evolutionary computation has been applied to solve different software engineering problems, in particular related to testing. SBT is an active research area that has targeted the testing of not only classical programs, but also complex systems such as ADSs. In this chapter, we have reviewed different SBT approaches for ADS, by considering different aspects: test objectives, definition of search space, scalability, and handling noisy simulations. The reviewed approaches are all related to the generation of scenarios. However, search approaches have been applied to tackle other testing problems for ADSs, such as test case prioritization [52], and sensitivity analysis of ADS parameters [45, 78].

Chapter 11 Fault Localisation and Understanding

Xiao-Yi Zhang

University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, China

11.1 Introduction

In the industry 4.0 era, software applications, such as cyber-physical systems (CPS), server systems, machine-learning-based systems, database systems, and real-time systems, are playing an increasingly important role in both the industrial world and our daily life. On the other hand, the dependability of these systems is essential, as failures or requirement violations of these systems may lead to disruptive results, even the loss of human lives. Thus, activities for software quality assurance, such as testing and debugging, are becoming increasingly important. However, current software systems tend to be composed of various components and exhibit complex behaviours, making these quality assurance activities extremely resource-consuming. Investigation results show that the process of testing and debugging takes up to 50% — 80% of resources in the classical cycle of software development and maintenance [11, 52].

In this chapter, we discuss the activity of Fault Localisation (FL), which is the first and most important step of debugging, aiming to identify the faulty components in the subject program (or system). Let PG denote the subject program composed of the set of components C = {c1 , c2, …}; here, the components can be program statements, functions, classes, or some high-level modules in a system. Suppose that, during testing, at least one failure was detected. Then, by doing FL, we aim to find a subset of components Cf ⊆ C which are the root causes leading to these detected failures.

Intuitively, if FL can be effectively and efficiently automatised, the whole process of debugging can be accelerated. To date, various studies focusing on the automation of FL have been conducted, accompanied by countless strategies to improve its accuracy and efficiency. According to the survey conducted by Wong et al. [49], these approaches can be categorised as: slice-based techniques [4, 20, 26, 45, 55, 64], program spectrum-based techniques [1, 2, 52, 58], statistics- based techniques [31-33, 48], program state-based techniques [19, 41, 54, 62, 62], machine learning-based techniques [47, 50, 51], model-based techniques [35, 36, 44], and data mining-based techniques [8, 13, 63].

In this chapter, we take the most widely-used and light-weighted FL technique, called Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation (SBFL), as a representative to show how we can apply SBFL in practice. The implementation of SBFL is introduced in Section 11.2. In Section 11.3, we briefly review the state-of-art studies on the improvement of SBFL. Then, in Section 11.4, we discuss the extension of SBFL to Deep Neural Networks (DNN) and Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS), respectively, which are popular domains in Industrial 4.0. Finally, we summarise this chapter in Section 11.5.

11.2 Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation and Its Applications

In this section, we introduce the most popular and widely applied FL, called Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation (SBFL). Note that in this section, we consider statements as program components under analysis, but other program elements (e.g., functions or classes) could be used as well.

11.2.1 Description of SBFL

Let S = {s1,s2,…,sn} be the set of statements of the program PG to debug. Assume PG contains a faulty statement sf; then, the problem of fault localisation is to find sf in S. SBFL takes as input the test information and predicts the faulty component sf from the statements’ set S. The detailed description of SBFL is presented as follows.

Assume a test suite including m test cases, i.e., T = {t1,t2,... , tm} has already been generated and executed. For each test case t in T, we record its coverage information, i.e., which statements are exercised, and its output correctness, i.e., whether its output reveals a failure or not. Here, for each t ∈ T, let Ct denote the statements’ set that are covered by t during execution; also let O(t) ∈{ Pass, Fail} denote the output correctness oft: O(t) = Pass and O(t) = Fail denote that the output oft is passed and failure-revealing, respectively. Then, based on T, SBFL calculates the following quantities for each statement s:

  • ef(s): the number of failure-revealing test cases that exercise statement s, i.e., |{t ∈ T|s ∈ Ct, O(t) = Fail}|;
  • ep(s): the number of passed test cases that exercise statement s, i.e., |{t ∈ T|s ∈ Ct, O(t) = Pass}|;
  • nf(s): the number of failure-revealing test cases that do not exercise statements, i.e., |{t ∈ T|s ∉ Ct, O(t) = Fail}|;
  • np(s): the number of passed test cases that do not exercise statements, i.e., |{t ∈ T|s ∉ Ct, O(t) = Fail}|.

Also, let F and P denote the total number of failure-revealing and passed test cases, respectively. Note that, for any statements, we have ef (s) = F — nf (s) and ep(s) = P — np(s).

SBFL predicts the suspiciousness of each statements using a metric, which is a formula involving the above quantities (i.e., ef, ep, nf,…, np, F, and P). Here, let Rx denote the metric with name “X”. For example, one of the earliest proposed metrics, Tarantula [24], denoted by RTar, is expressed as follows:

(11.1)
$$R_{Tar}(s) = \frac{ef(s)/F}{ef(s)/F + ep(s)/P}$$

As another example, Abreu et al. [1] proposed the Ochiai metric Roch, which has been observed to have better performance than RTar:

(11.2)
$$R_{Och}(s) = \frac{ef(s)}{\sqrt{F(ef(s) + ep(s))}}$$

Furthermore, Naish et al. [37] and Xie et al. [52] proposed a metric called Op, in which the term ef has the major influence on the suspiciousness.

(11.3)
$$R_{Op}(s) = ef(s) - \frac{ep(s)}{np(s) + ep(s) + 1}$$

They proved that ROp is the maximal metric under the single-fault condition. In other words, if the program has only one faulty statement, we cannot find another metric that always performs better than ROp.

To date, hundreds of metrics have been proposed. Although different metrics produce different calculations, they all follow the two heuristics:

  1. the larger ef(s) is, the more suspicious statement s is, and
  2. the lower ep(s) is, the more suspicious statement s is.

These two heuristics are in accordance with our intuition. Namely, if some statements are exercised by more failure-revealing test cases, they are more likely to be the root cause that triggers the detected failures. Thus, the metric R should be a function that increases with the growth of of and decreases with the growth of ep.

Finally, as the output, SBFL provides a list of statements, denoted by L, in which the statements are ranked in descending order according to their calculated suspiciousness. Namely, statements with higher suspiciousness values will rank higher than those with lower suspiciousness values. If SBFL is accurate, the faulty statement sf will have a high ranking. Then, testers can find them earlier by inspecting L.

11.2.2 SBFL for the Function of UAVPP

Here we take a concrete example to show how SBFL can be applied. Consider a function, called UAVPPSolver, to solve the unmanned aerial vehicle path planning (UAVPP) problem, [72, 73] and its faulty version as shown in Fig. 11.1. In the domain of robotic control, UAVPP describes a situation in which a Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) is performing its task in an environment involving the UAV itself, some obstacles (e.g., walls) and a target (i.e., an objective node); the goal is to plan the actions of the UAV, such that it can reach its target efficiently without collision with the obstacles. The UAVPPSolver function realises a path planning approach that relies on three path planning algorithms: the classical Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree [25], denoted by RRT, the accelerated RRT, denoted by MRRT [34], and a DNN-based approach (e.g., reinforcement learning based path planning [56]), denoted by NN. During the path planning, UAVPPSolver takes the status of the current UAV as input, which can be simplified as tuple ⟨ob jDis,wallDis⟩. Here, objDis represents the distance between the subject UAV and the target, and wallDis denotes the distance between the subject UAV and its nearest obstacle. Then, it will assign the next action for the UAV according to the algorithm selected from the candidates (i.e., RRT, MRRT, and NN). Specifically, UAVPPSolver assigns the path planning algorithms as follows. If the UAV is far from the obstacles, NN will be selected to guide the UAV to the target following a smooth path. Conversely, if the UAV is close to the obstacles (WallDis < 8), the step value (indicating its velocity) will decrease to avoid collision. Moreover, methods with strong randomness, i.e., RRT, will be selected to let the UAV escape from the obstacles as soon as possible. Finally, if the UAV is very close to the target, MRRT whose execution largely relies on the value of objDis, will be adopted to let the UAV reach its target soon. Now we assume that UAVPPSolver has a faulty statement. Namely, in statement s5, we set the variable step with a wrong value when wallDis < 8.

Here, each column represents the behaviour of a test case and each row represents the spectrum of a statement. Each black point in a cell indicates that a test case exercises a specific statement. For example, we can know that test case t2 exercises the statement s4. The Pass and Fail in the last row denote the test cases that are passed and failure-revealing, respectively. Note that, in UAVPPSolver, a test case is considered as failure-revealing if, during execution, the UAV collides with the wall or cannot reach the target before time out. From Fig. 11.2, we can know that there are three failure-revealing test cases (t1, t4, and t5) and two passed test cases (t2 and t3). Then, based on the test information, we can calculate the quantities ef, ep, nf, and np for each statement. For example, for statement s5, it is exercised by all the three failure-revealing test cases. Thus we have


ef(s5) = 3, nf(s5) = 0

Moreover, s5 is not exercised by any of the passed test cases. Thus, we have


ep(s5) = 0, np(s5) = 2

Furthermore, we use a metric to calculate the suspiciousness for the statements. Here the metric Rop expressed in Equation (11.3) is applied. Then, the suspiciousness of statement s5 is calculated as follows:


ROp(s5) = 3.0 − 0/(0 + 2.0 + 1.0) = 3.0

Finally, we rank all the statements according to their suspiciousness and get the rank list L ⟨s5, 3.0⟩, ⟨s2, 2.3⟩, …. Now, we find that statement s5 is ranked the first and it is indeed the faulty statement in UAVPPSolver. This means that if we use SBFL for UAVPPSolver we can find the faulty statement immediately.

11.3 Issues in SBFL

In Section 11.2.2, we have shown an example where SBFL is applied successfully in identifying the faulty statement. However, due to the complexity of real-life programs, test strategies, and the potential faults, we may encounter various situations that challenge the effectiveness FL. Figure 11.3 illustrates different activities necessary for performing SBFL, including the execution of test cases (i.e., testing), the collection of test information, and the calculation of statements’ suspiciousness (i.e., SBFL metrics). For each activity we can propose a specific technique to handle the constraints/issues that could exist in the implementation of SBFL, such as the budget of testing and the lack of test oracles. In this section, we summarise the potential issues related to SBFL, and then review the related works that, to some extent, can be taken as solutions.

Table 11.1 lists the perspectives of research works in terms of Problems, Descriptions, and Related Works. Specifically, the issues related to SBFL include quality testing information, multiple-fault scenarios, test oracles, and metrics selection; each of them will be reviewed in this section.

Table 11.1: Related works of conducting SBFL under different situations.
Problems Description Related Papers

Test oracles How to tackle the oracle problem within the context of SBFL Xie et al. 2013 [53]; Zhang et al. 2018 [72]

11.3.1 Quality of Test Information

Since testing is the activity preceding fault localisation and provides all the essential information for SBFL, the quality of the information pool derived during testing is important. Yu et al. [59] have observed that fault localisation effectiveness may vary a lot by using different test strategies to generate the test suite. Thus, we expect that the test suite obtained during testing has high quality, such that, by applying SBFL based on this test suite, we can get an accurate localisation of the faulty statement.

We here take an example to show how different test strategies can affect the FL effectiveness. Figure 11.4 shows the program MEDIAN that calculates the median value among the inputs u, v, and w. It also shows its faulty version on the right. Specifically, in line 14, we misused v instead of u.

Now we intend to generate some test cases to test MEDIAN. Note that each test case is with the form t = ⟨u,v,w⟩. Assume that following a given adopted test strategy, two test cases are generated, t1 = <3, 5, 2> and t2 = <1, 3, 0>. We execute both t1 and t2 and get the test information as shown in Fig. 11.5. Suppose we want to use the coverage of t1 and t2 to do fault localisation. Since both t1 and t2 are failure-revealing, we can infer that at least one statement covered by t1 and t2 is faulty. Unfortunately, although t1 and t2 are two failure-revealing test cases, they have the same execution trace, i.e., w < u < v, and cover the same statements, s2, s3, s10, s13, s14, and s15. Thus, we cannot distinguish the fault proneness among these statements by only examining t1 and t2. Now we adopt a different test strategy and generate another test suite including t1 and t3. Although t3 is a passed test case and we only have one failure (i.e., t1), t3 covers a different branch of program execution w < v < u. As a result, we can somehow distinguish s14 (i.e., the faulty statement) and the other statements.
