To date, various studies focusing on improving the quality of test information have been conducted. Test strategies identify the scheduling of generation or execution of each test case. In this context, studies try to achieve high-quality test information to fit the goal of SBFL efficiently. Baudry et al. [5] introduced a metric based on Dynamic Basic Block (DBB) to evaluate the quality of test cases for fault localisation. Campos et al. [7] found that the test suite is suitable for fault localisation if test cases in this test suite cover half of the statements on average. Yoo et al. [57] introduced the fault localisation prioritisation problem and devised a solution method borrowed from the concept of information entropy. Jiang et al. [23] applied several popular test case prioritisation strategies to perform fault localisation. They found that the adequacy criterion and the percentage of a prioritised test suite that is utilised are important factors affecting the effectiveness of SBFL, and they also found that Random Testing (RT) and Adaptive Random Testing (ART) are effective test strategies. Moreover, they found that SBFL can be more effective if the test suite satisfies the MC/DC-adequacy criterion [22].

11.3.2 Multiple Faults

Another important issue related to SBFL is the presence of “multiple faults” in a program. Whenever we are writing code, we may make errors. Studies have shown that, for an industrial code, the number of bugs per 1000 lines could range between 0.5 and 25 [6, 21]. This means that in a project with a large scale (e.g., one million lines of code), it is likely that multiple faults exist. Furthermore, it has been observed that the interactions among multiple faults can indeed influence the distribution of program spectra, and hence degrade the accuracy of SBFL [12, 14].

Here, we take an example to show the influence of multiple faults. Assume that a program (See Fig. 11.6) has five statements s1, s2, s3, s4, and s5, in which both s3 and s4 are faulty and assume that, once any of them is exercised, a failure will occur. If we intend to find at least one fault using SBFL, we may expect that one of s3 and s4 has a large ef value. However, since s5, although it is a non-faulty statement, belongs to the block of tackling exceptions, it will be triggered by the failures brought by both s3 and 54. Thus, it will have a large ef value, even larger than the ef values of s3 and s4.

Figure 11.6: Example of multi-fault situation.

main():

failure_tackling():
s1 # Non-faulty s5 # Tackling failure

if input < 0:

return fail
s2 # Non-faulty

return
if 0 < input < 1:
s3 # Fautty
failure_tackling()
if input > 1:
s4 #Faulty
failure_tackling()

According to the above example, if the program contains multiple faults, the interference among different faulty statements could largely affect the program spectra, and hence degrade the accuracy of SBFL. Currently, various studies have been conducted focusing on alleviating the negative effects caused by multiple faults. A general idea is to identify which failures are caused by which faults. After knowing this, we can eliminate the failures that are caused by non-relevant faults during fault localisation.

For example, Abreu et al. [3] proposed an approach based on Bayesian reasoning to consider the suspiciousness of combinations of statements based on their spectra. Liblit et al. [32] tried to cluster the failure-revealing test cases such that the failures triggering different faults can be isolated [32]. Podgurski et al. [38] proposed a fault identification strategy involving both supervised and unsupervised patterns based on testing reports. Gao et al. [17] proposed a clustering approach called MSeer, designed for localising multiple faults in parallel. Although the interactions and interference can have negative effects on SBFL accuracy, it has been observed that SBFL can have similar accuracy for at least one dominant fault, but which fault will be found is unknown [14]. So, in many cases, it is feasible to fix the bugs iteratively: we can focus on fixing one bug at a time, and after each fixing, turn to find other bugs based on the information from regression testing.

11.3.3 Test Oracle

In software testing, the term test oracle identifies the artefact to specify the expected output of each test case and determine whether the observed outputs are correct or not.

However, in most practical cases, the test oracle does not exist or it is incomplete. For example, considering the sin(.) function, although it is easy to know the correctness of the outputs of some special inputs such as sin(π), for most test cases (e.g., sin(1.83)), the correctness of their outputs cannot be easily identified automatically. In the context of testing, various approaches have been proposed to solve the oracle problem. For example, Chen et al. [9, 10] propose a methodology called Metamorphic Testing (MT). Instead of using a test oracle, MT aims to detect the potential failures by checking some system properties involving multiple inputs, called Metamorphic Relation (MR).

In the context of SBFL, since the calculation of the spectrum (i.e., ef, ep, nf,…, and np) relies on the information of whether each test case is passed or failure-revealing, in the absence of an oracle, SBFL cannot be applied. To date, to solve the oracle problem in the context of SBFL, various studies have been conducted. For example, Xie et al. [53] adapt MT to the context of SBFL by proposing the concept of “metamorphic slice”, which is a trace involving the coverage of multiple test cases. With their approach, we can perform SBFL effectively even if the oracle does not exist. Moreover, Zhang et al. [72] propose an approach to tackle to situation that the test oracle is incomplete, leading to the fact that only some test cases are labelled (i.e., we know their output correctness) while the other test cases are unlabelled (i.e., we do not know whether they are passed or failure-revealing). Specifically, they design a test classifier to assign each unlabelled test case a “predicted label” according to the already labelled ones. In this way, we can use more test cases, including both the labelled and unlabelled ones, and hence the effectiveness of SBFL can be improved.

11.3.4 Suspiciousness Metrics

Finally, as the core part of SBFL, the suspiciousness metric is also an important issue related to the effectiveness of SBFL. In this line of research, studies focus on enriching the theoretical foundations of SBFL. Although all the metrics, such as Equations (11.1) and (11.2), are based on basic intuition of the larger ef and lower ep that a statement has, the more suspicious it is, there is no approach or theory to provide an optimal trade off between ef and ep.

To date, hundreds of metrics have been proposed [1, 24, 46]. Naish et al. [37] innovatively make a theoretical comparison among various metrics and group them into several equivalent categories. Based on this, Xie et al. [53] explicitly prove the performance relation among these equivalent categories and propose two groups of maximal metrics. Furthermore, Yoo et al. [58] proposed a genetic algorithm to mine useful metrics automatically. Zhang et al. [71] propose a visualisation approach to reproduce the results of [53]. Furthermore, they extend the work to a general framework to review existing SBFL works and make qualitative evaluation for the metrics.

11.4 Adaption of Fault Localisation to Other Domains

SBFL is the most popular and widely used technique for automatic fault localisation. The main reason is that SBFL is not only effective but also light-weighted. The implementation of SBFL requires only the statement coverage and the outputs information, and does not need too complex information, such as data dependencies. Thus, for all the systems for which we can define the concepts of “component coverage” and “failures”, SBFL can be adapted. Of course, for different artefacts, the distribution of execution spectra could be largely different. Hence, the localisation results may not be as precise as for conventional programs. However, for all the systems, by adapting SBFL, we can get more understanding about the potential system hazard without spending too much computational efforts. In this section, we review some recent works related to SBFL for systems different than conventional programs. Specifically, we mainly introduce two kinds of artefacts, Deep Neural Networks (DNN) and Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS).

11.4.1 SBFL for Deep Neural Networks

Recently, the combination of Deep Learning (DL) and fault localisation has been widely studied. The works in [40] and [39] borrow the concept of fault localisation to identify the potential buggy weights in a DNN model. Moreover, Gerasimou et al. [18] and Sun et al. [42] apply fault localisation to identify the important neurons and input elements for the DNN models. According to different tasks (e.g., regression, classification, and decision making), the outputs of a DNN are also different. In this section, we discuss the task of image classification.

Here, we introduce the work proposed by Eniser et al. [16] that adapts SBFL to localise suspicious neurons. Let M denote a DNN model containing N neurons n1, n2,… , nN. In DNN testing, the test suite is a test dataset. For example, if we use a Convolution Neural Network (CNN) for image classification, the test suite is an image dataset such as MNIST [30], and each test case is an individual image. In addition, each test input t is attached with a label C(t), indicating the correct classification of t. For example, in the MNIST dataset, we may have C(t) = “7”, and in the CIFAR10 dataset [27], we may have C(t) = “dog”. Let C = {l1, … ln} denote the set of labels (also called classes). Now, given a test case t to execute the DNN, the propagation process is triggered, and the neurons are either activated or not by their activation functions. Let ϕ(t,n) denote the function to calculate the activation status of neuron n under input t. Here, we set ϕ(t,n) is 1 when the output of n is above a certain threshold, otherwise it is set to 0. The output is a predicted class of the input image, denoted by PC(M,t). Furthermore, if C(t) = PC(M,t), we say the input t is correctly classified, denoted by f/(t, M) = 0; otherwise, if C(t) # PC(M,t), we say t is misclassified, denoted by fl(t, M) = 1.

Figure 11.7 illustrates the execution information of a DNN model that can be used to do fault localisation. Instead of statements as in classical SBFL for programs, we analyse neurons n1, n2, …. The concept of “failure” here is the misclassification of an image, e.g., misclassifying “7” to “8”, or misclassifying “horse” to “vehicle”. The test “coverage” is associated to the activation of neurons. For example, if neuron n is activated by test case ti, we say ti covers neuron n.

According to the test information of the DNN, similarly to conventional SBFL, we can also calculate the values of efn, epn, nfn, and npn, respectively. They denote the spectrum of neuron n after executing all the inputs in T. Specifically, the meaning of efn, epn, nfn, and npn can be summarised as follows:

  • efn: the number of times that neuron n is activated by the misclassified inputs, i.e., I{t ∈ T | ϕ(t,n) =1 ^ fl(t,M) =1}|;
  • epn: the number of times that neuron n is activated by the correctly classified inputs, i.e., I{t ∈ T | ϕ(t,n) =1 ^ fl(t,M) =0}|;
  • nfn: the number of times that neuron n is not activated by the misclassified inputs, i.e., I{t ∈ T | ϕ(t,n) =0 ^ fl(t,M) =1}|;
  • npn: the number of times that neuron n is not activated by the correctly classified inputs, i.e., I{t ∈ T | ϕ(t,n) =0 ^ fl(t,M) =0}|;

Finally, the suspiciousness metrics, as shown in Equations (11.1) and (11.2), are used to calculate the suspiciousness of each neuron. If a neuron is suspicious, this neuron could be responsible for the misclassifications. The fault localisation results can provide evidence for evaluating DNN’s performance and hence predicting the potential hazards when the DNN is applied to safety-critical systems. Furthermore, Duran et al. [15] discuss the potential masking effect if we consider all misclassifications for a given class together during the calculation of the values of of and ep, and suggest a more fine-grained way (i.e., considering each misclassification individually) when applying SBFL to DNN.

11.4.2 Analysing the Hazard of Autonomous Driving Systems

Nowadays, personal mobility and goods transportation are undergoing a big transformation thanks to autonomous driving. However, errors in Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) may lead to disruptive economic damages, even the loss of human lives. Thus, it is meaningful to analyse the potential hazard for ADSs once some failures have been exposed during testing.

An ADS system takes as input the signals received by the environment or provided by the system operators. Moreover, the system contains various components performing different tasks. The goal of hazard analysis is to identify which components are the causes of potential system hazard. By knowing this, engineers can use the analysis results to re-engineering the system to improve its safety.

However, since the structure of ADS is complex, it is difficult to do formal verification to prove that the system is safe or dangerous. On the other hand, for ADS, we should execute many test cases before putting them into practice.

Thus, it makes sense to propose a data-driven approach to analyse the system hazard through the derived test information. In this section, we introduce a hazard analysis approach proposed in [65] following the idea of SBFL. Specifically, we consider an ADS whose components are configurable with some parameters; some configurations can lead to more(less) safe driving. The goal of the work is to consider the relation between the parameters’ values and the potential hazard.

Let M be a model of ADS under analysis. We assume that the components of M can be described as a set of parameters P = {p1,…, pn}, in which each parameter pi is defined within its own domain Di. M is configurable. If a concrete value vi is given to each parameter pi, a simulation instance, denoted by M (v1, …., vn) can be constructed. Then, we can run M (v1, … , vn) and obtain, as output, a signal over time o. Here, we define a simulation t as the pair t = <(v1,… , vn), o>. Given system model M and simulation set T, assume M is subjected to hazard (i.e., some simulations t ∈ T can cause system failures). Then, the fundamental problem is:

How to identify the parameters that are the main cause of system hazard?

To do this following the idea of SBFL, we need to know the coverage and result information for each test case. However, the ADS parameters have continuous values at each test execution. Also, due to the complexity of the ADS, it is difficult to have a crisp partition at each parameter. As a result, it is difficult to identify which components are covered and which are not. As a solution, the work in [65] introduces the concept of fuzzification-based coverage.

Specifically, to characterise the system parameters, the concept of fuzzy set borrowed from fuzzy logic [60] is introduced. Considering a parameter p defined in the domain D, let FP = {f1, f2, fm} denote the set of fuzzy sets that describe certain concepts of p. Each fuzzy set f ∈ Fp is defined by a membership function. For each concrete value v of p, f assigns a membership degree between 0 and 1, i.e., f : D → [0,1], indicating the degree that v belongs to f.

Suppose we have simulation t with parameter values (v1,… , vn). We define the coverage of parameter pk over t as the vector CPk,t = [f1(vk), … , fm (vk)], where, for each fi, we have fi ∈ Fp. Furthermore, we define the fuzzification- based coverage of the entire model M overt as Ct = {CPk,t |p ∈ P}. For example, we have a parameter p having domain D = [150,350] and during the execution of a test case t the value of p is 200. Then, we can say that test case t covers both the fuzzy set Small and Slight Small with 0.5 degree.

Furthermore, considering the correctness of a test case, let φ be a specific safety requirement of M. The satisfaction of φ over a given simulation t can be quantified as R(t) within the interval [0,1], indicating how strongly φ is satisfied. Then, we calculate the hazard degree of t, denoted by h(t), as h(t) = 1 — R(t).

After the definition of both the test coverage (i.e., fuzzification-based coverage) and correctness (i.e., hazard degree), we predict the hazard-related parameters following SBFL. That is to say, we finally assign a hazard impact score to each parameter p indicating its relation to the hazard. Specifically, we introduce the scoring metrics from SBFL and extend them to our context. Given model M and simulation set T, for each simulation t ∈ T, we know Ct and h(t). Then, concerning system hazard, we define

(11.4)
$$a_{h}^{f^{p_{i}}} = {\sum\limits_{t \in T}\left( {f^{p_{i}}\left( v_{i} \right) \cdot h(t)} \right)}$$

Similarly, concerning system safety, we define

(11.5)
$$a_{s}^{f^{p_{i}}} = {\sum\limits_{t \in T}f^{p_{i}}}\left( v_{i} \right) \cdot (1 - h(t))$$

Here, ahfpi and asfpi represent the degrees that fuzzy set fPi of parameter pi contributes to the hazard and safety, respectively. Specifically, if t covers fuzzy set fPi at fPi(vi) degree, then we consider the term fPi(v1). h(t) as the contribution of fPi to the hazard at t. Then, we sum fPi(vi) · h(t) for each t to calculate ahfpi and we calculate asfpi similarly. Finally, we use a metric, involving both asfpi and ahfpi, to calculate the final hazard impact score, denoted by Φ(fPi):

(11.6)
Φ(fpi) = ahfpi/(ahfpi+asfpi)

In [67], we adapted the fuzzy-set-based approach to analyse the hazard of a path planner provided by our industrial partner; the approach was later extended in [66], but, for the sake of space, we here only describe the approach in [67]. The path planner can automatically calculate an available path for the ego vehicle at run time. A possible driving scenario for this path planner is shown in Fig. 11.8.

During path planning, the path planner decides the action for the ego vehicle, step by step. At each time point τ, it generates some short-term paths as candidates, and then selects the least costly one, using a scoring function that employs some parameters w to give different importance to driving characteristics such as maximum speed, lateral acceleration, curvature, etc. Specifically, for each short-term path, denoted by stp, the path planner records some runtime flags, indicating whether the driving characteristics corresponding to these runtime flags are high (i.e., exceed the given threshold) or not in stp. For example, if the maximal acceleration is high, then the corresponding runtime flag rfaccma. is set to 1. Then, during path selection, the cost of stp is calculated by aggregating the parameters whose corresponding driving characteristics have runtime flags set to 1. Generally speaking, setting a parameter w to be high means that we expect the corresponding driving characteristics being low, i.e., the corresponding runtime flag being 0. The parameters analysed here as well as the corresponding runtime flags are listed in Table 11.2.

Table 11.2: Driving characteristics, runtime flags, and parameters
Driving characteristic Runtime flag Weight Description
(forward) acceleration rfaccmax WaccMax the parameter is aggregated to the total cost if the maximum acceleration is over a given threshold
deceleration rfdecMax WdecMax the parameter is aggregated to the total cost if the maximum deceleration is over a given threshold
lateral acceleration rflatg Wlatg the parameter is aggregated to the total cost if the maximum lateral acceleration is over a given threshold
speed rfspd wspd the parameter is aggregated to the total cost if the speed is over a given speed limit
curvature rfcurvature Wcurvature the parameter is aggregated to the total cost if the curvature of the short-term path is over a given threshold
safety distance rfsafeDist Wsaf eDist the parameter is aggregated to the total cost if the vehicle violates the safety distance with other scenario vehicles

Now we intend to adapt FL to analyse the system hazard of both parameters and runtime flags. Since the parameters have continuous values, we can calculate their hazard impact scores using fuzzification-based coverage presented before. Instead, since the runtime flags have binary values, we can simply collect their coverage and then calculate their hazard impact scores as in classical SBFL.

The outputs of such hazard analysis are two rank lists indicating, respectively, the correlations (1) between the parameters and the hazard, and (2) between the runtime flags and the hazard. Finally, through integration of the two lists, we can get an overall explanation about the potential system hazard, such as “if we set the parameters to these values, we obtain a specific activation of the runtime flags, which may be the cause of a potential collision”.

For example, we analyse a RightTurn scenario, in which, at the intersection, the ego vehicle must turn right, while another vehicle is crossing from right and another vehicle is crossing from the opposite direction, as shown in Fig. 11.9. The analysis result is shown in Table 11.3a. From the results, we can see that, in the rank list of parameters, parameter wlatg with fuzzy set VL is assigned with the highest hazard impact score of 0.63, which means that setting the parameter of lateral acceleration Very Large could lead to hazard. Moreover, the corresponding runtime flag rflats has a low rank with hazard impact score 0.15, which is consistent with the results of the analysis of the parameters; indeed, when the parameter value is high, its corresponding runtime flag is likely not activated (as the path planner prefers not to implement that driving characteristic); this is why a low hazard score is instead associated with the activation of the runtime flag. Thus, we can get the final explanation as:

In this situation, the ego vehicle needs to make a sharp turn to avoid the collision with the other vehicle coming from the opposite side, which requires a high lateral acceleration. However, since we have set the parameter of lateral acceleration very large, during the turning, the ego vehicle prefers the actions having low lateral acceleration. As a result, the hazard of collision in this traffic situation exist.

11.5 Conclusions

In this chapter, we have introduced the basic concept of software fault localisation (FL) and reviewed some representative automated FL techniques. Then, we have taken Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation (SBFL) as an example, and explicitly described how we can apply this technique in practice. With SBFL, we can (semi-)automatically localise the potential faulty statements in a program. Due to the complexity of current systems and software, various factors can influence the accuracy of fault localisation. Thus, we have reviewed some state-of-art progresses aiming to solve various issues related to SBFL, such as the limitation of test information, the test oracle problem, and the selection of SBFL metrics. Finally, we have discussed the possibility of adapting SBFL to analyse more complex models and systems. Particularly, we have presented two approaches that follow the idea of SBFL to analyse the hazard in the models of Deep Neural Network (DNN) and Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS), respectively. These models and systems have been widely adopted in the era of industrial 4.0. The presented approaches provide a possible way to investigate the potential faulty elements (e.g., neurons or system parameters) in these systems. The output of these approaches can provide useful information to improve the safety during system re-engineering and repairing.
